en: The Second Chapter.

[In this second chapter, titled "Non-contradiction," in its first quarter (pāda), the removal of contradictions to the Vedānta harmony is accomplished through the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Kāraṇāda, and others, as well as by the arguments employed by the Sāṃkhya and other schools.
Now begins the second chapter.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss; to the one who acts without effort; to the Guru who is known through the Vedānta and who is the witness of the intellect. //1//

I worship the Lord of Jānakī, who follows the established tenets of Vedānta and is unshaken by the arguments of the Smṛtis such as Sāṃkhya; who is not understood through various rootless scriptures; whose birth and dissolution are like those of space and other elements; who is devoid of beginning and end, whose body is consciousness, who is all-pervading, and who, though designated as an agent by the subtle body (liṅga), is not limited by a physical form. //2//
START BsCom_2,1.1.1 1.
The Section Concerning Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇam). Sūtras 1–2.
In the first chapter, it was established that the omniscient Lord of all is the cause of the origin of the world.
It is the cause of the persistence of the arisen world by acting as its controller, just as clay, gold, and so forth are for jars, earrings, and the like;
it is like a magician is for his illusion.
Furthermore, He is the cause of the re-absorption of the expanded universe back into His own self,
just as the earth is for the fourfold collection of living beings;
and it has been established through the demonstration of the harmony of the Vedānta texts that He alone is the Self of all.

The theories of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and other such causes have already been refuted on the grounds that they lack scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*). Now, [the author] addresses the removal of contradictions with tradition (*smṛti*) and logic (*nyāya*) regarding his own position,
as well as the fact that the theories of primordial matter and the like are merely bolstered by fallacious reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*).
The second chapter is commenced in order to demonstrate that the process of creation and so forth is consistent across all Vedāntas, and to establish this collection of meanings.
Therein, first of all, he introduces and then refutes the objection regarding contradiction with Smṛti:
"If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for Smṛti, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.1)
As for the statement that Brahman alone is omniscient and the cause of the world, that is incorrect;
why? Because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis.
Furthermore, there are the Smṛtis known as Tantras, composed by supreme sages and accepted by the learned, as well as other Smṛtis that follow them;
if [the Sāṅkhya doctrine were true], these would be rendered untenable.
For in those works, the insentient Pradhāna is described as the independent cause of the world.

The Smṛtis of Manu and others, however, provide scope [for application] by fulfilling the requirements expected from the collection of dharmas characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā), such as the Agnihotra; for instance,
they specify that for this particular class [of people], at this particular time, the initiation (upanayana) is to be performed according to this rule,
and such is the conduct.
In this way, they prescribe the study of the Vedas and the union with a wife for the practice of dharma;
likewise, they ordain the various duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-dharma) which serve the goals of human existence.
The Smṛtis of Kapila and others have no scope regarding matters to be performed [in the ritual sphere],
for they were composed specifically concerning right vision (samyagdarśana) as the means to liberation.
If they were to find no scope even there, it would follow that they are utterly purposeless.
Therefore, the Vedānta texts must be interpreted in a manner that does not contradict that [conclusion].

But how can the meaning of the Śruti, which has been determined through reasons such as "because it sees" (*īkṣati*) and so forth to be that Brahman alone—the omniscient—is the cause of the world, be challenged again by the objection regarding the lack of scope for Smṛti?
This is not a challenge for those whose intelligence is independent.
However, people who possess dependent wisdom (paratantra-prajñā), being generally unable to determine the meaning of the Śruti independently, would rely upon Smṛtis composed by renowned authors.
By means of those [Smṛtis], they would seek to understand the meaning of the Śruti;
for they would not place their trust in an exposition produced by us, due to the great respect they have for the authors of the Smṛtis.
Furthermore, the unimpeded knowledge of Kapila and others is recorded in tradition;
there is also a Vedic scripture stating: "He who in the beginning sustains with his knowledges the seer Kapila when he is born, and beholds him as he is being produced" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.2).
Therefore, it is impossible to conceive that their doctrine is not in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, they establish this matter by relying on reasoning;
therefore, there is a renewed objection that the Vedāntas should be interpreted by the force of Smṛti as well.
The resolution of that is: "No, because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis."

If the doctrine of God as the cause were to be rejected on the grounds that it would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, then other Smṛtis that likewise maintain God as the cause would also be left with no room;
we shall cite them: "That which is subtle and unknowable"—referring thus to the Supreme Brahman—"for He is the inner Self."

Having stated, "And he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of all beings," he further says, "Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest (avyakta), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), was produced.
Likewise, elsewhere he says, "O Brahmin, the unmanifest dissolves into the qualityless Puruṣa.
And thus: "Listen therefore to this summary: Nārāyaṇa is all this, the ancient one."
"He creates everything at the time of creation, and he consumes it again at the time of dissolution," so it is said in the Purāṇas.
And in the Bhagavadgītā: "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe" (BhG 7.6).
Furthermore, Āpastamba recites with reference to the Supreme Self itself: "From Him all bodies originate; He is the root, eternal, and everlasting" (DhSū 1.8.23.2).
Thus, in many ways, the Lord is revealed as both the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) through the authority of Smṛti.
Since I shall provide an answer by the very authority of Smṛti to one who objects on the basis of Smṛti, this presentation of the defect regarding the lack of scope for other Smṛtis is made.
However, the intent of the Śrutis toward the doctrine that the Lord is the cause has already been demonstrated.

And when there is a conflict among the Smṛtis, since one must necessarily either accept one or reject the other, those Smṛtis that follow the Śruti are authoritative, while the others are not to be relied upon.
This has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "In case of contradiction, however, [the Smṛti] would be unauthoritative, for there is indeed [contrary] inference" (Jai.Sū. 1.3.3).
Furthermore, it is impossible to conceive that anyone could perceive supersensuous matters without the aid of Śruti, because of the absence of any means [for such perception].
If it is argued that this is possible because perfected beings (siddhas) such as Kapila possess unimpeded knowledge, we say no; for even perfection is dependent upon other factors.
Indeed, perfection depends upon the practice of dharma.
And that Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
Consequently, the meaning of an injunction established from of old cannot be called into doubt on the basis of the words of a person whose authority is established only later.

Even if one resorts to the hypothesis of reliance upon perfected beings (*siddha*), since there are many such perfected beings, when contradictions arise among their traditions (*smṛti*) in the manner already shown, there exists no means of determination other than reliance upon the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

Even for one possessing dependent wisdom (*paratantra-prajñā*), it is not reasonable to exhibit partiality toward a particular object of memory without cause; for if such partiality were to occur in anyone toward anything, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that reality could not be established due to the diversity of human intellects.
Therefore, even for such a person, wisdom must be guided onto the true path by means of presenting contradictions in their memories and by discerning the objects that follow from those memories.
As for the scripture that was cited as demonstrating Kapila’s preeminence in knowledge, one cannot rely on it to have faith in the doctrine of Kapila even if it contradicts the Vedas,
because "Kāpila" is merely a commonality of name;
furthermore, there is the traditional memory of another Kapila, named Vāsudeva, who tormented the sons of Sagara.
Furthermore, an observation of another matter cannot establish a point if it is devoid of a supporting scriptural injunction (*prāpti*).

Indeed, there exists another Vedic revelation proclaiming the greatness of Manu: "Whatever Manu said was indeed medicine" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.2.10.2). And by Manu himself: "The Self in all beings and all beings in the Self..."
Indeed, perceiving this, the self-sacrificer attains sovereign rule.
(12.11) Thus, by praising the vision of the self-nature of all, it is understood that the doctrine of Kapila is being censured; for Kapila does not accept the vision of the self-nature of all,
since he maintains the distinction between individual selves.

In the Mahābhārata as well, after deliberating on the question, "O Brahmin, are there many Puruṣas, or is there indeed only one?", and having set forth the opposing view— "O King, for those who investigate Sāṃkhya and Yoga, there are many Puruṣas"— it refutes that [view] with the following: "Just as it is said that there is a single source for many Puruṣas..."
In that same way, I shall describe to you that universal Person who is preeminent in qualities.
Having begun with these words: "My inner self, yours, and those of others who reside within bodies—all these, he is the witness; he cannot be grasped by anyone, anywhere."
With the universe as his head, the universe as his arms, and the universe as his feet, eyes, and nose,
he moves alone among living beings, wandering at will and according to his pleasure.
Thus, the state of being the Self of all is definitively established.

And there is a scriptural passage regarding this state of being the Self of all: "When, for the one who knows, all beings have become the Self alone, then what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that unity? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7).
Such is the nature [of his system].

Consequently, it is established that Kapila’s treatise is contrary to the Vedas and contrary to the words of Manu who follows the Vedas, not merely because of his independent postulation of primordial matter (prakṛti), but also because of his postulation of a plurality of selves (ātman).
For the Veda possesses independent authority regarding its own subject matter, just as the sun does with respect to visible forms.
The authority of human words, however, depends upon another source and is mediated by the memory of the speaker; thus, there is a distance [between them].
Therefore, it is not a defect that Smṛti finds no scope when the subject matter contradicts the Veda. //1//
FN: "In the second [chapter], there is no contradiction with Smṛti and Tarka; the other [systems] are defective.
There is also no contradiction with the Śruti concerning the past enjoyer and the Śruti concerning the subtle body"—this is the summary verse (saṃgrahaśloka).
The Supreme Sage is Kapila.
Others [are those] composed by Āsuripañcaśikha and others;
the meaning is that they would understand the meaning of the Veda in a figurative sense.
"Subtlety" means being beyond the reach of the senses.
"Incomprehensibility" means being inaccessible to other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"The bodies" refers to Brahmā and the others.
"Eternal" means unchanging and immutable.
In the event of conflict with Śruti, the authority of Smṛti is to be disregarded and rejected;
for it is only when there is no such conflict that an inference from Śruti occurs.
[This refers to] the burner of one who is being burned.
"He is the head of all" because he is reflected everywhere;
this should be applied similarly to "the arms of all" and so forth.

According to the Śruti, "I shall manifest name and form," he is the manifester of names and forms, even though he is the creator of the body of names, by means of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra).

The meaning is: "I worship Him"—the Supreme Self who is non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), the controller of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), who is celebrated and renowned as the "Agent" and the "Part.

In connection with the Smṛti, he recounts what has been previously stated in order to explain the relationship between the subject matter of the preceding and following chapters, beginning with the words "In the first chapter":
starting from the Sūtra on the "Origin and so forth," it was established that Brahman is the cause of the origin and other states of the world.

The meaning is that in such sūtras as "But by the vision of the scripture" (*śāstradṛṣṭyā tu*), it has been stated that He alone is the non-dual Self of all; and by the sūtra beginning with "That which is inferable" (*ānumānikam*), it has been shown that any other cause is not based on the scriptures.

Having thus restated the subject matter of the first chapter, he now briefly explains the subject matter of the second chapter—which concerns the removal of contradictions regarding that same topic—section by section, starting with the words "Now" (*idānīm*).

In this regard, in the first pāda, the removal of contradictions regarding the harmony (*samanvaya*) [of the Vedānta texts] with the Smṛtis and arguments of the Sāṃkhya and other schools is accomplished.
In the second pāda, it is stated for the sake of non-contradiction that the scriptures (*āgama*) of the Sāṃkhya and others are rooted in error.

In the third pāda, the absence of contradiction is established by explaining the order of the birth and dissolution of the great elements, such as space, as well as the creation Śrutis and the Śrutis concerning the individual self (*jīvātman*) in each Vedānta text.

The meaning is that in the fourth quarter (pāda), there is no contradiction regarding the scriptural texts concerning the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra). This very point is summarized in a verse for the sake of easy understanding: "In the second [quarter], there is no contradiction through Smṛti and reasoning; [then follows] the sublation of others."
The scriptural statements regarding the enjoyer of the elements and the scriptural statements regarding the subtle body (liṅga) are likewise not contradictory.

Thus, since it is impossible to resolve doubts regarding contradiction when the subject matter is not yet known, it is logical that the chapter on non-contradiction (*avirodhādhyāya*) follows immediately after the chapter on harmonization (*samanvayādhyāya*).
Regarding this, he states the purport of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words "Firstly... and so forth.

Since this section (pāda) is intended to remove contradictions regarding the concordance with the Śruti, its connection is with the Śruti, the Śāstra, and the chapter (adhyāya). Because all the topical discussions (adhikaraṇas) consist of the establishment of one's own view, they are connected to this section.

Here, the distinction is that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the result is the failure to establish the stated concordance due to contradiction with Smṛti, whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), that concordance is established.
In this context, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts as declared by Brahman.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the *Sāṃkhya-smṛti* or not—depending on whether the authority of that *smṛti* is accepted or rejected—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "As has been stated.
*Tantra* refers to the scripture (*śāstra*) taught by Kapila, so called because "by means of it" (*anena*) the fundamental principles (*tattva*) are woven together (*tantryante*) or expounded.
Furthermore, there are other [doctrines] propounded by Pañcaśikha and others;

if this were the case, the Vedāntas would be rendered purposeless in their systematic exposition (*samanvaya*) of non-dual Brahman—this is the meaning. To the objection that there is no contradiction because those [other doctrines] also have Brahman as their sole object, he says: "For in them... (*tāsu hi*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the Sāṃkhya tradition is accepted for the sake of establishing its authority, would not the Smṛtis of Manu and others then lose their authority? Anticipating this, he says "Manu and others," meaning that since those [Smṛtis] have scope regarding *dharma*, they possess authority.

If it is then argued that the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others should likewise have authority regarding *dharma* through their primary intent, and that there is no contradiction because the ultimate reality (*tattva*) is indeed Brahman alone, he says: "Not so."

Since conceptual construction is untenable regarding reality, it is appropriate to explain the Śruti in accordance with Smṛti that leaves no room for alternative interpretation; this is because of the maxim that between that which has scope and that which has no scope, the latter is stronger. Thus he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt).
He raises an objection, saying "How so? (katham), on the grounds that since the lack of authority of Smṛti is accepted when it contradicts Śruti, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is not tenable.

He says "it might be" (*bhavet*) to indicate that this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) would not apply to those capable of understanding the meaning of the Veda independently, but it would indeed apply to those who have faith in the Sāṃkhya elders.
He further says "and of Kapila and others" (*kapilaprabhṛtīnām ca*) to show that because they possess knowledge of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*), faith in them would arise.
One should behold him as the Supreme Lord, who at the beginning brought forth the sage Kapila as he was being born, and who sustained him with his knowledges once he was born.
Such is the application of the scriptural passage (*śruti*).

He establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) as follows: "Just as you argue that the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*) must be abandoned because it contradicts the *Sāṃkhya* tradition (*smṛti*), so too do I argue that the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhānavāda*) must be abandoned because it contradicts other traditions. This is the resolution (*samādhi*) to that [objection].

Therefore, from that Brahman, the unmanifest— the world in its subtle form— remains dissolved in Māyā. Having thus stated the words of the Itihāsas, he expresses the consensus of the Purāṇas with the words "ataśca" (and therefore).
"Prabhava" means that from which something originates; it is the cause of birth.
"Pralaya" means that in which something dissolves; it is the substratum of dissolution.
Therefore, from that Lord who is the agent, Brahmā and the others originate.
That very [Self] is the root and the material cause;
is it subject to transformation? No, it is eternal and immutable.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is eternal.
Now, one might ask: why was the contradiction with Śruti not mentioned? To this he says: "by the strength of Smṛti.
[The question arises: when there is mutual contradiction among the Smṛtis, how can there be a determination of the truth?
Regarding this, he says: "But it has been shown" (*darśitaṃ tu*). The meaning is that the determination of reality is established by the Śruti scriptures alone.
To the question, "What then is the status of the Smṛtis?", he says: "And in case of conflict" (*vipratipattau ca*).

The meaning is this: since a conceptual alternative (vikalpa) regarding a real entity is impossible when there is mutual contradiction among Smṛtis concerning the true nature of reality, those Smṛtis whose basis is an established Śruti are authoritative, whereas others, whose basis is a merely inferred Śruti, are not authoritative.
Regarding the point that a Smṛti is not authoritative when it contradicts an established Śruti, he states the Jaiminīya principle: "It has been said."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the Smṛti rule, "It should be entirely covered," which contradicts the direct Vedic revelation (śruti), "One should chant the udgītha while touching the Audumbarī post," is authoritative or not:

the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) being that it is authoritative because one can infer a foundational Śruti for it, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: when there is a contradiction with an established Śruti, the authority of the Smṛti is *anapekṣam*—meaning devoid of expectation [of corroboration] and thus to be rejected.

The meaning is this: since scriptural inference occurs only when there is no contradiction, whereas here, because a contradiction exists, scriptural inference is impossible; thus, due to the absence of a source, the Smṛti regarding the total covering [of the sacrificial post] is not authoritative.
To the objection that the Sāṃkhya Smṛti might have perception as its source, he says: "And not... [na ca].

It may be suspected that it is possible for yogins to possess supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*) by virtue of the greatness of their spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*); thus it is said, "it is possible. [The opponent argues: "Indeed, Kapila and others first ascertained the authority of the Veda and, through the practice of *dharma*—the subject matter of that Veda—attained spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). By means of that accomplishment, they composed the *Smṛtis*, and according to those *Smṛtis*, it is not proper to contradict the beginningless *Śruti*, because that would involve a contradiction with what must be relied upon (*upajīvya*). [The author] refutes this: "No."
"Even from the perspective of established proof" means "to entertain excessive doubt";
that is to say, it is impossible to suspect that the Vedas have abandoned their primary meaning and possess only a figurative sense.
If it is argued that the Veda is not dependent on anything else because it is self-established (*svataḥsiddha*), we say no;
for there is no evidence for the self-establishment of one who is not God (*anīśvara*).
Even granting this, he says "established" (*siddha*).

The meaning is that even when postulating the meaning of the Vedas by relying on the words of the Siddhas, if there is mutual contradiction among those statements of the Siddhas, it is proper to determine the meaning of the Vedas solely through the reasonings of Manu and others which rely upon the Śruti.

The literal sense is that the mere word of a Siddha, without the support of the Śruti, is not a cause for determining the ultimate truth. Now, one might ask: "If a person of dull intellect has faith in the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, how can his mind be led onto the path of Vedānta? To this, he says: "By the words beginning with 'paratantra'..."
[Objection: But surely, since scripture declares Kapila to be omniscient, faith in his doctrine is unavoidable; to this, he replies with the words "But that which...
It is improper to be deluded into thinking that the author of Sāṃkhya is mentioned in the Śruti merely by the name "Kapila," because it is impossible for a dualist such as he to be omniscient.
And here, Kapila—who is known as such because he is endowed with all knowledge—is indeed a portion of Vāsudeva;
for the sense is that he is "all-knowing" (sarvajña) because he teaches the Vedic Sāṃkhya, which is the knowledge of the self-nature of all things.
[The term] *prataptuḥ* means of the one who causes burning.
Furthermore, it is enjoined that "one should see that Lord who sustains Kapila through his cognitions";
thus, the mention of Kapila’s omniscience—which serves another purpose as a subordinate element to the realization of the Lord—is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Since this [omniscience] is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and cannot therefore serve to establish its own meaning, omniscience is not proven by a mere restatement; so he says: "anyārtha" (for another purpose).
Having refuted the scriptural authority of Kapila, the proponent of dualism, he states that Manu, the proponent of Brahman, possesses scriptural authority with the words "And it occurs...
He further states that non-duality is shown even in the Itihāsas by means of a censure of the Kāpila doctrine with the words "In the Mahābhārata also...":
the purpose of this inquiry is whether individual persons (puruṣas), which are the selves, are in reality distinct, or whether there is but one inner self (pratyagātman) of all objects of perception.

Just as the earth is the single source and material cause for many bodies in the form of persons, so shall I describe that Person, the Self, as the universe— consisting of all things because He is the material cause of all— and as endowed with qualities such as omniscience. He is "the one whose head is the universe" (*viśvamūrdhā*), meaning that all the heads of gods, animals, humans, and others, which are well-known in the world, belong to Him alone.
Because the one alone has entered into all fields by way of reflection,
there is thus the application of terms such as "the one who joins with the universe" (viśvayuj).
He moves through and understands all beings as one.
The meaning is "everywhere. Acting according to his own will means being independent; there is no one whatsoever who restrains him.
The meaning is "the Lord of all.
"According to one's pleasure" means,
in other words, "having the nature of sorrowless bliss."
Having stated the contradiction of the *Kāpila-tantra* with the *Smṛtis* rooted in the Veda, he states its direct contradiction with the Veda itself: "And the Śruti...

The connection is as follows: it is established that at the time of [this] knowledge, not only is there something contrary to the Veda through the mere postulation of an independent *prakṛti*, but also through the postulation of a plurality of selves (*ātman*).
To the objection, "In the case of a contradiction with Smṛti, why should the Veda itself not be rendered invalid?", he says: "For of the Veda..."
The authority of the Veda is self-established because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

The authority of human statements is to be known through the postulation of their own recollection and the experience that is its basis; thus, there is a remoteness consisting in "extrinsic validity" (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) due to this mediation.
This is the literal meaning of the phrase "the distinction between Śruti and Smṛti."
For when two rules conflict, that which has no scope is sublated by that which has scope.

Here, because of the disparity between intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) and extrinsic validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*), and because the Vedic statement—whose validity is immediately ascertained and which has not yet encountered a contradiction—sublates the Smṛti that is in conflict with it; this is the intended meaning.
Therefore [it is said].
The meaning is "due to a distinction";
the intention is that it is possible for [the opponent's position] to be rooted in error. //1//
And because the others are not perceived (BBs 2.1.2):

those other things than the *pradhāna*—namely, the *mahat* and so forth—which are not conceived in the *smṛti* as being transformations of the *pradhāna*, are not perceived either in the Veda or in the world.
At least the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) can be remembered [as having been taught], since they are well-known in both the world and the Veda.

However, because the great principle (*mahat*) and the others are well-known from both common experience and the Vedas, it is not possible for there to be a Smṛti [text] concerning them, just as there is none for the sixth sense-object.

As for the fact that in some places a scriptural passage appears to have them as its primary purport, that too has been explained—under the Sūtra "And for some, it is inferential" (Brahmasūtra 1.4.1)—as not having that as its primary purport.
The intention is that since the Smṛti concerning the effects lacks authority, it is logical that the Smṛti concerning the cause also lacks authority.

Therefore, even for this reason, the objection that there would be no room for the Smṛti is not a fault; however, he will refute the reliance on reasoning starting from the sūtra "Not so, because of the difference in characteristics" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.4). 2.
First, the Great Principle (mahat) and the Ego (ahaṅkāra) are unestablished;
since the subtle elements (tanmātras) are also unestablished due to their having the ego as their material cause, they cannot even be remembered [as such]. Thus he says, "And of the others.
Now, one might object that the Great Principle and the rest are well-known from the scripture stating, "The Unmanifest is beyond the Great Principle"; therefore, he says, "Even that which..."
He states the purport of the Sūtra with the words "kārya" (the effect), etc.
The meaning is that it is determined that the authority of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti does not extend even to Pradhāna, just as it does not extend to Mahat and the other [evolutes].
To the question, "Even if the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is sublated, how can its stated arguments be sublated? he says: "tarka" (reasoning), etc. //2//

Section on the Refutation of Simultaneity (Yogapratyuktyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 3.
"By this, Yoga is refuted" (BBs 2.1.3).
By this refutation of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, it is indicated that the Yoga Smṛti is also to be regarded as refuted;
for there too, in contradiction with Śruti, the Pradhāna is [asserted to be] the independent cause.
Furthermore, effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, which are well-known in both common worldly experience and the Vedas, are postulated.
Now, this being the case, since the same logic applies, this matter is already covered by the previous [section]; for what purpose is it extended here again?
Indeed, there is a specific doubt that arises in this instance.

For yoga is prescribed in the Veda as the means for attaining right vision (*samyagdarśana*), as in [the passage]: "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5). Furthermore, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, an extensive exposition of the rules of yoga is seen, beginning with the description of the posture and other requirements: "Having placed the body even, with the three [parts] raised," (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8), and so forth.
Furthermore, thousands of Vedic indicators concerning yoga are found, such as: "They consider that steady control of the senses to be yoga" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.18),
and "This knowledge and the entire method of yoga" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.18),
and other passages of this kind.

In the Yogaśāstra as well, it is accepted that "Yoga is the means for the vision of reality" (*atha tattvadarśanopāyo yogaḥ*), precisely as a means to right vision (*samyagdarśana*). Therefore, since it shares a portion of its subject matter with [the Vedas] that is already agreed upon, the Smṛti of Yoga will likewise be beyond reproach, just like the Smṛtis concerning the Aṣṭaka and other rites.
This further objection is also refuted by the principle of extension (*atideśa*).
This is because we observe that even when there is agreement on one part of the subject matter, there is disagreement regarding another part of it, as previously stated.

Furthermore, although there exist many Smṛtis concerning internal subjects, an effort has been made specifically to refute only the Sāṃkhya and Yoga Smṛtis; for these two are renowned in the world as the means for attaining the supreme goal of human life.
They are accepted by the learned and are reinforced by indicative marks rather than by direct Vedic revelation,
as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.13): "Having known that God, who is reached through Sāṃkhya and Yoga and who is the cause of that [world], one is released from all bonds."
The refutation, however, is that the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is not attained through Sāṃkhya knowledge or through the path of Yoga independent of the Veda.

For the Śruti excludes any means to the supreme good other than the Vedic realization of the oneness of the Self, stating: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).
Indeed, those Sāṃkhyas and Yogins are dualists; they do not perceive the oneness of the Self.

As for the statement regarding the vision, "That cause is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga," it should be understood that it is specifically Vedic knowledge and meditation that are denoted by the terms Sāṃkhya and Yoga due to their close proximity.
Insofar as they do not contradict [the Vedas], the authority of the Smṛtis on Sāṃkhya and Yoga is indeed accepted.

For example, the purity of the Person (puruṣa), which is well-established in such scriptural passages as "For this Person is indeed unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.16), is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas through their description of the Person devoid of qualities (nirguṇa-puruṣa).
Likewise, it is also accepted by the Yogins: "Now, the wandering mendicant, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, and without possessions" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 5).
Thus, this state of being established in renunciation (*nivṛtti*), which is well-known from the Vedas, is followed by the instruction on wandering mendicancy (*pravrajyā*) and so forth.
By this, all logical arguments (*tarka*) and traditional codes (*smaraṇa*) are to be refuted.
If it is argued that these too assist in the knowledge of reality through reasoning and logical proof, let them indeed assist.

Knowledge of reality, however, arises only from the statements of the Vedānta, according to such scriptural passages as: "One who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.7), and "I ask you about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26). // 3 //
FN: That body in which the three—the chest, the neck, and the head—are elevated is called "three-elevated" (*tryunnata*).
*Tarka* (reasoning) is inference (*anumāna*) as that which is to be assisted;
*upapatti* (logical proof) is the supporting argument (*yukti*). This is the distinction.

There being a doubt as to whether the reconciliation stated regarding Brahman is contradicted by the Yoga-smṛti of the Pradhāna proponents or not, [the Sūtra] extends the previous reasoning: "By this, Yoga is refuted.
Since this is an extension (atideśa), the connection and so forth should be understood as before.
He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) which was not explicitly refuted previously: "For there exists here... and so on.
Nididhyāsana is yoga.

That body in which the three—the chest, the neck, and the head—are elevated is called "trirunnata" (threefold-elevated); if the reading is "trirunnatam," it is Vedic (chāndasa). The word "yuñjīta" (one should yoke) is to be supplied as the verb.
He says "and the indicative marks" to show that there are not only injunctions regarding yoga, but also explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that provide knowledge of yoga.
Those who know yoga consider that aforementioned concentration (*dhāraṇā*) to be yoga and the supreme austerity.
The connection is as follows: having obtained this knowledge of Brahman, the rule for yoga, and the method of meditation from the grace of Mṛtyu, Naciketas attained Brahman.
The meaning is that even with respect to portions of reality such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth, Smṛti must be accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because it possesses the nature of having a portion of its subject matter established as authoritative and consistent with yoga.

In the section on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*), it was stated that Smṛtis such as "the *Aṣṭakā* sacrifices should be performed" and "the teacher should be followed" possess authority by means of inferring a foundational Śruti, since their content is not contradicted by the Veda.

Having restated the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)—that since the Smṛti of Yoga is authoritative regarding yoga, it must also be authoritative regarding the portion concerning reality (tattva)—the author establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "This [Smṛti]...

One might ask: why are the Smṛtis of the Buddhists and others not refuted here? To this he replies: "Even though they exist... The sense is that these are disregarded here because they are well known as being deceptive, because they are accepted by those who are unrefined and like beasts, and because they stand outside the Veda.
Regarding the phrase "the cause of that":

having known the God who has entered—that is, attained—as the inner self (pratyak) by means of discernment and meditation through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which are the causes of those aforementioned desires, one is released from all fetters such as ignorance;
this is the meaning.

To the question, "Why has the refutation of both Smṛtis been performed even though they possess a root [in the Veda]? he says: "But the refutation... The word "iti" indicates the reason. The word "kṛtam" (was performed) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Because of proximity" means that the words *sāṃkhya* and *yoga* found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) grasp meanings belonging to their own class [of scriptural terms].
Is it, then, that the Smṛti is non-authoritative in all its parts?
He says "no," [explaining] "by which part" and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that the doctrine of Brahman contradicts the views of Kaṇabhakṣa and others, he extends the argument with the word "by this," meaning "by contradiction with the Śruti."

Anticipating the objection that "the sublation of that which is beneficial is not logical," [the author] states, "Even those... [to show] that the part which is beneficial is not to be sublated, but rather the part concerning reality (*tattva*).
Reasoning (*tarka*) is inference (*anumāna*); the means of supporting it is logic (*yukti*), which is *upapatti* (justification). //3//

Section on the Difference in Nature (Vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 4–12 START BsCom_2,1.3.4 END BsCom_2,1.2.3 The world cannot have Brahman as its material cause because it is of a different nature [from Brahman]. Furthermore, [the world] is not an effect of Brahman because it possesses the qualities of being gross, insentient, and impure, whereas Brahman possesses the opposite qualities. Moreover, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is characterized by suffering, while Brahman is characterized by bliss; and because the world is subject to destruction, whereas Brahman is eternal. Nor can the world be an effect of Brahman because it is composed of parts and lacks consciousness, while Brahman is partless and conscious. Additionally, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is finite and non-pervasive, whereas Brahman is infinite and all-pervasive. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to change and transformation, while Brahman is immutable and unchanging. Finally, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is a collection of diverse elements, whereas Brahman is a single, uniform reality. Therefore, since the world is of a different nature from Brahman, it cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: This is not so, for there are instances where effects possess qualities different from their causes. For example, fire, which is hot, produces smoke, which is cold; and gold, which is bright, produces ornaments that are dull. Likewise, Brahman may produce a world that is of a different nature. [Reply: That is not correct, because the examples cited do not establish the point. In those cases, the difference in quality is merely a matter of degree or manifestation, and not a fundamental difference in essence. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is perceived as having a beginning and an end, whereas Brahman is without beginning or end. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is characterized by multiplicity and diversity, while Brahman is characterized by unity and simplicity. Since these points have been established, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: Even if the world is of a different nature, it may still be an effect of Brahman, just as a spider produces a web that is different from itself. [Reply: That is not so, because the spider’s web is not fundamentally different from the spider’s own body, which serves as its material cause. In the case of Brahman, however, no such material cause exists within Brahman itself from which the world could arise. Therefore, the world is not an effect of Brahman. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is designated as "this" (idam), just as a pot is designated as "this" when it is made from clay. [Reply: That is not so, because the designation "this" applies to the world only after it has come into existence, whereas Brahman is designated as "that" (tat) even before the world arises. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is perceived as being distinct from Brahman, just as a jar is distinct from the clay. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to the laws of karma and moral causation, whereas Brahman is free from such constraints. Since these arguments have been presented, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is permeated by the power of Brahman, just as the body is permeated by the soul. [Reply: That is not so, because the analogy is flawed. The body is not an effect of the soul in the sense that the soul is its material cause; rather, the body is an effect of the elements, while the soul is merely the instrumental cause of its animation. Similarly, the world is an effect of the elements, not of Brahman. Therefore, the world is not an effect of Brahman. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is designated as "Brahman's world," just as a cloth is designated as "Devadatta's cloth. [Reply: That is not so, because the designation "Brahman's world" refers to the fact that Brahman is the presiding deity and sustainer of the world, not that it is the material cause. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is characterized by ignorance and delusion, whereas Brahman is characterized by knowledge and purity. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to birth and death, whereas Brahman is unborn and immortal. Since these points have been established, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is taught in the scriptures that "all this is indeed Brahman. [Reply: That is not so, because that scriptural passage intends to show that Brahman is the inner controller and the ultimate reality underlying the world, not that the world is a literal transformation of Brahman. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is perceived as being composed of parts and lacking consciousness, while Brahman is partless and conscious. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to change and decay, whereas Brahman is eternal and unchanging. Since these arguments have been presented, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is designated as "Brahman's creation," just as a painting is designated as "the artist's creation. [Reply: That is not so, because the designation "Brahman's creation" refers to the fact that Brahman is the efficient cause and the source of the world's manifestation, not that it is the material cause. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is characterized by suffering and imperfection, whereas Brahman is characterized by bliss and perfection. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is finite and limited, whereas Brahman is infinite and limitless. Since these points have been established, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is taught in the scriptures that "from Him comes the origin, the sustenance, and the dissolution of this universe. [Reply: That is not so, because that scriptural passage intends to show that Brahman is the cause of the world's origination, sustenance, and dissolution in the sense of being the presiding deity and the ground of its existence, not that it is the material cause. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is perceived as being distinct from Brahman, just as a reflection is distinct from the object reflected. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to the laws of karma and moral causation, whereas Brahman is free from such constraints. Since these arguments have been presented, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is designated as "Brahman's body," just as the earth is designated as "the body of Viṣṇu. [Reply: That is not so, because the designation "Brahman's body" refers to the fact that Brahman pervades and sustains the world as its inner self, not that the world is a literal transformation of Brahman. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is characterized by multiplicity and diversity, whereas Brahman is characterized by unity and simplicity. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to birth and death, whereas Brahman is unborn and immortal. Since these points have been established, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is taught in the scriptures that "He created all this. [Reply: That is not so, because that scriptural passage intends to show that Brahman is the creator of the world in the sense of being the presiding deity and the source of its manifestation, not that it is the material cause. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is perceived as being composed of parts and lacking consciousness, while Brahman is partless and conscious. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is subject to change and decay, whereas Brahman is eternal and unchanging. Since these arguments have been presented, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. [Objection: The world is an effect of Brahman because it is designated as "Brahman's manifestation," just as light is designated as "the manifestation of the sun. [Reply: That is not so, because the designation "Brahman's manifestation" refers to the fact that Brahman is the source of the world's appearance, not that it is the material cause. Furthermore, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is characterized by suffering and imperfection, whereas Brahman is characterized by bliss and perfection. Also, the world is not an effect of Brahman because it is finite and limited, whereas Brahman is infinite and limitless. "Because of its dissimilarity, it cannot be such; and [this is known] from scripture.
(BBs 2.1.4) The objection against the position that Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of this world—which was based on *smṛti*—has been refuted.
Now, the objection based on reasoning (*tarka*) is being refuted.
Furthermore, once this meaning of the scripture has been ascertained, what room is there for an objection based on reasoning?
One might object: "But surely, with respect to Brahman, the scripture ought to be independent [of other means of knowledge], just as it is with respect to Dharma.
This would be a valid position if this subject matter were cognizable through scripture alone and inaccessible to other means of knowledge, like Dharma, which consists of things to be performed.
But Brahman is understood as the perfectly established reality (*pariniṣpanna-rūpa*);
and regarding a perfectly established entity, there is scope for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of earth and so forth.
And just as when there is mutual contradiction among scriptural texts (*śruti*), the others are interpreted in accordance with one [of them], [so it is here].
Thus, even when there is a conflict with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the scripture (*śruti*) should be interpreted according to that very [other means].
Furthermore, reasoning (*yukti*), which supports an unseen matter through its similarity to what is seen, is closer to direct experience (*anubhava*);
the scripture, however, is more remote, as it denotes its own meaning merely by way of tradition (*aitihya*).
The realization of Brahman, which culminates in direct experience, is held to be the remover of ignorance and the means to liberation because it yields its fruit through immediate perception.

Furthermore, the Śruti, by enjoining reflection (*manana*) in addition to hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the passage "It is to be heard and reflected upon," shows that reasoning (*tarka*) is also to be respected in this matter. Therefore, a further objection based on reasoning is raised with the words, "Not so, because of its being of a different nature."
As for what was stated— that Brahman, being conscious, is the cause of the world and its material source— that is not tenable.
Why?
Because this modification is of a different nature from its material cause:
for this world, which is intended to be the effect of Brahman, is observed to be non-intelligent and impure,
whereas Brahman is heard in scripture to be of a different nature from the world— intelligent and pure.
Furthermore, a relationship of material cause and modification is not observed between things that possess different characteristics;
for instance, modifications such as necklaces do not have clay as their material cause, nor do bowls and the like have gold as their material cause.
Rather, modifications are produced from clay alone and are endowed with the qualities of clay, and from gold alone and are endowed with the qualities of gold.

Likewise, this world, being insentient and endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion, must be the effect of a cause that is itself insentient and consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion; it cannot be the effect of something of a different nature.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this world is distinct from Brahman because it is observed to be impure and insentient.

For the world is indeed impure, as it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion—serving as the cause of joy, agony, despondency, and so forth—and because it comprises the diverse manifoldness of heaven, hell, and other high and low states.
Furthermore, this world is insentient because it enters into a state of being an instrument for the sake of the sentient through the relationship of cause and effect;
for when there is equality [of status], the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary does not exist.
Indeed, two lamps do not benefit one another.
[Objection: But surely even a conscious cause-and-effect relationship will benefit the enjoyer, according to the analogy of a master and a servant. [Reply: No;
for even in the case of a master and a servant, it is only the unconscious portion that benefits the conscious one.

Indeed, it is only that part consisting of the conscious elements such as the intellect (*buddhi*) which constitutes the appropriation of one conscious being that benefits another conscious being; a conscious entity itself does not directly benefit or harm another conscious entity.
For the Sāṃkhyas maintain that those who are conscious are indeed non-agents;
therefore, cause and effect are unconscious.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the consciousness of wood, clods of earth, and the like.
Moreover, this distinction between the conscious and the unconscious is well-established in the world;
therefore, because it is of a different nature from Brahman, this world cannot have that as its material cause.

Even if someone were to say, "Having heard that the world has a conscious material cause, I shall understand by that very authority that the entire world is conscious," [the answer would be as follows].
Because the modification is observed to be permeated by the nature of the primordial matter (*prakṛti*),
the non-manifestation of consciousness will occur due to a particular transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*).

Just as the consciousness of selves (*ātman*), though possessing clear consciousness, is not manifested in states such as sleep or fainting, so too the consciousness of wood, clods of earth, and the like will not be manifested.

And precisely because of this distinction created by being cultivated or uncultivated, as well as by the presence or absence of form and so forth, there will be no contradiction in the relationship of primary and subordinate between causes and effects or between selves—even though they are indistinguishable in their sentience—just as, for example, although earthiness is common to all, meat, soup, boiled rice, and so on, mutually assist one another due to the distinctions existing within each individual thing; so it will be here as well.
Furthermore, the established conventional distinction [between them] will not be contradicted for this very reason.
By that [argument], the difference characterized by being conscious or unconscious might somehow be avoided;
however, the difference characterized by being pure or impure is not avoided at all.
And since even the other kind of difference cannot be avoided, he says: "And its suchness [is known] from the word."

Indeed, this sentience of all things in the world, which is not actually perceived, is merely imagined by those who rely solely on the authority of scripture because of the scriptural hearing that the world has sentience as its nature;
yet even that is contradicted by the scripture itself,
since from the scripture one understands that such is not the case.
The term "suchness" (*tathātva*) expresses the state of being distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

The scripture itself, in the passage "both consciousness and non-consciousness" (*vijñānaṃ cāvijñānaṃ ca*, Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), by making known the insentience of a certain portion [of reality], declares the world—which is non-conscious—to be distinct from the conscious Brahman. // 4 //

that is to say, by way of tradition alone, as something beyond direct perception.

Since recollections (*smṛtis*) lack authority, there is no contradiction in their being consistent [with scripture]; thus, by way of restating what has already been established, he states the purport of this section (*adhikaraṇa*)—which serves as a definition of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—in the words: "Brahman is this... (*brahmāsya...*).

For Brahman, which is accessible through the Veda alone and independent of other means of knowledge, there is no entry for reasoning consisting of inference.

He supports the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that there is a contradiction because what is established is accessible through another means of knowledge and thus shares the same object—with the words "This might be so.
