Now, one might argue that even if there is a contradiction due to having the same object, let another means of knowledge (*māna*) alone be sublated because of its conflict with scripture; to this he says, "And as...

The meaning is that just as a weak scriptural statement is sublated by a stronger one, it is proper to interpret a scriptural statement that has a possible scope (*sāvakāśa*) through secondary figurative application (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) by means of another means of knowledge that has no possible scope (*niravakāśa*).

Furthermore, since reasoning (*tarka*) is an internal auxiliary (*antaraṅga*) to the direct realization of Brahman—which is the cause of liberation—because it has as its object an immediate reality, just like the principal [realization], insofar as it has for its sphere of operation examples that are immediately perceived.
But since verbal testimony concerns objects that are beyond the senses, it is extrinsic; therefore, it is sublated by reasoning. Thus he says:
"perceived," etc. That is to say, by mere tradition, i.e., by way of being beyond the senses.
He demonstrates the primacy of direct experience with the words, "and ending in experience.

Anticipating the objection that reasoning (*tarka*) is prohibited by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "This understanding is not [attained] through reasoning," he says, "The Śruti also [says so]," meaning that such an objection is not valid because it would contradict an injunction.

Having thus raised this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts—which maintain that the conscious Brahman is the cause [of the world]—[is established].
When there arises a doubt as to whether the argument— "the earth and so forth do not have consciousness as their material cause,
because they are effect-substances,
like a jar"— is contradicted by the logic of Sāṃkhya and Yoga or not, [the former view holds] that the Smṛti is weak due to its lack of a foundational source (mūla).

He raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example, stating "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*), on the grounds that inference is more powerful due to its being rooted in universal concomitance (*vyāpti*).
The result, as in the previous case, is that the former position entails the failure of the concordance (*samanvaya*), while the latter position establishes it.
The world does not have Brahman as its material cause,
because it is of a different nature from it;
for whatever is of a different nature from something else does not have that thing as its material cause.
The meaning is that just as necklaces and other such objects possess the characteristic of clay;
likewise, pleasure, pain, and delusion are the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Thus, the world, being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, possesses a common primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Because it is endowed with that [nature], whatever is thus is so, just as jars and other objects are endowed with clay; thus he says, "by clay alone.
He establishes its dissimilarity by stating, "and being different from Brahman."
For just as a single female body produces pleasure, distress, dejection, and so forth for a husband, a co-wife, and a paramour respectively,
so too should other entities be understood.
In this context, "pleasure" (prīti) is happiness (sukha).
Paritāpa is grief;
viṣāda is delusion;
by the word "etcetera," passion and so forth are included.

One might object that because both are equally conscious, there can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary; this is incorrect, as the case of master and servant provides a counter-example. To this, he replies with "No," etc., stating that there is no such deviation, since it is precisely the body of the servant that benefits the conscious master.
He states that "because sentient beings are devoid of increase or decrease, they do not act as mutual benefactors" by saying, "they are unsurpassed. From that [lack of mutual benefit],

he raises the view of certain partial thinkers— that the world is indeed conscious— by the force of its being composed of the nature of conscious entities heard [in scripture], saying, "As for him who..."
Since the sentience of jars and the like is sublated by non-perception, he says: "But [it is due to] non-manifestation.
The meaning is that consciousness, though existing, is not perceived because it is not a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The point is that the manifestation of consciousness occurs only when there is the coloring of a modification (*vṛttyuparāga*) by something other than the internal organ, and not otherwise.
Regarding the illustration for the non-manifestation of consciousness when there is an absence of a function (vṛtti), he says "just as" (yathā).
To the question, "If both the Self and the non-Self are conscious, how can there be a relationship of master and servant? he replies, "precisely from this.

Even though they are equal [in being conscious], there is a relationship of being the subordinate (śeṣitva) due to the specific nature of each; regarding this, he provides an illustration with "and just as" (yathā ca).

To the question of how there can be a distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, he says: "By means of differentiation," which means by the manifestation or non-manifestation of consciousness.
The Sāṃkhya offers a rebuttal by accepting the position of a certain school (ekadeśin) that everything is conscious: "Even by him, in some way..."
Having abandoned the initial admission, he refutes [the opponent's position] with the remainder of the sūtra, beginning with "And not," etc.
"The other" refers to the nature of being sentient or insentient.
"Dissimilarity" is the meaning of the term *tathātva*.
The meaning is that presumptive testimony based on what has been heard (śrutārthāpatti) is sublated by the verbal testimony [of scripture]. //4//
[Objection: But is it not the case that even sentience is heard of in some instances regarding the elements and the sense organs, which are otherwise considered to be insentient?
For instance, there are scriptural passages concerning the elements that attribute consciousness to them, such as "The earth spoke" and "The waters spoke" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.1.3.2–4),
and "That fire thought" and "Those waters thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3–4).
Such are the scriptural texts regarding the elements that speak of their sentience.

The subject matter of the senses is also indicated by such passages as, "These vital breaths (*prāṇas*), disputing among themselves as to who was superior, went to Brahmā" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.7), and "They said to Speech: 'Do thou sing the Udgītha for us'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2).
Thus, it concerns the senses and their objects.
To this, he recites the following:
"But there is a designation of the presiding deity, because of distinction and because of following after.
The word "but" (tu) dispels the doubt.

Indeed, one should not suspect that the elements and the sense organs possess consciousness on the basis of scriptural passages such as "the clay spoke," for this is a designation of the presiding deities. It is the conscious deities— the presiding deities of clay and so forth, and the presiding deities of speech and so forth— who are designated as engaging in activities such as speaking and conversing, which are appropriate for conscious beings, and not the mere elements and sense organs.
Why?
Because of distinction and conformity.
For the distinction between the enjoyers and the elements and sense-faculties—characterized by the differentiation between the conscious and the unconscious—has already been stated previously.
Moreover, it would not be possible for that [breath] to possess consciousness in every respect.

Furthermore, in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the Kauṣītakins distinguish [the breaths] with the word "deity" (*devatā*) in order to exclude the suspicion that they are mere instruments and to establish them as presiding conscious entities, stating: "These deities, indeed, were disputing among themselves as to who was the best."
And [it is said]: "Thus, all these deities, having recognized the highest good in the vital breath... (2.14).
Furthermore, conscious deities presiding over [the elements] everywhere are understood from mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), histories, and Purāṇas, such as:
"Agni, becoming speech, entered the mouth" (Ai. Ā. 2.4.2.4).
Scriptural passages such as these show that there are deities who accompany and assist the organs.

Furthermore, in the supplementary portion of the dialogue among the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), it says: "Those vital breaths went to their father Prajāpati and said" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.7), indicating their journey to Prajāpati for the purpose of determining which among them was the most excellent.

And from those words, through positive and negative concomitance by means of each successive exclusion, the pre-eminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established. Furthermore, the worldly practice observed in such passages as "To him [the breath] an offering is brought" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.13)— which is similar to the usage among ourselves and others— confirms that these designations refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānin*).

It should be understood that even the statement, "That heat [tejas] thought," refers to this very act of seeing belonging to the Supreme Deity alone, who is the presiding controller and who persists through its own transformations.

Therefore, when it is objected that this world is indeed different in nature from Brahman, and because of this difference in nature, it cannot have Brahman as its material cause (prakṛti), he provides the following rebuttal. // 5 //

FN: *Saṃvadanaṃ* means dispute. The ellipsis is "they distinguish the speech and other [organs] from the vital breath and other [organs]. *Ahaṃśreyase* means for the sake of one's own respective superiority.
The term *niḥśreyasa* means the highest good (*śraiṣṭhya*).

One raises an objection—intended to be refuted by the subsequent sūtra—to the effect that [the doctrine] is not sublated because it is supported by scripture (*śruti*), beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
This is because scriptural passages concerning clay and so forth refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānin*) of those elements, since they possess qualities such as being speakers.

The Sāṃkhya replies that it is not tenable for the expression "consciousness and unconsciousness" (*vijñānaṃ cāvijñānaṃ ca*)—which distinguishes between the conscious and the unconscious—to have a figurative meaning. He states: "the one possessed of self-conceit" (*abhimānin*).
"Conversation" (*saṃvadana*) means dispute.
It is neither the mere elements (*bhūta-mātra*) nor the mere sense organs (*indriya-mātra*) that are designated as being conscious.
The meaning is that there can be no sublation of the distinction well-known in common worldly usage and in the Vedas.
He states another meaning for the word "viśeṣa" with the words "api ca" (furthermore).

Since the vital breaths, described as "quarreling for their own respective excellence" (*ahaṃśreyase*) for the sake of their own superiority, have been qualified by the term *devatā*, which denotes a conscious being, the meaning is that the words "prāṇa" and so forth refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānin*).
The meaning is that having realized the supreme good and preeminence in Prāṇa, they became dependent upon Prāṇa.
He explains "following after" (anugati) in various ways with the words "and they followed after. For that Prāṇa...
The offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) by means of speech and so forth was performed as the surrendering of one's own qualities, such as being Vasiṣṭha and the like.
As for the observation of "splendor" (*tejas*) and so forth, it should be understood that this has already been explained in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* as residing in a conscious being.
Therefore, the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: "Because the world lacks consciousness, [it cannot be the Self]. //5//
But it is indeed seen. (BBs 2.1.6)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
As for what was stated— that this world does not have Brahman as its material cause because of their dissimilarity—
that is not an absolute rule.

For it is observed in the world that from things well-known as sentient, such as humans, there arises the production of hair, nails, and so forth, which are of a different nature; and from things well-known as insentient, such as cow dung, there arises the production of scorpions and the like.
[Objection: But surely the bodies of humans and others, though themselves insentient, are the causes of the insentient hair, nails, and so forth.
Furthermore, the bodies of scorpions and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the effects of insentient things such as cow dung.
To this it is replied: even so, there is indeed a distinction, in that some insentient things become the substratum for consciousness while others do not.

Moreover, there is a great transformational disparity between the nature of humans and the like and that of hair, nails, and so forth, due to the difference in their essential forms and other characteristics.
The same applies to cow dung and the like in relation to scorpions and the like.
Furthermore, if there were absolute similarity [between cause and effect], the very relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) would vanish.

Now, it might be argued that there is some inherent nature, such as "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*), which persists in the hair and nails of humans and so forth, just as it does in cow dung and the like in relation to scorpions and the like.
In that case, even Brahman’s own nature, characterized by existence (*sattā*), is observed to persist in space and other such entities.

Furthermore, regarding the argument that the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause (*prakṛti*) on the grounds of their being "dissimilar" (*vilakṣaṇatva*): you must state whether this dissimilarity is intended to mean the non-persistence of the *entirety* of Brahman’s nature, or merely the non-persistence of some particular aspect of it—such as consciousness (*caitanya*).

In the first alternative, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total annihilation of both the primary cause (*prakṛti*) and its modifications (*vikāra*); for it cannot be said that something is a modification of a primary cause when there is no excellence [in the former]. In the second case as well, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For it has been stated that the nature of Brahman, characterized by existence (*sattā*), is indeed observed as persisting in ether and other such things.
However, in the third case, there is an absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For what instance could be cited before a proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*) to show that whatever is not permeated by consciousness is seen to have a non-Brahman nature?
This is because it is accepted that the entire collection of entities has Brahman as its material cause (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, the contradiction with scripture is indeed well-known,
since it has been established that the purport of scripture is that conscious Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world.
As for the claim that because Brahman is fully established (*pariniṣpanna*), other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) might apply to it—
that too is a mere wishful thought;
for, due to the absence of form (*rūpa*) and other such qualities, this object is not within the domain of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, because there is an absence of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, this matter cannot be known through inference and the like;
rather, it is to be understood solely through scripture (*āgama*), just like *dharma*.

Thus says the Śruti: "This understanding is not to be attained by reasoning; it must be declared by another [who has realized it] for the sake of easy knowledge, O dearest one" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9).

And these two verses— “Who indeed knows, who here has declared, from whence this creation was born? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.30.6)— demonstrate that the cause of the world is difficult to understand even for perfected lords.
There is also a traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "Those entities which are indeed inconceivable—one should not attempt to apply reasoning to them.
And [it says]: "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable, this is said to be unchangeable" (Gītā 2.25).
"Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin."
And there are other such passages as: "For I am the source of the gods and of all the great seers in every way" (Gītā 10.2).
Furthermore, it has been argued that the very scripture, by enjoining reflection (*manana*) in addition to hearing (*śravaṇa*), shows that reasoning (*tarka*) must also be respected.
By this pretext, the establishment of dry logic (śuṣka-tarka) is not possible here;
for it is only logic supported by scripture that is resorted to here as an auxiliary to direct experience (anubhava).
Because of the mutual deviation between the states of dream and waking, the Self is shown to be unaffected (ananvāgata).
And in the state of serene composure (*saṃprasāda*), through the abandonment of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is the attainment of the nature of Being (*sadātman*);

thus, because conceptual proliferation originates from Brahman, there is non-difference from Brahman according to the principle that the effect is not other than its cause—such is the kind of reasoning [implied]. "Because reasoning is unstable" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.11).

And thus he will demonstrate that mere reasoning is non-deceptive. Furthermore, as for one who, solely by the power of hearing about a conscious cause, imagines the entire world to be conscious— even for him, the scriptural statement "consciousness and unconsciousness" [regarding the two forms] serves to refute that view, since it shows the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious through the differentiation of consciousness and its absence.
It can indeed be so applied;
however, even this hearing of the division is not tenable for the opponent alone.
How so?
For here it is proclaimed that the Supreme Cause exists as the very self of the entire world, according to the text: "It became both conscious and unconscious.

In this regard, just as the state of being unconscious is not possible for that which is conscious because their characteristics are dissimilar, so too the state of being conscious is not possible for that which is unconscious.
Since the argument regarding the difference in characteristics has already been refuted, the cause must be understood exactly according to the scriptural text.
[Note: "Pāriṇāmika" means consisting of the specific transformations found in hair and so forth.
This understanding arising from the Vedānta scriptures is not to be set aside by mere reasoning or one's own speculative conjecture; it is not subject to sublation.

Alternatively, the meaning is that it cannot be attained through reasoning; rather, when it is proclaimed and awakened by another skillful teacher, it leads to right knowledge—that is, to direct realization. "O dearest one" (*preṣṭha*) is an address to Naciketas by Yama.

From where—by what cause—did this emission, the creation beginning with space, arise? And by whom was its stability attained? Truly, in reality, who knows? No one at all. Who has declared it? No one has been a proclaimer.
"Deceptiveness" means the failure to establish the specific nature of the object.
Is it some slight difference that serves as the reason, or a great difference?
Regarding the first case, he states the fallacy of deviation: "This is not an absolute rule."
"It is indeed seen" [is said].
He raises the objection that there is no deviation because the reason (*hetu*) is non-existent, saying "But surely... [nanu].
He states that there is deviation because there exists some slight difference [between the cases], saying "It is replied... [ucyate].
The meaning is that there exists a distinction between the body and its hair and so forth, consisting in their being respectively insentient and sentient.
Regarding the second [case] as well, he points out a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very same context with the words "the Great [Self]" (mahān),
meaning that which is subject to transformation (pariṇāmika).
The meaning is that [the transformation] consists of a change occurring within the hair and so forth themselves.

Furthermore, regarding those two things between which there is the relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), one who asserts their similarity must state whether that similarity is absolute or merely partial.
He states the fault in the first case [absolute similarity] as follows: "If it were absolute... (*atyanta*...).

Anticipating a second objection—that since Brahman and the world both possess existence (*sattva*), their relationship as material cause (*prakṛti*) and effect (*vikṛti*) is established—he says "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
Having analyzed the nature of their difference (*vilakṣaṇatva*), he states another refutation with the words "By way of being different" (*vilakṣaṇatvena*) and so forth.

In the position that the world is not the effect of Brahman because no universal characteristic of Brahman, such as sentience (*cetanatva*), persists in it, it would have to be said that the relationship of material cause and effect exists only when there is complete similarity between them.
He says that this is inconsistent: "In the first [case]," and "But in the third, there is an absence of an illustrative example.
Nor should it be argued that there exists an illustrative example such as, "The world does not have Brahman as its material cause because it is insentient, like ignorance (avidyā)."
This is because beginninglessness (*anāditva*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Nor is there a lack of pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*) in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), since that too, being of the nature of a causal impression (*kāryasaṃskāra*), is an existent (*bhāva*) and thus has Brahman as its material cause; and when it is not apprehended as a non-existent (*abhāva*), beginningless existence (*anādibhāvatva*) remains the limiting condition.
Now he states the defect common to all three alternatives, beginning with "āgama" (scripture).

Having restated what was said previously, he says "yattu uktam" (as for what was stated), etc., asserting that there can be no objection based on reasoning (*tarka*) because Brahman cannot be the object of dry logic (*śuṣkatarka*).

Due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), or the ground for the application of a word (*padapravṛttinimitta*), [Brahman] is not within the scope of inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), or verbal testimony (*śabda*).
The meaning is that Brahman, as characterized by its own nature, is to be known solely through the Veda.
This understanding regarding Brahman is not to be removed by independent reasoning, nor is it to be established by such means;
or rather, it is not to be sublated by fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*).
The understanding taught by a teacher who knows the Vedas, and not by a fallacious logician, leads to right knowledge, to experience, and to its fruit.
"O dearest one," "O beloved"—these were the words of Death addressed to Naciketas.
Who truly knows, in direct perception, that from whom this manifold creation has come forth on all sides?
Let alone feeling; who in this world has spoken it, or rather, has proclaimed it?
[The form] "prāvocat" is a Vedic instance of the elision of a long vowel.
The meaning is that there is not even one who speaks [of Me] as I truly am.
They do not know My origin—that is, My birth—because, being the beginning of all, I have no birth.
"By a pretext" means under the guise of the rule for meditation.

"Dry" (śuṣka) means independent of scripture (śruti). "Supported by scripture" (śrutyanugṛhīta) refers to that which is grasped after the reality has been ascertained through scripture, for the purpose of subsequently eliminating doubts regarding human defects such as the impossibility [of the teaching]. He states this with the words "svapnānta" and so forth.
The identity of the individual soul—which possesses states and is associated with the manifold world of the body and so forth—with the non-manifold Brahman is impossible;

furthermore, the non-duality of Brahman is untenable because it contradicts the means of valid knowledge that apprehend duality. When such impossibility regarding the meaning of the Vedic texts arises, in order to dispel it, [the text shows] that the Self, which persists through all its own states, is not followed by and is untouched by those changing states, as the states themselves are subject to change.

The meaning is as follows: since it is impossible for the nature [of Brahman] to deviate from itself—just as heat does not deviate from fire—if the error of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-bhrānti*) were absent in deep sleep, then the possibility of identity with the non-phenomenal Brahman would arise from the realization of non-difference expressed in the words, "O dear one, it was non-existent" (*asat somya*).
Thus, one resorts to reasoning such as: "Just as jars and other objects are non-different from clay, so too the world is non-different from Brahman because it is born from that," and so forth.
The sense is that there is no room for the objection based on reasoning, because other kinds of reasoning cannot penetrate this Brahman, whereas this [specific kind of reasoning] is favorable to it;
thus, dry reasoning has no access to Brahman.
He states that this is the consensus of the Sūtras by saying, "Because reasoning is not firmly established" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*).
Deceptiveness means the state of not being a means of valid knowledge (*apramāpaka*).

As for the objection raised by the Sāṃkhya against the partial proponent (*ekadeśin*)— namely, that if it were asserted that the entire world is sentient, the scriptural teaching of differentiation (*vibhāga-śruti*) would be untenable—
that is not correct.

In this regard, it can be argued by that partial proponent (ekadeśin) that the scriptural mention of a distinction can be reconciled through the manifestation and non-manifestation of consciousness; however, for the Sāṃkhya, this criticism becomes like an adamantine coating, because if everything were an effect of the Pradhāna, all would be insentient, and thus a distinction between sentient and insentient effects would be impossible. This he states with the words beginning "yo 'pi... and so forth.

If it is asked how Brahman can be the material cause (prakṛti) given that the established doctrine (siddhānta) accepts a distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, he says: "Because it has been refuted.
This means it has been discarded by the two [reasons] of being non-conclusive (aprayojakatva) and deviance (vyabhicāra). //6//
If it be argued that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because [the statement] is a mere negation. (BS 2.1.7)

If you maintain that Brahman—which is conscious, pure, and devoid of sound—is the cause of an effect that is its opposite (i.e., unconscious, impure, and possessed of sound and other qualities), then it would follow that the effect is non-existent prior to its production. And this is undesirable for you, who are a proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*). If [this objection is raised]:
This is not a fault, because it is a mere negation.
For this is a mere negation; there is no object to be negated by this negation.
For this negation cannot negate the existence of the effect prior to its production.
How so?
Because just as this effect even now exists in reality by way of its causal nature, it is understood to be likewise existent prior to its production.
Even now, this effect does not exist independently, apart from the nature of its cause;
for there is scriptural testimony such as: "Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).
However, the existence of the effect in the form of its cause is undifferentiated prior to its production.
But surely, Brahman, being devoid of sound and other qualities, cannot be the cause of the world? Certainly it can.
However, an effect characterized by sound and other qualities does not exist—whether prior to its production or at present—devoid of the nature of its cause;
therefore, it cannot be said that the effect was non-existent prior to its production.
We shall explain this in detail in the discussion on the non-difference between cause and effect. // 7 //

Anticipating the objection that the effect must be non-existent prior to its production because it is impossible for it to exist in the form of its own contradictory cause—which would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own established tenets—he provides the following resolution with the words beginning "If it be said that it is non-existent," and so forth: since the effect is illusory (mithyā), its existence in the form of the cause throughout the three periods of time is not contradictory; thus, the denial of its existence [prior to production] is meaningless. This is the sense of the phrase "from the unreal" (asatyāt).
He cites scripture (*śruti*) regarding the absence of conventional truth (*kāryasatyatva*): "All that," and so forth.
Having restated the doubt of one who does not recognize its falsity, he refutes it with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*), and so on.
And this has been explained in detail.
The meaning is "falsehood. //7//

Here it is said: If it is admitted that the effect—which possesses the properties of grossness, having parts, insentience, finitude, impurity, and so forth—has Brahman as its cause, then at the time of dissolution (*apīti*), when the effect is being reabsorbed and attains non-distinction from the cause, it would defile the cause with its own properties. Consequently, because of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cause, Brahman, would likewise possess impurity and other such qualities just like the effect, [Brahman] could not be omniscient.

This Upaniṣadic view that Brahman is the cause of the world is inconsistent. Furthermore, since all distinctions reach a state of non-distinction [at dissolution], there would be no cause for regulation during subsequent production; thus, production would not occur according to the distinction between enjoyers and objects of enjoyment, which makes it inconsistent. Moreover, if the re-emergence of those who have attained non-distinction from the supreme Brahman were admitted even when causes such as karma are dissolved, it would follow that even the liberated could be reborn, which is inconsistent.
Moreover, even during dissolution, this world would remain distinct from the supreme Brahman;
thus, dissolution itself would be impossible, and it is untenable that an effect could exist as non-different from its cause. Therefore, [the theory] is indeed inconsistent. // 8 //

He explains the sūtra that raises the objection—stating "here he says"—for the purpose of establishing the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*): "If there is no difference between the effect and the cause, then the cause would also be subject to impurity and so forth, just like the effect. He provides the explanation of the term *pratisaṃsṛjyamāna* as "the cause," meaning that just as salt dissolving in water vitiates the water, so it is in this case.
He states another interpretation of the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (*apica*).
The meaning is that if all effects were to merge back into their cause, they would necessarily result in having a single uniform nature, just like the cause itself.
He states yet another point with the words "Moreover."

The meaning is that since karma and other causes of production exist even during dissolution, then just as [beings] arise for those who are enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*), so too would there be the undesirable consequence of the arising of even those who are liberated.
He states another interpretation preceded by a doubt: "Now (*atha*)" etc.

If, even at the time of dissolution, the effect were separate from the cause, then—just as during the period of maintenance—there would be the consequence of no dissolution occurring, and because of the resulting duality with the effect, this view would be inconsistent; such is the meaning. //8//

But it is not because of the existence of a [counter-]example. There is no inconsistency whatsoever in our own philosophical system regarding what was stated:
that "the effect, upon merging into the cause, would defile the cause with its own properties."
That is not a valid refutation.
Why?
Because there is no supporting example (dṛṣṭānta).
For there are indeed examples showing how an effect, when returning to its cause, does not defile that cause with its own specific qualities.

For instance, transformations such as bowls and the like, which have clay as their material cause and exist in states of high, low, or middling distinctions during their period of differentiation, do not, upon returning to their material cause, contaminate it with their own specific qualities.
Furthermore, even though earrings and other such items are modifications of gold, they do not merge with the gold by means of their own specific properties upon dissolution.

Likewise, the fourfold collection of beings, which is a modification of earth, does not merge with the earth by means of its own specific properties upon dissolution. However, for your position, there is no illustrative example whatsoever.
Indeed, merging itself would not be possible if the effect were to persist in the cause by means of its own attributes.

Even though the effect and the cause are non-different, we shall explain under *Brahmasūtra* 2.1.14 that it is the effect that possesses the nature of the cause, and not the cause that possesses the nature of the effect, based on the scriptural texts concerning "originating material" (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, it is far too little said to claim that upon merging, the effect would merely blend with the cause through its own attributes.
This same undesirable consequence applies even to the state of persistence, because you admit the non-difference between cause and effect,
as in: "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).
"Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);
"This immortal Brahman alone is before [us]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11);
"All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
For by such scriptural passages as these, the non-difference of the effect from the cause is declared without distinction throughout all three periods of time.
In this regard, the solution— that the cause is not affected by the effect or its attributes because they are superimposed through ignorance—
is equally applicable even at the time of dissolution.

And there is this other illustration: just as a magician is not touched by the illusion he himself has projected at any of the three times because it lacks substantial reality, so too the Supreme Self is not touched by the illusion of saṃsāra.

And just as a single dreamer is not touched by the illusion of the dream-vision— because he is unaffected by the transition from dreaming to waking— so too the one unchanging witness of the three states is not touched by the three changing states.
For this manifestation of the Supreme Self in the form of three states is indeed mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), like the appearance of a rope as a snake and so forth.

Regarding this, it has been stated by the Teachers who know the tradition of the Vedānta meaning: "When the individual soul (*jīva*), sleeping through beginningless *māyā*, awakens, then it realizes the non-dual (*advaita*) which is unborn, sleepless, and dreamless" (Gauḍapāda Kārikā 1.16).

In this regard, what was stated— that upon dissolution, the cause would also be subject to defects such as grossness just like the effect— is incorrect. Furthermore, as for the claim that since all distinctions reach a state of non-distinction, no regulating cause can be established for their subsequent emergence through differentiation—
this too is not a fault.
Precisely because of the existence of the illustrative example:

for just as even in deep sleep, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and so forth, although there is an actual attainment of non-distinction due to the innate nature [of the Self], yet because false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) has not been removed, distinction arises again upon waking just as before; so it is here as well.
And there is a scriptural text (*śruti*) on this point: "All these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know that they have merged into Being."
"Thus, whatever they become here— whether a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito— they become that very thing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2, 3).
For just as even though there is no division within the Supreme Self, the empirical usage of division, obstructed by false knowledge, is seen to persist unimpeded like a dream.
Even so, even in these two cases, the power of differentiation is inferred to be strictly bound by false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
By this, the objection that liberated beings might be subject to rebirth is refuted,
because false cognition has been eliminated by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Furthermore, as for this other alternative imagined at the end—that even upon dissolution, this world might remain distinct from the supreme Brahman—that too is refuted simply by the fact that it is not accepted [by our school]. Therefore, this philosophical view of the Upaniṣads is perfectly consistent. 9. @----------------------
FN: "Approaching" (apigacchat) means merging.
The state of differentiation is the period of persistence (sthitikāla).
The statement regarding ignorance—"they do not know," having become one in Brahman while it exists—is an expression of nescience.

In this context, the statement regarding "differentiation" means that those things which become differentiated by birth and so forth prior to deep sleep appear in exactly the same way again at the time of waking; thus,
upon dissolution, the world does not defile its own cause,
because it has merged into that cause.

He explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*), "Like a blue jar and so forth in clay and the like," with the words beginning "not at all" (*naiva*). "Dissolving" (*apigacchat*) means merging or being absorbed.
"The state of division" (*vibhāgāvasthā*) refers to the period of duration.
Regarding the phrase "of your position":
since sweet water is not the cause of saltiness, it is not a valid example.
Furthermore, he says "only non-absorption" (apītiḥ), meaning that if there were a state of effect as in the case of salt, there would be a defect in your argument.
When the effect is non-existent, its connection with the properties of the cause is not possible;
the sense is that when the substratum (dharmin) is absent, its properties (dharmas) are also absent.

Now, one might object: "In the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), since the effect exists even during dissolution through its non-difference from the cause, this [argument] would constitute a flaw. To this, he says: "Even though there is non-difference..."

The meaning is that while the substrate possesses the attributes of the imagined [effect] due to their non-difference, the substrate does not possess the attributes of the imagined effect, because it exists separately from that effect.

Furthermore, he resolves [the objection] by means of a *pratibandha* (reductio ad absurdum), stating that the qualification "in dissolution" (*apītau*) is redundant, with the words "And this is too little.
Having explained the analogy of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he explains the analogy of illusory appearance (*vivarta*) with the words "If it exists... (*asti ceti*).
Out of dissatisfaction with the claim that illusion (māyā) is without a material cause (anupādāna), he states another example, beginning with "just as" (yathā).
Since it might be argued that contact is indeed perceived during the time of a dream, he says "upon waking" (prabodha).
The meaning is that because the self is untouched by the dream both in the waking state and in deep sleep, it is likewise untouched at the time of the dream itself.

If there is no contact with the states of the individual soul (jīva), then what need is there to speak of the Omniscient One? Thus he states the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "evam" (thus).

Alternatively, the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the waking state constitute the three states of the Lord (*īśvara*). To express the consensus of the elders regarding His lack of attachment to these, he says "atroktam" (it is said here).

The meaning is that when one awakens at the time of the instruction "That thou art" and abandons the sleep of *māyā*, one then experiences the non-dual Lord—who is devoid of the states of birth, dissolution, and persistence—as one's own Self.
He states the established conclusion with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
Having restated the second inconsistency, he refutes it by means of that very same Sūtra with the words "as for what [was said] again" (*yat punar*).
He states the scriptural authority (*māna*) for the existence of ignorance during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and for the reappearance of differentiation: "And scripture [says so].
The statement regarding ignorance—"being unified in Brahman, they do not know"—refers to the state of non-cognition.

The statement regarding differentiation—"whatever [distinctions] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth by which they were divided prior to this deep sleep, at the time of waking again they become exactly as they were"—refers to the reappearance of division.

Now, one might ask: "If the power of ignorance (ajñāna) that causes differentiation exists again in deep sleep, how can its existence be established at the time of universal dissolution (sarvapralaya)? To this, he says: "Just as...

Just as in deep sleep, even though all effects are undifferentiated within the Supreme Self, there exists the power of ignorance which is the cause of future differentiation; so too, at the time of absorption—that is, the great dissolution—the power for the differentiation of creation is inferred from the connection with false ignorance.

Since the conventional practice of differentiation, which is the effect of false knowledge, persists now and is seen as uncontradicted— just like a dream— due to the absence of the awakening to reality,
the meaning is that the existence of the cause is established from the observation of its effect.

The underlying sense is that because the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti) persists even during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), there is a necessity for the rebirth of ignorant individual souls (jīvas).
"By this" means by the absence of the power of knowledge regarding the cause of birth. //9//
And because of the faults in one's own position. (BBs 2.1.10)
Moreover, these common defects would arise for the opponent's own position.
How so? It is said:
as for what was asserted—that this world is not derived from Brahman as its material cause because of their dissimilarity—[that is untenable].
This [objection] applies equally even to the theory that the Pradhāna is the primordial material cause,

because it is admitted that the world, which possesses sound and other qualities, arises from the Pradhāna, which is devoid of sound and other qualities. And for this very reason— namely, the admission that an effect of a different nature arises— the consequence of the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect prior to its production (asatkāryavāda) is equally applicable.
Nevertheless, since it is admitted that the effect undergoes dissolution into the cause, the same undesirable consequence applies here as well. Thus,

when all modifications in which every distinction has been obliterated have reached a state of non-distinction upon dissolution, those specific determinations belonging to each individual person— which existed prior to the dissolution, such that "this is the material cause for this person" and "this is for that"— cannot be restricted in the same way during re-emergence, because their cause is absent.

If a restriction were accepted without a cause, then because of the equality of the absence of a cause, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even those who are liberated would be bound again. If it is argued that some particular differences attain non-distinction upon dissolution while others do not, then those which do not attain it would fail to be effects of the *pradhāna*. Thus, since these defects are common to both positions, they should not be raised against only one side; this serves to confirm that these objections are indeed without fault [for the opponent].
Because it must necessarily be resorted to. [10] [The opponent might argue:
"They would manifest (*prāduṣyuḥ*), that is, they would become manifest.
Since defects such as heterogeneity (*vailakṣaṇya*) and so forth are faults even in the Sāṃkhya position, he states "svapakṣa... [etc. to say that we need not exert ourselves to refute them.
He explains the sūtra with the word "sva" (one's own).
"Prāduḥṣyuḥ" means they would manifest.
"Ata eva" (for this very reason) [is used].

It should be understood that this fault belongs only to the Sāṃkhya, who maintains that the effect is real, because it is impossible for that which is real to exist in the form of its contradictory cause; it does not belong to the proponent of the falsity of the effect (*kāryamithyātvavādin*).
He states the fourfold fault mentioned in the Sūtra "In dissolution" (*apītau*) with the words: "Likewise, in dissolution...
[The fault is as follows: there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the Pradhāna, like the effect, would possess form and other qualities.

There would be no fixed rule such that "this karma and so forth is the material cause for this person" or "this is the object of enjoyment for this person," nor would there be the established distinction between the bound and the liberated. If, for the sake of establishing this distinction, it is said that the specific aggregates of the liberated dissolve into the *pradhāna* while the specific aggregates of the bound do not dissolve, then for those that have not dissolved, there is a contradiction with their being effects, just like the *puruṣas*.
This is the meaning. //10//
"Because reasoning is not firmly established, if it is argued that there must be another way to infer [the truth], even so, there would be the consequence of no liberation. (BS 2.1.11)
Furthermore, one should not oppose a matter that is accessible through scripture by means of mere reasoning alone;
for in such a case, reasonings— which lack scriptural authority and are based solely on human imagination— become unstable,
because imagination is unrestrained.

For instance, we observe that arguments (tarka) which have been laboriously devised by some experts are refuted by other experts; and those very arguments, having been devised by them, are in turn refuted by yet others. Thus, because of the diversity of human intellects, it is impossible to rely upon the stability of such arguments.
Now, if it be maintained that reasoning is established as being accepted by someone of renowned majesty— be it Kapila, or another— even so, it remains unestablished;
for we observe mutual contradictions among the founders of systems (tīrthakaras), such as Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and others, even though they are acknowledged by those of renowned majesty.
To this it may be said: otherwise we shall infer in such a way that the fault of instability will not occur;
for it cannot be said that there is no reasoning whatsoever that is stable.
Indeed, even this instability of reasonings is established by means of reasoning itself.
Because some forms of reasoning are seen to be unstable, other reasonings of that same class must also be unstable.
And if all reasoning were unstable, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of worldly convention;
for it is observed that people act toward the future in order to obtain pleasure and avoid suffering by means of the analogy between past and present time.

Furthermore, when there is a conflict regarding the meaning of the scriptures, the determination of the correct meaning by means of refuting fallacious meanings is accomplished precisely through reasoning (*tarka*) in the form of an investigation into the function of the sentences.
Manu also holds this view: "One who desires purity in dharma should ensure that the triad of perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions is well understood."
Thus it is said:
"He who examines the instruction on Dharma given by the sages with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows Dharma, and no other."
By saying this [in verses 12.105–106],
he shows that non-establishment itself is the very ornament of reasoning (*tarka*).
For it is in this way that, by means of abandoning [faulty] reasoning, one comes to understand reasoning that is free from reproach.
If it is argued that there is no proof whatsoever that because one's ancestor was deluded, one must oneself also be deluded—
and therefore the instability of reasoning (*tarkāpratiṣṭhāna*) is not a fault—
even so, the consequence remains that liberation is impossible.

Although in some matters the stability of reasoning (*tarka*) may be observed, nevertheless, regarding this present subject, there inevitably follows the fault of instability, and thus liberation through reasoning is impossible.
For this extremely profound reality of existence, which is the basis for liberation, cannot even be conceived by imagination without recourse to scripture (*āgama*).
Indeed, because it lacks form and other sensory qualities, this matter does not fall within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, we have already stated that because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and other such factors, there can be no inference or other means of knowledge [regarding the Self].
Moreover, it is the consensus of all proponents of liberation (*mokṣavādin*) that liberation results from right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*);
and that right knowledge is of a single form, because it is dependent upon the reality of the object itself.
For that object which exists in a single form is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
In the world, knowledge having that as its object is called "correct knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*), just as [the cognition] "fire is hot.
This being the case, it is untenable for there to be any disagreement among persons regarding such correct knowledge.

However, regarding the cognitions based on reasoning (*tarka*), disagreement is well known because they contradict one another. For what has been established by one logician as "this alone is correct knowledge" is refuted by another; and what has been established by him is, in turn, refuted by yet another—this is well known in the world.
How could there be a correct cognition arising from reasoning that has as its object a single, non-abiding form?
Furthermore, the proponent of *pradhāna* is not the foremost among those skilled in reasoning such that he would be accepted by all logicians, whereby we might accept his view as correct cognition.
Nor is it possible to assemble all past, future, and present logicians in one place and at one time, so that their consensus on a single form and a single object might constitute a correct cognition.

Since the Veda is eternal and is the cause for the arising of knowledge, it is established that its subject matter is fixed; therefore, the correctness of the knowledge produced by it cannot be denied even by all logicians—past, future, and present alike.
Thus, it is proven that this very knowledge derived from the Upaniṣads is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Otherwise, since correct knowledge would be impossible in any other way, the consequence would be that liberation from saṃsāra could never occur.

Therefore, by the authority of scripture and by reasoning that conforms to scripture, it is established that conscious Brahman is both the cause and the material source (*prakṛti*) of the world. (11) [Note:
Reasoning devoid of supportive scripture is merely "solitary."]
The purity of Dharma is the definitive distinction from non-Dharma;
it is the state of being exceedingly profound, the attainment of the scriptures, and the fitness for the one and only [goal];
it is the reality of existence as found in its cause, which is non-duality.
Liberation from bondage consists in the state of being exclusively one with existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidekatānatva*).

Furthermore, since reasoning (*tarka*) is subject to potential defects, the faultless systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta cannot be sublated by it; thus [the author] says: "Also because of the instability of reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānād api*).
One might raise the objection: "Even though human intellects are diverse, one may place trust in the reasoning of Kapila because he was omniscient"—this is expressed by the word "now" (*atha*).
He refutes [the objection] with the maxim: "If Kapila is omniscient, what proof is there that Kaṇāda is not?"—thus he says, "Even so.
He explains the portion of the doubt situated within the Sūtra with the words, "Now it might be said.

The meaning is: even if reasoning (*tarka*) based on dissimilarity and so forth is unstable, some reasoning endowed with pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) will be established; by that, the Pradhāna may be inferred.

[Objection: But surely that [inference] is also non-established, because it belongs to the class of *tarka* (speculative reasoning), like "having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) and so forth. To this he says: "Not so.
Regarding the phrase "because it belongs to the class of *tarka*": is the *tarka* itself established or not?
In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because within this very [instance], the probandum—non-establishment—is absent.
Intending to show that even in the second case, it is not the case that all forms of reasoning (*tarka*) are non-conclusive due to a lack of evidence, he says: "This too...
Furthermore, [the action] whose ripening is yet to come is a means to achieve the desired goal, because it is a cooking (*pāka*).

He states "by all reasoning" (*sarvatarka*) to show that there is no lack of foundation, because reasoning—consisting of an inference that establishes what is desired, such as "like cooking that has already occurred"—is the cause for the worldly activities of engagement and withdrawal.
"Path" (*adhvan*) means the object, such as cooking and eating, or consuming poison and so forth.

By means of that generality, such as the nature of being cooked (*pākatva*), one infers that future objects like cooking will be causes of pleasure or pain; it is by this inference that engagement and other activities occur.

Furthermore, since the determination of the intended meaning of a statement is accomplished through reasoning (*tarka*) alone in both the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās, he says "the reasoning is established" with the words *śrutyartha* etc.

He also says "Manu" to show that Manu likewise considers certain types of reasoning to be established; "purity of dharma" (*dharmasya śuddhiḥ*) means the determination of its distinction from what is non-dharma (*adharma*).
He accepts the non-establishment of a certain type of reasoning with the words "this very [one].
The sense is that if all reasonings were established, there would be no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) at all.
Like the reasoning of the prima facie position, the reasoning of the final conclusion (siddhānta) is also non-established.
He mocks the one who says "because there is no difference in being mere reasoning" with the words "Not so.

Even if reasoning is established in some matters, there is no independence for reasoning regarding the specific cause of the world; he explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words beginning "Even though," etc.
The "extreme profundity" of Brahman means its being inaccessible to any means of knowledge other than the Veda.
The true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the existent cause of the world is non-duality (*advayatva*).
It is the basis for liberation and the objective support for liberation.
He shows that Brahman cannot be reached by means other than the Vedas with the words "from form" (*rūpāt*).
He states another point—that there is no liberation, meaning there is an absence of liberation—by means of the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*).

To the objection that even if the cognition of an object of a single nature were correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), why could it not be produced by reasoning (*tarka*), he replies: "In that case, such being so.
Because cognitions arising from reasoning are mutually contradictory, they do not possess the status of correct knowledge.
The meaning is that it is impossible for there to be a misconception regarding right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
The construction is as follows: how could that which arises from *tarka*—the object of which is not established in a single form—be right knowledge?

Anticipating the objection that "since Sāṃkhya is the most excellent [system], its knowledge is right," he states the non-establishment of the reason: "And not by means of the *pradhāna*... and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Could it not be that the intellect arising from reasoning determined by all logicians joined together is the cause of liberation? To this he says: "And they cannot [be so]. Therefore, since liberation is impossible through knowledge arising from reasoning, it is not proper to subvert the harmony of the Vedānta texts by means of reasoning; for if that were subverted, right knowledge would not be attained, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation. He concludes the meaning of this portion of the Sūtra with the words: "Therefore, elsewhere."
He concludes the meaning of the section, which results from the non-contradiction of the concordance with reasoning by means of logic, with the words: "Therefore, by scripture... (11).
Section on the Acceptance by the Learned (Śiṣṭaparigrahādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 12 4. [The section concerning] the acceptance by the learned. Sūtra 12.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are also explained.

Because it is closely related to the Vedic system, because it is endowed with the force of more weighty reasoning, and because it has been accepted in some respects by certain learned persons who follow the Vedas, one who— relying first upon the doctrine of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause— [employs] reasoning for its sake...
The objection raised regarding the Vedānta texts has been refuted.

Now, however, some of dull intellect, relying on the doctrines of the atomists (*aṇuvāda*) and others, may again suspect an objection based on reasoning against the Vedānta texts; therefore, [the author] extends the previous argument by the maxim of "defeating the chief wrestler" (*pradhānamallanibarhaṇanyāya*).
"Parigrahas" means those who accept [certain views]; "aparigrahas" means those who do not accept them—those who are not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭas*).

By this same reason for refuting the doctrine of Pradhāna as the primary cause under discussion, those theories of atoms and other causes which were not adopted by the learned authorities such as Manu, Vyāsa, and others— these too should be understood as explained as being prohibited and refuted; since the grounds for their refutation are identical, there is nothing further to be doubted here.

Even with equal measure, there is a refutation of such [objections] as the fact that the supreme, most profound cause of the world cannot be fathomed by logic, the instability of reasoning, the lack of liberation even through otherwise-correct inference, and contradiction with scripture. // 12 //
The subject matter is the Vedāntic harmony which asserts that Brahman is the material cause of the world.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the logic of the Vaiśeṣikas and others—according to which whatever is all-pervasive cannot be the material cause of a substance—the answer is that it is indeed contradicted; for although the elder Sāṃkhyas may lack skill in reasoning, the Vaiśeṣikas and others are renowned for their mastery of logical thought, and thus their reasoning remains unrefuted.
Having reached this conclusion by means of a counter-example, he extends [the rule] with the words "by this" (*etena*).

The result is as before. Now, one might object: why has the teaching of the Sāṃkhya doctrine been treated as the subject of instruction (*upadeśa*) while the doctrine of the Logicians (*tārkika*) has been treated as its extension (*atideśa*), when the reverse could just as well be the case? Anticipating this doubt, he states the reason for the relationship of instruction and extension between the preceding and succeeding sections: "of the Vedic... (*vaidikasya*).

The theory of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is proximate to the Vedānta system through such aspects as the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*), non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*), and self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*);
because it was accepted by learned authorities such as Devala and others on the basis of the aspect of the pre-existence of the effect, it is taught due to its strength.
The intention is that the theories of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth are not extended [to the Vedānta] because they are weak, being devoid of any scriptural foundation.
He says "because of equality" (*tulyatvāt*) to show that there is no need to ask what the reason for the refutation is.
He states the very reason: "it is equal" (*tulyam*).
As for what was said—that Brahman is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of substances because of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*)—[the same logic applies].
In this regard, it should be understood that there is a sublation by Śruti because it is that upon which the Smṛti depends for establishing its own position;
furthermore, the possession of great magnitude—that is, omnipresence consisting in conjunction with all things—is not established in Brahman, which is devoid of qualities.
Therefore, it is proven that there is no contradiction of the doctrine of *samanvaya* (harmonious convergence) by the logic of the logicians. //12//
END BsCom_2,1.4.12 START BsCom_2,1.5.13 5.
The Section Concerning the Attainment of the Enjoyer (Bhoktrāpatti-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 13.
If it be argued that there is no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman] because of the soul's becoming the enjoyer [of the fruits of action], it would be as in the world.
Otherwise, however, the doctrine that Brahman is the cause would be refuted by the force of reasoning alone.

Even though scripture is authoritative regarding its own subject matter, nevertheless, when its subject matter is sublated by another means of knowledge, it must be understood as having a different purport.
Just as it is with mantra and arthavāda,
so too reasoning (tarka) would be non-conclusive regarding anything other than its own specific domain, such as in the case of dharma and adharma.
What follows if this is so?
Therefore, this is improper: that the Śruti should subvert an object established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
But how can an object established by another means of valid cognition be subverted by the Śruti?

To this it is replied: For this distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is well-known in the world; the enjoyer is the conscious embodied self (śārīra), and the objects of enjoyment are the sense-objects such as sound and the rest.
Just as Devadatta is the eater and the rice is the food,
the non-existence of that distinction would follow if the eater were to undergo the state of being the food,
or if the food were to undergo the state of being the eater.
Otherwise, it would follow that the two attain a state of mutual identity because they are non-different from Brahman, the supreme cause;
yet, it is not proper to subvert this well-known distinction.
Just as the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is observed in the present, so too must it be postulated for the past and the future.

If someone should object, "Therefore, because this well-known distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed would result in non-existence, this determination that Brahman is the cause is untenable," one should reply to him: "It may be so, as in the world.
This distinction is indeed possible even in our view, because it is observed thus in the world.

For instance, although the foam, waves, ripples, and so forth—which are modifications of water—are not different from the ocean which is of the nature of water, a worldly transaction characterized by their mutual distinction and mutual conjunction is nevertheless perceived.
Furthermore, although the foam, waves, and other transformations are non-different from the ocean which consists of water, they do not undergo mutual transformation into one another;
nor, even though they do not undergo mutual transformation, do they become different from the nature of the ocean.
In the same way here as well, there is no mutual transformation between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
And there will be no otherness from the Supreme Brahman;
even though the enjoyer is not a modification of Brahman, [it is said]:
"Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).
Thus, since it is heard that the unmodified Creator himself becomes the enjoyer by entering into his own effects,

nevertheless, for him who has entered into the effect, there exists a distinction caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as there is for space caused by limiting adjuncts such as jars; therefore, even though non-difference from the Supreme Cause, Brahman, is established, the distinction characterized as the enjoyer and the enjoyed is also logically consistent.
It has been stated that this is according to the analogy of the waves of the ocean and so forth. [Note:
"Being directed toward something else" means having a secondary (figurative) sense;
"division" means birth. // 13 //
Alternatively, the refutation has already been stated by the word "even so" (*tathāpi*).
The subject matter is the Vedāntic harmony (*samanvaya*) which teaches that the world-creation and so forth proceed from the non-dual Brahman.
Is it the case that whatever is mutually distinct is not non-different from the non-dual cause, as in the case of a jar and a cloth produced from clay and thread respectively?

In the doubt as to whether [the non-duality of Brahman] is contradicted by perception of difference accompanied by reasoning (*tarka*) or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) asserts that it is indeed contradicted—despite reasoning being unestablished with respect to Brahman—because it is established with respect to the difference in the world; this is expressed in the sūtra: "Because of the attainment of the enjoyer" (*bhokrāpatter*). The result of the prima facie view is the failure to establish non-duality due to such contradiction.
The distinction is that in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that [truth] is established.

An objection is raised—beginning with "Even though"—that since the determination of the meaning of the scriptures occurs through independent revelation (*anapekṣa-śruti*), it is not proper to challenge it by means of reasoning (*tarka*). [The response is:
There is indeed no such challenge regarding the meaning of scripture when that meaning is inaccessible to other means of knowledge (*māna*).

He provides the following resolution: "Even so," etc. He argues that the non-difference of earth, water, and so forth from Brahman—which is due to their non-difference from the non-dual Brahman and which is the subject of the scriptural texts concerning Brahman as the material cause—is sublated by the means of knowledge establishing duality, because it is just like the meaning of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) "The sacrificial post is the sun," which is susceptible to other means of knowledge.
"Having another purpose" means having a figurative sense.

Since reasoning (*tarka*) is established regarding the differentiation of the world within its own domain, [the opponent] asserts that there is an objection based on that; thus he says, "Reasoning also...
[The opponent] raises a doubt: "What follows from this? even though reasoning and the like possess authority regarding duality?
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies: "From this... [it follows].

The meaning is that since reasoning (*tarka*) and other means of knowledge possess validity, it is improper for the Śruti to sublate duality; therefore, it is logical that the non-dual harmony (*advaita-samanvaya*) is sublated.
He clarifies this point by first raising an objection with the words "How? and so forth.

Anticipating the objection—"But by whom was the mutual identity of the enjoyer and the enjoyed ever stated?"—he says "Of those two" (*tayośca*), [indicating] that it is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the Śruti.
Because it is heard that those two are non-different from the one Brahman, their identity is postulated;
for if there were difference between two things that are non-different from one and the same thing, even that one thing would necessarily result in being different.
Therefore, the meaning is that difference would be sublated.
He rules out the acceptance of this [consequence] with the words "na cāsya" (nor of this).

The meaning is that since the Śruti has room for interpretation by virtue of its figurative sense, it is not proper for it to sublate the non-figurative, non-contingent authority of the non-duality [scriptures].
To the objection—namely, that because the division [of the self and the world] is recent, it is sublated by the non-dual Śruti which concerns the beginningless [reality]—he says "yathā" (just as).

The meaning is that the distinction [between the enjoyer and so forth] is beginningless and endless, because of the following inference: "Past and future times are the substrata for the distinctions such as the enjoyer, because they are time, like the present time."
This being the case, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) at first sight by means of the analogy of transformation (*pariṇāma*): "It would be as in the world" (*syāl lokavat*).

Anticipating the objection—namely, how there can be mutual difference among transformations that are non-different from a single ocean, or conversely, how they can be non-different from that one despite their difference—he replies with the principle: "For there is no impossibility in what is observed" (*na ca dṛṣṭenupapattiḥ*), saying: "And not... (*na ca...*).

Thus, he states that there is a mutual difference between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, yet non-difference from Brahman, with the words "In this way, here... He raises an objection regarding the disparity of the illustration, on the grounds that the individual soul (jīva) is not a modification (vikāra) of Brahman, with the words "Even though...
He then asserts the similarity to waves and so forth by noting that birth exists as something conditioned (aupādhika), with the words "Nevertheless..."
"Division" means birth;
or rather, the solution has already been stated by the word "even so" (tathāpi).
To the question, "How can there be a division of the enjoyer in each body?", he says: "of that which has entered into the effect."
He concludes the result regarding division based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-vibhāga) with the words "ityata" (therefore).

The meaning is that even though the enjoyer and so forth are non-different from the one Brahman, since difference is admitted—just as in the case of waves and the like—there is no contradiction of the monistic synthesis (advaita-samanvaya) by the evidence of duality. //13//
END BsCom_2,1.5.13 START BsCom_2,1.6.14 6.
The Section Concerning the Origin (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 14–20.
"The non-difference of that [the effect] from that [the cause] follows from such words as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa) and others.
Having provisionally accepted this conventional distinction characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the refutation was stated as 'it would be as in the world.
However, this distinction does not exist in the ultimate sense, because the non-difference of those two—the effect and the cause—is understood."
The effect is the world, consisting of manifold elaborations such as space and so forth;
the cause is the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, it is understood that from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is non-difference from that cause, meaning the effect has no existence apart from it.
Why?
Because of the words concerning "clinging" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.
First, there is the word concerning "clinging."

Having asserted that through the knowledge of one [thing] there is the knowledge of all, and in view of the need for an illustration, it is said: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the reality is simply 'clay'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1).

This is what is meant: when a single lump of clay is known in its ultimate sense as having the nature of clay, everything made of clay—such as jars, bowls, and water-pots—becomes known, because there is no difference in their being essentially clay.

For whatever modification there is, beginning with the mere verbal undertaking— that it exists— is merely a name consisting of speech alone, such as "pot," "bowl," or "water-jar. In reality, however, no such thing as a modification exists at all.
"For this is merely a name; it is unreal. 'Only clay is real'—this is the illustration taught regarding Brahman.
From the word *vācārambhaṇa* heard there, it is understood that even in the case of the illustrated subject (the dārṣṭāntika), the entire aggregate of effects has no existence apart from Brahman.
Furthermore, having stated that fire, water, and food are the effects of Brahman, the text declares that the effects of fire, water, and food do not exist apart from fire, water, and food itself:
"The fire-nature of fire has departed; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the three forms alone are real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1), and so forth.

From the phrase "from the word *ārambhaṇa* and others," the word "others" includes such passages as: "All this has that as its essence; that is the Truth, that is the Self; thou art That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7);
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6);
and "All this is indeed Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).

Furthermore, one should cite the collection of scriptural passages intended to establish the oneness of the Self, such as "The Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2) and "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).
And otherwise, the knowledge of all things through the knowledge of one would not be possible.

Therefore, just as the spaces within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth are non-different from the great space (mahākāśa), and just as the water of a mirage and the like are non-different from the saline soil and so forth—because their nature is seen and then lost, and because they cannot be defined by way of their own intrinsic nature; |||
Thus, it should be understood that this entire manifold of objects of enjoyment, enjoyers, and so forth, has no existence apart from Brahman.
Now, one might object: Brahman is multiform;
just as a tree possesses many branches, so too Brahman is endowed with the activity of manifold powers (*śakti*).
Therefore, both unity and plurality are indeed real.

Just as there is non-unity in the sense of "tree" and plurality in the sense of "branches," and just as there is unity in the nature of the ocean and plurality in the nature of foam, waves, and so forth.
Just as there is oneness in its nature as clay and plurality in its forms as jars, bowls, and so forth,

so too will the worldly and Vedic practices based on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) be established through the aspect of plurality, while the practice of liberation through knowledge will be established through the aspect of oneness.
And thus, the analogies of clay and so forth will be appropriate;
however, this would not be the case, because in the analogy, truthfulness is determined to belong to the material cause alone, as stated in the words: "Only 'clay' is real."
Furthermore, because the phrase "a mere beginning in speech" (vācārambhaṇa) declares that the entire collection of modifications is unreal;

and because, in the case of the illustrative example as well, the text—"All this has that as its self; that is the Truth"—determines that the single supreme cause alone is real; and because the text—"That is the Self; thou art That, O Śvetaketu"—teaches the identity of the embodied soul with Brahman.
For this identity of the body with Brahman is taught as something already self-evident, not as something to be accomplished through further effort.

Therefore, this scriptural realization of the identity with Brahman becomes the sublater of the natural notion of being the embodied self, just as the cognitions of a rope and so forth sublate the cognitions of a snake and so forth.

And once the identity of the embodied self [with Brahman] is sublated, all its natural worldly activity based upon that identity is likewise sublated; it is for the sake of establishing such activity that another aspect of difference is postulated in Brahman.
Furthermore, Scripture shows this:
"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
By such statements as these, [the text] declares the non-existence of the entire empirical transaction— characterized by action, agent, and fruit— for one who perceives Brahman as the Self.
Nor is it proper to say that this absence of empirical transaction is restricted to a particular state [of life],
because the identity of Brahman and the Self expressed in "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is not dependent upon any particular state.

By means of the illustration of the thieves, [the text] shows the bondage of one who intends falsehood and the liberation of one who intends truth, thereby demonstrating that oneness alone is the single ultimate reality (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16).
Diversity, moreover, is a manifestation of false knowledge;
for if both were real, how could a living being, even while engaged in the sphere of empirical activity, be said to "intend falsehood"?
