And by refuting the perception of difference in the passage, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19), [the scripture] demonstrates this very point;
moreover, in such a view, it is not logically tenable that liberation results from knowledge.
This is because no false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) that is to be dispelled by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is accepted as being the cause of saṃsāra.
For if both [unity and diversity] were real, how could it be said that the cognition of diversity is dispelled by the cognition of unity?

[Objection: But surely, if one accepts the absolute unity [of all things], then worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be contradicted because they would lack an object (*nirviṣayatvāt*), since diversity would not exist.
Just as cognitions such as that of a person arise with respect to a post and so forth,

so too the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions, being dependent upon duality, would be contradicted in the absence of that [duality]; likewise, the scripture concerning liberation, being dependent upon the distinction between the disciple, the teacher, and so forth, would also suffer contradiction in the absence of that [distinction].
And how can the truth of the oneness of the Self, as propounded by a scripture of liberation that is itself false, be established?
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because all worldly transactions are indeed established as true prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self.
It is like the conduct in a dream prior to awakening.

For as long as there is no realization of the oneness of the true Self, no one can conceive of the unreality of those modifications characterized by the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results.
Indeed, abandoning its natural state of being the Self that is Brahman, every living being perceives only these modifications through ignorance, in the form of "I" and "mine," as belonging to itself.
Therefore, prior to the awakening to the Self as Brahman, all worldly and Vedic activity is entirely tenable.

Just as for an ordinary person who has fallen asleep and is seeing various high and low objects in a dream, there arises a cognition that is certainly regarded as direct perception before waking, and at that time there is no intention that it is a mere semblance of perception; so it is in this case.
But how can the realization of the true identity of Brahman as the Self be established by means of an untrue Vedāntic statement?
For one does not die from being bitten by a rope-snake,
nor is the purpose of drinking or bathing accomplished by the water of a mirage.
This is not a fault,
because effects such as death are observed to be caused by the poison of fear and the like,
and because effects such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water are observed in one who is in the state of dreaming.
If it should be argued that its effects are likewise unreal,

we reply: although the effects— such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water— experienced by one in the state of dreaming are unreal, nevertheless, the cognition of them is indeed a real fruit, because it remains unsublated even for one who has awakened.

For no one who has awakened from a dream, considering the effects seen in the dream—such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water—to be false, would also consider the cognition of those effects to be false.
By this non-sublation of the cognition of the dreamer, the doctrine that the body alone is the self should be understood as refuted.
And so says the Śruti: "When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for desired objects..."
"In that dream-vision one should recognize prosperity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.9);
thus, [the text] shows the attainment of true prosperity through an unreal dream-vision.
Likewise, when certain ill omens are perceived by direct observation, one should know: "He will not live much longer."
Having said this, he shows that by means of various such unreal dream-visions—such as "Now, if one sees a man who is black with black teeth, he kills him"—true death is indicated.

And this is well known in the world to those skilled in the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): by such a dream-vision, the arrival of good fortune is indicated; by such [another], the arrival of misfortune.
Likewise, the comprehension of the true letters such as *ka* and so forth is seen to arise from the comprehension of the false letters represented by lines.
Furthermore, this final means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishes the oneness of the Self; beyond this, nothing further remains to be expected.

For just as in the world, when it is said "one should sacrifice," there is an expectation of "what [is sacrificed]," "by what [means]," and "how," it is not so when it is said "That thou art" or "I am Brahman"—nothing else remains to be expected.
This is because the realization has as its object the oneness of the self of all.
For if there were any remaining object [after this realization], there would be a desire for further knowledge;
however, apart from the oneness of the self, there is no other remaining object that could be desired.
Nor can it be said that this comprehension is not possible,
because of such scriptural passages as, "He understood that from him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.3).
Furthermore, because there are injunctions for the means of realization— such as hearing [the scriptures] (śravaṇa) and so forth, as well as the recitation of the Vedas (vedānuvacana) and so forth—
it cannot be said that this realization is purposeless or erroneous,
since its fruit is seen to be the cessation of ignorance (avidyā).

Furthermore, because there is no other subverting cognition [to contradict it], we have already stated that prior to the realization of the oneness of the Self, the entire worldly and Vedic discourse concerning truth and falsehood proceeds unimpeded. Therefore, once the oneness of the Self has been established by the final means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), all previous discourse based on duality is sublated; consequently, there is no room for the postulation of a Brahman consisting of multiple selves.

Objection: Is it not understood from the presentation of examples such as clay that the Śāstra intends Brahman to be subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*), for in the world, objects such as clay are known to be transformable? Reply: No, it is said.
"Verily, this great person is the Self—undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25);
"This very Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26);
"Neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).

Because Brahman is understood to be immutable from such scriptural passages as those which prohibit all modifications, it is not possible to maintain that the one Brahman possesses both the property of transformation and its absence; for [these two] cannot coexist in a single entity. If it be argued that this could be like the case of standing and moving, we say no.
Because of the qualification "of the immutable" (kūṭasthasya). For it is not possible for the immutable Brahman to be the substratum of manifold attributes such as staying and moving;
and we have already stated that Brahman is immutable and eternal because all modifications are denied of it.

Nor is it intended that the vision of Brahman as undergoing transformation into the form of the world should, like the vision of the oneness of the Self with Brahman, be a means to liberation independently for some specific fruit;
for there is a lack of authoritative evidence.

Indeed, the scripture shows that the fruit results solely from the knowledge of the Self as the immutable Brahman, beginning with "This is the Self, not this, not this" and concluding, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
Such is the nature of this [argument].

In this regard, the following is established: since the attainment of the fruit is accomplished solely through the vision of Brahman—which is devoid of all specific attributes—as taught in the context of Brahman (brahmaprakaraṇa), whatever is heard there that is not itself a fruit, such as Brahman’s transformation into the form of the world and so forth, is employed exclusively as a means for that vision of Brahman.
Just as it is said that "that which is without fruit in the proximity of that which has fruit is a subordinate part [of it]," it is not to be conceived as an independent means for attaining a result.
For it is not reasonable to say that from the knowledge of the Self's possessing transformation, the possession of transformation by the Self would be the resulting fruit.

If it is argued that because liberation is unchangingly eternal, there can be no relationship between a ruler and the ruled for one who maintains the doctrine of the identity of the Self with the unchanging Brahman— and thus there would be a contradiction with the scriptural proposition that God is the cause— [we reply]: No,
for omniscience depends upon the manifestation of the seeds of name and form, which are of the nature of ignorance.

From such scriptural passages as, "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), the following meaning has been proposed [in the Sūtra]: "The origin, etc., of this [world] proceed from that [Brahman]"— namely, that the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe proceed from the Lord, who is omniscient and omnipotent, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, and not from the non-intelligent Pradhāna or any other cause.
That proposition remains exactly as it was; no meaning contrary to it is stated here again.
How could it not be stated, given that the absolute oneness and non-duality of the Self are being asserted?
Listen to how it is not so stated: Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),

which are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), which are as if constitutive of the omniscient Lord, which are indefinable as being either identical to or different from reality, and which serve as the seed for the manifold world (*saṃsāra-prapañca*), are designated in the Śruti and Smṛti as the "illusory power" (*māyā-śakti*) and the "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) of the omniscient Lord.

The Omniscient Lord is distinct from those two, according to the Śruti: "That which is called space is indeed the evolver of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1);
and "Let me evolve name and form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), and "Having fashioned all forms and made names, the Wise One sits calling [them by those names]" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).
And from such scriptural passages as, "He who makes the one seed manifold" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.12),
the Lord becomes subject to the limiting adjuncts of name and form created by ignorance.
Like the ether, it conforms to limiting adjuncts such as jars and water-pots.

And that [Supreme Self] grants the status of being called "individual souls" (*jīva*)—which are conscious selves (*vijñānātman*) conforming to the aggregates of effects and instruments (the body and organs) produced by name-and-form presented by ignorance—to those very things that are its own self, standing in the place of the ether within a jar, for the sake of empirical usage.
Thus, the Lord’s status as Lord, His omniscience, and His omnipotence depend entirely upon the limitation imposed by adjuncts consisting of ignorance.

Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), no conventional discourse regarding a controller and the controlled, or omniscience and the like, is tenable in the case of the Self whose nature is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Thus it has been said: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūmā*)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1);
and likewise, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
And so on.
Thus, all the Vedāntas declare that in the state of ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is an absence of all conventional transactions (vyavahāra).
Likewise, in the *Īśvaragītā* as well: "The Lord does not create agency nor actions for the world..."
The connection with the fruit of action does not proceed from intrinsic nature.
"The Lord does not take on the sin of anyone, nor indeed their merit;
knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that living beings are deluded" (Gītā 5.14–15).
Thus, it is demonstrated that in the state of ultimate reality, there is an absence of conventional designations such as the ruler and the ruled.

However, even in the Śruti, the conventional usage of terms such as "Lord" (Īśvara) is stated in the context of worldly discourse: "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Likewise, it is said in the Īśvaragītā: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings."
"By means of Māyā, He causes all beings, mounted upon a machine, to whirl around" (Gītā 18.61).
The author of the Sūtras also, with the ultimate truth in mind, states that [the individual soul] is different from That;
however, with a view toward conventional usage, he says "it may be as in the world," thereby describing Brahman as being like the great ocean.

Without rejecting the manifoldness of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) and resorting to the process of transformation (*pariṇāmaprakriyā*), [the author] relies on it because it will be useful for the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*).

[Note: The connection is as follows: that which is "seen" means empirical; "perished" means impermanent; and since its own nature (*svarūpa*) is thus indescribable and devoid of existence and manifestation (*sattāsphūrti*), it is "non-different.
Here, "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); that which is produced by it is "natural" (*svābhāvika*).
The absolute state of oneness is isolation (*kaivalya*). [If it were otherwise,] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be contradicted; truth consists in the absence of sublation (*bādhā*).
The refutation is the certainty that [the letters] are unreal.
It is well known that through the illusion of lines having the form of the letter *a* and so forth, real *a*s and other letters are perceived.

Regarding the very first prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the primary resolution by means of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*): "In that case, there is non-difference."

Stating that the two refutations share the same subject matter (*samānaviṣayatva*) as their point of connection (*saṃgati*), he explains the difference in meaning between them based on their respective foundations in *pariṇāma* (transformation) and *vivarta* (illusory appearance), saying "having admitted" (*abhyupagamya*).

Having accepted the inherent validity (*utsargikaprāmāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge, the existence of both difference and non-difference were stated by means of the analogy of transformation for the sake of satisfying those of dull intellect;
now, that very accepted validity [is being examined].
The sense is that [the non-dual scripture] is established as being of a conventional nature by being removed from the status of revealing ultimate reality;
thus, there is no sublation of the non-dual scripture by the means of knowledge that apprehend the duality of illusion,
because one perceives a duality such as a staff or a garland in a single rope— this is the primary resolution.
Thus, in order to establish that there is no contradiction with the non-dual synthesis (*advaita-samanvaya*), he proves the falsity of duality [with the words] "because of those two.
Since the identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) would contradict the relationship of cause and effect, he says: "by way of distinction" (*vyatirekeṇa*).
The meaning is that what is being established is the effect's lack of existence apart from the cause, not their identity.

He applies the Śruti by stating "this has been said," explaining that the meaning of the particle *eva* is that speech is a mere name, a modification (*vikāra*), and does not exist apart from its cause.
He states another meaning for the word *ārambhaṇa* with the words "furthermore":
"the nature of fire has departed" means it has gone away because it is nothing but the cause.
It is true that the three forms of fire, water, and earth consist of the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra);
since even these are merely Being (sat-mātra), the intention is that "Being alone remains.
He says, "And not otherwise," meaning that if the individual soul (jīva) and the source of the world (gati) were different from Brahman, the initial proposition would be contradicted.
To demonstrate their non-difference through a sequence of examples, he says: "Therefore, just as...
The meaning is: by the force of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

The connection is as follows: that which is seen—that is, perceived—and which has perished—that is, is impermanent—is non-different from its own nature (*svarūpa*), because it is indefinable (*anupākhyatva*) in that form, being devoid of existence and manifestation (*sattāsphūrtiśūnyatva*).
Having stated his own doctrine of pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*), he raises the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) with the words "Now, [is it not the case]...":
the meaning is that [Brahman] is endowed with manifold powers (*śakti*) and their dependent primordial natures (*prakṛti*), as well as their transformations (*pariṇāma*).

Anticipating the objection that in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference all established order is secured, whereas absolute non-difference would subvert the means of knowledge for duality, he refutes it with: "It could not be so."

The meaning is that because the existence of modifications is negated by the word "only" (*eva*) and by the phrase "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is outside the scope of the Śruti.

Furthermore, if transmigratory existence were real, there could be no instruction regarding the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is characterized by that [existence], with Brahman, due to their contradiction; thus he says, "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*).

Anticipating the objection that this unity is to be accomplished through the combination of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*) for the sake of instruction, he says, "Himself" (*svayam*), because such a view would contradict the word "art" (*asi*).
Therefore, he says "and thus" (*ataśca*) to show that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is false because it is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
The meaning is: "because of the teaching established by itself.
As for what was stated—that plurality is real for the sake of conventional usage—[that is addressed here].
Is that [conventional reality] subsequent to knowledge for the sake of worldly transaction, or prior to it?
It is not the first case; thus he says: "And when sublated.
Here, "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) refers to ignorance; that which is produced by it is "intrinsic" (svābhāvika).
The meaning is that since the conventional usage of "subject" (*pramātṛ*) and so forth does not exist after [the attainment of] knowledge, multiplicity (*nānātva*) is not to be postulated.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for if conventional usage is established by means of a multiplicity postulated prior to knowledge, the reality of that multiplicity remains unproven.
As for the claim that the conventional usage of "knower" and so forth is indeed real and merely ceases in the state of liberation—that is not so; he says, "And this [is not so]...
For if transmigratory existence were real, the soul's identity with Brahman would not occur in that state.

Because difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same place at the same time, the meaning is that since the non-difference of Brahman from the transmigrating soul is understood to be eternal, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) must also be merely illusory.
Furthermore, just as in the world, if someone seized by soldiers on the suspicion of being a thief takes up a heated axe while speaking falsely, he is burned and bound; [so too is the case here].

Thus, one who asserts multiplicity is consumed by fire, whereas one who speaks the truth is not consumed and is liberated. Likewise, one who perceives oneness—realizing "all this has that as its self"—is liberated. Based on this scriptural illustration, he states "taskara... [and so forth], asserting that oneness is the truth and multiplicity is false. The sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is the basis for the conventional usage of multiplicity.
By censuring plurality, he states that unity alone is the truth: "From death...

Furthermore, in this view of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), liberation is held to result from the cessation of the cognition of difference through the knowledge of the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman; however, that is not tenable, because it is not admitted that the cognition of difference is an error (*bhrama*).
He states "and not in this [case]" because one valid cognition is not sublated by another valid cognition;
the implication is that the opposite could also be possible.

Now, he uncovers the seed of the prima facie argument—that the reality of manifoldness follows from the otherwise inexplicability of the validity of perception and so forth—beginning with "But surely," and so on.
The absolute oneness of unity is isolation (*kaivalya*). [If it were otherwise,] the means of valid cognition would be contradicted and rendered invalid.
The sense is that, for the sake of the validity of perception and other means upon which [the Vedāntas] depend, it is appropriate that the Vedāntas intend both difference and non-difference.

An objection might be raised: "Since the ritual (karma) and knowledge (jñāna) sections proceed by relying on an imagined distinction between the agents of action—such as the sacrificer—and the agents of knowledge—such as the disciple—their authority remains unimpaired because their own objects of cognition, such as dharma, are not sublated. Anticipating this, he says: "And how [could it be so] by means of the unreal? The sense is that there would result a sublation of the object of cognition, just as fire inferred from smoke imagined in dust is sublated.

In that regard, he states with the words "To this it is replied," etc., that in the domain of duality, the empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge is established as long as there is no sublation (*bādha*).
Truth (*satyatva*) is the absence of sublation;
sublation is the ascertainment of falsity (*mithyātva-niścaya*).

In reality, although [the world] is false, because there is no certainty of that falsity regarding modifications (vikāra), the operation of perception and other means of knowledge is possible; thus he explains the aforementioned example: "Just as for an ordinary person who has fallen asleep.

Having thus established the empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) of the means of dualistic cognition—that they convey objects free from sublation at the time of worldly transaction—he restates the objection in order to establish the ultimate validity (*tāttvika-prāmāṇya*) of the Vedāntas, which are the means of dualistic cognition, namely that they convey Brahman, which is free from sublation at all times: "But how [can it be so] by means of the unreal? etc.
Is it that truth does not arise from the unreal, or rather that there is no knowledge of the real?
In the first case, this is indeed accepted.
We do not maintain that the knowledge arising from words is itself real;
even granting that [such knowledge is real], he states the example: "This is not a fault.

The meaning is that there is no fixed rule that truth cannot arise from untruth, because we observe the occurrence of actual death, fainting, and so forth, caused by poison imagined through the delusion of being bitten by a snake, even when one has not been bitten by a snake at all.
He states another example with the words "In a dream," etc.

The meaning is that there is a deviation [from the rule], because from unreal things such as a snake or its belly, one observes an effect which is a real cognition, such as the knowledge of being bitten or bathing.
Taking the literal sense [of the opponent's argument], he raises an objection: "That effect also... and so forth.
He clarifies the point already stated with the words "In this regard, we say," and so forth.

"Cognition" (*avagati*) is the mental modification (*vṛtti*); or, even though it is real like a jar and the like, the meaning of the word "cognition" is consciousness (*caitanya*) manifested by the modification, which is the fruit of an object perceived in a dream that is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*).
He states "by this" (*etena*), indicating that by this [argument], the doctrine of the body being the self (*dehātmavāda*) has also been refuted as a matter of course.

If the cognition occurring while in a dream were a property of the dream-body, then upon waking, there would be no recollection of the uncontradicted cognition in the form, "I experienced such a dream.
Therefore, since we observe such recollection despite the difference in bodies, the meaning is that the one who recollects is other than the body.
Regarding the second rule—that knowledge of the real does not arise from the unreal—the author states that there is an exception to this by scripture: "And so says the Śruti."

Nor should it be argued that, even though women are false, knowledge of a true accomplishment arises from seeing them because they are themselves real; for the reason is that the vision itself is false by virtue of being qualified by its object, and thus in the present case as well, knowledge is possible through consciousness associated with the false Vedas, even though Brahman is real. Having stated that knowledge of a desired truth can arise from the untrue, he now states that knowledge of the undesired also arises: "In the same way," etc.
Regarding the cognition of the real from the unreal, he provides another illustration: "likewise, the letter 'A' and so forth.
The meaning is that it is well known that the real letters 'A' and so forth are cognized through the error of [perceiving] lines as having the form of the letter 'A' and so forth.
Thus, by stating that the real arises from the unreal, the rule that "that which performs a purposeful action (arthakriyā) is real" is refuted.

By stating that truth is known through untruth, the following pervasion (*vyāpti*) is destroyed: "That which is accessible through the production of untruth is sublated, like fire inferred from a counterfeit mark.
Thus, the sense is that even though the Vedāntas are imagined, their capacity to bring about the knowledge of the true Brahman is possible; therefore, they possess ultimate validity (*prāmāṇya*).
As for what was said—that both [unity and diversity] are real for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of unity and plurality—that is not so.
Because it is impossible to conceive of the reality of a difference that is established by worldly consensus as being in contradiction with a non-difference that possesses an unprecedented fruit;
furthermore, if the practical usage of both were to occur simultaneously, then their reality might indeed be possible,
but such is not the case.

He says, "Moreover, the final [cognition]," because unity, being independent, completely sublates plurality through its finality, just as the cognition of mother-of-pearl sublates the [appearance of] silver.

To the objection that the realization of unity does not arise due to conflict with the non-dualistic means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) upon which it depends, he replies, "And this [realization] is not..."

The meaning is that Śvetaketu indeed understood the reality of the Self from the words of his father, because the arising of knowledge is heard [in scripture] and because the causal conditions were present. Relying upon the conventional distinction between teacher and disciple and so forth, the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence being known depends upon the conventional validity residing in perception and other means of knowledge;
and that is not contradicted by the realization of ultimate oneness.

However, the sense is that because of its contradiction with that [non-dual realization], the ontological validity of perception and other means of knowledge—which cannot otherwise be sustained—is sublated.
Furthermore, since the cognition of oneness possesses the status of a fruitful valid cognition (*pramā*), the fruitless delusion of duality must be sublated; thus he says, "And this [cognition]...
Now, if all duality were false, how would worldly transactions such as "the dream was false, the waking state is true" be possible?

Anticipating the objection— "How can the Vedic statement 'Truth and falsehood both became truth' be justified?"— he recalls the previously mentioned analogy of a dream, stating that "just as in a dream there is the conventional usage of 'this is true' and 'this is false' based on temporary sublation or non-sublation, so it is also in this long dream. This is what is meant by "prāk ca" (and previously).
He concludes that the conceptualization of multiplicity as being real for the sake of conventional usage is inconsistent, stating "therefore" (tasmāt).
He raises an objection, suggesting that this is not merely imagined but is indeed heard in scripture, stating "but surely" (nanu).

He provides the rebuttal— “It is said: No”— to show that this illustration applies to the aspect of the non-difference between cause and effect, and not to the quality of being subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva), because that would contradict the scriptural texts concerning the immutability (kūṭasthatva) of Brahman.

He raises an objection by means of an illustration, stating "sthitau" (in the state of persistence), suggesting that being subject to transformation during creation and its absence during dissolution are not contradictory when considered sequentially.
He replies with "no," stating that for that which is immutable (*kūṭastha*), any modification at any time is untenable, because it would contradict its very nature as immutable.
Anticipating the objection that its immutability is unproven, he says "of the immutable."

The point is that because it is impossible for the immutable (kūṭastha) and partless [Brahman] to undergo transformation (pariṇāma) consisting of a change of state by abandoning its prior nature, the phenomenal world (prapañca) is merely an illusory manifestation (vivarta), like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Furthermore, since the fruitless world is mentioned as being subordinate to the knowledge of the fruit-bearing, non-phenomenal Brahman, it is not real; this he states with the words "nor as... and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that—based on the scriptural text, "In whatever way one meditates upon Him, that very thing one becomes"—the fruit for the knower is the attainment of Brahman through the realization of Brahman's capacity for transformation—he replies: "For [it is] not... due to possessing transformation," and so on.

The meaning is that since the possibility of the fruit of liberation—which is immutably eternal—has been established by the Śruti text, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it is illogical to conceive of a fruit characterized by suffering, impermanence, and transformation.

Now, an objection is raised: previously, in the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," a proposition was made regarding God as the cause; now, in establishing non-difference through the concluding statement "the non-difference from That," there would be a contradiction because of the absence of the distinction between the ruler and the ruled. Thus he says: "Kūṭastha... (immutably eternal).
He states the absence of contradiction—through the words beginning with "no"—that while lordship and so forth exist in relation to imagined duality, in the ultimate sense there is non-difference.

The meaning is that name and form, which constitute ignorance, are merged within the conscious Self; their "unfolding" is creation in its gross form, and since lordship and the like depend upon that [unfolding], there is no contradiction.
He explains the summarized meaning through the words beginning with "therefore."
Regarding the phrase "by way of identity or difference":
it is impossible to assert that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) possess the nature of the Lord (īśvara), because they are insentient;
nor can they be different from the Lord, because that which is imagined lacks both independent existence and independent manifestation. This is the meaning.

He says "māyā" with the intention of expressing the identity of ignorance (*avidyā*) with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which consist of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). If name-and-form were the very self of the Lord, then the Lord would be insentient; therefore, he says "different from those two. Regarding this difference and his manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*), he cites scripture beginning with "ether" (*ākāśa*).

He states that, through the distinction imagined by limiting adjuncts such as ignorance (avidyā), the one occupying the position of the original image (bimba) possesses the nature of the Lord (īśvara), while those who are reflections (pratibimba)—the individual souls (jīvas)—possess the nature of being governed; thus he says, "And He [governs] those who are His own self. Furthermore, one should not be deluded into thinking that multiple individual souls are mentioned here in the Bhāṣya.
Because difference is taught through the distinction between the aggregate of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth;
however, it has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is one alone as a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*).
To cite scripture regarding the absence of duality such as "Lordship" (*īśvaratva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he says: "And thus... (*tathā ca*).
To the question, "How then [is there] agency and so forth?", he says: "But its own nature...
The meaning is that beginningless ignorance itself functions in the form of agency and the rest.
Regarding the claim that the Lord possesses real lordship because He destroys the sins and merits of the devotee and the non-devotee respectively, he says: "He does not take [it]..."
The meaning is that it does not withdraw [the self].
Because of that obscuration of the knowledge of one's own true nature, people wander in delusion, thinking: "I am the agent," "I am the Lord," or "He is my controller.
To show that the stated meaning is approved by the author of the Sūtras, he says: "The author of the Sūtras also... [sūtrakāro 'pīti].

The transformational process (*pariṇāma-prakriyā*) is not resorted to merely for the sake of worldly convention, but also for the purpose of meditative worship (*upāsanā*); thus he says, "and the transformational process. As it has been said: "One whose mind is wretched perceives transformation; but one whose intellect has destroyed its impurities perceives illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). //14//
And because [the object] is perceived when there is existence. (2.1.15)
For this reason as well, the effect is non-different from the cause:
because the effect is perceived only when the cause exists, and not when it does not exist.
For example, a jar is perceived when clay exists, and a cloth when threads exist.

Furthermore, it is not observed as a rule that the perception of one thing occurs only when another thing is present; for instance, although a horse is different from a cow, it is not perceived only when the cow is present,
nor is a jar perceived only when the potter is present.
Even though there exists a relationship between cause and effect, [the two] are distinct entities.
Now, is it not observed that the perception of one thing is necessarily contingent upon the existence of another, as in the case of smoke when fire exists?
This is not so;
for even when the fire has been extinguished, smoke is observed coming from things such as cowherds' huts.
Alternatively, one might qualify the smoke by its particular state, saying that "such smoke does not exist in the absence of fire."
Even so, there is no fault whatsoever; for we state that the cause for the non-difference between cause and effect is the intellect (buddhi) being colored by the existence of that [effect].
And this [coloring] does not exist in the case of fire and smoke.
Or rather, the aphorism may be read as: "And because it is perceived through its existence."
The meaning is that the non-difference between cause and effect is established not only by the word [of scripture], but also because of the existence of direct perception;
for there exists a direct perception of the non-difference between cause and effect.

For example, in the case of a cloth formed by the arrangement of threads, no effect called "cloth" is perceived apart from the threads; rather, only the threads themselves, possessing lengthwise and crosswise extensions (*ātāna-vitāna*), are perceived through direct perception.
Likewise, there are fibers within the threads, and the parts of those fibers within the fibers.
From this direct perception of the three colors—red, white, and black—it is to be inferred that there is merely air and merely space.
Beyond that is Brahman alone, without a second; regarding this, we have already stated that all means of valid knowledge find their ultimate rest. 15.
FN: The meaning of the sūtra is that because the effect exists and is perceived when the cause exists and is perceived, there is non-difference [of the effect] from [the cause].
Thus, having resolved the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding that non-difference, he states the inference: "And when [the cause] exists," etc.
The meaning of the sūtra is that because the effect exists and is perceived when the cause exists and is perceived, there is non-difference [of the effect] from [the cause].
The pot is non-different from the clay, because its existence and perception are necessarily restricted to the existence and perception of the clay, just like the clay itself.
Anticipating the objection that this reason might not be conclusive— asking why it should not also apply even if they were different— the author refutes it with the words "and not" (*na ca*).
The meaning is that if there were difference between the clay and the jar, as there is between a cow and a horse, there would be a severance of the causal relationship (*hetūcchitti*).

Because a cow and a horse lack the relationship of cause and effect (*nimittanaimittikatva*), there is an absence of causality. Therefore, by that very reason, the relationship of cause and so forth is established for the clay and the jar, and not their non-difference; thus, he raises the objection regarding their being distinct entities with the words "And not by the potter... (*na ca kulāla...*).

Nor is there a difference in entity by way of the relationship between material cause and its effect, because even in the case of the example of clay, that relationship exists despite the absence of [intrinsic] difference; furthermore, if there were difference, such a relationship would be impossible, just as it is between a cow and a horse. This is the intended meaning.
For although the potter and the jar stand in the relationship of efficient cause and so forth, they are nonetheless distinct entities.
The literal meaning is that the perception of a jar is not restricted solely to the presence of a potter.
He raises an objection regarding the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason found in the sutra as it was heard: "But surely...
He replies, "No," stating that the reason consisting of a restrictive rule—that the perception of smoke occurs only when fire is present—does not apply in that case.

One might raise the objection that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because a rule exists in the case of smoke situated in a long, continuous column where the root is not severed; thus he says, "Now [if]... He replies, "Not so," because what is intended as the reason is: being an object of a cognition colored by the cognition of that [other thing], while its own existence is necessarily dependent upon the existence of that [other thing]. The phrase beginning with "provided that" (*sati*) is included to exclude deviation in the case of color (*rūpa*), which is grasped by a cognition colored by the cognition of light.
There is no deviation [in the rule] because objects such as jars exist even in the absence of light.
The meaning is that there is no deviation in the case of the aforementioned specific smoke, since it is perceived even without the cognition of fire.
Thus, the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that [the cognition] is "colored" (anuraktā)—that is, accompanied—by the existence (bhāvena), i.e., the presence, of those two, namely cause and effect.

Alternatively, we state that the reason is "the state of being that," namely co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in being graspable by a cognition whose object is that [co-referentiality].

The meaning is: because we observe a cognition of co-referentiality in the case of "the clay pot" (*mṛd-ghaṭaḥ*), whereas we do not observe such a cognition in the case of "fire and smoke" (*agni-dhūmaḥ*).

Having explained the Sūtra as having the purpose of inference (*anumāna*), he now explains it as referring to perception (*pratyakṣa*) by means of an alternative reading: "And because of existence" (*bhāvācca*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the term "woven together" (*ārambhaṇa*) mentioned in the preceding Sūtra. Furthermore, the perception that "this is one cloth" is not a proof for the separate existence of the cloth from its threads.
This is because it is also logically consistent [to explain the perception] as having for its object a false effect that lacks a separate existence [from its cause].

Therefore, the meaning is that there is non-difference [of the effect from the cause], since the direct perception exists that "the threads themselves, possessing the conjunctions of lengthwise and crosswise extension, are the cloth.
He extends this principle of the cloth to the case of the threads and so forth with the words beginning "In the same way" (tathā).
The meaning is that through direct perception, in each respective effect, only the cause remains as a residue.
Where there is no direct perception, the effect therein is non-different from its suspected cause,
because it is an effect.
He says "by this" [referring to the phrase] "it is to be inferred like a cloth.

One might object that if there is a residue of causes, then the *pradhāna* and so forth would be the residue, not Brahman; to this he replies with "therein, all... [referring to the phrase] "all... [and so on].

The meaning is that since it has been stated that the purport of all the Vedāntas lies in Brahman, that alone remains as non-dual; no other cause remains, because such a thing lacks any basis in authoritative means of knowledge. //15//
And because of the existence of another [cause]. (BBs 2.1.16)
For this reason as well, the effect is non-different from the cause:
because it is heard in scripture that before its production, the effect exists in the cause in the very form of the cause, as in:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

This is because, in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (Ai. Ā. 2.4.1.1), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the effect—comprised by the word "this"—and its cause;
and whatever does not exist in something by way of its own nature cannot arise from that thing.

Just as oil cannot be produced from sand, therefore, because the effect is non-different from the cause prior to its production, it is understood that even once produced, the effect is indeed non-different from the cause. And just as the cause, Brahman, does not deviate from existence throughout the three periods of time, so too the effect, the world, does not deviate from existence throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, there would be only a single sentient being, because the effect is non-different from its cause. // 16 //

The author of the Sūtras states "and because of existence" (sattvāt ca) to show that the world, even after its production, is non-different from its cause; for the scripture, through the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, "this world is indeed the Existent Self" (*idaṃ jagat sadātmaiva*)—teaches that prior to creation the effect exists by way of the nature of the cause, and since this cannot be otherwise accounted for, the world remains non-different from its cause even once produced. Furthermore, he provides a logical argument for the meaning of the scripture: "And whatever [exists] at whatever time, by whatever nature... (*yaccayadātmanā*).

The meaning is that a jar and so forth exist previously in the form of clay and so on, because they are produced from that [clay], just as oil [is not produced] from sand; this is based on a general negative concomitance (*sāmānyato vyatireka*). Since the effect possesses existence just like its cause, and there is no evidence for a difference in their existence, the effect has an existence non-different from its cause—this is another interpretation of the Sūtra’s meaning, which he states with the words "And just as... Now, since it is impossible for an existing effect to be non-existent at earlier or later times, its existence is invariable.
And that reality is the one, all-pervading pure consciousness alone.
By virtue of its non-difference from that [consciousness], the meaning is that there is no otherness between cause and effect—such as "the clay exists" and "the jar exists"—as they appear. //16//
Nor should it be argued that, because of the non-difference of a single existence (*sattva*), there would likewise be no distinction between a jar and a cloth.
In reality, because non-difference is intended by way of the nature of a single entity;
if so, what is the distinction between clay and a jar?
We reply: it is identity (*tādātmya*).
In reality, although existence (*sattā*) is one and the same everywhere, there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between a jar and a cloth because their existences are distinct;

however, since the distinction between cause and effect does not entail a distinction in existence, they possess non-different existence, which constitutes their identity—this is the specific distinction. //16//

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [non-existent] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for there is another attribute [intended], as is clear from the remainder of the passage. (BS 2.1.17)

Now, one might object: does not the Śruti sometimes designate even the non-existence of the effect prior to its production? For instance, it says, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), and "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1). Therefore, because of these designations of non-existence, it may be argued that the effect does not exist prior to its production.
We say: no.

For this designation of the effect as "non-existent" prior to its origination is not intended to mean that it is absolutely non-existent. Rather, because it possesses manifested name and form (*nāmarūpa*), its state of having unmanifested name and form is a different attribute (*dharmāntara*); it is by means of this different attribute that there is this designation of the existent effect—prior to its origination—as "non-existent," while it remains non-different from its cause in the form of the cause.
How is this understood?
From the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). A sentence whose meaning is doubtful at the beginning is determined by its remainder.

Moreover, in this context, that very thing which was indicated at the beginning by the word "non-existent" (asat) in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," is again referred to by the pronoun "that" and qualified as "existent" in the statement, "That became existent.
Furthermore, because the non-existent has no connection with prior or subsequent time, the use of the verb "was" (āsīt) would be untenable.
Even in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," there is no absolute non-existence, because the supplementary sentence, "It made itself by itself," provides a qualification.

Therefore, this designation of the effect as "non-existent" prior to its origination is due solely to its being a different state [of being]. For in the world, a thing that has been differentiated by name and form is well known to be worthy of the term "existent.
Consequently, because it had not yet been differentiated by name and form, it is figuratively said to have been "as if non-existent" or "as if it were not. // 17 //
FN: The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that "in the beginning there was only emptiness; from emptiness alone the world arose.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, this world—in the beginning, prior to creation—was Brahman alone, which, being unmanifest in name and form (*nāmarūpa*), was non-existent and thus equivalent to non-being, yet extremely subtle. From that Brahman, the existent world, with its manifest name and form, was born.

Having raised the objection that the prior existence of the effect in the form of the cause is unestablished, he provides the resolution with the word "asat" (non-existent). The meaning is as follows: just as in the opening statement, "One should place the sugar-cubes smeared [with ghee]," when there is doubt as to what they are smeared with, the conclusion is reached from the supplementary sentence, "Ghee, indeed, is brilliance," that they are smeared with ghee; so too here, the certainty that [the effect] exists is reached from the supplementary sentence, "That is real" (*tat sat*).

Because of the statement regarding its connection with past time in the phrase "it was," he says that it was indeed non-existent and unmanifested, not empty; thus he states, "and of the non-existent, [there is] prior and posterior.
He extends the aforementioned reasoning to another sentence with the words "or as non-existent. The point is that the qualification "being made" is impossible for that which is empty. //17//
On account of reasoning and because of another scriptural word. (BS 2.1.18)
Through reasoning (*yukti*) and through other scriptural statements (*śabdāntara*), it is understood that prior to its production, the effect exists and is non-different from its cause.
First, the reasoning is described as follows: in the world, those seeking specific effects such as curd, jars, or golden ornaments are seen to employ specific causes such as milk, clay, or gold.
For those seeking curd do not take up clay, nor do those seeking a jar take up milk; this would not be possible under the theory that the effect is non-existent [in the cause] (*asatkāryavāda*).
Since prior to production everything is equally non-existent everywhere, why is it that curd arises only from milk and not from clay, and why does a jar arise only from clay and not from milk?
If, despite this equal non-existence prior to production, there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to the curd in milk alone and not in clay, [then the theory is untenable].
If it were said that there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) in the clay alone and not in the milk,

then, because of possessing such excellence, the previous state would no longer be "non-existent," resulting in the abandonment of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) and the establishment of the theory of the existent effect (*satkāryavāda*).

Furthermore, the capacity (*śakti*) of the cause, which is postulated for the purpose of restricting the effect, could neither restrict the effect if it were something other [than the cause] nor if it were non-existent.
Because there is no distinction in their non-existence and no distinction in their difference,
the power is of the very nature of the cause, and the effect is of the very nature of that power.

Furthermore, because there is no cognition of difference— such as that between a horse and a buffalo— between cause and effect, or between substance, quality, and so forth, their identity must be accepted.

Even if one postulates inherence (*samavāya*), if a relation between inherence and its inherent relata is admitted, then another mutual relation would have to be postulated for each of those, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is not admitted, there follows the consequence of a total disconnection.
Now, if it is argued that inherence, being itself of the nature of a relation, becomes related without depending on any further relation;
In that case, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as well, being itself of the nature of a relation, would be related without depending on inherence (*samavāya*).
Furthermore, since substances, qualities, and so forth are perceived as identical [with their parts], the postulation of inherence is useless.
Moreover, how does the effect—the composite substance—subsist while existing within its causes, the constituent substances?
Does it exist in all the parts collectively, or in each part individually?
If it were to exist in all the parts collectively, then the non-perception of the whole would follow as a consequence,
because it is impossible to bring all the parts together simultaneously.
For multiplicity residing in all its substrates collectively is not grasped by the perception of individual substrates.

Furthermore, if it were to reside in all of them part by part, then one would have to postulate parts of the whole distinct from its constituent parts—parts by which the whole could reside part by part within those constituent parts; for a sword occupies a sheath by means of parts distinct from the parts of the sheath itself.
Furthermore, an infinite regress would result,

because for the [whole] to reside in each of those various parts, other parts would have to be postulated. Alternatively, if it were to reside in each part individually, then while it is active in one place, it would be inactive elsewhere.
For Devadatta, while being present in Srughna, cannot at that very same time be present in Pāṭaliputra as well;
for if he were to exist in multiple places simultaneously, it would follow that he is multiple,
just like Devadatta and Yajñadatta who reside respectively in Srughna and Pāṭaliputra.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the whole] is fully present in each part, just as "cowness" and so forth are, we say:
no, because such a perception does not occur.

If the whole were fully present in each part like "cowness," then just as cowness is perceived directly with respect to each individual cow, the whole would likewise be perceived directly with respect to each individual part.
And it is not perceived as being thus restricted.

Furthermore, since the whole (avayavin) is involved in its effect through its completion in each individual part, and because that [whole] is a single entity, it would follow that the horn could perform the function of the breast, and the chest could perform the function of the back;
yet this is not observed.
Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent prior to its production, then production would be without an agent and devoid of a self-nature.
Moreover, production is indeed an action, and like motion and so forth, it must necessarily have an agent.
Furthermore, it would be a contradiction for there to be an action that is without an agent.

If the arising of a jar were said to occur, it could not have the jar as its agent; rather, one would have to assume it has another as its agent. Likewise, if the arising of the shards and so forth were said to occur, they too would have to be assumed to have another as their agent.
And this being the case, when it is said that "the jar arises," the state of arising is perceived for the potter and others as well,
because their state of having already arisen is also perceived. Now,
if it is argued that "arising" is simply the connection with the existence of its own cause, and that "attainment of self" (ātmalābha) is the effect [coming into being], then—
It must be explained how that which has not yet attained self-nature (*anātman*) could be connected;
for a connection is possible only between two existing things, not between an existent and a non-existent, nor between two non-existents.
Furthermore, because non-existence (*abhāva*) is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), it is untenable to establish a temporal limit (*maryādā*) such as "prior to arising."

For in the world, a boundary is observed for existing things such as fields and houses, but not for non-existence. Indeed, it is not possible [to say] that the son of a barren woman was king prior to the consecration of Pūrṇavarman by means of such a cause for establishing a boundary; nor is it possible [to say] that the indefinable son of a barren woman was king prior to the consecration of Pūrṇavarman by means of such a cause for establishing a boundary.

By establishing a limit, the son of a barren woman—who is indefinable—is qualified as having been a king, being a king, or being about to become a king. And if even the son of a barren woman were to come into existence after the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), then one might also expect this: that the absence of an effect (*kāryābhāva*) would likewise come into existence after the operation of causal factors. We, however, see that since there is no difference between the son of a barren woman and the absence of an effect in their common state of non-existence, just as the son of a barren woman will certainly not exist after the operation of causal factors, so too the absence of an effect will not exist after the operation of causal factors.
"It will not come to be.
But if this were so, it would follow that the activity of the agent is purposeless;
for just as no one exerts effort to establish the nature of a cause because it is already established beforehand, [so too would it be for the effect].

Thus, because the effect is already established prior [to its production] and is non-different from that [cause], no one would exert effort even for the sake of establishing the effect's own nature; yet, people do exert effort.
Therefore, we conclude that the effect is non-existent prior to its production, so as to make the operation of the causal factors purposeful.
Regarding the phrase "of the effect":
this is not a fault,
because for one who establishes the cause by means of the form of the effect, the purposefulness of the causal operation is rendered possible.
It has been stated that even the form of the effect is indeed identical with the essence of the cause, because that which is not identical with it cannot be produced.
Furthermore, the mere perception of a difference does not constitute a difference in the substance itself;
for Devadatta, though seen in different states with his hands and feet contracted or his hands and feet extended, does not undergo a change in substance.
This is because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "it is that very same one.

Likewise, although fathers and others assume many different forms day after day, there is no change in the underlying substance, because of the recognition: "He is my father," "He is my brother," "He is my son."
If it is argued that [the term "birth"] is appropriate there because it is immediately preceded by the cutting off of birth, and not elsewhere, we say no;
for even in the case of milk and the like, the assumption of the form and configuration of curd and so forth is perceived directly.

Furthermore, even in the case of invisible things such as banyan seeds and the like, when they come within the range of perception through the state of sprouts and so forth—having been augmented by other constituent parts of the same kind—the designation "birth" is applied.
The notion of annihilation arises when those very *āyuvans* (life-forces) reach a state of non-perception due to their gradual diminution.

In that case, if it were held that a non-existent entity becomes existent because it is separated by such an annihilation of birth, then there would follow the absurd consequence of a difference between the being in the womb and the one lying on its back.
Likewise, there would follow the absurd consequence of a difference between the stages of childhood, youth, and old age.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of abolishing worldly conventions such as those regarding fathers and so forth.
By this same reasoning, the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) should be refuted.
Moreover, for one who maintains that the effect is non-existent prior to its production, the activity of the causal agents would be rendered objectless.
Since it is logically impossible for a non-entity to be an object [of action], it would be like employing various weapons such as a sword for the purpose of striking at empty space.
If it is argued that the operation of causal factors must have an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as its object, we say no;
for if the operation of causal factors directed toward one object were to produce something else, it would lead to the absurdity of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that the effect is merely a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) itself, we say no; for this would entail the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatā*).

Therefore, substances such as milk and the like, while persisting in the state of curd and so forth, receive the designation "effect. Thus, even in a hundred years, it is impossible to determine that the effect is anything other than the cause.
Likewise, the very root cause, like an actor, assumes the status of being the locus of all worldly transactions by taking on the form of various effects from the final effect onwards.
Thus, through reasoning, it is understood that the effect exists prior to its production and is non-different from the cause.
This is also understood from another scriptural statement.

Since a word designating the non-existent (*asad-vyapadeśin*) was cited in the preceding sūtra, a word designating the existent (*sad-vyapadeśin*) other than that is "another word" (*śabdāntara*). Starting with passages such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," and having introduced the position of non-existence with, "Now some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-being alone,'" and having raised the objection, "How could being be born from non-being?", [the scripture] concludes by determining: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

In this regard, because the identity (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the effect—denoted by the word "this"—with the cause—denoted by the word "Being"—is heard in scripture prior to its production, its existence and non-difference [from the cause] are established.

If, however, the effect were non-existent prior to its production and, being subsequently produced, were to inhere in the cause, then it would be something other than the cause. In that case, the scriptural statement, "By which the unheard becomes heard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3), would be contradicted.
In this way, this proposition would be undermined;
however, through the realization that sentient beings are not different [from the Buddha], this proposition is established. (18) [Note:
*atiśaya* refers to either the property of the effect or the property of the cause.]

The meaning is that "the non-existence of the effect" refers to the non-existence of the effect [prior to its production]. The grammatical connection is: "it would have been possible" (*upāpatsyata*) means "it would have been logically established" (*upapannam abhaviṣyat*). "Being another entity" (*vastvantaratvam*) means being distinct in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
By this, it is stated that the cause persists (*anvaya*) throughout all its effects.
To clarify the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), the example "like an actor" is given.
The author of the Sūtras states another reason for the non-difference of the effect from its cause: "by reasoning" (*yukteḥ*).

The meaning is that the existence of the effect prior [to its production] is established through its non-difference from the cause, by means of this reasoning: namely, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the activity of those seeking curd and the like toward milk and the like.

Anticipating the objection that activity toward a cause might still occur because one perceives it as a cause even though the effect is non-existent—thereby offering an alternative explanation—the author says: "For [if they were] indistinct," and so on.

The meaning is that since there can be no arising of what is non-existent, or else, if such arising occurred, it would follow that everything could arise from everything; consequently, there would be no directed activity toward specific respective material causes (*upādāna*).

As it has been stated by the elders of the Sāṃkhya school: "Because the non-existent cannot be produced, because of the necessity of grasping a material cause, because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything..."
"Because that which is capable produces only what is possible, and because of the nature of the cause, the effect exists [as a pre-existent entity].
This means that since a capable cause produces only an effect for which it has the capacity, the effect must exist as the object of that capacity; for what is non-existent cannot be produced.
Furthermore, the meaning of the latter half of the verse is that the effect is existent because it is non-different from its existent cause.
He raises an objection, saying "Now [if]... [with the thought]: "Even though the effect is non-existent, the restriction of activity is possible due to some excellence (atiśaya).
Is this excellence a property of the effect or a property of the cause?

Regarding the first case, he says: "In that case, because it possesses excellence," [pointing out] that since the effect, which exists in the form of its prior state, would be the locus (dharmin) of that excellence, its existence becomes unavoidable.
He says "And [if] power" because even in the second case, the existence of the effect would follow.
Power that is distinct from both cause and effect, like the effect itself, is either non-existent or it does not regulate the effect;

for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of anything else—such as a human horn—acting as a regulator, since the properties of being distinct and being non-existent are no different in the case of power than they are in other cases.
Therefore, for this reason, it must be accepted that the effect itself, when latent in the form of its cause, is what is called "potency" (śakti) by virtue of being the regulator of manifestation;
thus, the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) is established—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he says "apica" (moreover), because if the effect and the cause were different, there would be a cognition of difference, such as "the clay and the jar are two distinct things."

Anticipating the objection that even if the two [the cloth and its whiteness] are distinct, such a cognition does not arise because of inherence (*samavāya*), he refutes inherence with the words "inherence" (*samavāya*).
Is inherence connected with the inherent relata (*samavāyin*) or not?
In the first case, is that connection itself inherence or its own essential nature (*svarūpa*)?
In the first case, there would be an infinite regress of inherence;
in the second case, since even the relationship between clay and a jar is established through their own essential nature (svarūpa-sambandha) alone, inherence is not proven.
Regarding the position that they are unrelated, he states the fault: "if it were not accepted," and so forth.
The consequence would be the absence of qualified cognition regarding substances, qualities, and so forth;
the meaning is that it is impossible for that which is unrelated to be the regulator of qualified cognition.
For a relation is precisely what regulates qualified cognition.

It does not require another regulator, as that would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, he raises the objection that inherence (samavāya) is self-establishing and establishes others— beginning with "Now" (atha).

It is connected; the meaning is that it produces a qualified cognition of itself and its own relatum. He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a counter-argument: "Conjunction, too... and so forth.
As for the claim that conjunction requires inherence because it is a quality (*guṇa*) and not because it is a relation (*saṃbandha*),
that is not so,
because it is a property (*dharma*).
Furthermore, because inherence (*samavāya*) would itself entail another relation, we do not observe that the property of being a horse—which is unrelated [to it]—can be a property of a cow.

Moreover, since the qualities such as "sinlessness" and so forth are mentioned in the Śruti and Smṛti, and according to the technical definition that "a quality is a desired attribute in common usage," inherence itself must also be a quality.
The technical definition that "quality-ness is a specific genus" (*jātiviśeṣa*), however, only follows after the establishment of inherence.
The universal (*jāti*) is defined as that which is eternally inherent in many; this is because the cognition of a universal depends upon the cognition of inherence (*samavāya*).
Therefore, prior to the establishment of inherence, the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) remains unestablished—this is the general direction of the argument.
Furthermore, an entity must be accepted in accordance with its actual apprehension; otherwise, one could equally well claim that when a cow is perceived, a horse is its objective basis (*ālambana*).
And thus, since there is a cognition of non-difference in the form "the clay is the jar," non-difference alone must be accepted;
for it is impossible for *samavāya* (inherence), which is absolutely distinct from those two, to be their regulator. Thus he says: "tādātmya" (identity).
In this way, according to such cognition, the effect exists by virtue of the nature of its cause.

It has already been stated that [the whole] is false by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Furthermore, he states "And how? to show that it is false because its mode of existence (*vṛtti*) cannot be determined.

Therein, having restated the first [position], he refutes the first alternative—namely, whether the whole, such as a cloth, exists in its own nature within its parts, such as the threads, like the number three and so on, or whether it exists part by part—with the words beginning "If... (*yadi...*).

The meaning is that since the perception of an object existing as a distributed whole (vyāsajyavṛtti) is produced by the perception of all its substrates, it would follow as an absurd consequence that a folded cloth or the like could not be perceived, because none of its constituent parts would be perceived.
He raises a second objection with "Now [if you say]":
just as a sword, while residing part by part in both the hand and the scabbard, is perceived even when only the hand is grasped.

Thus, he refutes [the opponent's position] by pointing out that even if the apprehension of the whole (*avayavin*) were possible through the apprehension of some part, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of parts; this is expressed by the words "even then" (*tadāpi*).
Having set forth the first and second alternatives, he refutes them with the passage beginning "now, for each part" (*atha pratyavayavam*).
At the time when the cloth exists in one thread, it could not exist in another thread.
The meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of multiplicity in its subsistence.

He raises the objection—"In the case of 'cowness' (*gotva*)"—suggesting that just as there is no fault of multiplicity for a genus (*jāti*) even though it subsists simultaneously in multiple individuals, so it might be for a whole (*avayavin*).
He refutes this with "No," on the grounds that the subsistence of a whole like that of a genus is unestablished, as there is no such experience.
"So be it.
He states another fault with the words "pratyeka" (each individually),
because of the context and the connection.

The meaning is as follows: just as Devadatta performs his own work, such as studying, either in a village or in a forest; or just as a cow, which is a composite whole (avayavin), might produce its own effects, such as milk, even from its horns or tail—thus, by the failure to determine a mode of existence (vṛtti), the indeterminability (anirvācyatva) of the effect is demonstrated.
Now, he states another fault in the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*) with the words "prior" (*prāk*).

Just as when it is said "the jar moves," the jar's agency—consisting in its being the substratum for the action of moving—is manifested, so too, in the case of "the cloth is born," the cloth is experienced as the agent of the action of birth.
Therefore, the agent of birth must be asserted to exist prior to the birth.
The meaning is that if the agent is non-existent, it follows that the action itself must also be non-existent.
Although the fact that production has an agent is established by experience, he states an inference based on its being an action: "And production...

Anticipating the objection that even though agency is impossible for a jar that is non-existent at the time of its production, the potter and others can still be the agents because they exist, he says: "And of the jar..."
He extends the argument by saying "likewise" (*tathā*), [meaning] that the production of shards and so forth is like the production of a jar from what was non-existent.
Having restated the objection, he states the fault with "and if it were so" (*tathā ca*);
the meaning is that this contradicts experience (*anubhava-virodha*).

Having established the existence of the effect according to his own view—that the "origination" of an entity is its first modification—he now raises the objection based on the position of the logicians (*tārkika*), namely that the so-called "origination" of an effect is its inherence (*samavāya*) in its own cause or its inherence in itself as existence (*sattā*): "Now," etc.
Even according to that view, the existence of the effect is necessary.

He says "How? because that which is non-existent cannot possess the nature of being related. The phrase "or of two non-existent things" is a statement of an illustrative example. An objection is raised: "But surely an effect is not non-existent everywhere at all times like a human horn; rather, it is non-existent prior to its production and after its destruction, but existent in the interval. Thus, due to this difference, the possibility of its being related is established. Anticipating this, he says: "Of non-existence..."

Here, the words "non-existence" (*abhāva*) are to be explained as synonyms for the word "non-being" (*asat*). The meaning is that since non-being has no connection with time, it is not logical for it to possess "prior-ness. Now, one might ask: how can an effect that occurs subsequent to the operation of its causes be equivalent to the son of a barren woman? To this, he says: "And if... (*yadi ca*).

The logical connection is as follows: "the non-existence of the effect" means "the non-existent effect," and thus [the Sāṃkhya position] would have been established by itself; [if that were so, it] would have been proven. What, then, is the final determination?
To this he says: "We, however... and so forth.

The intention is that, according to the Smṛti statement, "There is no being for the non-existent," [the effect must exist]. He raises the objection regarding the futility of causal factors in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) with the words, "But surely" (nanu).
And he states that the effect is already established because it is non-different from its established cause, with the words, "And because of its non-difference from that" (tadananyatvāt ca).
He says, "This is not a fault," meaning that the operation of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) is for the purpose of manifesting the cause in the form of an effect that is otherwise inexpressible.
For the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain the reality of the effect and advocate the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the fault of the uselessness of causal factors would arise,
because even manifestation is already existent.

For the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), however, everything is logically consistent with their observations—like a dream—by virtue of the power of Māyā, which is skillful at bringing about the manifestation of the impossible.
When scrutinized, everything is untenable; for if it were tenable, the consequence would be duality (dvaita). This is the primary resolution, as there is no other resolution possible.

One might object: "Why not simply accept the solution that what is different from the cause is indeed non-existent when it arises? Anticipating this, he says, "The form of the effect also... and so on, reminding us of the refutation of the position of non-existence (*asatpakṣa*). Therefore, the sense is this: since [the effect] cannot be definitively established as either different or non-different from the cause, and is distinct from both existence and non-existence, the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvācya*) is the fruit of the operations of indeterminable causal factors; thus, this very position is the best. One might further object:
"But surely, specific states such as broadness and flatness, though not seen in the clay, are observed in the jar."
And thus, [the opponent might argue] that "a pot is different from clay, because it possesses qualities contradictory to it, like a tree"; to this he says: "Nor... (na ca).
In reality, "otherness" (anyatva) means true difference.
He states another instance where the reason is inconclusive: "likewise, day by day.
Even though there is a change in state in the bodies of parents and others every day, since there is no birth or destruction [of the underlying substance], non-difference is logical.

Regarding the illustrative case (dārṣṭāntika), however, an objection is raised: "Since a jar or the like arises when the clay or other material perishes, the non-difference between cause and effect is not tenable because they possess contradictory properties in the form of birth and destruction.
