This is answered with "No," on the grounds that the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because there is no destruction of the cause.
The meaning is that since milk, clay, and so forth are perceived as persisting through their connection with effects such as curd and jars, their destruction is unproven.

[Objection: "But surely, where a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is observed, even if the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, there might still be the distinction between existence and non-existence because the reason exists—such as in the case of sprouts and the like, where the positive concomitance of fig seeds and so forth is not observed. To this, he says: "adṛśya" (unobservable). Even in that case, such as with sprouts and the like, because the parts of the seed and so forth persist, birth and destruction do not actually exist; rather, the conventional usage [of those terms] arises from the accumulation and diminution of other parts. Having raised the doubt that one might infer a difference in substance through the signs of accumulation and diminution, and thus conclude that what was non-existent arises and what was existent perishes, he states the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) with the words: "tatreḍṛg" (in that case, such...).
Regarding the claim that there is no deviation [from the rule] because difference exists even within the body of the father, he states the subverting argument: "pitrādi" (the father, etc.).
By the phrase "etena" (by this), the meaning is:
by the statement of the persistence of the cause in all its effects.

Having refuted the defect in his own position, he introduces the consequence for the opposing position with the words "But for one who... Since a non-existent effect cannot be the locus of an excellence produced by the operation of an agent, it might be argued that even though it is not an object [of action], clay and so forth could still be the object; this is the doubt raised with the words "the inherent cause" (*samavāyin*). He rejects the first alternative of the dilemma—whether the effect is different or non-different from the inherent cause—with the words beginning "No," and so on.
Anticipating the second objection, he states the acceptance of the desired conclusion: "samavāyī" (the inherent cause).
He summarizes the non-difference of effects from their intermediate causes with: "tasmāt" (therefore).
He states the resulting non-difference from the ultimate cause: "tathā mūla" (likewise, the root).

He states that in the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), there would be a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñābādha*): "But if [the effect were non-existent] prior to its production," etc. (18).
And it is like a cloth. (BBs 2.1.19)

Just as a rolled-up cloth is not clearly perceived—such that one cannot discern whether it is a cloth or some other substance—the very same cloth, when unrolled, is perceived as manifest through that unrolling, with the recognition: "That substance which was rolled up is indeed this cloth. Furthermore, just as at the time of being rolled up, although it is grasped as a "cloth," its specific length and breadth are not grasped, yet at the time of unrolling, those specific dimensions are grasped; it is not something other than the form that was rolled up.

"As when [one says] 'this cloth is torn'—in this way, the effect such as a cloth, which exists in an unmanifest state within its causes such as the threads, is perceived clearly and manifestly through the operations of agents such as the shuttle, the loom, and the weaver.
Therefore, by the analogy of a cloth that has been rolled up and then spread out, the meaning is that the effect is non-different from the cause. // 19 //
FN: *Āyāma* means length.

An effect is distinct from its material cause because, even when that [cause] is perceived, [the effect] is not perceived, and because it possesses a dimension greater than that [cause], just as a hare is distinct from a gnat. To show that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this [argument], the Sūtra says "and like a cloth" (*paṭavat*).
This clarifies the deviation of the second reason with the words "and just as by rolling up... (*yathā ca saṃveṣṭaneti*).
Length is extension. //19//
And as in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. (BBs 2.1.20)

Just as in the world, when the various vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna are restrained through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and they persist in the form of mere causes, only the effect of mere life is produced, but not other effects such as contraction and expansion;
yet when those same vital breaths resume their activity, other effects such as contraction and expansion, in addition to mere life, are also produced.

Nor is there any difference between the various modifications of the vital breaths and the vital breath itself which possesses those modifications, because there is no distinction in their nature as wind;
in this same way, the effect is non-different from its cause.

And therefore, because the entire world is an effect of Brahman and is non-different from it, this scriptural proposition is established: "By which, when heard, the unheard becomes heard; when thought, the unthought becomes thought; when known, the unknown becomes known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1).

In that very context, having raised the argument that "the effect possesses a distinct causal capacity because the effect is different from its material cause, since it produces a different effect, like [an agreed-upon example]," the author of the Sūtras states the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words: "And as in the case of the vital breaths, etc. (YS 4.2).

Thus, he concludes the meaning of the section by demonstrating that the proposition is established because the world of living beings is non-different from Brahman: "And therefore, of the entire... (20).
END BsCom_2,1.6.20 START BsCom_2,1.7.21 7 The Section Concerning the Designation as Other (Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 21–23.
"Because of the designation of another, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial, and so forth.
(BBs 2.1.21) Otherwise, however, the doctrine of an intelligent cause is challenged;
for when the process of the world's creation is based upon an intelligent being, defects such as the failure to perform what is beneficial necessarily follow.
Why?
Because of the designation of the other.
The scripture designates the identity of the other—the embodied soul—with Brahman: "That is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
This is because of such an awakening;
or else, [the text] designates the other Brahman as the embodied self of the individual soul in the passage: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).
Thus, because it is shown that the unmodified Creator, Brahman itself, enters into its effects and constitutes the embodied self;

and because the supreme deity, in the passage "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva), let me evolve names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), designates the living self with the word "self," demonstrates that the embodied self is not different from Brahman.
Therefore, that which constitutes the creatorship of Brahman belongs solely to his body;

consequently, being an independent agent, he would only do what is beneficial and conducive to his own well-being, and not what is harmful—the manifold web of evils such as birth, death, old age, and disease.
For no one who is not dependent on another would build a prison for himself and then enter it.
Furthermore, being himself utterly pure, he would not identify as his self a body that is utterly impure;
and whatever he had done that somehow caused suffering, he would abandon it by his own will,
and he would take up what causes happiness.
And one should remember: "This manifold reflection of the world was fashioned by me.
For every person in the world, having clearly performed an action, remembers: "This was done by me.
And just as a magician effortlessly withdraws at will the illusion he himself has projected, so too [does the Lord].
In this same way, the embodied soul (śārīra) would also have to withdraw this creation.
For even his own body, the embodied soul is not able to withdraw without effort;
thus, because no such beneficial action or other such signs are observed, it is understood that the process of the world is unjust [if attributed to him]. // 21 //

The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the Vedāntic harmony (*samanvaya*) which asserts that Brahman, non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*), is the cause of the world. Regarding the doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the logic that "if such a Brahman were to produce the world, it would not produce its own undesirable states such as hell, because it is an independent sentient being," [the author] relies upon the previously mentioned non-difference of the soul [from Brahman] and [concludes that] the defects of the soul [would indeed apply] to Brahman.
Taking up the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) sūtra, "They would follow as a consequence," he explains it with the words beginning "Because of the designation of the other" (itaravyapadeśāt).

The result is that in the prima facie view, the harmony (samanvaya) [of the Upanishadic texts] is not established because [Brahman] is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), that harmony is established.
In the phrase "hitākaraṇa" (non-performance of what is beneficial), by the transposition of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is explained as the fault of performing what is harmful (*ahitakaraṇa*).
By the words beginning with "and not himself" (*naca svayam*), he brings forward the delusion (*bhrānti*) and other factors mentioned by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). //21//
But it is something more, because of the designation of a distinction. (BBs 2.1.22)
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.

We declare that the creator of the world is that Brahman which is omniscient and omnipotent, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, and which is distinct from and superior to the embodied soul.
In that case, defects such as failing to act for the benefit [of others] do not apply;
for there is nothing beneficial that must be performed by him, nor anything harmful that must be avoided,
because his nature is eternally liberated.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction to his knowledge or obstruction to his power anywhere, because he is omniscient and omnipotent;
however, the embodied one is not of such a nature, and thus defects such as failing to act for the benefit [of others] would necessarily follow in his case.
But we do not say that he is the creator of the world. Why is this?
Because of the designation of difference.
"The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5);
"That is to be sought; that is to be understood" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1);
"Then, my dear, one becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).

The scriptural designation of distinctions such as agent and object, found in passages like "The embodied self is mounted by the conscious self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35), shows that Brahman is distinct from the individual soul (jīva).
But is it not true that designations of non-difference are also shown, such as "That thou art"?
How could difference and non-difference, being contradictory, possibly coexist?
This is not a fault,
because the possibility of both has been established in various places through the analogy of space and the space within a jar.

Furthermore, when non-difference has been realized through such an instruction of non-difference as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), then the transmigratory state of the individual soul (jīva) and the creative agency of Brahman vanish; for all conventional usage based on difference, which is a manifestation of false knowledge, is sublated by perfect knowledge.
In that state, how could there be creation, or how could defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others] exist?

For we have stated more than once that transmigratory existence—characterized by the failure to accomplish what is beneficial and so forth—is an error caused by the non-discrimination of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), namely the aggregate of body and organs produced by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) presented by ignorance (avidyā); it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), just like the conceit regarding birth, death, cutting, breaking, and so on.

However, as long as the conventional usage of difference remains uncontradicted, the superiority of Brahman—which is understood through such instructions concerning difference as "He is to be sought, He is to be known"—would entail the occurrence of defects such as the failure to accomplish what is beneficial.
It obstructs. // 22 //

Since there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), the defects of the individual soul and the world would belong to Brahman, and the qualities residing in Brahman—such as the power of creation and dissolution, and omniscience—would belong to the individual soul.

This is not an acceptable consequence, because the individual soul is never observed to possess the capacity for dissolution even within its own body. Having reached this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he explains the aphorism of the final conclusion (siddhānta-sūtra) with the words beginning "the word *tu*," and so forth.

The meaning of the Siddhānta text is that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is accepted as being like that between a reflection and its original in the world, and thus the systematic arrangement of their respective attributes is established. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: if we were to say that the individual soul is the creator, then faults would ensue; however, we do not say that.
Furthermore, are these faults to be imputed after the realization of non-difference (*abheda*), or before it?
He says "not so" with the words "apica" (moreover).
He clarifies what was stated regarding its being a manifestation of false knowledge with the word "avidyā" (ignorance).
In the context of the superimposition of the attributes of the intellect, such as agency, he provides the body's attributes as an illustrative example with the word "janma" (birth).
He states the second [objection] with the words "But when there is no sublation" (abādhite tu).

The meaning is that since the attributes such as being the creator are sublated after [the realization of] knowledge, whereas before [that realization] their establishment is possible through imagined difference, there is nothing faulty. //22//
And like a stone and so forth, that [transformation] is impossible. (2.1.23)

And just as in the world, among stones that are all equally endowed with the commonality of "earth-ness," one observes a manifold variety: some are precious gems such as diamonds and lapis lazuli; others are of middling potency, such as sun-crystals; and others are discarded stones fit only to be thrown away by dogs and crows.

Just as various diversities of leaves, flowers, fruits, scents, tastes, and so forth are observed among seeds—such as sandalwood and the *kiṃpāka* fruit—even though they all depend upon the same earth;
and just as even from a single essence of food there arise diverse effects such as blood and the like, as well as hair of the head and body;

in the same way, even from a single Brahman, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme conscious one (*prājña*), as well as the diversity of effects, is logically possible. Thus, there is no inconsistency in this [doctrine].
The meaning is that the faults imagined by others do not arise.

Furthermore, this is further supported by the authority of scripture (*śruti*), the fact that modification is merely a matter of speech (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), and the analogy with the variety of objects seen in a dream. (23) [FN:
*Kiṃpāka* is the fruit of the great *tāla* tree.]

But how can there be the diversity of individual souls (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as the diversity of their effects, within Brahman, which is of an indivisible and uniform nature? The author of the Sūtras removes this apparent inconsistency by means of examples: "And like stones, etc. (*aśmādivat*). *Kiṃpāka* is the fruit of the great *tāla* tree.

The intended meaning is that there is diversity due to the distinctions between beginningless potencies (*anādiśakti*) in the form of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of various respective effects.
He states the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra: "And because of scripture" (*śruteśca*).
[This implies that] Brahman would possess the defects residing in the individual soul (*jīva*).

Inferences such as "because it is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), [it must be like] the individual soul," are sublated by scriptural texts concerning its being self-evident valid knowledge and its faultlessness.

Furthermore, since modifications such as agency and enjoyership are illusory, even the individual soul possesses no defect; how then could the Supreme Lord—who stands as the archetype and perceives all distinctions—be subject to the charge of defect?
As for the argument that Brahman cannot be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of diverse effects because it is of a single nature, unlike clay, thread, and so forth;
That is not so;
the meaning is that there is a deviation [from the rule] because, even in a single form, one perceives the variety of diverse objects of perception as in a dream.
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction in the concordance [of all scriptural texts] with Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self. //23//

Section 8: The Topic on the Observation of Reabsorption (Upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 24–25. [The opponent argues: "Because we observe the reabsorption [of the organs] into the Self, [the Self is the cause]. Sūtra 24: "On account of the observation of reabsorption. [The opponent explains: Since we observe that the organs of sense and action are reabsorbed into the individual Self at the time of death—according to such scriptural passages as, "Then speech merges into the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.11)—it follows that the individual Self is the cause of the world. For it is a well-known principle that whatever is reabsorbed into something else is an effect of that thing. Therefore, the individual Self must be the cause. Sūtra 25: "[This is not so,] because [the scripture teaches] a different [reabsorption] into that which is established by its own nature. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. The reabsorption of the organs into the individual Self is not taught here as their final dissolution. Rather, the scripture teaches a different kind of reabsorption—namely, their merging into the Self as established by its own nature (the Supreme Self)—at the time of the soul's departure from the body. As the scripture says: "Having become one with the breath, he passes out with the very same" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Furthermore, the subsequent passage, "He goes to the light" (ibid.), shows that the individual Self, having departed, proceeds toward the Supreme Self. Thus, the organs are merely withdrawn into the individual Self for the purpose of its journey, and not dissolved into it as its final cause. Therefore, the individual Self is not the cause of the world. End of Section 8. Section 9 begins. Section 9: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 26. [The opponent objects: "But the non-difference of the cause and the effect is not possible. Sūtra 26: "But [the world is not non-different from Brahman] because of the difference of nature. [The opponent argues: We observe a difference in nature between the cause and the effect. Clay, for instance, is a substance, whereas jars, pots, and other vessels are objects possessing specific forms and functions. Since the world possesses qualities such as activity, agency, and enjoyment, while Brahman is devoid of such qualities, the world cannot be non-different from Brahman. Therefore, the doctrine of non-difference is untenable. End of Section 9. Section 10 begins. Section 10: The Topic on the Non-existence of the World (Prapañcāsattvādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 27. [The opponent asks: "If the world does not exist, how can there be liberation? Sūtra 27: "And because of the non-existence [of the world]. [The opponent argues: Since the world is perceived through valid means of knowledge, it cannot be non-existent. If it were non-existent, liberation would be impossible, as there would be nothing to be liberated from. Therefore, the world exists. End of Section 10. Section 11 begins. Section 11: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) continued. Sūtra 28. [The Siddhāntin replies: "But [the world is non-different] because of the designation of the cause as the effect. Sūtra 28: "But [the world is non-different] because of the designation of the cause as the effect. [The Siddhāntin explains: The world is indeed non-different from Brahman. Why? Because the cause is designated as the effect. In the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), the term "Being," which denotes the cause, is subsequently designated as the effect in the form of the earth, water, and fire. Since the cause is thus designated as the effect, the world is non-different from Brahman. End of Section 11. Section 12 begins. Section 12: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) continued. Sūtra 29. [The opponent objects: "But [the world is different] because of the difference of names and forms. Sūtra 29: "But [the world is different] because of the difference of names and forms. [The opponent argues: Although the cause is designated as the effect, we observe a difference between them due to the distinction of names and forms. Prior to creation, there was no differentiation of names and forms; after creation, however, the world is differentiated by various names and forms. Therefore, the cause and the effect are different. End of Section 12. Section 13 begins. Section 13: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) concluded. Sūtra 30. [The Siddhāntin replies: "But [the world is non-different] because of the existence [of the effect] in the cause, as in the case of a snake and its coils. Sūtra 30: "But [the world is non-different] because of the existence [of the effect] in the cause, as in the case of a snake and its coils. [The Siddhāntin explains: The world is non-different from Brahman. Why? Because the effect exists within the cause. Just as a coiled snake is non-different from the straight snake, so too the world, though appearing different through names and forms, is non-different from Brahman. The difference is merely an appearance caused by name and form. Therefore, the world is non-different from Brahman. End of Section 13. Section 14 begins. Section 14: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) concluded. Sūtra 31. [The opponent asks: "If the world is non-different from Brahman, then Brahman is subject to the faults of the world. Sūtra 31: "And because of the non-acceptance [of the world's defects]. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. The defects of the world do not apply to Brahman. Why? Because the scripture does not accept such a conclusion. Passages such as "That Self is free from sin" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1) declare that Brahman is devoid of all imperfections. Therefore, the world's defects do not affect Brahman. End of Section 14. Section 15 begins. Section 15: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) concluded. Sūtra 32. [The opponent asks: "If the world is non-different from Brahman, then the world's suffering applies to Brahman. Sūtra 32: "And because of the non-acceptance [of the world's suffering]. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. The suffering of the world does not apply to Brahman. Why? Because the scripture does not accept it. Passages such as "He who is without desire, who is freed from desire, whose desire is satisfied, whose desire is the Self—he has no fear from anything" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1) declare that the liberated Self is free from all suffering. Therefore, the world's suffering does not affect Brahman. End of Section 15. Section 16 begins. Section 16: The Topic on the Non-difference of the Cause and Effect (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) concluded. Sūtra 33. [The opponent asks: "If the world is non-different from Brahman, then Brahman is subject to transformation. Sūtra 33: "And because of the non-acceptance [of transformation]. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. Transformation does not apply to Brahman. Why? Because the scripture does not accept it. Passages such as "The True, Knowledge, Infinite is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) declare that Brahman is eternal
If it be argued that [Brahman is not the cause] because we observe the bringing together [of materials], we say no; for it is like milk.
That which was stated—that the conscious Brahman, one and without a second, is the cause of the world—is not tenable.
Why? Because...
Because we observe the bringing together [of instruments].

For in this world, potters and others who are the makers of jars, cloths, and so forth, are seen to perform their respective effects only after having gathered various causal factors—such as clay, staffs, wheels, and threads—and thus being equipped with the necessary means.
Since Brahman, according to your view, is without any assistance, how could its status as a creator be possible if it does not gather other means?
If it is argued that, for this reason, Brahman is not the cause of the world,
this is not a fault; because,
as in the case of milk, it is logically possible due to a specific nature inherent in the substance itself.
For just as in the world milk or water transforms itself into the state of curd or ice without depending on any external means, so too will it be here.
[Objection: But even milk and the like, when transforming into the state of curd and so forth, certainly depend on external means such as heat; how then can it be said that "it is like milk"?
[Reply: This is not a fault.

For even milk itself, to whatever extent it undergoes mere transformation, is prepared for the state of curd by heat and so forth; if it did not possess the inherent nature of becoming curd, it would never attain the state of curd even through the force of heat and other factors. Indeed, neither wind nor space attains the state of curd through the force of heat and such.
And its fullness is accomplished through the totality of its constituent parts;
however, Brahman possesses complete power,
and its fullness need not be accomplished by anything else.
And there is a scriptural passage: "Of Him, neither effect nor cause is found; neither one equal to Him nor superior to Him is seen.
His supreme power is heard of as indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent."
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.2).
Therefore, even for the one Brahman, a manifold transformation is possible due to its association with diverse powers, just as in the case of milk and other substances. // 24 // [FN:
The "conjunction" (upasaṃhāra) of causal factors refers to their combination.]

The subject matter [of this section] is the reconciliation of the texts that declare the creation of the universe from Brahman alone, without any assistant, based on the observation of the process of condensation— whereby milk is transformed into the state of curd through heat and other factors. This demonstrates rapidity and effectuation.

In the doubt as to whether this contradicts the worldly maxim that "that which is without assistance is not a cause," it was previously stated that because the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the defects of the soul do not attach to Brahman;

now, however, by way of a counter-example, he explains a portion of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) sūtra with the words beginning "cetanam" [the conscious one], stating that even apart from limiting adjuncts, there is no auxiliary cause such as an impeller for Brahman, because there is no plurality of Lords (īśvara).
The result [of this argument] is as before.
The "convergence" (upasaṃhāra) of the causal factors is their meeting together.
He establishes the final position—that the aforementioned reasoning does not suffer from deviation in the case of milk and so forth—by stating: "This is not a fault.
Indeed, it is precisely our accepted view that pure Brahman is not a cause [in itself].
With the thought that for the distinguished Lord, Māyā alone is the assistant, he says: "external" (*bāhyam*).

Anticipating the objection that even milk has assistants such as the act of churning (*ātañcana*), and thus there is no deviation from the reason of being "without assistance," he replies with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*) etc., stating that since some kind of transformation is observed in milk even in the absence of an assistant, the state of deviation remains as it was;
therefore, an assistant would be useless.
Regarding this, he says: "It is refined.
But surely, milk is refined for the sake of becoming curd; why then is it postulated that "quickness is produced"?
Why could it not be the case that milk, being inherently incapable, is made capable by means of an auxiliary?
Regarding this, he says, "If indeed... [referring to the phrase *yadi cet*].
To the question, "What is the purpose of providing assistance for that which is already capable?", he replies with the word "sādhana" (means/proof).
In the absence of a specific assistant, a certain transformation occurs in the milk.
The meaning is that in that case, the capacity for the state of being excellent curd is manifested by the two factors of churning and the addition of heat.
If it is then argued that a companion who manifests this potential must also be mentioned for Brahman, he says in response: "Perfect" (paripūrṇa).
The meaning is that it possesses the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) independently.
He states the proof for such a power: "And scripture (śrutiḥ)" [verse 24].
Also because, in the world, it is like [the case of] gods and so forth. (BBs 2.1.25)
This might be so:
it is observed that insentient things such as milk undergo the state of curd and so forth even without depending on external means;
however, sentient beings such as potters and others are seen to engage in producing an effect only by depending on a collection of means.
How could Brahman, being conscious and without a companion, proceed to act?
We reply: "Like the gods and others.
Just as in the world, beings such as the gods, ancestors, and seers—who possess great power and are conscious—act even without depending [on external means].

On account of their possession of a particular sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), we observe from the authority of the *mantras*, *arthavādas*, *itihāsas*, and *purāṇas* that certain external agents, by mere volition, spontaneously fashion many bodies of various forms as well as palaces, chariots, and so forth. Furthermore,
the spider (*tantunābha*) creates threads from itself alone.
The crane conceives a fetus even without semen;
and the lotus plant proceeds from one lake to another without requiring any means of transport.
In the same way, the conscious Brahman will create the world by itself, without depending on any external instrument.
If he should say: "Those examples of Brahman such as the gods and others that have been cited are not equivalent to the Brahman which is the subject of the illustration;
for it is only the insentient body of the gods and others that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the production of the splendor of other bodies and so forth, and not the conscious Self.
And in the case of the spider, saliva produced from the consumption of smaller insects attains a state of solidity and becomes the thread."
Furthermore, the crane conceives upon hearing the sound of thunder,
and the lotus plant, though devoid of consciousness, acts as if it were conscious by moving its body toward another pond;
therefore, these are not appropriate analogies for Brahman.
One should reply to him: "This is not a fault, because what is intended to be expressed is merely the difference from the examples of the potter and so forth.

For instance, although potters and the like, as well as gods and the like, are equally conscious, potters and others depend upon external means when beginning an effect, whereas gods and others do not.
Likewise, we shall explain this statement—that even though Brahman is conscious, it will not require any external means—by means of the examples of the gods and others.
Therefore, the intention is that there is no absolute rule; for just as the capacity of one is observed, so too must it be for all. (25) [Note:
*Loka* is that by which an object is perceived or known; it refers to the scriptures such as the Mantras and Arthavādas, as well as the usage of elders.]
*Abhidhyāna* means volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Just as in the *Mahābhārata*, the continuous succession of garments for Draupadī arose from the mere volition of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, so too does Brahman possess causality even though it is without external assistance.

Now, one might raise the following objection—which is the doubt to be set aside by the Sūtra: "Brahman is not the cause, because while being conscious, it is without assistance, like a potter who is devoid of clay and other materials. To this, he states the potential counter-argument: "This might be so... [and so forth].
He states "as in the case of gods and so forth" because that reason also suffers from the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding gods and others.
That by which an object is perceived or known is the "world" (*loka*), namely the scriptures such as the *mantras* and *arthavādas*, as well as the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
"Abhidhyāna" means volitional resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
Now, one might object: "In the examples ranging from the gods down to the spider, there is no consciousness in the bodies [of the agents].
In the cases of the crane and the lotus plant, which are conscious, the cloud's sound and the body respectively serve as auxiliary factors for their agency in setting forth the embryo.
Therefore, because of these specific causes, there is no deviation [from the rule]. This is the doubt raised by the words beginning with "If he should say... and so forth.
He offers a rebuttal, stating that there is indeed an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*), by saying: "One should say to him [the following].
This fault is known as the "dissimilarity of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntavaiṣamya*).

For in this case, the reason (*hetu*) must be understood as "consciousness" (*cetanatva*)—characterized by being the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃdhīviṣayatva*) and common to the body which has attained identity with the mind (*cittādātmyāpanna*)—and not as primary selfhood (*mukhyātmatva*).
Because in your example of the potter, there would be the fallacy of the probans being deficient;
furthermore, "being without assistance" for a conscious being means being devoid of any cause distinct from itself,
and since both [the properties of being without assistance and being conscious] exist in gods and so forth, there is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra).
Because the body is included within one's own self, it lacks any existence apart from that self.

Thus, gods and others differ from a potter in that they do not depend on anything external to themselves for effects such as a jar; and Brahman differs from the gods because He does not even require a body.
For kings, gods, and others, there is no single uniform set of causal materials at the commencement of an undertaking;
indeed, it is heard in the Mahābhārata that by the mere resolve of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a succession of garments arose for Draupadī.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the cause even when acting without assistance. //25//
END BsCom_2,1.8.25 START BsCom_2,1.9.26 9.
The Section Concerning the Consequence of the Whole Being [Involved] (Kṛtsnaprasakti-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 26–29.
Either there would be the consequence of [the cause] being entirely transformed, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its partlessness.

It has been established that Brahman—conscious, one, and without a second—is the cause of the world, transforming itself without depending on external means, like milk or like the gods and so forth. However, for the sake of purifying the meaning of the scripture, he now raises an objection.
There would follow the consequence of the transformation of the whole; that is, the entire Brahman would undergo transformation into the form of the effect, because it is partless.
For if Brahman were possessed of parts like the earth and other elements, then one part of it would transform while another part would remain as it was.
Furthermore, Brahman is understood from the scriptures to be partless: "Without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19);
"For the divine Person is formless, existing both within and without, and unborn" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
"This great being is infinite, boundless, and indeed a mass of consciousness alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12).
This is that Self which is "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26),
"neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8),
and so forth— passages which negate all specific attributes.
Furthermore, since a transformation of only one part is possible, if the consequence of a transformation of the whole were to follow, it would entail the destruction of the root [cause].
Moreover, the instruction regarding the object to be seen would become purposeless, because the effect would be seen without effort;
and since a Brahman distinct from that [effect] would be impossible, there would also be a contradiction with scriptural passages concerning its being unborn and so forth.

Now, if one were to accept that Brahman possesses parts (sāvayava) out of a desire to avoid this fault, even so, those scriptural passages cited as establishing its partlessness would be contradicted;
furthermore, if it has parts, the consequence of impermanence (anityatva) follows.
Thus, he objects: "In every way, this position cannot be maintained. // 26 //
[Otherwise,] it would have undergone transformation in one part while remaining untransformed in another; thus,
there would be the consequence of total transformation.

When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arises—based on the milk analogy—that Brahman undergoes transformation (pariṇāmin), this section (adhikaraṇa) is introduced to establish the definitive conclusion that the meaning of the scripture is illusory manifestation (vivarta) and not transformation. Thus, he states the connection between the preceding and the subsequent sections as being one of "the relation of the effect" (kāryatva-saṃgati) by saying: "The conscious... and so forth.
The subject matter is the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) regarding the creation of the world from the partless Brahman.

In the doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the logical principle that "whatever is partless cannot undergo transformation," or not, the author explains the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra—"In its entirety" (*kṛtsna*)—stating:
"By one who asserts that Brahman undergoes transformation, it must be stated whether Brahman is partless or possessed of parts."

It has been stated that, in the first case, the entire Brahman would exist in the form of a transformation; this he explains by means of a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta) with the words beginning "yadi brahma" (if Brahman...).
"Paryaṇaṃsyat" means it would have become transformed; and "ekadeśaśca avāsthāsyat" means one part would have remained untransformed.
He states the resulting defect, based on the establishment of partlessness from the aforementioned scriptural passages, with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

He states another defect with the words "The state of being visible" (*draṣṭavyatā*): if the fundamental Brahman-self does not exist apart from its transformation, then the instruction that "the Self is to be seen" would be devoid of meaning.

Furthermore, he states that if one accepts the birth and destruction of Brahman through its nature as a transformation, there is a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "unborn" and "immortal," using the words "Unbornness, etc. (*ajatvādīti*).
Anticipating the position that [the self] possesses parts, he refutes it with the remainder of the sūtra, beginning with "Now" (atha) and so forth. //26//
But on account of scripture, [the world] is [real], because it has its root in the Word. 2.1.27.
With the word "but" (tu), he refutes the objection:
indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in our position;
first of all, the consequence of the whole [cause] being [required for every effect] does not apply.
Why?
Because of scripture (śruti).
For just as the origin of the world from Brahman is heard in scripture, so too is the existence of Brahman apart from its modifications heard in scripture.

Because there is a designation based on the distinction between the cause and its modification, as in: "That deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate names and forms'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2);
and: "Such is his greatness, and the Puruṣa is even greater than that; all beings are one quarter of him, while his three quarters are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).

This follows from such passages as these, as well as from the statement that [the Self] has the heart as its abode and from the statement regarding union with Being (*sat-sampatti*): "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
If the entire Brahman were consumed by becoming the effect, [this would be impossible].
Thus, the qualification "having entered deep sleep" would be untenable;
for [the soul] is eternally united with the unmodified Brahman, and because there is no such thing as a modified Brahman.
Likewise, it is because the sense-objects of Brahman are denied, whereas it is logical that the sense-objects belong to a modification.
Therefore, there exists an unmodified Brahman;
nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding its partlessness,
for since partlessness is itself heard in scripture, it must necessarily be accepted.

Brahman has the word as its source and the word as its means of valid cognition; it is not based on the senses or other such means of knowledge, and must therefore be accepted exactly as the word declares it.
Furthermore, the word establishes both [attributes] of Brahman: the impossibility of its being entirely exhausted [in manifestation] and its partlessness (*niravayavatva*).
Even in the case of worldly things such as gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs, their powers are seen to have multiple contradictory effects due to the diversity of place, time, and causal conditions.

Even those [powers] cannot be understood through mere reasoning alone without instruction, such that one could know: "This entity has this many powers, these are its auxiliaries, these are its objects, and these are its purposes.
How much more so, then, would the nature of Brahman—which is of an inconceivable essence—not be defined without the Word?
Thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "Those entities which are indeed inconceivable, one should not apply reasoning to them."
And that which is beyond the primary natures (prakṛtis) is the characteristic of the inconceivable.
Thus, the comprehension of the true nature of supersensuous objects is rooted solely in verbal testimony (*śabda*).

Now, it may be objected that even by means of verbal testimony, a contradictory matter cannot be made known—for instance, that Brahman, which is partless, undergoes transformation and yet does not do so entirely.
If Brahman were indeed partless, it could not undergo transformation at all.
Or else, it would transform in its entirety;

or, if it were to transform in one form while remaining as it is in another, then by the conceptualization of such a differentiation of forms, it would necessarily follow that it possesses parts (*sāvayava*).

For regarding the domain of ritual action, in cases such as "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice" and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," [the same logic applies].
Even when a contradiction is perceived, resorting to an alternative (vikalpa) serves as the means for resolving that contradiction, because the performance [of an action] depends upon the person.

But in this case, even by resorting to an alternative, the resolution of the contradiction is not possible, because the reality of the object does not depend upon the person. Therefore, this [objection] is difficult to establish.
This is not a fault.
This is because we accept that the distinction of forms is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).
Indeed, a thing does not become possessed of parts merely by a distinction of form imagined through ignorance.
For the moon, though appearing as if it were many to one whose vision is impaired by cataracts, does not thereby actually become many.

Through the differentiation of form characterized by name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which is imagined by ignorance (avidyā), consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and being indefinable as either identical to or different from reality, Brahman becomes the locus for all worldly transactions such as transformation;
yet, in its ultimate nature, it remains beyond all worldly transactions and devoid of transformation.

Furthermore, since the differentiation of name and form is merely a verbal handle (vācārambhaṇamātra) and is imagined through ignorance (avidyā), the partless nature of Brahman is not contradicted. Nor is this scriptural text on transformation intended to establish actual transformation,
because no fruit is perceived in the realization of such a transformation.
This [scriptural passage], however, is intended to establish the nature of Brahman as the Self, which is devoid of all empirical transactions,
because its realization results in that very attainment; for,
having begun with "This is the Self described as 'not this, not this'," the text concludes, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
Therefore, in our position, there is no possibility of any fault whatsoever. // 27 //

Regarding what was stated—that the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is difficult to maintain—the author establishes the final conclusion through the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), saying "because of scripture" (*śruteḥ*).
By means of the word "but" (*tu*) and so forth, he demonstrates through the application of the Sūtra that the two previously mentioned defects do not exist in his own position.

He states, "That divinity... (*seyaṃ devatā...*), showing that there is no consequence of the entire [Brahman] being exhausted, because scripture declares the existence of the Lord as distinct from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which is the object of His vision and the object of His creative activity—by virtue of His being the Seer and the Transformer.
He says "tāvān" (so much) to show that its separate existence is heard in scripture even by way of deficiency or excess.
And he says "tathā" (likewise) to show that there exists Brahman as unmodified;
for according to the scriptural text, "That very Self is here in the heart," there exists Brahman distinct from the visible world.
The meaning is that this is because of the qualification "then," which refers to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
He states another inferential mark: "and likewise, the sense organs," etc.

Since modifications such as pleasure and pain fall within the range of the sense organs, while the Śruti—beginning with "It is not grasped by the eye"—denies that of Brahman, and since there is the Śruti stating that Brahman is beyond the reach of speech and mind, the meaning is that there exists an immutable Brahman.
Having stated that the fault of total pervasion (*kṛtsnaprasakti*) does not exist, he says "nor" (*na ca*) to indicate that the second fault also does not exist.
[Objection: But if Brahman exists both as the nature of the effect and as something separate, then its possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*) would be unavoidable.

Since it is impossible for a single partless entity to exist in two ways, the notion that Brahman—which has become twofold—is possessed of parts contradicts logic; thus, with a hidden intention, [the author] dispels the doubt of one who does not understand the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) by stating, "And because it is rooted in scripture.
For if the power of even those things perceived through the senses by ordinary people is inconceivable, what then need be said regarding Brahman, which is accessible only through scripture?
Therefore, both the partlessness of Brahman and its bifurcation must be accepted exactly according to the scriptural word;
it is not to be subverted by reasoning—this is the meaning.

The meaning of the Smṛti is that that which is beyond the primordial material causes (prakṛti), which are the natures of things perceived through direct perception, and which is distinct from them and knowable solely through instruction, is of an inconceivable nature.
He raises an objection due to a failure to understand the underlying intention: "But [the cognition] by means of a word also...

Alternatively, he challenges the interpretation of the *siddhāntasūtra* presented by certain partial adherents (*ekadeśin*) who hold that Brahman is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmī*), stating: "But...
The meaning is that a word depends upon the knowledge of its semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).
Now, one might argue that by resorting to the dilemma of whether Brahman possesses parts or is partless, all scriptural statements could be reconciled; to this, he says: "Action" (kriyā).

If Brahman were partless, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its being the material cause (prakṛti); if it possessed parts, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural term "partless."
Furthermore, conceptual construction (vikalpa) is untenable with respect to a real entity;

therefore, since no other mode [of operation] is perceived, the validity of the scriptures (śruti) is difficult to establish. To this objection, the author reveals his own intention: "This is not a fault.

Because it is accepted that even a partless and immutable reality undergoes transformations of name and form imagined through ignorance (avidyā), the fault of being "difficult to establish" does not apply.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction, because actual immutability [is maintained] while [the world] has the nature of imagined modification.
Anticipating the objection that if a difference in form were admitted, it would follow that [Brahman] possesses parts, he explains this with the words "for not... and so forth.
Having rejected the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being affected, he rejects another defect with the words "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*).
Now, one might ask: how can the transformation taught in the Śruti be of a false nature?
To this he replies: "And this [is not so].
It has been stated more than once that creation is merely restated as being subordinate to the non-dual Brahman, and is not what is being primarily established.
Therefore, he concludes that there is no fault whatsoever in the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavāda) with the words: "tasmāt" (therefore). //27//
And likewise in the self; for [the appearances] are indeed manifold. (BBs 2.1.28)
Furthermore, one should not dispute here as to how a manifold creation could occur within a single Brahman without the destruction of its own essential nature;

for it is taught that even within a single self acting as a dreamer, a manifold creation occurs without the destruction of its own essential nature: "There are no chariots there, no yoking of chariots, nor roads, yet he creates chariots, yoking of chariots, and roads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10).

As stated in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10 and elsewhere, even in the world, various creations such as elephants and horses are seen among gods and magicians without the destruction of their own nature.
Likewise, within the one Brahman, a manifold creation of diverse forms will occur without the destruction of its essential nature. // 28 //
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is a change of state through the destruction of the previous state,
as in the case of milk becoming curds;
illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is a change of state without the destruction of the previous form.

Just as the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, the author of the Sūtras clarifies the doctrine of Māyā by strengthening the view that Brahman is the material cause through the analogy of the witness of a dream, stating: "And [it is seen] in the Self" (sūtra 3.2.3).
"Rathayogāḥ" refers to horses. //28//
And because of the faults in one's own position. (BBs 2.1.29)
This same fault applies equally to the other side as well.

For even for the proponent of *pradhāna*, his own position is that the *pradhāna*—which is partless, unlimited, and devoid of sound and other qualities—is the cause of an effect that possesses parts, is limited, and has sound and other qualities.
In that case too, either the consequence of the whole [cause] being consumed follows because the *pradhāna* is partless, or else there is a contradiction with the very admission of its partlessness.
Now, it might be argued that they do not indeed accept the *pradhāna* as being partless;

rather, the three qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are eternal, and their state of equilibrium is the *pradhāna*. Thus, because it possesses those very qualities as its parts, it is "with parts" (*sāvayava*).
However, the fault under discussion cannot be avoided by such a form of "having parts."
For even among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, each one individually possesses the same partlessness (*niravayavatva*);
and since each one, when assisted by the other two, serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for its own class of manifestations (*prapañca*), the objection against our own position applies equally.
If it is argued that they must possess parts (*sāvayavatva*) because reasoning cannot be established otherwise, [we reply:]...
Even so, the fault of impermanence and other defects would still follow.
Now, if the intention is that the potencies themselves— indicated by the diversity of effects— are the constituent parts,
then those [potencies] remain as much a feature for the proponent of Brahman (brahmavādin) as they do for others.

Likewise, for those who maintain the theory of atoms (*aṇuvādin*), if an atom, when conjoining with another atom, were to do so in its entirety because it lacks parts, then, since expansion would be impossible, the consequence would be that it remains merely an atom.

If, on the other hand, it were to conjoin by means of one part, even then the admission of its being partless would be contradicted. Thus, this same fault applies equally to one's own position as well; and because it is equal, it should not be attributed to one side alone.
The proponent of Brahman has thus avoided the defect in his own position. [29] (FN:
For the Vaiśeṣikas, the process is as follows: two atoms, having conjoined, produce one dyad; and by three such dyads, one triad is produced.)
Furthermore, since defects such as the consequence of the whole [pradhāna] being involved apply to the positions of the Sāṃkhyas and others as well, they should not be raised against us;

this is according to the maxim: "The defect which is equal for both sides. Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "svapakṣa... (In his own position...). He raises an objection here: "nanu" (But surely...), regarding whether pradhāna is partless or possesses parts—if it is partless, there is the consequence of the whole being involved; if it possesses parts, there is a contradiction with the accepted doctrine that it is partless.
Is the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas* a modification (*vikāra*) or a collection (*samudāya*)?
In the first case, it would not possess the status of the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
Because it is a transformation;
in the second case, there is an absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
because the aggregate, being non-substantial, lacks a root.

Now, if it is argued that the partless qualities themselves are the material cause (*prakṛti*) of various transformations, then [the author] refutes this with the words "not so" and so forth, intending to show that the total exhaustion of the root would be unavoidable.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Therefore, because [the objection] is equal [to our own position], we are not to be questioned."

If each [quality], such as *sattva* and the others, were a partless (*niravayava*) material cause accompanied by the other two qualities, then—since it has been stated that this would entail the entire material cause being transformed into the form of the effect, resulting in the destruction of the root—this reasoning intended to prove partlessness is fallacious. Therefore, because the qualities possess parts due to their capacity for transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), like clay and so forth, there is no consequence of the whole being transformed, as transformation can occur in only one part; thus he raises an objection with the word "tarka" (reasoning).
He offers a rebuttal, stating "even so," [meaning] that even in the absence of this fault, another fault would arise.

Anticipating the objection that the qualities (*guṇas*) are not the constituent parts (*avayavas*) of the cause— like threads [are for a cloth]— but rather are powers (*śaktis*) residing therein inferred from the diversity of effects— he states "now" (*atha*) and so forth, showing that the Brahman too would possess parts (*sāvayavatva*) by virtue of its illusory powers (*māyika-śakti*), which is an equal [logical] consequence.
He states that even in the case of the atomic theory (*aṇuvāda*), the fault is equal, saying "likewise" (*tathā*).
The connection is that the fault is the same as in the Sāṃkhya system.
Regarding two partless atoms (*paramāṇu*), their conjunction must be either all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*) or non-all-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

In the first case, there would be the consequence that its effect, possessing double the dimension, would become a mere single atom, because a larger magnitude (prathiman) is impossible. For when one atom is pervaded by another from above, below, and on all sides, a substance greater than that cannot possibly exist. In the second case, the consequence is that atoms would possess parts (sāvayavatva). This is the meaning. [The opponent objects: "But is it not improper to state an equality of faults, like saying 'You are a thief' when the reply is 'You too are a thief'?"; to this, he says: "But it has been refuted... etc.

For it has been stated that in the doctrine of Māyā, everything is consistent, like a dream; therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction in the concordance [of the Vedānta texts] with respect to the partless Brahman. //29//

"And [the world] is endowed with all [qualities] because of seeing that [Brahman].
(BBs 2.1.30) It has been stated that the manifold expansion of transformations is possible for even a single Brahman due to its connection with diverse powers.
But how, then, is it understood that this is the supreme Brahman?
This is stated:
"And she is endowed with all [perfections] because she is seen as such";
it must be accepted that the supreme deity is possessed of all powers.
Why?
Because that is seen.

For scripture demonstrates the possession of all powers by the supreme deity: "He whose work is all, whose desire is all, who possesses all odors, all tastes, who has pervaded all this, who is without speech and without regard."
"One whose desires are true, whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4);
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
"By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart"—such passages as these [establish this]. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9) // 30 // [FN:
*Abhyāttaḥ* means pervaded on all sides.]
"Avākī" means devoid of the faculty of speech;
"anādara" means free from desire;
"sarvopetā" means endowed with everything.

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a contradiction—by the principle that "the unreal cannot proceed from the real"—with the *samanvaya* (harmonization) which declares the creation of the world by Brahman, who possesses the power of *māyā*, on the grounds that Brahman is bodiless; and regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is indeed a contradiction because the reasoning is not fallacious; [the author], stating the connection (*saṅgati*) as being one of the same subject matter through the corroboration of the previously mentioned possession of power, explains the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) with the words beginning "of the one," and so forth.

It has already been stated that the result [of the inquiry] is the contradiction or non-contradiction between the prima facie and final positions; this should be understood as extending to the end of the chapter.
"Abhyātta" means pervaded on all sides.
"Avākī" means devoid of the organ of speech.
Disregard is the absence of desire. //30//
If it is argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of organs (*vikaraṇatva*), that has already been answered. (BS 2.1.31)

It might be argued as follows: the scripture teaches that the supreme deity is devoid of instruments, stating such things as, "without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
How, then, could she, despite being endowed with all powers, be capable of producing effects?
For gods and others, though they are sentient and endowed with all powers, are known to be capable of performing their respective functions only when equipped with internal organs and instruments.
If it is asked: "How can the possession of all powers be possible for a deity from whom all distinctions have been negated by the statement 'not this, not this' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.23)?"
What needs to be said regarding this has already been stated previously.
This most profound Brahman is to be realized through scripture alone; it is not to be realized through logic.
Furthermore, there is no rule that whatever capacity is observed in one thing must necessarily exist in another as well.

It has already been stated that even for Brahman, from whom all distinctions have been negated, the possession of all powers is possible by means of presenting the differentiation of forms imagined through ignorance.
And so the scripture says: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19).
Thus, it shows that even though Brahman is devoid of instruments, there is a connection with all capacities.
Having restated the logic of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes it with the words "because of being devoid of organs" (vikaraṇatvāt).
It is observed that even for sentient beings such as gods who possess power, agency is seen only when there is identification with a body; in its absence, as in deep sleep, it is not seen.
Therefore, although Brahman possesses power, it lacks agency because it is bodiless.
The meaning of the objection is that power is not possible for one who is bodiless.
[The response is: Although agency is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) which is devoid of organs, it is possible for the Lord (īśvara);
this was stated in the sūtra, "And also like the gods and others in the world."

In this regard, the meaning of the resolution is that since it is impossible for the imagined body to be the substratum of *māyā*, it is logical that only consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of distinctions is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of *māyā*. //31//

Section 11: The Topic on Having a Purpose. Sūtras 32–33. END BsCom_2,1.10.31 START BsCom_2,1.11.32 11 prayojanavattvādhikaraṇam. sū. 32-33. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: Now, it might be argued that since the world is seen to have a purpose, the Supreme Lord must likewise have a purpose for creating the world. To this, we reply: No, because He has no unfulfilled desire. For the Lord is eternally satisfied; He has no unfulfilled desires to be fulfilled by creation. Furthermore, creation would be purposeless for Him who is already perfect. Moreover, if the Lord were to create out of mere sport (līlā), He would be subject to the fault of partiality and cruelty, as He would favor some and harm others. Therefore, the Lord creates the world not for His own purpose, but for the sake of the souls, providing them with the fruits of their own past actions (karma). Thus, the Lord is free from all defects, and the world proceeds according to the law of karma. END BsCom_2,1.11.32 START BsCom_2,1.12.34 12 vaiṣamyanairghṛṇyādhikaraṇam. sū. 34-36. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: Furthermore, it may be objected that the Lord is subject to the faults of partiality and cruelty, because He creates some beings happy and others miserable. This is not so, because the inequality of the world is due to the inequality of the souls' own past actions. The Lord is like rain, which falls equally upon all, yet the plants grow differently according to their seeds. The Lord merely provides the common cause (nimitta) for the manifestation of the fruits of karma; He does not create the inequality itself. Therefore, the Lord is neither partial nor cruel. END BsCom_2,1.12.34 START BsCom_2,1.13.37 13 sarvadharmopapatyadhikaraṇam. sū. 37. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: Moreover, in the case of the individual soul (jīva), certain attributes such as agency and enjoyership are observed, whereas in the case of the Supreme Lord, attributes such as omniscience and omnipotence are observed. These attributes are not contradictory, for they belong to different levels of reality. Just as fire possesses both the power to burn and the power to illuminate, so too the Lord possesses both the power to create and the power to know. All the attributes of the Lord are logically consistent with His nature as the Supreme Reality. Therefore, the Supreme Lord is established as the cause of the universe. END BsCom_2,1.13.37 START BsCom_2,1.14.38 14 racanānupapattyadhikaraṇam. sū. 38-41. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: It may be argued that the world cannot be created by an intelligent being, because its construction is so vast and complex that it is beyond the capacity of any finite intellect. To this, we reply: No, for we observe that even small things are constructed by intelligent beings. A house, though large, is built by a skilled architect; why then should the entire world be impossible? Furthermore, the world is not a single, solid mass, but is composed of diverse parts and functions, which indicates a design. Therefore, the world must have been created by an intelligent being. END BsCom_2,1.14.38 START BsCom_2,1.15.42 15 pravṛttyanupapattyadhikaraṇam. sū. 42-43. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: Moreover, it may be argued that an intelligent creator is unnecessary, because the world proceeds spontaneously like grass growing in spring. Similarly, the world, being a highly organized system, requires an intelligent architect. Furthermore, if the world were spontaneous, there would be no reason for its periodic dissolution and re-creation. Therefore, the world is the work of an intelligent being. END BsCom_2,1.15.42 START BsCom_2,1.16.44 16 payombuvaccettatrāpi. sū. 44. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: If it be argued that just as water turns into ice or milk into curds without an external agent, so too the world arises spontaneously, we say: Even in those cases, there is an unseen cause (adṛṣṭa) or a change in conditions that acts as the efficient cause. Water does not turn into ice without cold, nor does milk turn into curds without heat and time. Therefore, the analogy does not hold, and the world requires an intelligent creator. [The following is the translation of the relevant portion: If one were to infer a creator who is different from the one described in the scriptures, such a being would be devoid of the power of knowledge required for creation. END BsCom_2,1.22.50 START BsCom_2,1.23.51 23 abhisandhyādiṣvapi caivam. sū. 51.
[The world] does not [arise from a conscious creator], because it possesses a purpose (*prayojanavattvāt*).
Otherwise, one would imply that the world has a conscious creator;
however, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), being conscious, is certainly not capable of fashioning this manifold image of the world.
Why?
Because all activities are purposeful.
For in the world, a conscious person who acts with deliberation is never observed to undertake even a slight activity that does not serve his own purpose.
How much more so, then, in the case of this activity which involves an even greater intensity of effort?

And there is a Vedic scripture that echoes what is well-known in the world: "Verily, not for the sake of all does everything become dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
Indeed, this undertaking—which consists in fashioning the cosmic image of the world with its manifold variety—is an activity of the greatest intensity.

If this activity of the conscious Supreme Self were also postulated as being for the sake of its own purpose, then the scriptural teaching of the Supreme Self’s complete contentment would be contradicted;
or, in the absence of a purpose, there would likewise be an absence of activity.
If it should be argued that even though he is conscious, the Supreme Self will act just like a madman who, due to a lapse of intellect, acts without any personal purpose, [we reply: no.
If that were the case, the omniscience of the Supreme Self as heard in scripture would be contradicted.
Therefore, creation from a conscious being is untenable. // 32 // [FN:
The "error of the intellect" refers to the absence of discrimination.]
It is not so, because it possesses a purpose.
The subject matter under consideration is the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) which asserts that the world originates from a complete Brahman.
Does this [concordance] contradict the principle that a conscious being who is not deluded does not fashion a fruitless object? It does not.

In this doubt, since the agency [of the Lord] was previously stated by asserting His capacity even while bodiless on the strength of scripture, he explains the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra—beginning with "Otherwise," etc.—by way of an objection to that.
Anticipating the objection that the Lord might still engage in creation for the sake of another's purpose even in the absence of a fruit for Himself, he cites the scripture: "And it happens," etc.

It is a worldly convention that whatever activity is undertaken by a discerning person is for the sake of its own fruit; nor is there any deviation from this rule in the case of the activity of a compassionate person,
because even that is motivated by the desire to eliminate one's own mental agitation caused by an inability to endure the suffering of others— this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, he says "gurutara... [in the verse] to state that the fruit of such great exertion must be explained.
If it is then argued that even for Īśvara there is activity for his own sake, he says "yadiyamapi...":
the meaning is that if it were not for his own sake, the absence of activity previously mentioned would follow.
Fearing the objection that the Lord might not be a conscious being, he states the contradiction with scripture beginning with "Now" (atha) and so forth.
The fault of the intellect is the absence of discrimination. //32//
But, as in the world, his activity is solely for the sake of sport (līlā). 2.1.33.
With the word "tu" (but), he refutes the objection:
just as in the world, certain activities of one who has fulfilled all desires occur in the form of mere play during sports and diversions, having no other purpose in view;
and just as inhalation, exhalation, and so forth occur by their very nature, without aiming at any external purpose.
In this way, even for the Lord, there will be an activity consisting solely of divine play (*līlā*), arising from his own nature alone and without depending on any other purpose.
For no other purpose of the Lord can be established through either reasoning or scripture;
nor can one's inherent nature (*svabhāva*) be subjected to questioning.
Although this construction of the cosmic image appears to us as if it were an undertaking of great effort, nevertheless, for the Supreme Lord, this is merely sport (*līlā*),
because His power is unlimited.
Even if some subtle purpose might be imagined in the case of sports in the world, even so, no purpose whatsoever can be imagined here.
Because of the scriptural statement that [the Lord] has all desires fulfilled;
nor is there a lack of activity or activity like that of a madman,
because of the scriptural statement regarding creation.
And because of the scriptural statement that [the Lord] is omniscient.

Furthermore, it must not be forgotten that this scriptural account of creation does not have ultimate reality as its object, since it pertains to the sphere of conventional usage involving names and forms imagined through ignorance (avidyā), and because its primary purpose is to establish that Brahman is the Self. // 33 //
Note: "Distinct" means distinct from *līlā* (divine play).
The distinction is this: there is no lack of authority for the scriptural teaching on creation, nor is there any insanity regarding the scriptural teaching on omniscience.

He explains the *siddhāntasūtra*— that the aforementioned principle is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the pastimes (*līlā*) of kings— with the word "but" (*tu*). "Distinct" (*vyatirikta*) means distinct from the pastimes (*līlā*).
The meaning is: "in those delightful places which consist of the forms of play.

Although it might be conceivable that even the play (*līlā*) of kings and others has some fruit, such as the manifestation of pleasure, nevertheless, while there is purposeful activity by wise persons regarding [the cessation of] sighing and so forth, there is no fruit intended for themselves therein; thus, he states another instance of deviation with the words "and as... (*yathā ca*).
The nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is mobility, or rather, its *prārabdha* [karma] is the cause of inhalation and so forth;
the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*) is *māyā* accompanied by time and karma. Now, why is it said that the Lord’s creation of the world is merely for the sake of sport (*līlā*)?
Let some kind of fruit indeed be postulated; regarding that, he says: "No."
The meaning is that it would contradict [the Lord's] state of having all desires fulfilled.
Now, one might ask: why does the Lord not remain silent?
Why does He create a world that is fruitless for Himself and brings suffering to others?
Regarding this, he says: "And not by way of intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that since creation is unavoidable when the collection of causes—time, dharma, and so forth—is present.
As for what was stated, that "a result must be asserted because of the great effort involved," [that too is addressed].
Regarding that, he states the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) with the words "Even though... and so forth.
He states the sublation of the reasoning—that even for one who acts little, a result must be spoken of because it is observed to be so in the world—with the words "Even if... and so forth.
There is no non-activity [of the world] regarding the scriptural teaching of creation (*sṛṣṭiśruti*).
The distinction is that there is no madness in the scriptural teaching of omniscience.
He states, "And this [creation] is not [futile]," because, like the creation in a dream, this creation is mere illusion (māyāmātra) and thus has no expectation of a fruit;
nor is there any pointlessness in the scriptures concerning fruitless creation.
The meaning is that one must not forget that [the Self] is endowed with purposefulness and other qualities by virtue of being the remainder after the successful realization of Brahman. //33//

END BsCom_2,1.11.33 START BsCom_2,1.12.34 Section on Inequality and Cruelty; Sūtras 34–36. [The opponent argues: "If it be so that the Lord creates the world out of compassion for all beings, then He would create it as entirely uniform. Furthermore, since He does not create some beings to experience happiness while creating others to experience suffering, He must be accused of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*). [The Siddhāntin replies: This objection is not valid. For the Lord creates the diversity of the world based on the specific karma of each individual being. It is like a rain-cloud which pours down rain equally upon all, yet the seeds that sprout according to their own nature produce various kinds of plants. Thus, the Lord is neither partial nor cruel, as He merely provides the common cause while the specific cause lies in the karma of the beings themselves. Furthermore, the Lord’s compassion is indeed proven by the fact that He grants liberation to those who have performed good deeds.

Therefore, the charge of partiality and cruelty does not apply. [The opponent asks: But how can there be such a variety of karmas at the beginning of creation, when no beings existed before? [The reply: This is not a fault, because the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless. Just as the sequence of seed and sprout has no discernible starting point, so too the succession of karma and its fruits has no first beginning. Consequently, the diversity of the world is established through the beginningless variety of karma. Thus, the Lord remains free from the charges of partiality and cruelty. [The opponent objects: If the Lord depends on karma, then His status as the independent creator is lost. [The reply: No, for He is the dispenser of the fruits of karma. Karma alone cannot produce results without the supervision of an intelligent agent, just as food cannot digest itself without the aid of a physician. Therefore, the Lord is the supreme ruler who ordains the fruits of actions according to the merit or demerit of each being, remaining eternally free from partiality and cruelty. Thus ends the section on Inequality and Cruelty. Sūtras 34–36. End.
