"Neither partiality nor cruelty [can be attributed to Him], because He has regard for [the merit and demerit of beings]; for thus [scripture] shows.

Furthermore, the status of God as the cause of the world's birth and so forth is challenged once more—following the maxim of "firmly planting a pillar"—in order to strengthen the point already asserted:
that it is not logical for God to be the cause of the world.
Why?
Because it would entail the consequence of partiality and cruelty;
for [if he were the creator], he would make some, such as the gods and others, partakers of extreme happiness, [while making others suffer].

For if God were to fashion such an uneven creation— some beings, like animals and the like, experiencing extreme suffering, and others, like humans and the like, experiencing moderate enjoyment— it would follow that passion and hatred arise in Him just as they do in an ordinary person;
consequently, the very nature of God, established by the Śruti and Smṛti as being characterized by purity and other such qualities, would be destroyed.

Likewise, even by base people, mercilessness and extreme cruelty would be censured; for [if God were the cause], these would follow from His inflicting suffering and from the destruction of all living beings.
Therefore, since this would entail the consequence of partiality and mercilessness, it follows that God is not the cause. To this we reply: partiality and mercilessness do not apply to God.
Why?
Because [the Lord] is dependent.
For if a solitary, independent Lord were to fashion an unequal creation, these two faults—partiality and cruelty—would indeed follow;
however, there is no such thing as the creatorship of one who is independent.
For the Lord creates an unequal world while being dependent on something.
If it is asked what he depends upon,
we reply that he depends upon merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*).

Therefore, since the diversity of creation depends upon the merit and demerit of the living beings being created, this is not the fault of the Lord. Rather, the Lord is to be regarded as being like the rain-cloud;
for just as the rain-cloud is the common cause in the production of rice, barley, and other crops, [so too is the Lord].
However, regarding the diversity between rice, barley, and so forth, the specific and uncommon potencies residing in their respective seeds are the causes;
likewise, God acts as the common cause in the creation of gods, humans, and others.

But regarding the diversity among gods, humans, and so forth, the specific and uncommon karmas residing in those respective individual souls are indeed the causes. Thus, because God is dependent [on these factors], He is not tainted by partiality or cruelty.
How, then, is it understood that the Lord creates the transmigratory world—low, middling, and high—in dependence [upon other factors]?

For the Śruti demonstrates this: "For He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; and He alone makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down" (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 3.8).
And [it is said]: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).

Smṛti as well shows that the Lord's quality of being a bestower of grace depends precisely upon the specific actions of living beings—for instance, in passages such as: "In whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.11). // 34 //
FN: A *pṛthagjana* is a common person.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "This Lord (*īśvara*) causes him whom he desires to raise up—that is, to lead upward—to act rightly.
There is neither partiality (*vaiṣamya*) nor cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*).
The subject matter is the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) regarding the creation of the world by a faultless Brahman.

When there is doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the maxim that "one who acts unjustly is possessed of defects," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set forth with the words "And again," etc., following the connection of the objection: "That very creatorship which was previously stated to be for sport (*līlayā*) is not tenable if it depends on karma and other factors, because that would result in [Brahman] being non-supreme; yet if it were independent, it would result in the presence of defects such as passion."
The proposition that Brahman alone is the cause of the world was established in the *Janmādi-sūtra*.
An ordinary person is a commoner;
as for the scripture, it says, "Blameless and stainless."
The Smṛti states: "There is none dear to Me, nor any hateful.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "transparency and so forth," immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) is included;
the compound is analyzed as "that which consists of transparency and so forth, and which is the very nature of the Lord."
If [the Lord] were to act unfairly without regard for causes (nimitta), there would be defects such as partiality;
however, the author establishes the established tenet that the Lord does not lack dependence on causes, beginning with the words "evam prāpte" (this being the case).
Nor does dependence on causes imply a lack of lordship.

[The opponent objects: "Since the status of being a king or a lord remains constant regardless of whether one performs service [or not], let the diverse creation proceed from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) alone; what is the use of a Lord (*īśvara*)? To this, he says: "But the Lord is like the rain-cloud.
Since a specific cause produces its effect only when accompanied by common causes, the Lord is not redundant.
The sense is that otherwise, there would be the consequence of the rain-cloud being rendered useless.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "This Lord causes that person whom He desires to lead upward (*unninīṣate*)—that is, wishes to elevate—to perform good deeds.
Nor should it be argued that partiality remains a persistent flaw in one who causes some people to perform good deeds while causing others to perform evil deeds; [for this is not the case].

The meaning is that because the Lord is the common cause for the engagement of people in various actions according to their own nature—namely, the tendencies toward good and evil acquired since beginningless time—the Lord is therefore beyond reproach. //34//
If it is argued that [the distinction between souls and matter] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say no, because [the cycle] is beginningless. (BS 2.1.35)
"O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Since this determination of non-differentiation prior to creation is made, there is no karma depending upon which a diverse creation could occur;
for karma depends on the differentiation of bodies and so forth, which exists only after the time of creation.
Furthermore, since the differentiation of bodies and so forth would depend upon karma, a mutual dependency (itaretarāśrayatva) would result.

Therefore, let it be granted that the Lord acts in dependence on karma after the initial differentiation; however, prior to that differentiation, because karma—which is the cause of diversity—does not exist, it follows that the first creation must be uniform. If this is argued:
This is not a fault, because saṃsāra is beginningless.
This fault would arise only if saṃsāra had a beginning.

However, in the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the operation of both karma and the inequality of creation through a causal relationship—like that of a seed and its sprout—is not contradictory. // 35 //

The author of the Sūtras raises an objection—that because there is no karma caused by inequality in the first creation, it would have to be uniform, and consequently, all subsequent kalpas would likewise be so—and then provides the resolution: "Not due to karma.

Anticipating the doubt that the inequality in the first creation might be caused by karma existing after that creation, he points out the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) with the words: "After the creation... (sṛṣṭyuttara).
The phrase "the first creation" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should be understood that if there were uniformity at the beginning, then because there would be no cause for the emergence of diverse actions in the interim, it would be difficult to avoid the consequence that subsequent creations as well would necessarily be identical.
The refutation [of this objection] is easy to understand. //35//
But how, again, is it understood that this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is beginningless?
To this, he replies:
"It is both logically consistent and perceived.
It is logically consistent that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless.

For if saṃsāra had a beginning, it would follow that it arises spontaneously; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of even those who are liberated being born again into saṃsāra, as well as the consequence of encountering what has not been done (akṛtābhyāgama),
because the inequality of pleasure, pain, and so forth would be without cause.
It has been stated that Īśvara is not the cause of inequality;
nor is ignorance alone the cause of inequality,
because it is uniform in nature.
However, ignorance (*avidyā*), depending upon karma projected by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*), would be the cause of inequality.
Furthermore, a body cannot come into being without karma, nor can karma come into being without a body; thus, there is the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
However, if [the world] is beginningless, no fault arises because it is logically established through the analogy of the seed and the sprout;
moreover, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is perceived in both Śruti and Smṛti.
In the Śruti, for instance: "By this living self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

Thus, by designating the embodied self at the beginning of creation with the word "jīva"—on the basis of the etymological reason of "sustaining the vital breaths" (prāṇadhāraṇa)—the text demonstrates that transmigratory existence is beginningless.

For if it had a beginning, how could it have been designated at the start of creation with the word "jīva," based on the reason of sustaining the vital breaths, when its vital breaths were not yet established?
Nor could it have been so designated on the grounds that it *would* sustain them in the future.
For a past connection is stronger than a future connection,
because it has already been established:
"The Creator fashioned the sun and moon as they were before" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3).
And thus the wording of the mantra shows the existence of previous kalpas.
In the Smṛti as well, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is found: "Neither its form is perceived here in such a way, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation" (Gītā 15.3).
And in the Purāṇa it is established that there is no limit to the number of past and future kalpas.

He asks for the proof that there is no such thing as a "first creation" with the words, "But how? He shows that the proof consists of reasoning, scriptural testimony, and so forth, by commenting on the Sūtra with the words, "It is logically established. The meaning is that if one were to accept creation without a cause, the sections of the Veda dealing with knowledge (jñāna-kāṇḍa) and ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa) would become purposeless.

Raising the objection that "surely either God or ignorance must be the cause of the disparity in pleasure and so forth," he refutes this in succession with the words beginning "nor is it God. He then states what the cause actually is: "attachment and so forth."

Attachment, aversion, and delusion are the afflictions (*kleśa*); by their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), actions (*karman*)—consisting of a mixture of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—are projected.
It is with reference to these that ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the cause for the diversity of creation, such as pleasure and so forth.
Therefore, the sense is that one must accept an beginningless stream of afflictions and actions, acting as the auxiliary causes for ignorance.
Furthermore, if creation were to have a beginning, the production of the first body would be impossible due to the absence of a cause;
nor can karma be the cause.

Because action is impossible prior to the body, all disputants must therefore accept the beginninglessness of saṃsāra in order to avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence between action and the body; thus he says, "And not...

At the commencement of creation, at the very beginning of the world, even though the inner self (pratyagātman) has not yet acquired vital breath, one might suggest that it could be called by the term "jīva" based on the future act of sustaining [the body]; to this he replies, "And it will not sustain..."
The sense is that, in such passages as "A householder should take a wife of equal status," one must resort to a future state [of life] out of necessity.
Without instruction, the true nature of this tree of worldly existence—whether it is real or illusory—is not perceived;
and without knowledge, there is no end to it either.
Nor is a beginning perceived, precisely because of its non-existence;
nor is there a middle abiding, which is a state of persistence.
The meaning of the statement in the Gītā is that [the world] has a nature that perishes as soon as it is seen.
Even though saṃsāra is beginningless, its falsity establishes the restriction [found in scripture] that "Brahman is one only, without a second.
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction with the concordance [of all Vedānta texts] regarding the faultless Brahman. //36//
END BsCom_2,1.12.36 START BsCom_2,1.13.37 13.
The Section on the Arising of All Dharmas. Sūtra 37.
And because all phenomena arise [from it].

Having determined that the meaning of the Veda is that Brahman, which is consciousness, is the cause and the material source (*prakṛti*) of the world, the Teacher has refuted the defects such as "having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) and so forth, which were raised by opponents.
Now, intending to begin the section primarily concerned with the refutation of opposing views, he concludes the section primarily concerned with the acceptance of his own position.

Since all the attributes of a cause are logically established in the manner shown when this Brahman is accepted as the cause—namely, that "Brahman is omniscient, omnipotent, and possesses great illusory power (māyā)"—therefore, this philosophical view of the Upanishads is not to be doubted. // 37 //
And because all things arise [from it].

Regarding the subject matter—the Vedāntic synthesis which asserts that Brahman, though devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world—there arises a doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the logical principle that "whatever is devoid of qualities cannot be a material cause, just as color-form [is not the cause of sound]. To this, [the opponent] might argue: "Let the Lord be the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the unequal creation, since there exists karma which acts as its instigator."

But [it may be argued] that it cannot be the material cause because its pervader, the possession of attributes (*saguṇatva*), is absent; having reached this point by way of a counter-example, the author states the intent of the Siddhānta-sūtra: "The conscious [Brahman].

Even for that which is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), being the material cause through illusory transformation (*vivarta*) is not contradictory, because there exists the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*), which is the necessary condition for being the substratum of error.
The point is that possessing qualities (*saguṇatva*) is not a pervading [characteristic], because we observe the delusion of permanence and so forth even regarding qualities such as sound.

Although omniscience and omnipotence are not well-known in the world as attributes of a cause, it is nevertheless well-established that whoever is the creator of something is the knower and the possessor of power over all of it;

and since it is heard in scripture that God is the creator of everything, by following this established principle, His unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence are established by implication—this is what he intends when he says, "omniscient and omnipotent."
Regarding the term "Mahāmāyā":
it was stated [in this way] to wash away the mud of all doubts by describing [the Self] as both the agent and the material cause.
Therefore, it is established that there is no fault whatsoever in the Vedāntic doctrine. //37//
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīrakamīmāṃsā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda. // 1 //

Thus ends the first pāda of the second adhyāya in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //1//

Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Removal of Contradictions to the Concordance of Vedānta by means of the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Kaṇāda, and others, as well as by the Reasonings employed by the Sāṃkhya and other schools.
[Now begins] the second quarter of the second chapter.
I bow to that preeminent scion of the Raghus, whose true nature the followers of Sāṃkhya, the logicians, the Buddhists, the Jains, the Pāśupatas, and others do not know. (1)
START BsCom_2,2.1.1:
And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [to prove the existence of God].

(BBs_2,2.1) Although this scripture is engaged in determining the purport of the Vedānta passages, it is not like a school of logic (*tarka-śāstra*) which seeks to establish or refute some doctrine by means of divine reasonings.

Nevertheless, even while explaining the Vedānta texts, those views such as Sāṃkhya which stand in opposition to right vision (*samyagdarśana*) must be refuted; for this purpose, the subsequent quarter (the second chapter) proceeds.

Furthermore, since the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta serves the purpose of attaining right vision, the establishment of one's own position was performed first through that determination, as it is more important than the rejection of the positions of others.

Now, one might object: for those seeking liberation, it is proper to establish only one's own position in order to define right vision (*samyagdarśana*) as the means to liberation; what is the use of refuting the positions of others, which only incites hatred toward them?
Certainly, that is so.

Nevertheless, having observed that great systems such as Sāṃkhya and others—accepted by the great masses of people—have set forth under the pretext of teaching right vision, there may arise in some of dull intellect the expectation that these too should be adopted for the sake of right vision.

Likewise, because it is possible for them to possess profound consistency and because they were spoken by the Omniscient One, faith is placed in them; therefore, an effort is made to demonstrate their lack of substance.

Now, [it may be argued]: "Because of seeing, that which is not based on scripture is not [the cause]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5), and "And because of desire, there is no need for inference" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.18).

Furthermore, by the statement, "By this, all [other views] are explained, they are explained" (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.28), the refutation of the positions of the Sāṃkhya and others was already established previously;
so what is the point of repeating it?

This is explained as follows: The Sāṃkhyas and others, in order to establish their own positions, even cite Vedānta passages and explain them by interpreting them solely in accordance with their own views; that such an explanation of theirs is a mere semblance of an explanation and not a correct one has already been established.
However, the distinction here is that we now proceed to refute their reasoning independently, without reliance on the specific scriptural passages.

In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas maintain: Just as in the world various differentiated objects such as jars and bowls, being permeated by the nature of clay, are seen to be preceded by a commonality consisting of clay;
so too, all external and internal differentiated entities, being permeated by the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, must be preceded by a commonality consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

That commonality which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion is the Pradhāna (Primary Matter), composed of the three *guṇas*. Like clay, it is insentient, yet it brings about the purpose of the sentient *puruṣa* through its own diverse modifications by its very nature.
Regarding the phrase "it evolves":
likewise, one infers that very same Pradhāna by means of such marks as transformation (pariṇāma) and so forth.
To this we say: if this were established solely on the strength of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta),...
In this world, no insentient thing is ever seen to independently fashion modifications capable of accomplishing specific human purposes unless it is presided over by sentience.

For in the world, houses, palaces, beds, seats, pleasure-grounds, and so forth, are seen to be constructed at the proper time by wise artisans as being suitable for the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering.
Likewise, this entire external universe, beginning with the earth, is suited for the experience of the fruits of various karmas.

Moreover, how could the insentient *pradhāna* construct the internal body and so forth— which are endowed with various species, possess a specific arrangement of limbs, serve as the locus for experiencing the fruits of manifold karmas, and are seen by the most eminent wise men to be impossible even for the mind to conceive, let alone for craftsmen to create?
Because such [complexity] is not seen in clods of earth, stones, and the like;

yet, even in the case of clay and so forth, a specific form and arrangement is observed when they are presided over by a potter and others—by that same logic, it follows that the Pradhāna must also be presided over by another conscious being.

Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule that the primary cause should be determined solely on the basis of the properties inherent in the material cause (such as clay) and not on the basis of external agents such as potters.
This being the case, nothing is contradicted;
on the contrary, scripture is supported by the presentation of an intelligent cause.
Therefore, for the reason that "the formation [of the world] is otherwise inexplicable," one must not accept that the non-intelligent is the cause of the world.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "because of the impossibility of positive concomitance and so forth," he combines the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason.
For a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of external and internal distinctions with the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is not tenable,
since pleasure and the rest are perceived as being internal.
Furthermore, because sound and the other objects are perceived as not having that [pleasure's] nature,
and because they are perceived as being the causes thereof;
and because, even when there is no difference in the sound and so forth, a specific pleasure or the like is experienced due to a specific mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
Likewise, having observed that limited differentiated entities such as roots and sprouts are preceded by a combination [of causes], one who infers that external and internal differentiated entities—

because they are limited— are likewise preceded by a combination, faces the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* must be preceded by a combination, since they too possess the specific quality of being limited.

However, since the relationship of cause and effect is observed in the case of beds, seats, and so forth, which are produced through prior deliberation, it is not possible to postulate that external and internal entities, by virtue of their causal relationship, are preceded by something insentient. // 1 // [FN:
*Apadeśena* means by way of a pretext.]

Having raised the objection that just as all phenomena are possible in *brahman*, they might likewise be possible in *pradhāna*, [the author] refutes it: "And because the arrangement [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [for *pradhāna*].

Now, one might object: this treatise was commenced in order to determine the purport of the Vedāntas so as to remove obstacles to the ascertainment of the meaning of the [Vedāntic] sentences for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), and that [purport] has been determined as being free from defects;
therefore, this chapter consisting of the refutation of opposing views is not relevant to this treatise.
He raises an objection, saying "Even though," because the refutation of that [opposing view] is not required by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
He replies with "Nevertheless," stating that since it is impossible to establish one's own position without first refuting the opposing position, that must be done.
Then, to the question of whether the rejection of the opposing position should be performed even before establishing one's own position, he says, "The meaning of the Vedānta..."
The determination of the purport of the Vedānta is of primary importance because it is included within the means for attaining fruitful knowledge.
One might object: "Since it functions as a cause of passion and aversion, the refutation of other doctrines should not be undertaken"—this is the doubt expressed by the word "nanu.
Indeed, this discourse has been commenced with the primary aim of determining the truth.
The determination of reality cannot be accomplished without a lack of faith in other doctrines;

that lack of faith cannot be accomplished without the certainty that those doctrines are rooted in error; and that certainty cannot exist without this [fourth] chapter. Therefore, because it serves to protect one's own established tenets and to establish the primary objective, this chapter is appropriately integrated into this treatise.

Intending to show that [the practice] must be performed even by one free from passion because it is consistent with reason, he provides a resolution by accepting [the objection] with the words "Certainly," and so forth. "By way of pretext" means by means of a stratagem.
The meaning is that since there are many causes for the faith of those of dull intellect in those [practices], an effort is made here to dispel them.
However, faith in one's own doctrine and hatred for the doctrines of others are accepted because they serve the purpose of establishing one's primary position.
Nor is this [hatred] true hatred;

for it should be understood that rejection brings about hatred only when it is done with the thought that it is the "opponent's side," and not when it is performed with the desire to determine the truth as it actually is.
He raises the objection of tautology with the words, "But [it was said] because of the word *īkṣati*.
Previously, the non-Vedic nature of the Sāṃkhya and other systems was stated by refuting their authors who claim to support the meaning of the Śruti;

now, however, their independent arguments—which do not depend on the Śruti—are being refuted. Thus, since there is a difference in meaning, he says, "That is being explained," to show that this is not a mere repetition.

The subject here is the Sāṃkhya tenet that the non-conscious *pradhāna* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world; in the face of the doubt as to whether this is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or on error (*bhrānti*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated—showing its basis in valid knowledge through the connection of the objection that "since the qualities mentioned in the sūtra 'and because all attributes are possible' are possible in the *pradhāna*, that alone must be the material cause"—with the words: "In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas..."

The connection of this section with the preceding one is that the knowledge of one's own established doctrine (svasiddhāntajñāna) depends upon the refutation of the views of others (paramatanirāsa). Since all the topical discussions (adhikaraṇas) consist of the refutation of the views of others, they are connected to this section.

In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the result is the failure to establish the systematic harmony (samanvaya) of the meaning of the stated scriptures, due to contradiction with doctrines rooted in [erroneous] means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The proof of that [non-difference] is to be seen throughout this entire chapter (pāda), as it is established in the final conclusion (siddhānta).
The connection with the Śruti is the specific point of this chapter, because its purpose is to strengthen the fundamental harmony (samanvaya) with the Śruti.
"Bheda" means differences, which are modifications (vikāra).
He states the pervasion— that whatever modifications are endowed with something, they have that as their material cause— by means of the word "yathā" (just as).
Every effect has as its material cause an entity consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because it is endowed with those [qualities].
He states the inference "like a jar, etc. with the word "tathā" (so).
To the question "For what purpose does the Pradhāna undergo transformation?", he replies with the words "of the conscious one" (*cetanasya*).
The "object" (artha) consists of enjoyment and liberation;
for that purpose, [Prakṛti] proceeds by its very nature, and is not impelled by any conscious agent—this is the meaning.
As it has been said: "The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; the instrument is not caused by anyone."
He recalls the other inferences stated by them with the word "tathā" (likewise):

for it has been said— "On account of the finite measure of diverse objects, their commonality, their activity proceeding from a potency, the distinction between cause and effect, and the non-distinction of the manifold universe."
Thus,
in this verse, the logical mark (*liṅga*) "because of the coordination" (*samanvayāt*) has been explained;
the remaining [marks] are now being explained.
For instance: the unmanifest (avyakta) is the cause of the diverse effects such as earth and so forth, because they are finite, like a jar.
Nor is there a deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya) in the example.
Because even clay is unmanifest due to its being characterized by effects such as pots that are unmanifest prior to their production;

and likewise, since pots and the like proceed from the power of their cause, it must be stated that the effects beginning with the *mahat* also proceed from the power of their cause— that cause possessing such power is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Furthermore, the differentiation of an effect from its cause is observed as birth; for instance, clay is born from earth, and from that [clay] comes a jar.
Likewise, non-differentiation is observed as dissolution in the reverse order: the jar’s dissolution into clay, that [clay] into earth, earth into water, and water into fire.

These two—differentiation and non-differentiation—which are observed in the diverse multitude of entities (*vaiśvarūpya*) and which, when considered separately, find their rest in some cause because they possess the nature of differentiation and non-differentiation, [rest] in clay... [as in the case of the jar].
The meaning is: "like the division and non-division of a jar.
He states the established conclusion: "In this regard, we say..."—is it being argued by means of inferences that the world has an insentient nature as its material cause?
Or [the alternative is] that its nature is independent and insentient.
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because we ourselves accept the beginningless *māyā* composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the second point, he states "if" [in the verse] because the probandum is unestablished in the example of the jar and so forth.
That is to say, the thesis that "Prakṛti is independent and insentient" could only be established by the force of an example if such an example existed somewhere;
however, the logical connection is that no such example is observed anywhere.
He states the independent category [of the subject] as "not presided over by a conscious being.

Having stated the non-establishment of the opponent's probandum (*sādhya*), he states the counter-probans (*satpratipakṣa*) by expressing the pervasion (*vyāpti*): "Whatever effect consists of a diverse arrangement, that has for its material cause the insentient presided over by a conscious being"—as in the case of a house.
This world has for its material cause the insentient presided over by a conscious being.
The formal argument is: "Because it is an effect, like a house.

To state the subverting tarka (reductio) mentioned in the Sūtra—namely, that a diverse arrangement would be impossible in the absence of an intelligent cause—he describes the variety of the world with the word "tathā" (thus).
The distinction is that external objects such as earth and so forth are the objects of enjoyment, while internal objects such as the body and so forth are the locus of enjoyment.
The meaning is: that which possesses a specific, non-common arrangement—that is, a particular configuration—of its constituent parts.
"How could such a diverse world be created by an insentient primordial nature (prakṛti) that is not presided over by consciousness?"—
the meaning is "not at all.

He states the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— "that which is insentient and not presided over by consciousness does not produce an effect"— which is rooted in reasoning, using the example of a clod of earth (*loṣṭa*).
The meaning is that clay and other such materials, when impelled by consciousness, are not seen to possess causal efficacy [on their own].
Furthermore, the primordial nature (prakṛti), which is insentient and beginningless, is presided over by consciousness,
because it is subject to transformation.
He says "like clay, etc. to this effect.
Now, in the examples of clay and so forth, both [properties] exist: insentience and being presided over by a sentient agent.

In that case, among these, it is insentience alone that pervades the reason of "being subject to transformation" (pariṇāmitva), because it is internal [to the probandum] as the very nature of clay and the like.

However, being presided over by a conscious agent (*cetanādhiṣṭhitatva*) is not a pervading property (*vyāpaka*), because it depends upon external factors such as clay and the potter, and is thus an external condition (*bahiraṅga*).

Thus, one might suspect that even though there is transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is connected only with the attribute of insentience (*acetanatva*) and not with being presided over by a conscious agent; anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "not so" (*na ca*).

The point is this: in the example of the kitchen, the nature of the kitchen itself—which is internal—does not possess the quality of being pervaded by smoke; yet fire, which is external and distinct from it, does possess that quality. Thus, being "internal" is not the determining factor for being a pervader (*vyāpakatve*).

Furthermore, since there is no sublation (contradiction) in accepting the principle that whatever is insentient transforms only when presided over by a sentient being—and indeed, because such an acceptance is supported by scripture—he says: "And this being so... [na caivaṃ sati...].

He states that the word "and" (ca) is used in the Sūtra for the purpose of indicating the non-establishment of the reason "because of the concomitance with pleasure, pain, and delusion," saying: "And because concomitance and so forth are untenable.
The meaning is that inference is not tenable.
The word "and so forth" (ādi) is intended to include [the reasons] such as dimension (parimāṇa) and the rest.

Because sound and the other sense objects are experienced as being external, it is unestablished that they consist of internal pleasure and so forth; furthermore, because [pleasure] has them as its cause.
For there is no connection between a cause and its effect by way of identity, since this is not observed in the case of a staff and a jar—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, if pleasure and so forth were inherent in the object—just as clay is in a jar—and were conjoined with sound and other qualities, then pleasure and so forth would be perceived by everyone without distinction, just as the clay in a jar is.
Since such perception does not occur, the absence of the probans is established through non-perception of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*); thus he says, "sound and so forth.

Even though the object is one and the same, due to the diversity of individual mental impressions (*vāsanā*), one person perceives it as pleasure, another as pain, and another as delusion; therefore, objects do not have pleasure and so forth as their intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that they do not exist.
Having thus refuted the reason "because of conjunction" (*samanvayāt*), he refutes the reasons such as "because of limited magnitude" (*parimāṇāt*) and so forth with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

Since it is established that intellect (*buddhi*) and the other [evolutes] are preceded by conjunction because they possess limited magnitude, it follows that there must be multiple, conjoined entities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The Sāṃkhya’s position is that Brahman cannot be established because conjunction is impossible in a single entity.
What is this "limitedness"? It is certainly not limitation by space.
Because it does not exist within the space contained in the subject (pakṣa), its existence as a property is unestablished;
nor is there delimitation by time,
since the Sāṃkhyas do not admit the existence of time.

Furthermore, because [the reason] is already established through the association with the qualities of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no real delimitation (*pariccheda*). Moreover, even though *sattva* and the other qualities are mutually distinct, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of the probandum; thus he says: "sattva... and so forth.
As for what was said— that where the distinction between cause and effect ceases, that is Pradhāna—
that is not so,
because such cessation is possible in either Brahman or Māyā.

Nor is there a pervasion (vyāpti) such that whatever is the dissolution of an effect is completed in an insentient entity not presided over by a conscious being, because one observes the presiding of a conscious being in all insentient things; thus he says, "kārya...
By this, non-differentiation (avibhāga) is also explained.

As for the other pervasion— that whatever is limited is preceded by the unmanifest primordial nature (avyakta-prakṛti)— that too is subject to deviation, since the qualities (guṇas), though beginningless, are limited. By this, the argument that because the relationship of material cause and effect exists only between similar things, the material cause of insentient effects must itself be insentient, is also refuted.
Even if the insentient nature [of the world] is presided over by consciousness, similarity remains possible;
furthermore, the rule of similarity was refuted in the [sūtra] "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (BS 2.1.4).

Thus, since the activity of the effect can arise from the causal power dependent on consciousness, the probans "activity from power" (śaktitaḥ pravṛttiḥ) is established as being otherwise accounted for (anyathāsiddha). This is the intended meaning. //1//
And because of the activity [of the world]. (BBs 2.2.2)
Let this [specific] arrangement stand aside for now;

even that activity directed toward its accomplishment— which consists in the displacement from the state of equilibrium, the assumption of the relationship of principal and subordinate among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and the engagement toward a specific effect— is not possible for the insentient *pradhāna* acting independently.
This is because such activity is not observed in clay and the like, nor in chariots and the like;

for neither clay and the like, nor chariots and the like—which are themselves insentient—are ever seen to engage in activity directed toward a specific effect without being presided over by sentient agents such as potters or horses. Since the unobserved is established on the basis of the observed, an insentient cause for the world cannot be inferred from the reason that such purposeful activity would otherwise be impossible.
But surely, the activity of even a conscious being is never observed in isolation.
True, this is so;
nevertheless, the activity of non-conscious things such as chariots is observed when they are conjoined with a conscious being.
It is not observed that a conscious being, when conjoined with an unconscious thing, possesses activity.
What, then, is logical here? Is it that the activity belongs to that in which it is observed, or that it belongs to that with which it is conjoined?
Is it not the case that it is logical for activity to belong to that very thing in which it is observed, since both [the body and the conscious principle] are perceptible?
However, the pure conscious principle is not perceived as the substratum of activity, like a chariot or similar objects;

rather, the existence of the conscious principle is established only as conjoined with the body and so forth, which serve as the substratum of activity, since the living body is seen to differ from purely insentient things such as chariots.
For this very reason, the Lokāyatikas have concluded that consciousness belongs to the body alone, because it is observed when the body is present and not observed when it is absent.
Therefore, they maintain that activity belongs only to that which is insentient.
To this, it is replied: we do not say that activity does not belong to that insentient thing in which it is observed.
Let it belong to that very [person];
however, we say that it arises from volition (cetanā),
because it exists when that [volition] exists and does not exist when that [volition] is absent.

Just as the transformation characterized by burning and illumination—though dependent on wood and other materials—is not perceived when occurring in fire alone, yet occurs only from fire itself because it is seen when there is contact with it and not seen when there is separation from it; in the same way, even for the Lokāyatikas, the conscious body is seen to be the activator of unconscious things such as chariots. Thus, the capacity of the conscious to act as an activator is uncontradicted.

If it is objected that, even for you, since the activity of the Self—even when conjoined with the body and so forth—is untenable apart from its nature as pure consciousness, its status as an instigator is unestablished; we say no.
For, just like a magnet or like color and other qualities, it is possible for that which is devoid of activity itself to be an instigator.
Just as a magnet, though itself devoid of activity, becomes the instigator of iron.

Or, just as objects such as visible forms, though themselves devoid of activity, become the movers of the eyes and other sense organs, so too it is logical that the Lord—though himself devoid of activity—being omnipresent, the self of all, omniscient, and possessing all powers, should set everything in motion.
If it is argued that because of his oneness there is no object to be moved, and thus being a mover is untenable, we say: no.
This is because it has been repeatedly stated that [the world] is under the influence of the illusory manifestation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) produced by ignorance (avidyā).
Therefore, activity is possible when the cause is omniscient, but not when the cause is insentient. // 2 // [FN:
Of both the activity and its substratum.]

An independent, insentient entity should not be inferred as the cause, because its engagement for the purpose of creation is untenable; thus, the sūtra should be construed by connecting the word "untenability" (*anupapatti*) with the particle *ca*.
Anticipating the question of what the difference is between "arrangement" (*racanā*) and "engagement" (*pravṛtti*), he states the nature of engagement [in the words] beginning with "sāmya."
Indeed, the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas* is the dissolution (*pralaya*) of the principles; at that time, no effect exists, because it would follow that there is no dissolution [of the world].
Rather, at the beginning, there arises a state of disequilibrium (*vaiṣamya*) consisting of the departure from equilibrium.

Then, due to the predominance of one quality through its manifestation as the principal factor (*aṅgin*) and the subordination of another as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), there arises a relationship of principal and subordinate; when that exists, there is activity consisting in the production of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth,
and by means of that activity, there is "arrangement," which is the differentiation of various effects— this is the meaning.
"The activity of the guṇas is preceded by the superintendence of a conscious being, because it is an activity, like the activity of a chariot and so forth"—thus he says: "That too... (sāpi).
The meaning is that independent activity is impossible for that which is opposed [to the subject].

However, some explain the logical mark "activity from capacity" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛttiḥ*) as follows: because differentiated entities possess the power of activity, they must have an insentient nature that is not presided over by a conscious being.
This [reason] is also inconclusive with respect to the *guṇas*.
Furthermore, if the qualification "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is added, there is a contradiction (*viruddhatā*);

for in the case of jars and the like, which possess the capacity for activity and are effects, one observes a pervasion (*vyāpti*) with that which is contrary to the stated probandum—namely, having a conscious being as their presiding cause. This was indicated by the Sūtra: "And because of activity" (*pravṛtteśca*).
Now, even if activity is not observed in the world among independent insentient things, let that activity be established in the case of *pradhāna*.
Regarding this, he says: "And because [it must be] from what is seen.
The meaning is that for you, who rely on inference, it is impossible to establish supersensuous objects without an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now, the Sāṃkhya raises an objection: "But surely..."—meaning that while the activity of *pradhāna* is being refuted, one must state the activity of a conscious being (*cetana*) in creation, and that [activity] is not tenable. Thus he suspects: "But surely... and so forth.
He accepts that activity is impossible for one whose consciousness is pure, saying: "True.
In that case, the activity of a purely insentient entity must be established, otherwise creation would be impossible;
to this he replies: "Even so."
The point is that even though the pure conscious principle (*cetana*) does not act by itself, the activity of creation proceeds from the mutual relationship between the conscious and the unconscious.
The Sāṃkhya criticizes this Vedāntic conclusion,
saying "But not so," because every observed activity is seen to have its locus solely in the unconscious.
However, the activity of a conscious being is never observed to arise through a connection with the unconscious;
therefore, the meaning is that creation does not proceed from a conscious being. Having heard these two views, the neutral party asks: "But what [is it]?"

The meaning of the question is this: Is the Sāṃkhya view correct—that the activity observed in insentient things such as chariots belongs to those very objects themselves and that a conscious being is not the cause therein—or is the Vedāntin view correct—that the activity is impelled by a conscious being, such as a horse or driver?
The Sāṃkhya replies with "nanu" (is it not so?).
"Of both" means of both the activity and its substratum.
The point is that since the occurrence of activity is established by the observed substratum alone, one should not postulate the activity of an unobserved conscious being.

If the self is not perceptible, how is its existence established? To this he replies with the word "pravṛtti" (activity). The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the distinction of the living body from chariots and the like, as well as the presence of breath and so forth, is observed as a mark (*liṅga*), the existence of a conscious being is thereby established.
The meaning is that the self is established by the inference: "the living body possesses a self because it has breath and so forth; otherwise, like a chariot and the like.
Furthermore, the activity of the body is accompanied by a conscious being distinct from its own substrate, just as knowledge [is].
The term "substratum of activity" (*pravṛttyāśraya*) is stated to indicate another inference, namely: "because it is an activity, like the movement of a chariot.
The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that the establishment of its existence alone does not constitute its being the motivator (*pravartakatva*).
The point is that if the mere existence of something inferred were a cause for activity, it would follow that even space (*ākāśa*) would be a cause in all cases.
Furthermore, he states "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) to show that even the error of the Cārvākas—who hold that the self (*ātman*) is not perceptible—is itself a logical mark (*liṅga*).
The meaning is: "precisely because [the self] is not perceptible."
The sense is that if the body were perceived as distinct from the self, error would be impossible.
[This follows] from observation;
the words "of activity and consciousness" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Having accepted the opponent’s claim that the insentient alone serves as the substratum for activity, the proponent establishes the sentience as the motivator, stating: "That is now explained.

He asserts that the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of a sentient being, such as a horse, with the activity of a chariot and so forth is evident; and by means of these two, the fact that the sentient being is the instigator is also agreed upon even by the Materialists (*Lokāyatikas*).

Someone raises an objection: "But surely..."—based on the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that whatever is an instigator must itself possess activity like a horse, [the objector argues] that since the pervading property (activity) is absent in the Self, it cannot be the instigator.
He refutes [the objection] by saying "No," on the grounds that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) because of the deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of gems and the like.
He says "No" because, even though there is unity in reality, a conceptualized duality exists as something to be set in motion; he explains this by saying "Ignorance" (avidyā).

The meaning is that there is no occasion for objection, because it has been stated that the Lord’s status as the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*) and so forth arises from the power (*vaśa*) or capacity (*sāmarthya*) of that imagined connection—the "entrance" (*āveśa*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*) into the manifold of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*) imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), which is itself of the nature of *māyā*. //2//
If it is argued that [the milk] is like water, then in that case as well: BBs_2,2.3.
It might be argued as follows:
"Just as insentient milk functions by its very nature for the sake of the growth of the calf,

and just as insentient water flows by its very nature for the benefit of the world, so too will the insentient *pradhāna* function by its very nature for the accomplishment of the purpose of the *puruṣa*."
This is not well said;
for even in that case, we infer that the activity of water and milk occurs only when presided over by a conscious being,
because activity is never observed in an insentient object alone, such as a chariot, which is admitted by both parties.

Furthermore, the scripture— in passages such as "He who dwells in the waters, yet is within the waters, and controls them" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.4) and "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9)— declares that all movement in the world is presided over by the Lord.
Therefore, because it is included within the class of things to be proven (*sādhyapakṣa*), the example of milk and water is not a valid instance;
for it is possible that the conscious cow causes the milk to flow through her desire for affection,
and because the milk is drawn forth by the sucking of the calf.
Nor is there absolute independence even in the case of water,
since its flowing depends upon such factors as low-lying ground;
however, dependence upon a conscious agent has been demonstrated in every instance.

Regarding the sūtra "If it be said that [the Self] is not [the cause] because we see the need for an external instrument, we say no, for it is like milk" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.24), it is shown from the perspective of worldly observation that an effect can arise even without depending on an external instrumental cause, provided it has its own substrate.
However, from the perspective of the sacred scripture (śāstra), the fact that everything everywhere depends upon the Lord (Īśvara) is not set aside. // 3 //

FN: Because it is equal to the subject (*pakṣa*) in its possession of the property to be proven (*sādhyavattā*), it is not put forward [as a counter-example] and is not a ground for investigation. The activity of that which is beginninglessly insentient occurs through [the influence of] consciousness and so forth.
It is established that [the world] is an effect because it is a product,

like the production of a chariot and so forth. In this regard, having raised the objection of an inconclusive deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of milk and the like, he explains the Sūtra— stating that since even those cases are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*), the establishment of the probandum through inference and scripture is not subject to such deviation— with the words beginning "syādetat" (this might be so).
"Regarding the phrase *sādhyapakṣa*": the meaning is "because it is equal to the subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*).
[Therefore, there is] no presentation [of it as a separate example].
This means that there is no ground for deviation.
Furthermore, he states "and of consciousness" because there is no deviation [in the case] of the cow and so forth, since they exist as the instigators regarding the milk.
This has been demonstrated.
The ellipsis is "by means of inference and scripture.

Having raised the objection that there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows for the author of the Sūtras—who said both "for [it is] like milk" and "in that case also"—he states that there is no contradiction because these two Sūtras are based respectively on the perspective of common worldly experience and the perspective of the Śāstra: "Upasaṃhāra...
START BsCom_2,2.1.4:
And because of the non-existence of distinction and because of independence.
(BBs_2,2.4) For the Sāṃkhyas, the three *guṇas* abiding in a state of equilibrium constitute the *pradhāna*.
Apart from that [puruṣa], there exists no external factor that could act as either an impeller or a restrainer of the primary cause (pradhāna).
Furthermore, since the puruṣa is indifferent—being neither an impeller nor a restrainer—the primary cause is independent;

and because it is independent, it would be illogical to claim that the primary cause sometimes transforms into the form of the great principle (mahat) and so forth, while at other times it does not transform.
But for the Lord, because of his omniscience, omnipotence, and possession of great illusory power (māyā), both engagement and non-engagement are not contradictory. // 4 //
Having raised the objection that perhaps *dharma* and other factors, or even the *puruṣa*, might be the instigators of the activity of *pradhāna*, the Sūtra proceeds;
he explains it with the words beginning "of the Sāṃkhyas," etc.

The meaning is that since action cannot exist apart from *pradhāna*, and because the *puruṣa* is indifferent (*udāsīna*), it is illogical to claim that there is sometimes the commencement of creation and sometimes dissolution [based on such instigation].
The point is that since karma—which consists of primary matter (pradhāna)—is insentient and exists eternally, it cannot be the regulator of occasional activity. //4//
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the self] is not like grass and so forth. (BBs 2.2.5)
It might be argued as follows:

"Just as grass, creepers, cow dung, and so forth transform into the form of milk and the like by their very nature, independent of any other cause, so too will the *pradhāna* transform into the forms of the *mahat* and the rest.
And how is it understood that grass and the like transform independently of any other cause?
Because no other causal sign is perceived.
For if we were to perceive some causal sign, then we could, according to our desire, produce milk by taking grass and so forth; however, we do not so produce it.
Therefore, just as the transformation of grass and so forth is inherent, so too would the transformation of the Pradhāna be inherent.
To this it is replied: the transformation of the Pradhāna might be inherent like that of grass and so forth, if the inherent transformation of grass and so forth were admitted;
however, it is not so admitted.
Because another characteristic is perceived.
How is another characteristic perceived?
Because it is absent elsewhere.
For it is grass and the like, once consumed by a cow, that becomes milk, not what has been discarded or consumed by an ox and such.
If this [transformation] were causeless, then grass and the like would turn into milk even elsewhere, simply through a connection with the body of a cow.
Nor does something become causeless merely because it cannot be produced at will by human beings.
For there are some effects to be accomplished by human effort and some to be accomplished by fate.
Humans, too, are indeed able to produce milk by employing appropriate means, such as gathering grass and other fodder;
for those desiring abundant milk cause the cow to graze on abundant pasture.
And from that, they obtain abundant milk;
therefore, the transformation of the Pradhāna is not inherent (svābhāvika) like that of grass and other such things. // 5 // [FN:
*prahīṇa* means destroyed.]

Again, having raised the doubt that the primary cause (pradhāna) acts spontaneously and only occasionally by the force of an analogy, the author of the Sūtras refutes it with the words beginning "anyatra" (elsewhere).
He asks: "How? The answer is: "By another efficient cause (nimitta)."
He establishes the final position (siddhānta) that there exists another cause, such as a cow and so forth, by stating: "To this it is replied.
"Abandoned" means destroyed.
As for what was said—that milk is natural because it cannot be produced at will—that is addressed here.
Regarding this, he says: "And not according to one's desire. (Sūtra 5)
It has been established that the activity of the *pradhāna* is not inherent (*svābhāvikī*).
Nevertheless, even if we were to concede to you out of deference to your faith and accept that the activity of the *pradhāna* is indeed inherent, the fault would still necessarily follow.
Why?
Because of the absence of a purpose.

If it is asserted that the activity of the *pradhāna* is inherent and does not depend on anything else here, then just as it does not depend on any auxiliary cause, it likewise would not depend on any purpose; therefore, the *pradhāna*— [The sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

The proposition that "it proceeds in order to accomplish the purpose of the Puruṣa" would be abandoned. If he were to say, "It does not depend on anything else except its auxiliaries, nor even on a purpose," even so, the purpose of the primary principle's activity must be distinguished: would it be experience, or liberation, or both?
If it were enjoyment (*bhoga*), what kind of enjoyment could there be for a person (*puruṣa*) to whom no excellence can be imparted?

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*); if it were liberation (*apavarga*), since liberation would already be established even prior to activity, such activity would be purposeless.
Moreover, there would be the consequence of the non-perception of sound and other objects.

Even if one accepts that [the activity] serves both purposes, there would still be the consequence of no liberation, because the primary constituents (*pradhāna*) to be experienced are infinite. Furthermore, activity does not occur for the sake of satisfying a desire; for it is impossible for the insentient *pradhāna* to have a desire.
Furthermore, there is no longing in the pure and partless Puruṣa.

If it is argued that his activity proceeds out of fear that the powers of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) and creation (*sarga-śakti*) would otherwise be rendered useless, then—just as the power of vision is never severed—the power of creation would likewise never be severed; consequently, because saṃsāra would not be terminated, the undesirable consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa*) would follow.
Therefore, the claim that the Pradhāna acts for the sake of the Puruṣa’s purpose is untenable. // 6 //

FN: Because of the absence of objects, there would follow the non-existence of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). "Objects of experience" (*mātrā*) refers to enjoyments, so called because they are measured out (*mīyante*) or experienced (*bhujyante*), and are devoid of any excellence consisting in the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain.

The first point is that the primordial matter (pradhāna) does not act of its own accord; for if one were to admit that it acts spontaneously, it would follow that there is no dependence upon the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha). To refute the objection that this consequence is acceptable, he says: "Therefore, the primordial matter... [and so forth].
The meaning is that if the aforementioned consequence were accepted, there would be a loss of one's own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).

Anticipating the objection that there can be no spontaneous activity because it is impossible for such a purpose to exist, he states another point beginning with "If that [activity]... (*sa yadi...*).
He then says "Even so" (*tathāpi*) to indicate that if a purpose is required, it must be stated.
Since it is impossible to produce an excellence such as intrinsic happiness in the immutable *puruṣa*, and since superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not admitted, experience (*bhoga*) is not tenable.

Furthermore, if the activity of *pradhāna* were for the sake of experience, there would be the consequence of non-liberation due to the absence of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the cause of liberation;
conversely, if its purpose were liberation, the activity would be useless because liberation, consisting in abiding in one's own nature, is established by itself.
The meaning is that there would follow the consequence of the absence of enjoyment (*bhoga*).
He refutes the third [position] with the words "for the sake of both":
*mātrā* refers to objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), so called because they are measured out (*mīyante*) or experienced (*bhujyante*).

He refutes the statement in the *kārikā*—“Just as the world engages in activities for the sake of satisfying its longing, so the unmanifest (avyakta) operates for the sake of the liberation of the Person (puruṣa)” —with the words “And not...”.
The meaning is that longing, which is a specific kind of desire, is not appropriate for either a purely insentient entity or for the Self (ātman).
However, the Person possesses the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) because his nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).

If it is argued that the primary cause (pradhāna) possesses the power of creation because it consists of the three qualities (guṇas), and that the activity of the pradhāna toward creation occurs because those two powers cannot be purposeful without the manifestation of the visible world—[we reply: no;
since the powers are eternal, it would follow that creation is eternal. Thus he says: "The power of vision... (verse 6).
If it is argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so [the fault remains]. (BBs 2.2.7)
It might be argued as follows:

just as a certain man who possesses the power of sight but lacks the power of action—a cripple—presides over and sets in motion another man who possesses the power of action but lacks the power of sight—a blind man;
or just as a magnet, though not moving by itself, moves iron.
Thus, the objection is raised again by means of an illustrative example, namely that the Puruṣa will set the Pradhāna in motion.
To this it is replied: even so, there is no escape from the fault;
for first of all, the fault of abandoning what has been accepted follows.
This is because it is admitted that the *pradhāna* acts independently, whereas it is not admitted that the *puruṣa* is an instigator; furthermore,
how could the indifferent *puruṣa* set the *pradhāna* in motion?
For even a lame man impels a blind man by means of speech and other such means;
however, the Puruṣa possesses no such activity of impelling whatsoever,
because it is devoid of action.
Nor could it set [the mind] in motion by mere proximity, like a magnet;
for since its proximity would be constant, there would follow the consequence that activity would also be constant.
In the case of a magnet, however, its proximity—which is its own operation—is non-constant.
Furthermore, since this [Prakṛti] requires such things as being polished, the analogy of the man and the stone is not applicable.
Likewise, because the Pradhāna is insentient and the Puruṣa is indifferent, and because there is no third entity to connect them, a connection between the two is logically untenable.
Moreover, if the connection were based on a capacity for union, then because that capacity would never cease, it would follow that liberation is impossible.
As in the previous case, the absence of an external object must also be considered here.
However, there is a distinction: the Supreme Self possesses neutrality based on its own essential nature, whereas its agency is based on *māyā*. // 7 //

Although the agency of the *puruṣa* has already been refuted, it is raised once more by means of an analogy and then denied. To the Sāṃkhya who says, "If [it be argued] that it is like a person and a stone, even so," [the author] replies, "How so?"— thereby stating two reasons to show that the *puruṣa* possesses neither physical motion nor the quality of effort (*prayatna*), while asserting that the Sāṃkhya's own accepted principles— the independence of *pradhāna* and the neutrality (*audāsīnya*) of the *puruṣa*— would thereby be abandoned.
Because both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* are eternal and all-pervading, their proximity is eternal;
whereas for a stone, there is the activity of wiping and placing it upright, which constitutes a non-eternal proximity.
Thus, [the opponent's] argument is not a valid presentation, meaning that the example cited is not analogous.

[Objection: Surely there exists the fitness for the relationship of seer and seen between consciousness and insentience; by that [fitness], their status as such constitutes their connection. To this he says: "fitness. The meaning is that because the fitness consisting of the nature of consciousness and insentience is eternal, it would follow that the connection is also eternal.

Just as the position that the Pradhāna acts independently—whether for the sake of experience, liberation, or both—was refuted by means of these alternatives, so too must the position that the Pradhāna acts under the control of the Puruṣa be refuted on account of the absence of a result; thus he says, "as before.
Anticipating the objection as to how the Supreme Self, being indifferent, can be the instigator [of activity], he says, "the Supreme Self."
In the Sāṃkhya system, both [the cause and its effects] are contradictory because they are [both considered] real.
In our system, however, there is no contradiction between the imagined and the unimagined; this is the distinction. //7//
And because the status of being the principal [member] is untenable. (BBs 2.2.8)
For this reason as well, the activity of the *pradhāna* cannot be admitted.

For that state in which *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* exist merely in their own essential natures (*svarūpa*) in equilibrium, having abandoned their mutual relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities—that is the state of the *pradhāna*.

In that state, since these [qualities] possess independent essential natures, a relationship of mutual subordination and predominance is impossible, for fear of the destruction of their own essential natures.

Furthermore, due to the absence of any external agitator, the production of the Great Principle (mahat) and the subsequent evolutes, which is caused by the imbalance of the qualities (guṇas), would not occur. // 8 //
Is the state of the Pradhāna eternal like that of the immutable (kūṭastha), or is it subject to modification?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "In that [state]," etc.
The meaning is that if there were a relationship of part and whole (aṅgāṅgibhāva), there would be a destruction of the nature of identity;
consequently, because of the fear that this would result in the collapse of immutability (kauṭasthya), the relationship of part and whole is untenable, and thus creation is untenable.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the external" (bāhyasya).
The meaning is that there is no cause to be stated for the loss of that equanimity which has endured for a long time. //8//
And because there would be an inference otherwise, it would follow from the absence of the capacity for knowledge. (BBs 2.2.9)
Now, it might be argued: "We infer otherwise, so that this immediately preceding fault does not follow.
For we do not accept that the qualities (*guṇas*) have an independent nature or are immutable (*kūṭastha*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a claim.
Rather, the nature of the qualities is accepted on the basis of their effects."
In whatever manner the production of an effect is possible, in that very manner their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is accepted.
Furthermore, there is the accepted doctrine that "the functioning of the qualities (guṇas) is mobile.
Therefore, even in the state of equilibrium, the qualities remain as being precisely capable of undergoing disequilibrium.

Even so, the previously mentioned defects— such as the impossibility of creation due to the Pradhāna being devoid of the power of cognition— remain exactly as they were. Furthermore, one who infers even the power of cognition in it would cease to be a true opponent,
because this would entail the doctrine of Brahman (Brahmavāda), namely that a single conscious entity is the material cause of the manifold world.

Even though the *guṇas* are capable of undergoing disequilibrium (*vaiṣamya*), they would not undergo it while in a state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*) due to the absence of a cause; or, if they were to undergo it, they would necessarily undergo disequilibrium at all times because the absence of a cause remains the same. Thus, this very same fault mentioned immediately above follows as a consequence. // 9 //

It has been stated that there is no inherent inequality among the *guṇas* because their natures are mutually independent; anticipating the objection that the reason for this is unestablished (*asiddha*), the author of the Sūtras refutes it with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
If, on the contrary, one were to infer from the dependence of the *guṇas* upon one another that they are not independent by nature, then the defect mentioned in the preceding Sūtra would not apply.

Nor does this constitute a departure from established tenets (apasiddhānta), because the nature of the qualities (guṇas) is accepted in accordance with their effects; thus he says, "the functioning of the qualities is mobile.

Having accepted that there is no fault regarding the impossibility of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (aṅgāṅgitva) mentioned in the previous sūtra, he provides the rebuttal: "even so."

The meaning is that if one were to postulate a power of cognition for the sake of accomplishing an effect, it would result in the doctrine of Brahman (brahmavāda). He abandons this admission with the words "vaiṣamye" [verse 9].
And because of contradiction, [the Sāṃkhya system] is inconsistent. (2.2.10)
Furthermore, this admission of the Sāṃkhyas is mutually contradictory:
in some places they enumerate seven sense-faculties, while in others they enumerate eleven.
Likewise, in some places they teach the creation of the subtle elements from the Great Principle (mahat), while in others from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Similarly, in some places they describe three internal organs, while in others only one.
However, there is indeed a contradiction with the Śruti which teaches that the Lord is the cause, as well as with the Smṛti that follows it;
therefore, for this reason also, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is inconsistent.

To this, [the opponent] says: "But is not the view of the followers of the Upaniṣads also inconsistent, since they do not admit a difference in nature between the sufferer and the causer of suffering?"

For those who accept that there is indeed one Brahman, the self of all, which is the cause of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), it must be admitted that the sufferer and the causer of suffering are merely two specific states of that single Self and do not constitute different classes of being.

And if these two—the sufferer and the causer of suffering—were merely specific states of the one Self, then that Self would never be liberated from those two states of suffering and causing suffering; consequently, the scripture which teaches right vision for the sake of pacifying suffering would be rendered useless.
It would not be so; for it is not possible for a lamp, whose nature consists of heat and light, to be liberated from those two while remaining in that very same state.
As for the analogy presented regarding water, waves, ripples, foam, and so forth—

In that case as well, since the various particularities such as waves—which are of the nature of water—are eternal in the form of manifestation and disappearance, it follows that the water-nature cannot be liberated from the waves and so forth; thus, the situation remains the same.
Furthermore, this difference in kind between the sufferer and the cause of suffering is well-established in the world.
For instance, the seeker and the object sought are perceived as mutually distinct.
If for the seeker there were no object other than himself,
then that which constitutes the object of a seeker’s desire would be eternally established for him, and thus he would have no desire for that object;
just as for a lamp, whose nature is light, the object called "illumination" is eternally established, and thus it has no desire for that object.
For if the object were not yet attained, the seeker would indeed possess the state of being a seeker;
likewise, the object itself would not possess the state of being an object.
If it did so possess it, it would simply be its own object.
But this is not the case;
for these two words, "artha" and "artha," are relative terms.
A relationship can exist between two related entities, not within a single entity alone.
Therefore, these two—the object and the seeker of the object—are distinct;
likewise are the non-object and the seeker of the non-object.
For the seeker, the object is favorable and the non-object is unfavorable; thus, by way of a single conceptual turn, he is connected with both.
In that regard, because the benefit is so slight and the harm so great, both benefit and harm are in fact nothing but harm; thus, it is called the "tormentor.
The "tormented," however, is the single person who is connected to both in turn. If the tormentor and the tormented were of one and the same nature, liberation would be impossible.
But if they exist as distinct categories, then through the removal of the cause of their conjunction, the possibility of liberation might indeed arise at some time.
To this it is replied: No;
because precisely due to their oneness, the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is untenable.
This fault would arise if, within a single selfhood, the sufferer and the causer of suffering were to enter into a mutual relationship of object and subject.
This is not so, precisely because of its oneness.

For fire, being one, does not burn or illuminate itself, even though there exists a difference in its attributes such as heat and light, and even though it is subject to transformation. How, then, could the relationship of the "tormented" and the "tormentor" be possible in the case of the single, immutable Brahman?
But where, then, could this relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering exist?
It is said in reply: Do you not see that the living body, acting as the object of action, is the sufferer, while the sun is the cause of suffering?
[Objection: But "suffering" (tapti) is indeed pain; and that belongs to the conscious being, not to the insentient body.
For if the affliction belonged to the body alone, it would perish of its own accord upon the destruction of the body; thus, no means for its destruction would need to be sought.
To this it is replied: even in the absence of the body, affliction is never observed in the pure conscious principle (cetanasya) alone.
Nor do you yourself admit that affliction, which is a modification, belongs to the conscious principle in its isolated state.
Nor can there be a conjunction of the body and consciousness, because that would entail defects such as impurity.
Furthermore, one does not admit that heat itself is heated.

If you ask, "How then, even in your view, can there be the relationship of the sufferer and the causer of suffering?"—if you say, "Sattva is the sufferer and rajas is the causer of suffering"—we say no.
Because it is impossible for the conscious [self] to be composed of those two [pleasure and pain].
If it is argued that the conscious [self] also "as if suffers" because it conforms to the state of being a sentient being,
then it follows from the use of the word "as if" that, in the ultimate sense, it does not suffer at all.
If it does not burn, the word "not" does not constitute a fault;
for a *ḍuṇḍubha* does not become poisonous merely by being compared to a snake, nor does a snake become non-poisonous merely by being compared to a *ḍuṇḍubha*.
