Therefore, one must admit that this relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering (*tapyatāpakabhāva*) is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and is not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).
This being so, nothing is impaired in my position either.

However, if you instead maintain that the state of being a sufferer for the conscious entity (*cetana*) is indeed ultimately real, then for you alone the consequence of no liberation at all (*anirmokṣa*) would follow even more strictly.
If it is argued that because the tormentor is admitted to be eternal,

even though the powers of the tormented and the tormentor are eternal, there arises the necessity of depending on a cause for their conjunction; and that when the non-perception— which is the cause of the conjunction— ceases, the conjunction comes to an absolute end,
whereby absolute liberation is established— this is not so.

Because darkness, which is non-perception, is admitted to be eternal, and because the emergence and suppression of the qualities (guṇas) are not fixed, the cessation of the cause of conjunction is also not fixed; thus, since disjunction too would be unfixed, for the Sāṃkhya alone, liberation would be unavoidably impossible.

For the follower of the Upaniṣads, however, because he admits the oneness of the Self, because the relationship of object and subject is untenable for a single entity, and because the scripture declares that the diversity of modifications is merely a matter of words, the doubt regarding non-liberation is like [the doubt] in a dream.
Even so, it does not arise [in ultimate reality].

However, in conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), since the relationship between the afflicted and the afflictor is observed in a certain way in a given case, it remains exactly as it was seen there; thus, it neither needs to be challenged nor refuted. // 10 // [Note:
Indeed, the sense-faculty of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) is a single entity capable of grasping multiple forms and other objects.]
There are five sense organs and the mind as the seventh; thus, there are seven organs.
There are five organs of cognition, five organs of action, and the mind; thus, there are eleven.
Intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—these are the three.
"One" refers to intellect alone.
He explains the Sūtra [with the words] "mutually," etc.
The sense organ of cognition is the skin alone, which is a single entity that serves as the cause for the cognition of multiple objects such as sound and the rest;
there are seven organs consisting of the five organs of action, the mind, and [the skin];
or, including the five organs of cognition and the five organs of action along with the mind, there are eleven.
"Buddhi, ahaṃkāra, and manas—these three;
'one' means buddhi alone.

Having thus explained [the objection] on the grounds of internal contradiction between earlier and later statements, he states another point regarding the conflict between Śruti and Smṛti with the words "it is well known" (prasiddha).
Therefore, it is established that because the Sāṃkhya system is rooted in error, there is no contradiction between it and the faultless harmony of the Vedānta.
Unable to endure the inconsistency of his own doctrine, the Sāṃkhya objects, saying: "In this regard [the opponent] says...

The meaning is that the sufferer is the individual soul (*jīva*) and the cause of suffering is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); since their difference is not admitted [by the Vedāntin], the well-known worldly relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering would be subverted.
He explains: "For [if] one...

and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that it would be inconsistent [to claim] that the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) is lost, since there is indeed a mutual difference between those two even though their material cause (*upādāna*) is one, just as there is between heat and light, both of which have fire as their single essence.

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, there is no loss of conventional usage," he says "And if... and so forth, [meaning] that liberation of the self from those two would not occur, just as it does not for fire.

Anticipating the objection that "even while the substratum (dharmin) exists, liberation is possible through the destruction of its own nature, since we observe the destruction of waves and the like even while the water remains," he states the failure of the example with "Even that which... and so forth.

Furthermore, he states "and it is well-known" (*prasiddhaśca*) because accepting a distinction [between the object and its cognition] results in a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), while not accepting it contradicts common worldly experience.
For an object is called "tormenting" (*tāpaka*) because it afflicts one who desires it through the lack of acquisition, loss, and so forth.
He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the non-difference of the seeker (*arthin*) and the object (*artha*) with the words "If...

Since there is no object other than the seeker, it would follow by implication that there is no "object-ness" (*arthatva*), just as there is no "seeker-ness" (*arthitva*); thus he says, "In the same way, [there would be] no object either.
He refutes the acceptability of this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) with the words, "And this is not the case."

For being an end-in-itself (*arthatva*) consists in being the object of desire; and that [status] could not belong to anything other than the desired object, because there would be no desirer [distinct from it].
Indeed, a thing cannot be its own end-in-itself, since it is impossible for the very object of desire to be the desirer.
Therefore, the meaning is that difference must be admitted.
He states "and for this reason there is difference" with the words "the related," etc.; likewise, the syntactical connection is that the object and the seeker of the object are also distinct.

Having first stated the essential nature of the beneficial (*artha*) and the harmful (*anartha*), he clarifies their capacity to cause affliction (*tāpakatva*) with the words: "favorable to the seeker. Having explained the impossibility of liberation according to the Advaita school, he states its possibility according to his own school with the words: "in another birth. The meaning is as follows: the conjunction of the *puruṣa* with that afflicted intellect (*buddhi*)—which is the relationship of owner and owned—is caused by beginningless non-discrimination (*aviveka*). Its removal is through discrimination (*viveka*). Therefore, even for the eternally liberated *puruṣa*, liberation is established in some sense through figurative usage (*upacāra*).

Just as victory and defeat, which actually reside in the warriors, are metaphorically attributed to the king, so too bondage and liberation, which reside in the intellect (buddhi) that is entirely distinct from the person (puruṣa), are metaphorically attributed to the person.
As it has been said: "That [intellect] alone is bound and that alone is liberated.
He establishes his own conclusion with the word "here" (atra).

Is it said that the relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering is untenable from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), or from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-dṛṣṭi*)?
It is not the former; thus he says: "No."
"Because of oneness alone"—
the word "faultiness" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
He explains its lack of faultiness with the words beginning "it might be," and so forth.
The meaning is that this relationship of being the object and the subject is not real;

rather, it exists only where the state of being the sufferer and the inflictor is observed. Adopting the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), the proponent (*siddhāntin*) says, "Do you not see?
[the opponent] objects, "But surely... [fearing] that if the body were the sufferer, it would result in the doctrine that the body is the self (*dehātmavāda*).
The Sāṃkhya, who asserts that there is no suffering for the insentient body alone, must state whether suffering belongs to the pure conscious principle,
or to that which is conjoined with the body,
or to the suffering itself.
Or does it belong to a sentient being?
He says "it is not the first" by stating "it is said," and he says "nor the second or third" with the words beginning with "not even."
He raises a doubt regarding the fourth [point] with the words "sattvam" (the quality of goodness).

He refutes [this] with the words "na tābhyām" (no, by those two), [arguing that] if *sattva* and *rajas* were the sufferer and the tormentor respectively, there would be no bondage for the *puruṣa*, and thus the commencement of the treatise would be purposeless.

He raises the objection that even though the *puruṣa* is unattached (*asaṅga*), there is suffering because of its reflection in the *sattva* which is subject to suffering—this is expressed by the word "sattva.

He replies with "paramārthataḥ" (in the ultimate sense): if that were so, then suffering would be merely false, like the movement of the moon in water, and thus our own position would have been reached.

If it is asked how the falsity of suffering is understood from the mere word "iva" (as if), that is explained: the word "iva" expresses a similarity between the intellect (*buddhi*) as *sattva* and the one who suffers.

And he demonstrates that if this similarity—which consists in the person's state of being subject to suffering—is merely imagined, it is not real because, in fact, there is no suffering; thus he says, "If not.
The meaning is: if the person is in reality devoid of suffering, then the word "as if" (iva) does not constitute a fault, because its purpose is to indicate false suffering.
If it is argued that a false similarity itself is a fault—
He says "no"—that is, "not so.
The meaning of the word *eva* (only) is that both having an object (*saviṣayatva*) and being without an object (*nirviṣayatva*) are to be regarded as merely imagined (*kalpita*).

The sense is: since for the Sāṃkhya the states of being the sufferer and the causer of suffering are products of ignorance (*avidyaka*), nothing at all is faulty in my view; rather, it simply results in what is empirically observed (*dṛṣṭam eva saṃpannam*).

If, out of fear that admitting the capacity for suffering would constitute a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), it is asserted that the person (*puruṣa*) truly possesses the capacity for suffering, even so there would still be a contradiction of tenets, because its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) would be lost;
furthermore, there would be no liberation.
He says "Now" (*atha*) and so forth because truth (*satya*), like the self (*ātman*), cannot be subject to cessation.
Furthermore, he says "Because of its permanence" (*nityatva*) because suffering is constant due to the permanence of *rajas*.
Here, the Sāṃkhya raises an objection: "The one who suffers... (*tapyeti*).
The *sattva* or the *puruṣa* is the power to be afflicted (*tapyā-śakti*), while *rajas* is the power that afflicts (*tāpakā-śakti*).

Ignorance (*aviveka*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), consisting of a false perception; being accompanied by this, the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is "with its cause" (*sanimitta*). The meaning is that this conjunction, which consists in the *puruṣa*'s state of being the master of the *guṇas*, exists because it is dependent upon that [instrumental cause].
Liberation is the absence of suffering.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) refutes [the opponent's view] with "No," on the grounds that there is no liberation because of the non-cessation of the causal signs (*nimitta*).
To the objection that liberation occurs through cessation by means of discernment even in the absence of the cessation of darkness (*tamas*), he says: "And of the qualities (*guṇānām*)."
The sense is that this follows from the acceptance of the principle that "the functioning of the qualities (guṇas) is mobile.
Having stated the impossibility of bondage and liberation according to the opponent's position, he concludes his own position with the words "But for the follower of the Upaniṣads...
Since, in reality, there is no bondage due to oneness, there is no occasion for the suspicion that liberation might not exist.

The meaning is that, since conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) accepts difference, the relationship between the afflicted and the afflictor constitutes bondage; and because its cessation through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is logically established, there is no occasion for objection. //10//
END BsCom_2,2.1.10 START BsCom_2,2.2.11 2.
The Section Concerning the Great and the Long (Mahaddīrghādhikaraṇam) / Sūtra 11.
The doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause has been refuted. Now, the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the cause must be refuted.
In this regard, first of all, the objection that the proponent of atoms (*aṇuvādin*) imagines against the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*) is here addressed.

In this regard, the position of the Vaiśeṣikas is as follows: qualities inherent in the causal substance produce another quality of the same class in the effect-substance; for we observe that from white threads a white cloth is produced, and we do not observe the opposite.
Therefore, if Brahman, who is conscious, is accepted as the cause of the world, then consciousness should also be inherent in the world, which is the effect.
"Because that [consciousness] is not seen [in the effect], the conscious Brahman cannot be the cause of the world.
He refutes this position by means of the very same method [of the opponent]:
"Or like the large and the long from the short and the spherical" (BBs 2.2.11).

This is their system: it is said that atoms, possessing color and other qualities as appropriate, and having the dimension of sphericity (*pārimaṇḍalya*), remain for some time without having initiated an effect.

Subsequently, preceded by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and others, and aided by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), they initiate the entire range of effects through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the qualities of the cause produce another quality in the effect.
When two atoms (paramāṇu) initiate a dyad (dvyaṇuka), then the specific qualities such as whiteness and so forth residing in the atoms initiate other [qualities] such as whiteness in the dyad.
However, the specific quality of the atom, namely sphericity (pārimāṇḍalya), does not initiate another sphericity in the dyad,
because it is accepted that the dyad possesses a different dimension (parimāṇa).
For they describe minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) as dimensions residing in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).
Even when two dyads initiate a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*), the capacity to initiate [qualities] such as whiteness inherent in the dyads remains the same.
However, minuteness and shortness, though inherent in the dyads, do not initiate [corresponding qualities] at all.
This is because it is accepted that the tetrad possesses the dimensions of magnitude and length.
Even when many atoms, or many dyads, or an atom together with a dyad, initiates an effect, the same reasoning applies.

Thus, just as from an atom which is spherical, a dyad is produced that is minute and short, and a triad and so forth that are large and long, yet not spherical; [so too is the case for the subsequent effects].

Or, just as from a binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*)—which is both minute (*aṇu*) and short (*hrasva*)—a tertiary atomic compound (*tryaṇuka*) arises that is large (*mahat*) and long (*dīrgha*), and is neither minute nor short; likewise, if you do not accept that the non-conscious universe is produced from the conscious Brahman, what is lost to you?

Or, if you think: "I maintain that because the effect-substance, such as the binary atomic compound, is occupied by a contrary dimension (*parimāṇa*), the dimensions residing in the causes, such as sphericality (*pārimaṇḍalya*), do not initiate [the effect]."

But there is no other quality (guṇa) opposed to consciousness by which the world would be so pervaded that the consciousness residing in the cause would not initiate another consciousness in the effect;
for there exists no such quality called "unconsciousness" that is opposed to consciousness.
Because it is merely a negation of consciousness,
one might conclude that consciousness possesses the capacity for origination due to its difference from [inert qualities] such as spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*).
Do not think so.

Just as spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other qualities, though present in their causes, possess the very nature of not being productive [of further qualities], so too is it with consciousness (*caitanya*), because this aspect is common to both.
Nor can it be argued that spherical dimension and the like do produce [further qualities] by virtue of having passed into another dimension;
for it is accepted that even an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), once produced, remains for a single moment without qualities prior to the production of its own qualities.

Furthermore, since spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other such qualities are not distracted toward the production of another dimension, they do not initiate another dimension of their own kind; for it is accepted that the production of another dimension has other causes.
As stated: "The large [dimension] arises from the multiplicity of causes, from the largeness of the cause, and from a particularity of aggregation" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.9);
"The minute [dimension] is the opposite of that" (7.1.10).
"For by this [same reasoning], length and shortness are explained" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.17); for these are the sūtras of Kaṇāda.

Nor can it be argued that, due to a particular proximity or some other cause, only qualities such as multiplicity (*bahutva*) and the like initiate [larger dimensions], while sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and the like do not.
When another substance or another quality is being produced, all the qualities of the cause [contribute] due to a specific inherence in their own substratum.
Therefore, it should be understood that the non-productivity of sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth arises from their very nature,
and the same applies to consciousness (*cetanā*).

Furthermore, because we observe the production of substances and other categories that are of a different nature from their causes through conjunction, there is a deviation from the rule that things must arise from causes of the same genus.
If it is argued that, since the subject under discussion is substance (*dravya*), providing an example of a quality (*guṇa*) is inappropriate, we say no;
for by means of this illustration, what is intended to be shown is merely the fact of the commencement of something of a different nature.
Furthermore, there is no reason for any restrictive rule that a substance must be illustrated only by a substance, or a quality only by a quality.

Even your own author of the Sūtras has cited a quality as an illustration of a substance: "Because of the imperceptibility of conjunction [which inheres] in things that are perceptible and imperceptible, a body composed of five elements does not exist" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.2.2).

Just as the conjunction inhering in earth and ether—which are respectively perceptible and imperceptible—is itself imperceptible, so too the body inhering in the five elements, which are respectively perceptible and imperceptible, would be imperceptible.
It might be argued: "The body is indeed perceptible;
therefore, it is not composed of the five elements."
This is what is meant: conjunction is a quality and the body is a substance;
furthermore, in this context as well, the production of something distinct from its cause has been elaborated upon in the Sūtra, "But it is seen" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.6).
But if this is so, has this not already been covered by that [previous discussion]?
We say: no;
for that was refuted in relation to the Sāṃkhya.
This [objection] is directed against the Vaiśeṣika.

But surely, an extended application (*atideśa*) was also made on the basis of an identical principle in the passage: "By this, those systems not accepted by the learned are also explained" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.12).
True, that is so.
However, at the commencement of this Vaiśeṣika system, an elaboration has been made by means of an illustration following that system's own methodology. (11) [FN:
An atom is spherical; the dimension residing in it is sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*).
It should be read as "two and two."]

By way of restating the preceding topic (*vṛttānuvāda*), he states the connection of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) which establishes his own position through the aphorism "like the large and the long" (*mahaddīrghavat*) with the words "pradhāna... etc.

Although the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇuvāda*) ought to have been refuted immediately after the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position—since the establishment of one's own view is more appropriately connected to the *Smṛti-pāda* (the second chapter)—nevertheless, it was previously stated that the Pradhāna cannot be the material cause because its qualities, such as pleasure and so forth, are not present in the world.

The meaning is that the objection—that Brahman cannot be the material cause because the quality of consciousness (*caitanya*) is not inherent in Brahman—is here resolved by obtaining a connection with the illustrative example.
The subject matter is the Vedāntic synthesis (*samanvaya*) which asserts the creation of the world from the conscious Brahman.

Is it the case that whatever quality belongs to an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) produces a quality of the same kind in the resulting substance (*kāryadravya*), as in the case of the whiteness of a thread [producing whiteness in cloth]? [This is the point of comparison.]

When there is doubt as to whether [the world] contradicts logic (*nyāya*) or not, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it does contradict it because logic is non-deviant; the author explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*), beginning with "This," etc., to show that there is no such contradiction because logic is deviant.

Although it was established in the sūtra "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*) that the creation of the insentient proceeds from the sentient, nevertheless, this sūtra is intended to state the deviation of the Vaiśeṣika logic according to their own system.
It is not the case that the meaning has already been established.
At the time of dissolution, atoms remain motionless and uncombined; at the time of creation, however, action arises in them due to their conjunction with a self possessed of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
From that conjunction, the production of other substances occurs.
Having stated the general process— that the qualities of the cause produce another quality in the effect— he explains it specifically with the words "when two":
the atom is spherical, and the dimension residing in it is called sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*).
The meaning is that this constitutes an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the previously stated principle, namely that [an entity] does not originate a quality of its own kind.
He states another instance of deviation with the words "even when two":
the word *dve* should be read twice.

This being the case, the production of a four-atom aggregate (*caturaṇuka*) by means of four dyad-atom aggregates (*dvyaṇuka*) is logically consistent; however, according to the literal [interpretation], the production of a large four-atom aggregate from two dyad-atom aggregates is not tenable, because it must be understood that without either largeness or plurality residing in the cause, largeness cannot arise in the effect.

The authors of the *Prakaṭārtha*, however, state that this commentary belongs to the perspective of the ancient Vaiśeṣikas, as it is seen in the commentary composed by Rāvaṇa, which says: "The cause of the largeness observed in an effect produced from two dyads is what is called 'accumulation' (*pracaya*), namely, a loose conjunction of parts.
In any case, there is a deviation [from the rule] because the dimensions of shortness and minuteness residing in a dyad do not initiate [larger dimensions].

Although logicians postulate that a dyad (dvyaṇuka) arises from exactly two atoms and a triad (tryaṇuka) from three dyads, nevertheless, considering that reasoning lacks a firm foundation and thus there is no such fixed rule, he says: "even when many [atoms come together].
The qualities of the causal factors, such as whiteness and so forth, are the originators of qualities of their own kind.
The meaning is that the process is the same: the dimension of an effect-substance is not originated by the dimensions of its causes, but rather is originated by the number residing in the causes.
Having thus demonstrated this process, he states an exception while applying the Sūtra: "tadevam" (thus, in this way).
This was stated by relying on an indefinite process, namely, that "large and long [substances] arise from atoms alone."
Relying on the fixed rule (*niyataprakriyā*), he states an exception with the words "or as follows" (*yathā vā*).

The meaning is that an atomic substance (*aṇudravya*) is not produced from binary atoms (*dvyaṇuka*) that are minute and short, nor is even a short [substance] produced; thus, there is an exception (*vyabhicāra*).
In the sūtra, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*), intended to include the unmentioned atom (*aṇu*).
And thus, the application of the sūtra is that from the short and the spherical—the dyad and the atom—arises the large, the long, and the minute, namely, the non-conscious from the conscious.

In this regard, the distinction is that from the short arises the large and long triad (tryaṇuka), and from the spherical arises the minute dyad (dvyaṇuka). He raises an objection regarding the disparity between the example and the case at hand with the words: "Now, you might think..."
Because insentience itself is a contradictory quality, he says: "For [the effect] is not insentient.
Having accepted that the substance of the effect is pervaded by another dimension (parimāṇa), he states the equality of the intended portion: "It is not so.
He then abandons that acceptance: "And not..."
For a different dimension that has already arisen is contradictory [to the previous one];
since there is no such contradicting factor prior to its arising, the question is: why should spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) not be initiated in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)?
To the objection that a substance is produced simultaneously with its contradictory dimension, he says: "even though it has been initiated."
If they were produced simultaneously, it would contradict your own tenet;
therefore, the intended meaning is that the absence of contradiction is established.

Having raised the objection that because [substances] are occupied with initiating qualities such as atomicity (aṇutva), spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya) and so forth cannot initiate qualities similar to themselves, he refutes this with "And not... (na ca).
The state of being distracted is established otherwise;
the reason for this is "of another dimension.
He cites the sūtras regarding the existence of other causes: "the cause," and so forth.

Because the causes—the dyads—are many, there is largeness (*mahattva*) in the triad; because of the largeness of the clay, there is largeness in the jar; and in a very large mass of cotton produced from two cotton-balls, there is largeness due to accumulation (*pracaya*), which is a specific kind of conjunction of parts—this is the meaning.
He states that "that" (atomic dimension) refers to minuteness (*aṇutva*), which is the opposite of largeness, and which arises in the dyad through the number two residing in the atoms.

By the phrase "by this," he extends the principle: that which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of largeness is itself the non-inherent cause of lengthiness (*dīrghatva*) which coexists with largeness; and that which is the non-inherent cause of minuteness (*aṇutva*) is itself the non-inherent cause of shortness (*hrasvatva*), which is invariably concomitant with minuteness.
Therefore, the meaning is that since sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and the like are not causes for largeness and so forth, their exclusion from being [causes of] cognition is established.
One should not say that because they lack a specific proximity (*saṃnidhi*), they do not initiate qualities of the same kind; thus he says "nor" (*na ca*).

The meaning is that even in the case of atomic dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth, there is no difference in their residing in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), just as there is in the case of plurality (*bahutva*) and other such qualities.

He states the result of his argument—that in their non-initiation of [new] qualities, the fact that the effect-substance is occupied by contradictory qualities, its being distracted (*vyagratva*), or its lack of proximity (*asaṃnidhi*) is not the cause—by saying "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

As for the argument that— despite the deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of general qualities such as atomicity (pārimāṇḍalya) from the pervasion (vyāpti) that "a quality of the cause produces a quality similar to itself"—
there is another pervasion, namely, "whatever is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) residing in the inherent cause of a substance, it produces a quality of its own same class";
and since consciousness (caitanya) is a specific quality, its productivity is unavoidable.
That is weak;

for it must be understood that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the blue and other colors residing in the threads that cause a variegated cloth, since those are the causes of a variegated color of a different genus, and because consciousness lacks the status of a quality (*guṇa*) by virtue of being the self (*ātman*).
Therefore, it is established that the production of something of a different genus from consciousness is logical.
Regarding this, he states another example: "And from conjunction" (*saṃyogāt*).

Now, if it is argued that Brahman, being conscious, is a substance because it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the effect, and therefore a substance that is not of a different nature must be cited as an example of something producing an effect of a different nature—then [the following is said]:

He raises an objection, saying "In the case of substance," [suggesting] that conjunction, being a quality, is not an appropriate example. He replies, "No," [explaining] that this is an illustration regarding the aspect of producing something heterogeneous—namely, that from a conscious quality (guṇa) there arises an unconscious substance (dravya). He states, "The author of the Sūtras as well," [meaning] that Kaṇāda himself accepts this lack of restriction.
To the question, "How is there no fixed rule based on this much?", he says: "This has been stated.

He raises an objection, fearing that even in the absence of repetition by way of the principle of "not having different characteristics" (*navilakṣaṇatva*), there might be repetition by way of the section on extended application (*atideśādhikaraṇa*): "But is this not an extended application? (*nanvatideśa*).
He states "It is true" in order to refute the rule that the production [of a quality] must have qualities of the same kind, using the examples of sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth;
the meaning is that this is an extension (*atideśa*) of that very [rule]. //11//
END BsCom_2,2.2.11 START BsCom_2,2.3.12 3.
The Section on the Atom Not Being the Cause of the World (Sūtras 12–17)
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] is non-existent.

Now, he refutes the doctrine of atoms as the cause. That doctrine arises as follows: in the world, it is observed that substances possessing parts, such as cloth and the like, are produced by substances such as threads and so forth, which are accompanied by conjunction and follow their own respective movements.
By this general principle, it is understood that whatever possesses parts is all produced by those substances, assisted by conjunction, through their own inherent extension.
And that limit where this distinction between part and whole ceases is the atom (*paramāṇu*), which has reached the ultimate end of diminution.
Furthermore, this entire world, including mountains, oceans, and so forth, possesses parts.
Because it possesses parts, [the world] must have a beginning and an end;
and since an effect cannot exist without a cause, the intention of Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda) is that atoms are the cause of the universe.
Having perceived these four elements—known as earth, water, fire, and air—to possess parts, [he establishes] four kinds...
Atoms are postulated; because they have reached the ultimate limit of reduction, it is impossible to divide them further.
When earth and the other elements are being destroyed, their disintegration proceeds down to the level of atoms; that is the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).

Then, at the time of creation, motion arises in the atoms of air depending upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); that motion joins its own substrate, the atom, with another atom. Thereafter, air is produced through the sequence beginning with the binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*).
Thus is fire, thus is water, thus is earth;
even so is the body together with its sense-faculties. In this very way, this entire world arises from atoms.

The followers of Kaṇāda maintain that from the qualities such as color residing in the atoms, the qualities such as color in dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth arise, according to the analogy of the threads and the cloth.

To this, it is replied: first, the conjunction of atoms existing in a state of separation must be admitted as depending upon action (karma), because we observe the conjunction of things like threads which possess action.
Furthermore, since action is an effect, some cause must be admitted. If none were admitted, then, due to the absence of a cause, no initial action would occur in the atoms.
Even if one is admitted, whether it be effort (*prayatna*) or impact (*abhighāta*), etc., [the same problem follows].
If some cause for action were to be accepted as it has been observed, then because such a cause is impossible, there could be no initial action in the atoms.
For in that state, effort—which is a quality of the self—is not possible due to the absence of a body.
Indeed, effort, which is a quality of the self, arises when there is contact between the self and the mind, provided that the mind is supported by a body.
By this, other perceived causes such as impact and the like must also be rejected.
For all of those occur only after the time of creation; they cannot possibly be the cause of the primordial action.
Now, if it is argued that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is the cause of the primordial action, would that reside in the self (*ātman*) or reside in the atoms (*aṇu*)?
In either case, it is not possible for unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) to account for action within atoms, because the unseen is insentient.
For it has been stated in the Sāṃkhya system that what is insentient does not function or cause others to function independently unless it is presided over by a sentient being;
and in that state, the self is insentient because consciousness has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, because it is admitted that the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) inheres in the self, it cannot be the cause of motion in atoms due to the lack of a connection [between them].

If it is argued that there is a connection between the atoms and the person who possesses the *adṛṣṭa*, then, because that connection would be constant, it would follow that activity would be constant as well, since there is no other regulating factor.

Thus, in this way, since there would be no fixed cause for action among atoms, initial motion could not occur in them. Due to the absence of motion, the conjunction dependent upon it could not occur. And due to the absence of conjunction, the entire series of effects beginning with the dyad (dvyaṇuka), which depends upon that [conjunction], could not exist.
Furthermore, the conjunction of one atom with another must occur either through its entire self or by way of a single part.
If it were through its entire self, then because no increase in size would be possible, there would follow the consequence that [the aggregate] is merely an atom, which contradicts what is observed;
for it is observed that a substance possessing spatial divisions undergoes conjunction with another substance possessing spatial divisions.

If [the atom] were to join with another by means of one part, it would follow that it possesses parts. If it is argued that these parts of the atoms are merely conceptual constructs, then because conceptual constructs lack reality, the conjunction itself would be non-substantial; consequently, it could not serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for a substantial effect.
Furthermore, in the absence of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), an effect-substance such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) could not arise.

Just as at the initial creation (*ādisarga*), action (*karma*) cannot occur in atoms for the sake of producing conjunction due to the absence of a cause, so too at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), action could not occur in atoms for the sake of producing disjunction;
for even there, no fixed, observed cause for it exists.

Even if the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) exists, it serves for the accomplishment of experience (*bhoga*), not for the accomplishment of dissolution (*pralaya*). Therefore, due to the absence of such a cause, there would be no action of the atoms for the purpose of producing conjunction or disjunction;
and consequently, due to the absence of conjunction and disjunction, the non-existence of creation and dissolution—which depend upon them—would follow as a logical consequence.
Thus, this doctrine of atoms as the cause is untenable. 12.
[Note: "By their own concomitants" means by those things connected to themselves.
And the connection is that which consists of the relationship between the supported and the support; it is a composite whole (*samudāya*) that serves as the cause for cognition.
He begins the examination of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine: "In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [composite] does not exist."

Thinking that this [section] does not require a connection with the preceding incidental topic (*prāsaṅgika*), and intending to state its purpose by asserting that it follows the Sāṃkhya section through the connection of a counter-example—namely, that even if the Pradhāna is not a cause when uncontrolled by God, let atoms be a cause when controlled by Him—he says: "Now... (*itānīm*).
The subject matter here is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Vaiśeṣikas, namely, that the world is produced by atoms through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).

Regarding the doubt as to whether this is based on valid means of knowledge (*māna*) or on error (*bhrānti*), the author presents the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "And that" (*sa ca*).
The meaning is: by that [similarity] which consists in the fact that earth and so forth are effects and substances, just like cloth and other such things.

The formal argument is as follows: the subject under dispute, namely the earth and so forth, which possess parts, must be composed of multiple substances accompanied by a conjunction with substances of smaller dimensions, because they are effect-substances, just like a cloth and the like.
The qualifying attributes of the probandum (sādhyaviśeṣaṇa) are intended for the purpose of establishing the ultimate atom (paramāṇu) as desired by oneself.
Now, one might ask: "How is the establishment of the ultimate atom achieved by this much alone?
To that, he says: "And this [atom]..."

The meaning is as follows: "paramāṇu" (atom) is understood as the ultimate limit—the terminus of decrease—wherefrom the disputed state of having parts (sāvayavatva), which serves as the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka), ceases to exist.
The sense is that since the operation of inference proceeds only so long as there are parts, a dyad (dvyaṇuka) smaller than that is established as being partless (niravayava).
To one who argues that the reason "being an effect-substance" (kāryadravyatva) is unestablished because of the doctrine of the eternity of the world, he replies: "And all... (sarvaṃ ca).
The meaning is: the subject under dispute possesses a beginning and an end, because it has parts, like a cloth.
Having refuted the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*), he refutes its lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) with the words "nor" (*na ca*).
In response to the inquiry as to how many kinds these are, he says "those" (*tāni*).
Anticipating the objection that they cannot be the cause of the world because they too are destroyed at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), he says "and of them" (*teṣāṃ ca*).
The meaning is that the destruction of the whole does not occur through the division or destruction of its parts;

and because atoms are partless, causes of destruction such as the division of parts are impossible for them, and thus they are not destroyed. He states the sequence of creation resulting from their permanence with the words "tataḥ" (from that).

Thus, the result of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the doctrine of Kaṇāda is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is a contradiction with the systematic unity (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta, and therefore it is not established.
The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that there is no contradiction because that [doctrine] is rooted in error—with the words "In this regard, this... [and so on].
At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the conjunction of separated atoms must be explained as resulting from the action of one or the action of both.
Furthermore, an observed cause for action is effort and the like;
for example, bodily movement arises from the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort,
and the shaking of trees arises from the impact of wind and so forth.
In cases such as the striking of the hand, an instrumental cause is observed; likewise, is such a cause accepted for the action of an atom, or not?
In the second case, there would be no production of action; nor is the first case [tenable].
Since effort and the like occur only after the creation [of the world], action is impossible in either case.
Therefore, due to the impossibility of action, there can be no creation of dyads and so forth preceded by conjunction; this is the meaning of the Sūtra.

The distinction is that *abhighāta* (striking) is a specific kind of conjunction with a substance possessing velocity for a stationary object, whereas *nodana* (pushing) is the same for a moving object.

He raises the objection: "But [the action in] atoms arises from the conjunction of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) with the self, even in the absence of a visible cause. He then refutes this by means of a dilemma: "But that [unseen force]," etc.
It should be understood that this dilemma was formulated with the thought: "Why should the atom not be the substratum [of the adṛṣṭa], just as the inert self is?"
He applies the Sūtra here as well, saying "in both ways.
To the objection that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) presided over by the individual soul (*jīva*) may be the cause, he says "and of the self" (*ātmanaśca*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "because it is insentient (*acetana*), it cannot be a presiding agent."
The presiding agency of a separate Lord (Bhinneśvara) will be refuted later.
The lack of sentience in the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) has been stated as the reason for its not being caused by action.
He states another reason: "because it would be inherent in the self" (*ātmasamavāyitve*).

He raises the objection that, like gravity, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is also a cause of motion in that which is conjoined with its own substratum—this is expressed by the phrase "as in the case of the unseen force.

He refutes this by stating "due to the connection," meaning that because the conjunction with the omnipresent [Self] exists eternally in atoms, there would be a continuous state of motion, resulting in the impossibility of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).
Furthermore, he says "by another regulator" because, even if the occasional activity [of atoms] cannot be regulated by the unseen force, one might argue that the regulation comes from God (*īśvara*).

The meaning is that since eternal knowledge is not established—due to the contradiction with the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever knowledge exists is produced by a body"—the Lord does not exist as its possessor; and even if he did exist, because he would be eternally present, he could not function as a controller.
He concludes the meaning of the Sūtra with the words: "Thus, therefore... (tadevam).
Having refuted the causality of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he refutes its very nature with the words "And conjunction [of] the atom...

The meaning is that if conjunction were all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), one atom would be contained within the other; consequently, because the expansion of an effect would be impossible, every effect would be merely the size of an atom.

Furthermore, he states "It is observed... to show that since conjunction is observed to reside in only one part of a composite substance (*sāṃśadravya*), its all-pervasiveness cannot be postulated, as that would contradict observation.
The connection is that if the conjunction of an atom were by way of a single part;
since even the conjunction residing in a spatially conceived location—distinguished by direction—is itself merely conceptual, no effect could arise from it, or if it did arise, it would be false;
thus, this would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenet (apasiddhānta). This is the meaning.
Having applied the sūtra to refute the creation [theory] of the followers of Kaṇāda, he now applies the sūtra to refute their dissolution as well, with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
The process that [they propose]— that creation arises from the conjunction of atoms through action, and dissolution from their disjunction— is not tenable.

Since there is no observed cause— such as a directed impact— for the simultaneous disjunction of infinite atoms, and since the unobserved causes consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) cannot function as the motive for dissolution because they exist for the sake of pleasure and pain (and thus cannot produce a dissolution devoid of pleasure and pain), disjunction cannot occur through action motivated by the unobserved.

And thus, since the causes for both the perceived and the unperceived do not exist, action does not exist in either way—neither as having conjunction as its purpose nor as having disjunction as its purpose;
therefore, due to the absence of action, there is an absence of creation and dissolution, which are preceded by those [conjunctions and disjunctions]. This is the construction of the sūtra. //12//
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its similarity [to other categories]. (BS 2.2.13)
"And because of the admission of inherence, there is the non-existence [of the whole]"—this connects with the ongoing refutation of the atomic theory (*aṇuvāda*).
For you admit that a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) being produced from two atoms inheres in those two atoms, which are entirely distinct from it.
However, by one who admits this, the status of the atom as a cause cannot be established.
Why?
Because of equality and because of the resulting infinite regress.
For just as the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), being absolutely distinct from its two atoms, [is connected] to them by a relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*); [the same would apply to that relation].

In this same way, inherence (*samavāya*) as well, being absolutely distinct from its substrates (*samavāyin*), would have to be connected with those substrates by means of yet another relation characterized as inherence, since the state of absolute difference is identical [in both cases].
Consequently, one would have to postulate a further relation for each of those, and thus an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would necessarily follow.

But surely, in this case, inherence (samavāya), being perceivable through cognition, is grasped as being eternally connected with its inherent relata (samavāyin), and not as unconnected or dependent on another relation;
therefore, no further relation need be postulated for it, which would lead to an infinite regress.
To this, it is replied: "No."

This being the case, conjunction (saṃyoga) as well would be eternally connected with its conjuncts, and thus, like inherence (samavāya), it would not require another relation. If, on the other hand, conjunction were to require another relation because it is a distinct entity (arthāntara),
then inherence too would require another relation because it is likewise a distinct entity.
Nor is it reasonable to say that conjunction, being a quality (*guṇa*), requires another relation, whereas inherence (*samavāya*) does not because it is not a quality;
for the reason for such dependence is the same in both cases,
and the technical designation "quality" is irrelevant.
Therefore, for one who accepts inherence (*samavāya*) as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) necessarily follows.
And when an infinite regress occurs, since one thing remains unestablished, everything becomes unestablished; thus, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) could not possibly be produced from two atoms.
For this reason as well, the doctrine that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable. // 13 //

"And because of the admission of inherence (samavāya), there is the non-existence [of atoms]; the impossibility of the atomic theory follows by implication. This means that since dyads (dvyaṇuka) and inherence are equally distinct from atoms, just as a dyad would require another inherence, so too would inherence require another inherence, leading to an infinite regress (anavasthiti).
Now, one might argue: "Inherence, which is the regulator of specific cognitions such as 'the cloth is here in these threads,' does not depend on any other relation."
He raises an objection, saying "But here," on the grounds that [the relation] is eternally connected by its very nature.
He refutes this, saying "No," because conjunction (saṃyoga) also admits of being a connection by its own nature, and thus inherence (samavāya) would not be distinct.
If it is argued that [inherence is distinguished] because it is different from its relata, that requirement applies equally to inherence as well.
And regarding the "definition of quality" (*guṇaparibhāṣā*):

even in the absence of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*), since action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), and so forth are admitted to have inherence (*samavāya*), the property of being a quality is neither a pervader (*vyāpaka*) nor a pervaded (*vyāpya*) with respect to having inherence.

Since a quality (*guṇa*) can also exist through an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) just like inherence (*samavāya*), there is no supporting reasoning for its pervasion [with the need for another relation].

Therefore, being distinct from the related entities is itself the cause for requiring another relation; since this is equally true of inherence as well, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is unavoidable.
And that [inherence] brings about the destruction of its very root;
the meaning is that when inherence is not established, the dyad (dvyaṇuka) which is inherent in it cannot be established. //13//
And because [the self] exists eternally. (BBs 2.2.14)
Furthermore, atoms must be admitted as having either the nature of activity, the nature of cessation, the nature of both, or the nature of neither, since there is no other alternative.
Yet none of these four positions is tenable.
If they had the nature of activity, then because activity would exist eternally, it would follow that there could be no dissolution.
Even if its nature were cessation, since cessation would exist eternally, it would follow that creation never occurs.
Furthermore, having both as its nature is untenable due to contradiction.

If, however, it has neither as its nature, and activity and cessation are admitted to occur by virtue of external causes, then because such causes as the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) are eternally present, it follows that activity would be eternal.
Even if [the atoms] were not dependent [on a conscious agent], it would follow that there could be no occasional activity [of the world], since such things as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) are eternal.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable. // 14 //
He explains the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (api ca).
If [consciousness] has experience as its intrinsic nature, then its activity must be said to be contingent upon a cause;
yet, since causes such as time and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) are eternally present, it would follow that activity occurs eternally.
The meaning is that if it were signless (animitta), there would be an absence of activity. //14//
And because they possess form and so forth, the opposite [of being imperceptible] is observed. (BBs 2.2.15)

That which the Vaiśeṣikas accept— namely, that atoms are fourfold, possess color and other qualities, are the originators of the fourfold world of primary elements and their derivatives (bhūta-bhautika), and are eternal; and that these atoms, being substances with parts, are divided according to their parts until no further division is possible— that acceptance of theirs is entirely without foundation.
Because, since atoms possess form and other qualities, the opposite of their atomicity and permanence would necessarily follow;
that is to say, in relation to the ultimate cause, their grossness and impermanence would result, which is contrary to what is intended. Why?
Because it is observed thus in the world:

if a thing possessing form and so forth is seen in the world to be gross and impermanent in relation to its own cause— for example, a cloth is gross and impermanent in relation to its threads, and the threads are gross and impermanent in relation to their filaments— then [the same applies here].
Furthermore, these atoms are accepted by them as possessing color and other qualities;
therefore, they too must have causes, and in relation to those [causes], they would necessarily follow as being gross and impermanent.
As for the reason they have stated for their permanence—namely, "That which exists and has no cause is permanent" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.1)—[it is refuted as follows].

Even that [argument] being thus is not possible regarding atoms, because, in the manner already stated, it is established that even atoms possess causes. Furthermore, as for the second reason stated for their eternity: "And because there is no specific negation of the term 'non-eternal'" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.4).
Even that does not necessarily prove the permanence of atoms;
for if there were no permanent entity whatsoever, the formation of a negative compound with the word "permanent" would be untenable.
However, it does not depend specifically upon the permanence of atoms.
And that eternal, supreme cause, Brahman, certainly exists;

for the establishment of any object does not occur through the mere conventional usage of words and their referents, since such usage enters into operation only when the word and its referent have already been established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for the third reason stated regarding permanence— namely, "and ignorance" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.5)—
if this is explained as the non-perception by direct observation of existing causes whose effects are being perceived,
then it would follow that even the duality-atoms (dvyaṇuka) are permanent.
If it were further qualified by the phrase "provided it is not a substance," even so, only the state of being without a cause would be established as the ground for permanence;
and since that has already been stated previously, the phrase "and non-cognition" (*avidyā ca*) would be redundant.

Alternatively, it might be explained that because no third cause of destruction—other than the division of the cause or the destruction of the cause—is possible, this "non-cognition" (*avidyā*) demonstrates the permanence of the atoms.
There is no necessary rule that a perishing entity must perish by means of only two causes.
For this [rule] would hold true only if one were to admit that a substance is produced by another substance when it is accompanied by conjunction and consists of multiple substances.

However, when it is admitted that a cause—which is of a general nature and devoid of specific distinctions—becomes a producer by attaining a different state characterized by specific qualities, then, just as the hardness of ghee melts away, so too does the state of material form melt away.
Destruction would thus be possible.
Therefore, because they possess form and other qualities, there would be a contradiction of your intended position regarding atoms.
For this reason as well, the doctrine that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable. // 15 //

Furthermore, he states the system of the opponent in order to apply the following sūtra: "Moreover, atoms possess inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa), they are gross relative to their causes, and they are non-eternal, because they possess color, because they possess taste, because they possess smell, and because they possess touch, like a jar.

If it is objected: "In this case, 'atom-ness' (paramāṇutva) is the delimiting factor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka); how then can 'grossness' (sthūlatva), which is contradictory to it, be established as the probandum (sādhya)? The answer is: No.
This is because the properties of air-ness, fire-ness, and so forth, serve as distinct delimiters.
Nor is there a lack of logical necessity,
for if [the subject] were devoid of causes and yet eternal, it would be impossible for it to possess color and other qualities, just like the self (ātman).

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of a separate proof such as "air has a cause," there would be the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) even though the reasons such as "possessing color" (*rūpa*) lack the fault of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*);

for the point is that at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "wherever there is touch, there is a cause; wherever there is color, there is a cause"—the probandum is not established with respect to the delimitation (*avacchedaka*) of "air-ness" (*vāyutva*) and so forth.

Having raised a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) by stating, "Atoms are eternal because, while possessing existence, they lack a cause, like the self," he refutes it by showing the non-establishment of the qualified subject (viśeṣyāsiddhi), beginning with the words, "And as for that eternity..."
Existence (*sattva*) means the state of being an entity (*bhāvatva*), for the purpose of excluding prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
The negation of eternality (*nityatva-pratiṣedha*) possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogika*), because it is a form of non-existence (*abhāvatva*).

"Just as in the case of the absence of a jar," [it is argued that] when permanence is established in some [entity], since "the effect is impermanent" specifically negates permanence in the effect, permanence is thereby established in the atoms which constitute the cause; for otherwise, in the absence of a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the negation would be untenable. Having thus restated what was said by Kaṇāda, [the author] refutes it on the grounds of its being established otherwise, beginning with the words "As for that which...
(*yadapi*). Having accepted the conventional usage of negating permanence in the effect, he has stated the establishment of the counter-positive in Brahman.
In reality, however, the very conventional usage of "particularity" is unestablished;

for without the knowledge of the permanence of the cause through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible to employ the convention that "the effect is impermanent. Thus he says: "And not by verbal [testimony]," etc.
If there were another means of valid cognition regarding the permanence of the cause, then this conventional usage would have its root.

The point is this: prior to the fundamental cognition (*mūlajñāna*), there is no establishment of a real entity based on mere conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*), because that would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of establishing the existence of a *yakṣa* in a banyan tree simply through conventional usage. However, once the fundamental cognition has occurred, everything is established by that alone; thus, the introduction of conventional usage is redundant.
Having thus refuted two *Kaṇāda* sūtras regarding the permanence of atoms, he refutes the third with the words "As for that which... (*yadapi*).

If the meaning of the Sūtra were that the knowledge of the cause—by means of perception—of existing atoms whose gross effects are being perceived is ignorance (*avidyā*), then the fact of having an imperceptible cause would be the reason for their eternity.
That is not so, because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). This is the meaning.

If "being devoid of constituent substances" were the qualification of the reason (*hetu*), then the qualificand would become redundant and it would result in tautology; thus he says, beginning with "atha," etc.
[He asserts that] atoms are eternal.
He raises an objection regarding the meaning of the sūtra— "because destruction is not perceived, as in the case of the self"— with the words "Now, moreover" (athāpi).
It is observed that the destruction of cloth and the like occurs through the disjunction or the destruction of its constituent parts, such as the threads.
And since that duality does not exist in partless atoms, the meaning is that they are eternal.
He refutes this by saying "no," on the grounds that, according to the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), something capable of destroying the atoms is possible.
If it were thought that "origination" (ārambha) is the production of a distinct substance through the conjunction of parts, [then the objection would hold].
In that case, there would be the restriction that the destruction of a substance occurs only by two [causes].
However, there is no proof for its production [from parts], since a cloth distinct from the conjoined threads is not observed.
Therefore, on the strength of experience, one must accept that the cause itself, though inherently devoid of distinction, exists as the effect in the form of a state possessing distinctions.

Likewise, for even subtle (aṇu) things which are transformations of ignorance, destruction is possible through their attainment of the state of being a cause by means of the concealment of their individualized form as aggregates, caused by time and other factors at the time of dissolution.

This is just as the solidity of clarified butter melts upon contact with fire, without the destruction of the conjunction of its parts or the destruction of the parts themselves. Nor should it be suspected that this is not a valid illustration because solidity, being a qualification of conjunction, is a quality, and thus its case would not apply when a substance is destroyed; for [solidity here functions as a mode].

Because even a substance possessing qualities can undergo destruction from some cause, as illustrated by this partial example, and because the technical definition of a "quality" (guṇa) is not strictly binding;
for in reality, solidity— whether in ghee or a liquid— is simply the substance itself, being a specific transformation of the underlying ghee that persists through both states.
Nor should it be said that even though it is a substance, its destruction occurs solely through the disjunction of its parts;

for the meaning is that since clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is a single transformed entity (*pariṇāmin*), disjunction is impossible, and because such disjunction is likewise impossible when the hardness of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is destroyed.
Furthermore, since it is stated that "during dissolution there was no dust (matter), nor anything else," the destruction of atoms is established.
Therefore, they do not possess the status of being the ultimate cause; thus he concludes with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). //15//
And because there is a fault in both cases. (BS 2.2.16)
Earth is gross, possessing the qualities of smell, taste, form, and touch; water is subtle, possessing the qualities of form, taste, and touch;
fire is subtler still, possessing the qualities of form and touch.

Air has the quality of touch and is the most subtle; thus, these four elements are observed in the world to possess qualities that are accumulated or diminished, and to be endowed with a gradation of grossness, subtlety, and extreme subtlety.
In the same way, atoms too would have to be conceived as possessing qualities that are either accumulated or diminished, or not.
In either case, the attachment of faults would be unavoidable.

If one were to postulate that there is an increase or decrease in qualities, then for those with increased qualities, the consequence would be that they are no longer atoms due to the increase in their physical form (*mūrti*).

Nor can it be said that an increase in qualities occurs without an increase in physical form, because in the case of composite elements, an increase in physical form is observed whenever there is an increase in qualities.

If, however, in order to establish the equality of atomhood, the qualities of being increased or decreased were not postulated, and if instead all [atoms] were postulated as having only a single quality each, then there would be no perception of touch in fire,
nor of both color and touch in water,
nor of taste, color, and touch in earth.
Because the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of their cause;
for if it were assumed that all [elements] possess exactly four qualities, then there would be the perception of odor even in water.
In fire, there would be smell and taste; in air, there would be smell, color, and taste.
But this is not observed to be the case.
Therefore, the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] is also untenable. (16) [Commentary: "Because of the accumulation of form" means because of grossness (*sthaulya*).
Having stated the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that whatever possesses a greater number of qualities is gross—the author presents an alternative analysis by saying "tadvat" (in the same way).
It is postulated that the earth-atom possesses more qualities than those [other atoms], and therefore the water-atom and the others possess one fewer quality each; or is it not so?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "when it is being postulated," meaning because of the increase in form, that is, due to grossness.
An earth atom is grosser than a water atom because it possesses a greater number of qualities, just like a jar; thus should the argument be formulated.
He refutes the argument of lack of necessity with the words "and not without," the sense being that there would be a contradiction with what is observed.
On the alternative view that this is not the case, for the sake of equality among all atoms, they must either possess one quality each or possess four qualities each.
He states the fault in both cases with the words beginning "But if it is not postulated," etc. (verse 16).
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of expectation. (BS 2.2.17)

The doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause was even adopted by certain knowers of the Veda, such as Manu and others, with the intention of relying on aspects such as the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*).
However, this doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the cause has not been accepted in any respect by any of the learned; therefore, it must be utterly disregarded by those who follow the Veda.

Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas accept six categories (*padārtha*) which constitute the subject matter of their system—namely, substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—as being absolutely distinct from one another and possessing distinct characteristics.
Just as [one might speak of] a "human horse" or a "hare," so too,
having accepted that [the self is the substratum], they nevertheless accept that the remaining [qualities] are dependent upon a substance; that is not tenable.

How so? Just as in the world, things such as rabbits, kuśa grass, and palāśa leaves, being absolutely distinct from one another, do not possess a state of mutual dependence, so too, because substances and the other categories are absolutely distinct, it is impossible for qualities and the rest to have dependence upon substance.

Now, if it were the case that qualities and so forth are dependent upon substance, then—because they exist when substance exists and do not exist when substance is absent—it would follow that substance alone, through its various distinctions such as configuration and the like, becomes the object of multiple words and cognitions;
just as Devadatta, though being only one, becomes the object of multiple words and cognitions due to his association with different states.
This being the case, both the consequence of the Sāṃkhya doctrine and the contradiction of one's own established tenet would result.
But surely, even though smoke exists as something other than fire, its dependence on fire is observed.
True, it is observed;
however, because there is a perception of difference, the distinctness of fire and smoke is determined in that case.

In this case, however, as in the instances "a white blanket," "a red cow," or "a blue lotus," because each respective substance is perceived through its particular attribute, there is no perception of a difference between the substance and the quality— as there is, for example, between fire and smoke. Therefore, the quality has the substance as its very nature.
By this, the substantial nature of action, generality, particularity, and inherence is explained.
If it should be argued that qualities and so forth are dependent on substance because substance and quality are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*),
then that "inseparability" must be either non-distinctness of location, non-distinctness of time, or non-distinctness of intrinsic nature.
In every respect, this is not tenable.
First, if they were not located in different places, one's own accepted position would be contradicted.
How so?
For it is accepted that the region of the threads begins the cloth, but not the region of the cloth itself;
however, the qualities of the cloth, such as whiteness and so forth, are accepted as being in the region of the cloth, not in the region of the threads.
And thus they say: "Substances originate another substance, and qualities originate another quality" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.10).
For they indeed maintain that the causal substances, the threads, originate the effect-substance, the cloth;
and that the qualities residing in the threads, such as whiteness and the like, originate another quality, such as whiteness, in the effect-substance, the cloth.
That assumption would be contradicted if it were admitted that substance and quality do not occupy distinct locations.
If "non-separateness in time" were meant by "inseparability," then it would follow that the left and right horns of a cow are also inseparable.
However, if inseparability means non-distinctness in nature, then through such inseparability, a difference in essence between substance and quality becomes possible.
This is because [the cause] is perceived as being identical with that [effect].

Furthermore, their assertion that "conjunction is the relation between two things established separately (yutasiddha), whereas inherence (samavāya) is [the relation] between two things not established separately (ayutasiddha)" is false;
for it is impossible for a cause established prior to its effect to be "not established separately" from that effect.
Now, if this admission were made that inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation of an inseparably established effect with its cause,
even so, a relation of an effect that is previously unestablished and has not yet acquired its own nature with its cause is not possible, because a relation depends upon two terms.
If it is argued that it becomes related after having been established, [the response follows].

If it is admitted that the effect is established through a prior relation with its cause, then because there is no lack of separate existence (*ayutasiddhi*) between cause and effect, the claim that "conjunction and disjunction do not exist between them" would be wrongly stated.

Furthermore, just as the relation of a newly produced, inactive effect-substance with other all-pervading substances such as space is admitted to be conjunction alone and not inherence, so too its relation with the causal substance should be conjunction alone and not inherence.
Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) apart from their relationship.
If it is argued that their existence is established because we observe the words and cognitions "conjunction" and "inherence" distinct from the word and cognition "relationship," we say no;
for even in the case of a single entity, we observe multiple words and cognitions depending on its internal nature (*svarūpa*) versus its external form (*bāhyarūpa*).
Just as Devadatta, though being only one, comes to be the object of various words and cognitions in the world depending on his own nature and his relations—
such as "man," "brahmin," "learned in the Vedas," "generous," "child," "youth," "old man," "father," "son," "grandson," "brother," or "son-in-law"—
and just as a single line, by being placed in different positions, undergoes a distinction of words and cognitions such as "ten," "hundred," or "thousand."

Likewise, in the case of two related things themselves, their fitness for the words and cognitions "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and "inherence" (*samavāya*) occurs independently of any additional word or cognition of a relation, and not because of the existence of a separate entity;
thus, since that [separate entity] is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception, there is an absence of any other thing.
Nor does the fact that the words and cognitions of "relation" have related things as their object entail the consequence of those words and cognitions occurring incessantly.
This is because it has already been answered that [conjunction] occurs in relation to its own form and to other forms;

likewise, conjunction is not possible for atoms, the self, and the mind because they lack spatial divisions (apradeśatva), since conjunction is observed only between a substance possessing spatial divisions and another substance possessing spatial divisions.

If it is argued that spatial locations will be imagined for atoms, the self, and the mind, we say no; for if one imagines objects that do not exist, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of all objects being established.
This is because there is no restrictive cause to limit the imagination, such that "only this much—whether contradictory or non-contradictory—an existing object should be imagined, and nothing more."
Furthermore, since conceptualization is under one's own control and can be performed extensively,
there is no reason to prevent one from conceiving hundreds or thousands of objects beyond the six categories imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas.
Therefore, whatever anyone finds pleasing would be established for them.

A certain compassionate person might imagine that the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is full of suffering for living beings, should not exist at all; or another, being distressed, might imagine the rebirth even of those who are liberated. Who could be the preventer of these two?
Furthermore:
it is impossible for a composite dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) to be joined with two partless atoms, just as [it is impossible] for space to be joined [with anything].
For there is no joining of space with earth and so forth, as there is between lac and wood.
If it is argued that "inherence must necessarily be postulated because the relationship of the supported and the support between cause and effect would otherwise be untenable," we say no;
for this involves mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

For the establishment of the relationship of the supported and the support depends upon the establishment of the difference between cause and effect, and the establishment of their difference depends upon the establishment of the relationship of the supported and the support—just as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit—thus resulting in mutual dependence.
For the Vedāntins do not admit a difference between cause and effect, nor a relationship of the supported and the support,
because they maintain that the effect is merely a particular configuration of the cause.
Furthermore:

Since atoms are limited in extent, they must possess as many parts as there are directions—whether six, eight, or ten; and because they possess parts, they would be non-eternal. Thus, the accepted doctrine of their eternity and partlessness would be contradicted.
If it is argued that those very parts which you postulate as being distinct according to the different directions are themselves the atoms, we say no.

Because destruction is established through a sequence of degrees of grossness and subtlety, starting from the non-supreme cause; just as the earth, being the grossest among dyads and so forth, perishes despite being a real entity,
and thereafter other things of the same class as the earth— whether subtle or subtler— perish.
From that, the dyad [is destroyed]; likewise, even the atoms would perish because they belong to the same class as earth.
If it is argued that even when perishing, they perish only through the disjunction of their parts;
This is not a fault, because we have already explained that destruction can occur even as in the case of the melting of the hardness of ghee;

for just as in the case of ghee, gold, and the like, even though their parts are not being divided, the destruction of their hardness occurs through the attainment of a liquid state due to contact with fire.
In this way, even for atoms, there will be a destruction of their form and other qualities through their attainment of the state of being the ultimate cause.
Likewise, the commencement of an effect does not occur solely through the conjunction of parts,
since we observe the commencement of effects such as curd and ice from milk and water even without a further conjunction of parts.
