Consequently, in the case of gold and so forth—which are inherently devoid of any excellence—the sequence of effects such as earrings arises through a sequence of excellences produced by auxiliary factors such as heating with fire.
Nor should it be argued that if an excellence does not require another excellence, then the effect itself would likewise require nothing;

for if a cloth did not require clay, then because there is no difference in their status as effects, it would follow that a pot also would not require clay. Thus, dependence upon auxiliaries is established equally through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
As for what was said— that in the state where the effect is absent, it would follow that the cause is non-existent— that is not so;
for even that which is not a cause can be established as existent through the absence of sublation.
For existence is not merely the capacity for causal efficiency; since that [capacity] is impossible for what is non-existent, existence is distinct from it.
Indeed, the capacity for causal efficiency belongs to what exists, not to what does not exist.
Therefore, existence (*sattva*), which consists of an uncontradicted nature and serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of causality, is indeed distinct from causality itself.
Thus, the intention is that the status of being a cause is logically established for those entities that are pervasive and stable.
He also points out the contradiction with what was stated previously, saying "Moreover" (*api ca*). //26//
And thus, even for those who are indifferent, success is achieved. (BsCom_2,2.4.27)
Furthermore, if it were admitted that an entity arises from non-existence,
then even for people who are indifferent and making no effort, their desired goals would be accomplished,
because non-existence is easily available.

Even for a farmer who does not exert effort in the work of the field, there may be the production of grain; and for a potter who does not exert effort in the processing of clay, there may be the production of vessels;
and even for a weaver who does not weave threads, there is the acquisition of cloth as if he were weaving them.
Furthermore, no one would ever strive for either heaven or liberation in any way;
nor is this [striving] logical or accepted by anyone.
Therefore, this acceptance of the arising of existence from non-existence is also untenable. (27)
FN: For those who do not exert themselves, that is, those devoid of effort;
"amatra" refers to a vessel such as a jar.
It has been stated that if production occurred from non-existence, there would be production even from a rabbit's horn.
He states another over-extension [of the argument] with the words "of those who are indifferent": that is, of those who are inactive and devoid of effort.
"Amatra" refers to a vessel such as a jar.
This refers to one who is performing [the meditation] without engaging in [external] activity.

Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the doctrine of momentary external objects—which is rooted in delusion—and the systematic exposition (*samanvaya*) of the eternally immutable Brahman. //27//

"Not non-existence, because [things] are perceived.

(BBs 2.28) Thus, when the refutations regarding the impossibility of a composite whole and so forth have been raised based on the doctrine of external objects, the Buddhist Proponent of Consciousness-Only now responds:
"Indeed, observing the attachment of some to external entities, this system of the doctrine of external objects was elucidated in accordance with their inclination."
This is not the intention of the Sugata;
rather, his intended position is precisely the doctrine of consciousness as the sole aggregate (*vijñānaikaskandhavāda*).

And within that doctrine of consciousness, the entire conventional operation of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge is established as existing solely internally, in the form of mental representations.

Even though external objects exist, the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and results (*phala*) does not occur without their being ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*).
How, then, is it understood that all this conventional usage resides solely within [the mind], and that no external object exists apart from consciousness?
He says: "Because of the impossibility of that [external object]."
For if that external object is admitted, it must be either atoms or their aggregates, such as pillars and the like.
In that regard, atoms cannot first be the objects determined by the cognition of pillars and so forth (because no cognition arises that has the appearance of atoms).
Nor can their aggregates, such as pillars and the like, be so.
Because it is impossible to determine whether those [objects] are different or non-different from their atoms;
in this same way, one should also perceive universals (*jāti*) and so forth through direct perception.

Furthermore, regarding the cognition that arises with a common nature based on mere experience, there is this partiality toward each respective object—such as "cognition of a pillar," "cognition of a wall," "cognition of a jar," or "cognition of a cloth."
Since this [perception] is not possible without a specific quality residing in cognition, one must necessarily admit that cognition possesses a similarity of form (*sārūpya*) with its object.
And once that is admitted, since the form of the object is already contained within the cognition itself, the postulation of the existence of an external object is useless.
Furthermore, because they are invariably perceived together (*sahopalambha*), it follows that there is no difference between the object and the consciousness.
For there is no perception of one of these two when the other is not perceived; nor is this [perception] logical if they were distinct in nature,
because there would be no obstructing cause [to prevent their simultaneous perception].
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is an absence of external objects;
and this should be understood through examples such as dreams.

For just as the cognitions of dreams, illusions, mirages, water in a mirage, and cities of the Gandharvas occur in the forms of grasped object and grasping subject even without any external object, [so it is with all perceptions].
Thus, it is understood that even cognitions whose objects belong to the waking state— such as the cognition of a pillar and so forth— are capable of being [mere mental constructs],
because there is no difference in their status as cognitions.
But how, in the absence of an external object, is the diversity of cognitions possible?
He says, "Because of the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For in beginningless *saṃsāra*, the variety of consciousnesses and latent impressions—existing in a relationship of mutual cause and effect like a seed and its sprout—is not contradicted.
Furthermore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the variety of cognitions has latent impressions alone as its cause.
Because both of us admit that the variety of cognitions caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) occurs even without an external object— as in dreams and the like—
whereas I do not admit that the variety of cognitions caused by an external object occurs without latent impressions;
therefore, for this reason as well, the external object does not exist.
This being the case, we reply: "There is no non-existence, because [objects] are perceived.
Indeed, it is not possible to determine the non-existence of an external object.
Why?
Because of perception; for,
in accordance with each respective condition, an external object is indeed perceived— such as a pillar, a wall, a jar, or a cloth—
and it is not possible for that which is being perceived to be non-existent.
For just as someone who is eating might say, "I am not eating, nor am I satiated," even while the satisfaction resulting from the act of eating is being experienced by himself;

in the same way, how could one whose words are to be accepted be a person who, while perceiving an external object for himself through the contact of the senses, says, "I do not perceive it, nor does it exist"?
[The opponent objects: "But I do not say, 'I do not perceive any object at all'; rather, I say that I do not perceive anything distinct from the perception itself."
Indeed, you speak thus because of the unrestrained nature of your tongue;
however, you do not speak with reason.
For even the existence of an object distinct from its cognition must necessarily be admitted on the basis of that very cognition itself.
For no one perceives the perception itself as a pillar or a wall;

rather, all worldly people perceive pillars, walls, and so forth precisely as objects of perception. Even those who deny external objects explain them by saying that what is an internal form of the knowable appears as if it were external.

Even they, while apprehending a consciousness that is well-known to all the world and appearing as something external, and yet wishing to deny the external object, employ the expression "as if external" (*bahirvadati*).
Otherwise, why would they say "as if external"?
For no one would ever say, "Viṣṇumitra appears like the son of a barren woman."
Therefore, for those who accept reality according to experience, it is logical to accept that [the object] appears as external itself, and not that it appears as if it were external.

[Objection: But surely, because an external object is impossible, one determines that "it appears as if external. [Response: This determination is not correct, because possibility and impossibility are determined based on the operation or non-operation of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the operation or non-operation of valid means of cognition does not precede possibility and impossibility.
For whatever is apprehended by even one of the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception, that is possible;
but whatever is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition whatsoever, that is impossible.

In this case, however, since an external object is apprehended by all the respective means of valid cognition, how can it be said that it is impossible on account of conceptual alternatives such as being distinct or non-distinct [from consciousness], given that it is indeed apprehended?
Nor does the destruction of the object occur due to the cognition's conformity with the object,
because such conformity with an object is impossible when the object is non-existent,
and because the object is perceived externally.

Therefore, one must admit that even the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) between the cognition and its object is caused by their relationship as means and end (*upāyopeyabhāva*), and not caused by their identity.

Furthermore, in expressions such as "cognition of a jar" (*ghaṭajñāna*) and "cognition of a cloth" (*paṭajñāna*), the difference lies only in the qualifiers—the jar and the cloth—not in the qualified cognition itself.
Thus, its difference from both [the jar and the cloth] is established, as is the difference of those two from it.
Therefore, there is a distinction between the object and the cognition.
Likewise, this should also be understood in the case of "the perception of a jar" and "the recollection of a jar";
for here too, the distinction lies only between the two qualifiers—perception and recollection—and not in the jar, which is the qualified object.
Just as in the case of "the smell of milk" or "the taste of milk," there is a distinction only between the two qualifiers—smell and taste—and not between the qualified substance, milk; so it is here.

Furthermore, since two moments of consciousness occurring at earlier and later times are each exhausted by their own self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), it is logically impossible for them to stand in the relationship of grasper and grasped (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

Consequently, the thesis of the differentiation of consciousness, the thesis of properties such as momentariness, the doctrines of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the theory of the perfumable and the perfumer (*vāsya-vāsakatva*), and the various propositions concerning bondage and liberation through the influence of ignorance (*avidyopaplava*) regarding existent and non-existent phenomena—all these would be untenable.
Those [theories] contained in one's own treatises would be abandoned.
Furthermore,
for one who accepts that "consciousness is consciousness," it is logical to accept that external objects— such as pillars, walls, and the like— are not accepted at all.

Now, if you argue that consciousness, because its nature is luminosity, is experienced by itself like a lamp, whereas an external object is not so experienced, then you are accepting an action upon oneself that is utterly contradictory— like saying "fire burns itself"— while you do not accept the non-contradictory and world-renowned fact that an external object is experienced by a consciousness distinct from itself. Oh, what great scholarship has been displayed!
Nor is consciousness itself experienced as something non-distinct from its object, precisely because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
[Objection: If consciousness were to have an object graspable as distinct from its own nature, then that too would be grasped by another, and that by yet another, leading to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, since cognition is, like a lamp, of the nature of illumination, for one who postulates another cognition [to perceive it], the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator is untenable due to their equality; thus, such a postulation is purposeless. Both of these [objections] are incorrect, because when there is merely the apprehension of consciousness, no desire arises to apprehend a witness of that consciousness, and therefore the suspicion of an infinite regress is untenable.
Furthermore, because there is a difference in nature between the witness and its cognition, the relationship of perceiver and perceived is established;
moreover, since the witness is self-established, it cannot be denied.
Moreover:

By asserting that consciousness, like a lamp, manifests by itself without depending on another illuminator, one would be saying that consciousness is inaccessible to any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇagamya*) and lacks a cognizer,
just as the manifestation of a thousand lamps situated in the midst of a solid rock.
"Quite so," [the opponent replies].
If it is argued that because consciousness is of the nature of experience, your position is being accepted by me, we say no;
for we observe that another cognizer, whose instrument is the eye, is manifested by means of a lamp and so forth.
Therefore, since consciousness also possesses the same quality of being an object of illumination, it is understood that its manifestation occurs only when another cognizer exists, just like a lamp.

If it is argued that by suggesting the witness—the cognizer—is self-established, you have merely adopted my own position—that cognition manifests itself—through a different verbal formulation, we say: no.
This is because you admit that cognition possesses specific attributes such as arising, perishing, and multiplicity.
Therefore, like a lamp, we have established that cognition too is cognizable by something distinct from itself. 28.
FN: "Partisanship" (pakṣapāta) is the conventional usage [of a thing] as being qualified by a particular object.
"Affliction by ignorance" (avidyopaplava) is the association with ignorance.
"[The world] is not non-existent, because it is perceived."

Whether the Vedāntic doctrine— which asserts that Brahman is an indivisible, undifferentiated consciousness that is the material cause of external objects— is contradicted by the Yogācāra position, which holds that consciousness is diverse, possessed of forms, and momentary, and that no object exists apart from it, is a matter of doubt arising from whether that [Yogācāra] view is based on valid cognition or error. Taking as a premise the refutation of the previously mentioned theory of external objects, the author states the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

The result [of this analysis] is the contradiction or lack of contradiction between the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final (uttarapakṣa) positions. Now, one might object: "How can there be an intended meaning regarding both the existence and non-existence of external objects within a single Sugata’s scripture, given their contradiction? Anticipating this, [the author] states that there is no contradiction because of the difference in the capacities of the recipients (adhikāribheda).
Thus, by asserting that the Vijñānavādin is a knower of the Sugata’s intention, he [distinguishes himself] from the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādin), who are of inferior capacity.
He speaks of preeminence with the words "of some.

And it has been said by Dharmakīrti: "The teachings of the Lords of the World follow the dispositions of sentient beings. This means that the instructions of the Sugatas conform to the intellectual capacities of their disciples.
Now, one might ask: "If there is no external object, how can there be the conventional usage of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge?
To this he says: "In that [case]," etc.
Consciousness itself, by way of having the imagined forms of blue and so forth, is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

The meaning is that conventional usage proceeds through the conceptualization of distinctions: the fruit of cognition as having the nature of manifestation, the means of cognition as having the nature of power, and the knower as having the form of being the substratum of that power.
"Why should the difference not be primary? To this he says: "Even though [it exists]," and so forth.
For there is no conventional usage of the term "object of cognition" (*prameya*) for blue and the like that have not ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, the meaning is that only the form (*ākāra*) as it has ascended into the intellect is the object of cognition, not the external [object].
He sets forth arguments preceded by a question regarding the non-existence of external objects, beginning with "How so? and so forth:
the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) does not exist apart from cognition (*jñāna*), because it is impossible for it to exist apart from that [cognition].
He says, "like a human horn," and explains that it is because such a thing is impossible.
He clarifies this impossibility with the words, "for indeed...
If [the pillar were merely] atoms, there could be no cognition of a single, gross pillar.
The meaning is that the aggregate (*samūha*) is non-existent.
[An opponent might argue: "Even in the absence of a whole (*avayavin*), universals (*jāti*) and so forth could still be external objects.
To this, he says: "In this way" (*evam*).

The meaning is that if there were either non-difference or absolute difference between the universal (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*) on the one hand and the substratum (*dharmin*) on the other, then—just as in the case of the substratum itself or another distinct substratum—the relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) would not exist.
Furthermore, since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, categories such as universals and so forth do not exist.

Moreover, if cognition lacked a specific connection consisting of similarity with the object of knowledge (*jñeya-sārūpya*), it would follow that it could have everything as its object; therefore, a specific distinction must be admitted.

And thus, since it is only a specific feature residing in the cognition that is made an object by the cognition, there is no establishment of an external object due to the absence of proof and because of [logical] complexity (*gaurava*); so he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).
"Partisanship" (*pakṣapāta*) refers to the conventional usage of the distinction between the specific features of objects.
Furthermore, the knowable is non-different from the cognition.
"Because it is apprehended by a cognition whose apprehension is restricted to a single moment,
like cognition itself"— thus he says, "Moreover" (*apica*).
Even if there were a real difference between cognition and its object, their simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhana*) would still occur.
Regarding the claim that [the relationship exists] because of the state of the grasped and the grasper, he says: "And this is not so.
The meaning is that there is no relationship of grasped and grasper because there is no cause for a connection between momentary cognition and an object.
Furthermore, waking consciousness does not have an external object as its support.
He states "dream" [in the verse], meaning: "Because it is consciousness, like the cognition of dreams and so forth.
He raises an objection, saying "How?", implying that this inference is sublated by the impossibility of accounting for the diversity of cognitions.
He provides an alternative explanation with the word "vāsanā":
*vāsanā* is simply prior cognition included within the beginningless continuum;
by its power, the diversity of cognitions bearing forms such as blue arises, even when there is an interval of many moments.
The meaning is that it is just as the redness of cotton is due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the seed;

and because this is agreed upon by both parties, he says "moreover" (*apica*) to show that it is the latent impressions alone, and not external objects, that are the cause of the diversity of cognitions.

Since the doctrine of momentary consciousness-only (*kṣaṇika-vijñānamātra-vāda*) is rooted in valid means of knowledge, the objection arises that it contradicts the doctrine of eternal consciousness; to this, he explains the aphorism of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) beginning with "not non-existence" (*nābhāva*).
Is the non-existence of the external object due to its non-perception, or due to its non-perception as distinct from cognition?
It has already been stated that the first case is not so, because [the object] is indeed perceived.
He raises the second alternative: "But surely, 'I am not'..."

Since the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), by way of their relationship as subject and object, is established through the perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*), the assertion of non-difference contradicts direct perception; thus he says, "Certainly," and so forth. He further states, "And therefore," because if the external object were absolutely non-existent, its perception through direct perception would be impossible, [people] perceive the external object as distinct from knowledge even on the basis of your own words.
He says "otherwise" (*itarathā*) because [the word] would not exist externally due to its being an example and its impossibility.
He says "therefore" (*tasmāt*), for the particle *eva* is appropriate because of the uncontradicted experience of difference, whereas the particle *vat* is not.

He raises an objection with "but surely" (*nanu*), suggesting that the particle *vat* is used because the object of knowledge does not exist apart from cognition, as stated in the refutation of its possibility.
What is this "impossibility" (asaṃbhava)?
Is it non-existence, or the ascertainment of non-existence, or irrationality, or the absence of possibility—which consists of a doubt characterized by an extreme alternative?
It cannot be the first, because it would be indistinguishable from the probandum (sādhya).

It is not the second [alternative], because in the case of a collective cognition (samūhālambana) such as "the jar and the pillar are large," there is a determination of the existence of difference between two objects possessing contradictory properties—namely largeness, duality, jar-ness, and pillar-ness—from a single non-large cognition; thus, the charge of impossibility (*asambhava*) is unestablished. To this he says: "This is not correct."
"Occurrence" (*saṃbhava*) is the ascertainment of existence (*sattā-niścaya*), which depends upon valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

"non-occurrence" (*asaṃbhava*) is the ascertainment of non-existence (*asattva-niścaya*), which depends upon the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*). There is no reversal of this. He clarifies this very systematic arrangement with the words "For that which... (*yaddhi*). Stating the result of the aforementioned arrangement—namely, the occurrence of external objects through perception and other means—he simultaneously refutes the third [position] with the words "In this case... (*iha*).

It is not correct to conclude the non-existence of external objects such as pillars—which are established by valid means of cognition—merely on the grounds that they cannot withstand the dilemmas of being either identical to or different from their constituent atoms;
for this same untenability applies equally to your own position.

Indeed, it is not logical for a single, non-material consciousness to have as its object a gross, manifold collection [of atoms], since there can be no identity between the object and the consciousness.
Because that would entail the consequence of [the object] being gross and manifold.
Nor is this a desired conclusion,
for if collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) were abolished, the conventional usage of dual objects and so forth would be lost, since cognitions are mutually unaware of one another's contents.
Therefore, even if it is logically untenable, an object must be accepted as fit for conventional usage according to how it is experienced.
Nor is the fourth [alternative] possible, because such a possibility is of no use once [the object] has been ascertained.
The sense is that in some cases, [the similarity] serves as a prerequisite for the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the claim that there is no external object because it is established that only the similarity of the object residing within the cognition can be the objective support (*ālambana*) of that cognition, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
As for the objection regarding prolixity that was raised, it is not a valid criticism because it is supported by authoritative evidence; thus he says: "externally," etc.

Precisely because the distinction between cognition and its object is established by the direct experience of witnesses in all the world, for that very reason even the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is not a proof of non-difference; thus he says, "for that very reason.
And just as, although the form of a visible substance is invariably perceived along with the perception of light, it is not non-different from the light, [so too is the case here].
Likewise, there is no non-difference between the object and the cognition;
for even though they are distinct, the restriction [of their relationship] is established by way of the relation of apprehended and apprehender.
Nor is it the case that, because cognition is momentary, its connection with an apprehended object distinct from itself is impossible.
The intended meaning is "because of its stability.
Consciousness is distinct from multiple objects,
because it is unitary.
He states the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*), using the example "like cowness.
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*),
because the oneness of cognition is ascertained from the uniform cognition "cognition, cognition."
And that [cognition] does not have the universal as its object, because there is no determination of the difference between individuals; thus he says: "Not of the qualified object.
Having stated the difference between the jar and so forth from consciousness, he states the difference from the cognitive state (vṛttijñāna) with the words: "In the same way."
The meaning is that a jar is distinct from two [entities] because it is a single thing, like milk.

He states "Moreover" (*api ca*) to point out the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) that the abandonment of the conventional usage of one's own treatise would follow if objects distinct from cognition were not admitted.
It is both illogical and unaccepted that two successive, self-luminous, momentary cognitions could stand in the relation of the apprehended and the apprehender to one another;
likewise, the proposition of their difference is not tenable,
because the apprehension of difference is impossible without the mutual apprehension of the locus (*dharmin*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), as well as by another [cognition].
And thus, the stable self (sthāyī-ātman) that perceives the difference between those two must be admitted to be distinct from them.
In this way, in the absence of a distinction between the thesis, the probandum, the reason, and the example, the proposition "this is momentary" or "this is non-existent" is not tenable.
The particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the mere individuality (vyakti-mātratva) excluded from everything else.

The proposition that a universal is "followed by many" and consists in the form of the exclusion of what is not that (atad-vyāvṛtti) is not tenable, because all multiple objects would be nothing but cognitions, making it impossible for them to be mutually or otherwise known. Furthermore, the proposition that a subsequent cognition of blue is the impressed (vāsya) and a preceding cognition of blue is the impressioner (vāsaka) is not tenable,
because there is no distinct cognizer of those two.
The affliction of ignorance is its association with ignorance;
by means of that, "blue" is a real entity (saddharma),
while "a human horn" is a non-real entity (asaddharma).
"Formless" refers to the properties of existence and non-existence;

for it is difficult to maintain the thesis of formlessness regarding either existing consciousness or the non-existing horn of a man, because such a claim must be established through knowledge of multiple objects.
The proposition that "his bondage is through ignorance and his liberation is through knowledge" is to be accomplished by the knowledge of many things.

By the word "etcetera," the instruction for the benefit of the disciple—that what is generally desired is to be accepted and what is undesired is to be abandoned—is understood as being accomplished by manifold knowledge.
Therefore, the meaning is that for the sake of conventional discourse such as propositions and so forth, the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject must be admitted.
He states that there is another argument for the distinction between cognition and its object, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñcānyat*).
The meaning is that since there is no difference in the nature of their experience, it is logical to accept the existence of the object just as one accepts cognition.

He raises an objection: "Now, as for cognition... (*atha vijñānam*), suggesting that cognition is accepted because it has itself as its object, whereas the object is not, because it is apprehended by something else.
He states that the Buddhist disciple has demonstrated his own stupidity by accepting what is contradictory and rejecting what is not contradictory—namely, with the words "absolutely" (*atyanta*).
Having accepted that cognition is self-cognizable, he has fallen into folly; for in reality, self-cognizability is untenable, as he says with the words "and not" (*na ca*).

The meaning is that when [the self] is the agent (kartṛ) subordinate to the action, it cannot possess the status of an object (karman) termed "primacy" (pradhānatva); therefore, its being the object of a cognition whose agent is itself is non-existent.
Nor should it be said that "self-cognizability" (svavedyatva) consists merely in having oneself as one's own object;
for the point is that when there is non-difference, even the relation of object and subject is impossible.
He raises the objection that if cognition lacks self-cognizability (*svavedyatva*), two faults would ensue—introducing the phrase "nanu" (but surely).
He then refutes those two faults, namely "infinite regress" (*anavasthā*) and "parity" (*sāmya*), with the words "tadubhayamapi" (both of these as well).

Since impermanent cognition possesses birth and other such characteristics, it is insentient (*jaḍa*) like a jar; therefore, because it is impossible for it to grasp its own birth and so forth by itself, there arises a requirement for a cognizer (*grāhakākāṅkṣā*).
However, since witnesses (sākṣins) are independent with respect to both existence and manifestation, there is no infinite regress;
nor is there parity [between them],
because of the disparity between consciousness and insentience— this is the meaning.
To the question "Where is the witness? he says: "of that which is self-established.
The meaning is that if an independent witness were non-existent, the distinctions between momentary cognitions could not be established; therefore, such a witness must be accepted.
Furthermore, he states "moreover" to show that the witness must be admitted because he is the establisher of the nature of impermanent cognition.
By asserting that consciousness depends upon another cognition, one would be stating its lack of epistemic validity;
by asserting that it manifests by itself, one would be stating its emptiness of a knower.
And thus, because it is neither an object of a knower nor an object of a cognition, consciousness would be non-existent, like a lamp placed within a stone.
Therefore, the meaning is that its witness must be accepted.

The Buddhist objects: "It is precisely the absence of any cognizer other than itself that you [the Vedāntin] have established for consciousness; yet, one should not say that this leads to its non-existence simply because of the absence of a cognizer, for consciousness itself is the cognizer. To this, the Śākya replies: "Certainly."
He refutes [the objection] with "No," on the grounds that if there were no distinction, the relationship between knower and known would be impossible, and thus another knower would be necessary:
"The cognition under dispute has an object of knowledge distinct from itself, because it is an object of knowledge."
The meaning is "like the body. Is the transcendent witness known by another or self-known? In the first case, there would be an infinite regress.
He raises the following objection: "Regarding the witness (sākṣin)," [thinking] that in the second [verse], the Vijñānavāda itself might have been stated by way of a different formulation:
"You assert that consciousness is subject to birth and destruction;
therefore, since it is a rule that an effect is insentient, we have established that it must be cognizable by something other than itself."

It has also been stated that because the immutable conscious self (kūṭastha-cidātman) does not depend on a cognizer, there is no infinite regress; therefore, he refutes [the objection] by stating that there is a great difference between our two positions:
"Not so, because of consciousness... (Verse 28).
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like a dream and so forth. (BBs 2.2.29)

As for what was stated by the one who flees from external objects—that even cognitions within the sphere of the waking state, such as those of pillars and the like, might exist without an external object, just like cognitions in dreams and so forth, because there is no difference in their being cognitions—this must be answered.
To this it is said: waking cognitions cannot be like cognitions in dreams and the like.
Why?
Because of their difference in nature;
for there is indeed a difference in nature between dreaming and waking.

What, then, is the difference? We say it is sublation and non-sublation. For an object perceived in a dream is sublated by one who has awakened, thinking, "I falsely perceived a great assembly of people."
"It was not that I was in a gathering of many people; rather, my mind had become overcome by sleep, and because of that, this delusion arose.
In the same way, regarding illusions and the like, there is a sublation according to their specific nature.
However, an object perceived while awake, such as a pillar or the like, is never sublated in any state whatsoever.

Moreover, dreaming is memory (*smṛti*), whereas waking is perception (*upalabdhi*). Furthermore, the difference between memory and perception is directly experienced by oneself as consisting of separation from and union with objects, as in: "I remember my beloved son, yet I do not perceive him; I desire to perceive him."

This being the case, it is impossible for one who personally experiences the difference between the two to say, "The perception of the waking state is false, because it is a perception, like the perception of a dream.
Nor is it proper for those who consider themselves wise to deny their own experience.

Furthermore, since one is unable to assert that waking cognitions are inherently without an objective basis due to the contradiction with experience, one seeks to assert it instead by means of their similarity to dream cognitions.
Furthermore, a property that cannot exist for something by its own nature will not come to exist for it simply because of its similarity to another thing.
For fire, which is experienced as hot, will not become cold because of its similarity to water. However, the difference between dreaming and waking has already been demonstrated. (29)
Note: The phrase "connected with sleep" (nidrālagnim) is a designation for a defect of the instrument [of knowledge].
For cognition arising from mere mental impressions (saṃskāra) is recollection (smṛti);
experience born of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is apprehension (upalabdhi).
Thus, it has been stated that because the object is perceived just like the sensation and the cognition, there is no absence of external objects.
Now, he refutes the inference that waking cognition—unlike dream cognition and the like—does not have an external objective support, with the words "and because of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyācca*).
Here, what is the probandum (*sādhya*)? Is it mere objectlessness, or is it being devoid of an ultimately real object?
Alternatively, [the definition might be] "emptiness of empirical objects.
Not the first, because even delusions such as dreams have false objects as their objective supports, and thus the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).
Nor the second.
The meaning of the word "and" (ca) in the sūtra is that [the definition] would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Regarding the third [alternative], however, he states with the words "for it is sublated," etc., that in the state of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), the property of grasping a sublated object (*bādhitārthagrāhitva*) is the adventitious condition (*upādhi*).
"Afflicted by sleep" means...
This is a statement regarding a defect in the logical reason (*karaṇadoṣa*).
To exclude the possibility that [the reason] is too broad (*sādhanavyāpaka*), he says: "And it is not thus.

Furthermore, there is another point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): the experience born of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaja-anubhava*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), while dream-cognition, which is not born of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaja*), is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Accepting the view of the opponent that a dream is a form of memory, he says, "And also...
He states another difference between the perception of memory and direct perception: "because of the object being absent...
Since the object of memory is something unrelated and non-present, it may sometimes be the case that this [memory] is without a supporting basis (*nirālambana*).
The meaning is that it is not because of a perception (*upalabdhi*) that grasps only the present object associated with [the senses].

He states the result of expressing the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) regarding being produced from valid or invalid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-apramāṇaja*), as previously mentioned: "In that case, being so" (*tatraivaṃsati*).
The sense is: "given that there is such a difference in nature."

The sense is that the inference of "lack of objective support" (*nirālambanatva*) based on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "being produced from non-means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇajatva*) is not tenable.

He dispels the objection regarding the failure to establish the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-asiddhi*) with the words "nor" (*na ca*); he also states the sublation (*bādha*) with the words "moreover" (*api ca*).
In reality, if the property of being objectless were to belong to the experience of a jar and so forth, then what would be the use of citing an example,
since it could be stated even through direct perception?
For the heat of fire does not need to be stated by means of an example.
If, in reality, no such property exists, then what is the use of an example?
For that which has been sublated cannot be established even by a thousand examples.

Therefore, although you have begun to employ inference out of fear that the statement of self-nature being without an object would contradict the experience of its having an object, nevertheless, the contradiction does not let go. This is the meaning.
He says, "But it has been shown," [in verse 29], meaning that even the previously mentioned condition (upādhi) must not be forgotten.
There is no existence [of the object], because it is not perceived. (BBs 2.2.30)

As for what was also said—that the variety of cognitions can be accounted for solely through the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) even in the absence of an object—that must be refuted. To this it is replied: on your position, the existence of latent impressions would not be tenable, because external objects are not perceived.
For latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) arise in various forms corresponding to each object, having the apprehension of objects as their cause.
However, when objects are not being perceived, what could be the cause for these diverse predispositions?

Even if they were beginningless, such a state would be a bottomless regress according to the analogy of a succession of blind men; it would undermine conventional practice and fail to establish one's intended purpose.

Furthermore, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which the denier of external objects (*arthāpalāpī*) has put forward— namely, that this collection of cognitions is caused solely by mental impressions (*vāsanā*) and not by external objects—
should be regarded as refuted by this very [argument],
because mental impressions are impossible without the perception of objects.

Moreover, since they admit the perception of objects even without mental impressions (*vāsanā*), whereas they do not admit the arising of mental impressions without the perception of objects, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) likewise establish the actual existence of external objects.
Furthermore, what are called "mental impressions" are specific types of formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
and formative forces cannot be conceived without a substratum.
This is because it is observed thus in the world;
moreover, for you, there is no substratum for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as it is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [30] [Note:
*Bhāva* means arising, existence, or being.]
Having recalled what is to be refuted by the Sūtra, he refutes it with the words "As for what was also said," and so forth.
"Bhāva" means arising or existence.

Now, one might object: even if external objects are not perceived, let there be a variety of successive cognitions due to the power of preceding predispositions (*vāsanā*), because this process is beginningless, like the sequence of seed and sprout; to this, he says: "Even though it is beginningless."
The meaning is as follows: since a sprout is seen to arise from a seed, it is logical to postulate a causal relationship between two things of that same kind even when they are not perceived;

however, in this case, because the arising of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) independent of the experience of an object must be postulated at the very beginning, the postulation of beginninglessness is rootless, and thus the intended diversity of cognition is not established. [Objection: But surely, the diversity of cognition is observed in dreams to exist when independent latent impressions are present, and not to exist when they are absent; therefore, the infinite regress has its root. To this, he says: "As long as... (yāvat).

The meaning is that since it is not established that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are independent [of external objects] when they are the effects of the experience of external objects, there can be no observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.
He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) which establishes their being effects with the words "without" (*vinā*).

It has been stated that because it is impossible for latent impressions—which are the effects of the experience of objects—to be independent of them, your proposed observation of positive concomitance and so forth does not hold.

Furthermore, because the diversity of the apprehension of novel objects occurs even in the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). Thus, the diversity of cognition is not produced by latent impressions alone; rather, based on positive and negative concomitance—namely, that [diversity] exists when there is the experience of an object and is absent when it is not—it is established that it is produced solely by the object which delimits the experience rooted in latent impressions. This proves the existence of external objects; thus he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Whatever conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) exists in the world is observed to have a substratum (sāśraya), just as velocity and so forth have arrows and the like as their substrata;
therefore, there is no existence of the formations of consciousness because no substratum is perceived—this is the meaning of the phrase "apica" (furthermore). //30//
And because of momentariness. (BBs 2.2.31)

Furthermore, even that which is postulated as the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) by virtue of being the substratum for latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because its nature is not stable due to the admission of momentariness, cannot serve as the locus for latent impressions, just like the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). This is because there exists no single, continuous entity connected to the three periods of time— neither one that is immutable nor one that perceives all objects.
The conventional activities of depositing latent impressions (*vāsanā*), recollection, and the reconnection of memory are possible only by depending on place, time, and causal conditions.
However, if the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were of a stable nature, it would result in the abandonment of your own tenet.
Furthermore, since the acceptance of momentariness is common even to the Vijñānavāda, those arguments based on momentariness that apply to the theory of external objects [would likewise apply here].
The refutations that were raised—beginning with "Because the preceding has ceased when the succeeding arises," and so forth—are to be applied here as well.

Thus, both of these positions of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas)—the position of those who maintain external objects (Bāhyārthavāda) and the position of those who maintain consciousness-only (Vijñānavāda)—have been rejected.
As for the position of the Proponents of Emptiness (Śūnyavāda), however, since it is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), no further effort is made to refute it.

For this worldly convention, established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be denied without first apprehending another reality, because there is no exception to what is established by a general rule (*utsarga*). [Regarding the objection that] "let the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) be the basis," he says: "And because of momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvāt*). No heed is paid [to this], other sūtras are not composed; these very [sūtras] are applied through repetition (*āvṛtti*). Let the storehouse-consciousness be the basis—hence he says: "And because of momentariness."
He explains the Sūtra with the words "even that which...
Because it is impossible for there to be a relationship of support and supported between two things that arise simultaneously, like the left and right horns [of a cow];
and because, if there were a sequence of before and after, it would be impossible for that which is non-existent at the moment of being supported to function as a support.

The meaning is that because a sentient being (*sattva*) is momentary, the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) cannot be its substratum, since it too is momentary, just like the cognitions of blue and so forth.
If it is argued that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) must therefore have the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness as its substratum, the author says "no" (*na hi*).

If there is no persisting self (*ātman*), whether subject to modification or immutable, then—since a continuum is not a real entity—the depositing or placing of impressions in relation to space and so forth, as well as memory, recognition, and [the rest], [would be impossible].
The meaning is that legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is rooted in that [self], and therefore all of that [procedure] would be impossible.
He says "stable" (*sthira*) to show that if the self were to persist for the sake of legal procedure, then there would be a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
He explains the Sūtra also as having the purpose of an extended application (atideśa) with the words "Moreover" (apica).
He concludes the refutation of the two views with the word "Thus" (evam).

Having raised the objection that even the Madhyamika position—that because everything consisting of knowledge and the object of knowledge cannot withstand analysis in terms of existence or non-existence, only emptiness remains—is rooted in valid cognition, the author of the Sūtra asks: why? [is this so?]...

He did not reject [them]; therefore, he says "empty" (śūnya). This means that no separate sūtra is composed out of respect [for them], but rather these very [verses] are also applied for the purpose of refuting their doctrine.
For instance: there is no non-existence of cognition and its object, because they are apprehended through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
But [it may be argued]: waking and dreaming states are devoid of cognition and objects.
Because it is a state, like deep sleep; to this he says: "And because of its dissimilarity, it is not like dreaming and so forth.
Dreaming is the beginning of that which includes deep sleep; therefore, there is emptiness in the other two states [waking and dreaming].

The meaning is that there is no inference [proving the non-existence of the self], because it is sublated by the perception of an object of knowledge characterized by the difference between apprehension and non-apprehension; furthermore, even in deep sleep, the existence of self-knowledge persists, which renders the probandum deficient.
Moreover, since negation without a substratum is impossible, the substratum itself must be declared to be the reality.
But at its conclusion, there is no existence;
because it is not perceived through a means of valid cognition (māna), he says: "There is no existence, because it is not perceived.
To explain that meaning, he says: "For this [is not so]," and so forth.
That which appears is not non-existent; thus, by the general rule, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not empty.
The meaning is that it is not empty because there is no sublation (*bādhā*).
Nor is it empty due to being unable to withstand analysis in terms of existence or non-existence.
The intended meaning is that [the Sugata's teaching] is possible because of falsity.
Regarding the sūtra "And because of momentariness," it should be read as "And because of the teaching of momentariness.
The meaning is that the Sugata is a speaker of incoherent prattle, since he teaches momentariness, which is contradictory to emptiness. //31//
And because it is untenable in every respect. (2.2.32)
What need is there for much?
In every way, however this doctrine of annihilationism (vaināśika-samaya) is examined for its logical consistency, it simply falls apart like a well dug in sand.
We do not perceive even the slightest logical justification here.
Therefore, the conventional practice of the Nihilist school is untenable.

Furthermore, by teaching these three mutually contradictory doctrines—the external object, consciousness-only, and emptiness—the Sugata has clearly demonstrated his own state of incoherent prattle, or else it was out of malice toward the people, thinking: "May these people be bewildered by the comprehension of contradictory meanings."
The intention is that this doctrine of the Sugata (Buddha) is in every respect to be disregarded by those who desire their own welfare.
[Note: Here, "people" refers to those outside the Vedic fold. He concludes the inconsistency of the Sugata’s system with the word "sarvathā" (in every respect).
How could there be contradictory speech from one who is omniscient?
To this, he says: "Or hatred. Here, the term "people" (prajā) should be understood as those outside the Veda.
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the Vedānta doctrine and the doctrine of the Sugata, which is based on the single root of illusion. //32//
Section 6: The Topic of the Impossibility [of Contradictory Attributes] in One [Entity] (ekasminnasaṃbhavādhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 33–36.
Because [it] is impossible in a single [locus], the doctrine of the Sugata has been refuted. Now,
the doctrine of the naked ones (Jainas) is being refuted.

They maintain that there are seven categories (padārtha) recognized among these: namely, soul (jīva), non-soul (ajīva), influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa).
However, in brief, there are only two categories called soul and non-soul;
for they believe that, as appropriate, the others are included within those very two.

Regarding these two, they describe this further elaboration known as the five *astikāyas*: the *jīvāstikāya* (the category of souls), the *pudgalāstikāya* (the category of matter), the *dharmāstikāya* (the category of motion), the *adharmāstikāya* (the category of rest), and the *ākāśāstikāya* (the category of space).
They also describe the many kinds of internal subdivisions of all these, as imagined within their own system (*svasamaya*).
And in every case, they apply this logic known as the *saptabhaṅgīnaya* (the method of sevenfold predication).
It may exist, it may not exist,
it may both exist and not exist, and it may be inexpressible.
It may be that it both exists and is inexpressible; it may be that it does not exist and is inexpressible; and it may be that it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible.
In the same way, they apply this method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) even to such [attributes] as unity and permanence.
To this we reply: why is this position not tenable?
Because it is impossible for [contradictory attributes] to coexist in a single [subject].
For it is not possible for contradictory properties, such as existence and non-existence, to coexist simultaneously in a single substratum, just as cold and heat cannot.
These seven categories that have been determined—defined as being exactly this many and of such a nature—must either be exactly so or not be so at all.
Otherwise, if their form were undetermined, such that they might be either thus or otherwise, then cognition would be invalid, like a state of doubt, because its form would be unsettled.
[Objection: Surely, since a thing consists of multiple natures, a cognition that arises with a determined form cannot be invalid, just like a cognition of doubt.
[Reply: We say no.

For one who asserts that multiformity (anekāntatva) is unrestricted across all things, even determination itself—because it is a particular instance of a real entity (vastutva)—would be subject to the occurrence of conceptual alternatives such as "it might be" or "it might not be," and thus its very nature as determination would be undermined.
It might be so;
thus, for the one who determines and for the result of determination, there would be existence in one case and non-existence in another.

This being the case, how could a teacher who has become an authority (pramāṇabhūta) be able to instruct regarding the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing, all of which remain undetermined?
Or else, how could those who follow his intention proceed with regard to the matter taught by him when its specific form remains undetermined?
For it is only when there is a determination that the result is certain that the entire world proceeds toward the performance of the means to achieve it without confusion; otherwise, it does not.
Therefore, one who composes a treatise whose meaning is undetermined would have speech that is not to be accepted, like that of a drunkard or a madman.

Likewise, when one considers whether the number five of the five astikāyas exists or does not exist, it might indeed exist according to one position, but according to another position it would not; consequently, they would either fall short of the number five or exceed it.
Furthermore, it is not possible for these categories to be inexpressible (*avaktavya*).
If they were inexpressible, they would not be expressed;
yet they are expressed and called "inexpressible"—this is a contradiction.
Furthermore, while being expressed, they are both determined to be as they are and not determined to be so.

Likewise, if one were to prattle that right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the fruit of such ascertainment, either exists or does not exist, and similarly that its opposite, wrong vision (*asamyagdarśana*), also either exists or does not exist, this would belong to the camp of the intoxicated or the insane, not to the camp of those who are to be convinced. Furthermore, if there were no ascertainment— such as that heaven and liberation exist in one case and do not exist in another, or that they are eternal in one case and non-eternal in another— then purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) would be impossible.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the nature of the soul (*jīva*) and other categories established as beginningless in one's own scriptures would not be correctly determined.

Thus, since it is impossible for two contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to reside in a single substratum (*dharmin*) like the soul or other categories, and since it is impossible for the property of non-existence to exist alongside the property of existence within a single entity, and likewise impossible for existence to exist alongside non-existence, this doctrine of the Ārhats is incoherent.

By this, the various forms of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda)—such as the acceptance of unity and multiplicity, permanence and impermanence, or distinctness and non-distinctness—are to be understood as refuted.

As for the notion that [beings] arise from a collection of atoms designated as "pudgalas," that has already been refuted by the previous refutation of atomism; therefore, no separate effort is made to refute it here. // 33 //
Note: The soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva) are the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
the flow of the senses toward sense objects is influx (āsrava);
that which restrains this is restraint (saṃvara), consisting of the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth.
Nirjarā is that which wears away or destroys impurity; it consists of practices such as climbing heated stones and the like.
Bandha is karma.
Mokṣa is the continuous upward movement of one who has entered the space of the non-world (aloka-ākāśa) upon the destruction of the bonds of karma.
The term *astikāya* is conventional (*sāṃketika*) and denotes a category of reality (*padārtha*). Its etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: "it is a living being (*jīva*) and it is an *astikāya*.
*Pudgala*s are aggregates of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*); they are called *pudgala*s because they are filled (*pūryante*) and they go (*gacchanti*), and they are *kāya*s (bodies/accumulations).
The collection of the seven modes, beginning with "existence," is the *saptabhaṅgī*; its method (*naya*) is the logic (*nyāya*).
[The objection that it is] "not [valid], because of impossibility in a single [locus]" is raised.

Having refuted the doctrine of the Muktakacchas, the doctrine of the Muktāmbaras comes to mind; therefore, he states the connection by way of context (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) with the words "having been refuted."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the Vedic doctrine that Brahman is of a single form is contradicted by the theory of manifoldness (anaikāntavāda)—the doubt arising from whether that theory is rooted in valid cognition (pramāṇa) or in error—the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), intending to show that there is indeed a contradiction because the theory is rooted in valid cognition, introduces that position with the words "And seven...
[The categories are: the living being (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva), the enjoyer (bhoktṛ) and the enjoyed (bhogya).
The activity of the senses directed toward sense objects is *āsrava* (influx);
that which restrains this is *saṃvara* (restraint), such as the observances (*yama*) and restraints (*niyama*).
That which wears away or destroys impurity is *nirjarā* (dissociation), such as climbing upon heated stones and the like.
Bondage is karma;

liberation is the continuous upward movement of one who has entered the space of the Satyaloka upon the destruction of the fetters of karma. Now, since the influx (āsrava) and the other factors are included within the objects of experience (bhogya), how can there be exactly seven? To this, he says: "But in brief..."
Having stated the meaning through both concise and detailed [explanations], he provides another detailed exposition in the intermediate manner with the words "of those two" (*tayoḥ*).

The term *astikāya* is a conventional designation for a category of things (*padārtha*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is a *jīva* and it is an *astikāya*; thus, it is a *jīvāstikāya*.
"Persons" (*pudgala*) are so called because they fill (*pūryante*) and dissolve (*glānti*); "bodies" (*kāya*) are aggregates of atoms;
"dharma" is that which is to be inferred from correct activity;
and "adharma" is the cause for the retention of the soul (*jīva*), which by nature tends to move upward, within the body.
The meaning is that space (*ākāśa*) is the absence of obstruction.
He states the internal subdivisions of the five categories with the words "of all," which has this meaning:
the category of living beings (*jīvāstikāya*) is threefold; one type of living being is eternally perfected, such as the Arhat and others.
Some are currently liberated, while others are bound.
The category of persons (*pudgalāstikāya*) is sixfold: the four elements, beginning with earth; [and the remaining two].
It consists of the immobile and the mobile.
Dharma and adharma have been described as having the characteristics of facilitating motion and maintaining stability, respectively.
The astikāya of space (ākāśa) is of two kinds: the world-space (lokākāśa), which pertains to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), and...
The space of the non-world (*alokākāśa*) is the support for the liberated.
Bondage consists of eight kinds of karma: four destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*) and four non-destructive karmas.
Among these, the destructive karmas are: knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇīya*), perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇīya*), deluding (*mohanīya*), and obstructive (*antarāya*).
The knowledge that liberation does not result from the knowledge of reality is the first [type of] karma;
the knowledge that liberation does not result from hearing the Ārhata scriptures is the second;
and the failure to discern the distinction among the many paths to liberation shown by various teachers is deluding (mohanīya) karma.
Obstructing the engagement on the path to liberation is *antarāya* (obstructive karma).
These four are the *aghāti-karmas* because they destroy spiritual excellence (*śreya*).
Now, the four non-obstructive (*aghāti*) karmas are: *vedanīya*, *nāmika*, *gotrika*, and *āyuṣka*.
The conceit "I have a reality to be known" is the feeling-aspect (vedanīya); the conceit "I am this by name" is the name-aspect (nāmika);
the conceit "I have entered here into the lineage of disciples of the venerable Teacher, the Arhat," is the clan-aspect (gotrika).
Action for the sake of maintaining the body is *āyuṣka* (life-span karma).
Alternatively, *āyuṣka* is that which is mixed with semen and blood; its capacity for the transformation of the body in a manner conducive to the knowledge of reality is *gotrika* (genetic karma).
The specific activity that initiates the states of *kalala*— which consists of liquefaction— and *budbuda* for that potent [seed] is *nāman*;
the slight thickening of the active seed by means of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) and wind (*vāyu*) is *vedanīya*,
because it is conducive to the experience of reality (*tattva*).
These [eight types of karma] do not obstruct the purpose of the pure person (śuklapudgala) who reveals reality (tattva).
This eightfold karma is bondage because it has birth as its purpose; it acts through the gateways of influx (āsrava) and so forth.
By the phrase "imagined by their own systems" (svasamayaparikalpitān), he indicates that this process is devoid of authority.

The meaning is that they assert the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntatva*) of the categories (*padārtha*) mentioned, which are merely constructed according to the conventions of their own systems; thus he says, "In all cases.
Taking up two contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence, they apply this logic to every entity. The *saptabhaṅgī* is the combination of the seven modes, beginning with existence.
This is its method and reasoning:
for if a jar or the like were always of one and the same nature in its entirety, it would exist even as the very thing to be attained; consequently, no effort toward attaining it would be necessary.
Therefore, it exists in some way through such forms as "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva).
The intended meaning is that one must accept that every entity possesses multiple aspects, such as the fact that it does not exist in some way in terms of its being attainable and so forth.
What are those sevenfold modes (saptabhaṅga)? He states them:
"In some sense, it exists," and so on.
The indeclinable *syāt* is a substitute for a verbal form; it signifies "in some way" (*kathañcit*).
*Syād asti* means "it exists in some way."
The same applies to fire as well.
In that regard, when there is a desire to express its existence, the first alternative (bhaṅga) "it exists" (syād asti) proceeds;
when there is a desire to express its non-existence, the second alternative "it does not exist" (syān nāsti) proceeds.
If there is a desire to express both [existence and non-existence] sequentially, there is the third alternative: "it may both exist and not exist.
If there is a desire to express both simultaneously, because it is impossible to utter two words at once, there is the fourth alternative: "it may be inexpressible" (*syād-avaktavya*).
If there is a desire for both the first and the fourth alternatives, there is the fifth alternative: "it may both exist and be inexpressible."
The sixth alternative (bhaṅga) is "it may be that it exists and is inexpressible," arising from the desire for both the second and fourth [alternatives];
the seventh alternative is "it may be that it exists and is inexpressible," arising from the desire for both the third and fourth [alternatives]. This is the distinction.

Likewise, taking the pair of unity and plurality, there are: "it may be one," "it may be one and many," "it may be inexpressible," "it may be one and expressible," "it may be many and inexpressible," and "it may be one, many, and inexpressible."
In the same way, one should infer such [statements] as "it would be eternal" or "it would be non-eternal.
Thus, when an entity possesses multiple forms, worldly transactions such as acquisition and abandonment are possible;
however, if it possessed a single form, everything would exist everywhere and at all times, which would result in the collapse of all worldly transactions.

Therefore, since it might be argued that "everything is non-conclusive" and thus the doctrine of a single-natured Brahman is contradicted, the author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words "herein":
whatever exists exists everywhere and at all times, just as the Self, which is Brahman.
Nor should it be said that, if this were so, there would be no effort toward attaining it.
Because effort arises from the delusion that something has not been attained;
that which does not exist simply does not exist, such as a rabbit's horn and the like.

Since conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is indeed distinct from both [existence and non-existence], the doctrine of exclusivity (*ekāntavāda*) alone is logical, not the doctrine of non-exclusivity (*anaikāntavāda*).
To explain: is the non-existence of an entity in the very same form in which its existence occurs, or in another form?
In the second case, since the other form of the entity is itself non-existent, the entity possesses only a single, eternally existent nature.

For it is not the case that because the attainment of a village situated at a distance is non-existent, the village itself is also non-existent; for if the object to be attained were non-existent, the effort toward its attainment would be impossible.
Therefore, one must accept the uniformity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) according to conventional usage.
He says "not so" with the words "this is not. [Objection:
But surely the object under dispute is manifold in nature, because it is a real entity (vastutvāt).
If it is argued that [the pot] is like the man-lion (nārasiṃha), we say no;
for this is contradicted by the experience that "the pot exists right now.

Furthermore, regarding the seven categories such as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, is their existence as seven and their nature as being souls and so on necessarily existent or non-existent, or is it non-necessary?
He states "yaḥ" [in the verse] to show that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the first case;
he states "itarathā" to show that in the second case there would be no ascertainment of the object (padārthaniścaya);
and he raises the objection "nanu" to suggest that the ascertainment is simply that "everything is non-conclusive" (anaikāntika).
Is its nature as a certainty (niścaya) determinate or indeterminate?
In the first case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the property of being a real entity (vastutva) within that very single form of certainty.
In the second case, it would follow that it is a doubt (saṃśaya). To this he says: "We say, 'No'."
He extends the logic stated regarding valid cognition (*pramā*) to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and so forth by saying "in this way" (*evam*).
The meaning is: "of that [cognizer] which has as its result the determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the rest.
He says "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*) because, if there were no such determination in all these cases, there would be neither instruction nor unshakable engagement in action.
He states that even the fivefold nature of the *astikāyas* would not exist under the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anaikāntavāda*), saying: "In the same way, of the five...

As for what was stated regarding their being "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), does this mean they cannot be expressed by any word whatsoever, or that they cannot be expressed simultaneously by multiple words?
It is not the first, because it involves a contradiction; thus he says: "Nor is it the case that these..."
And they are said [to be so] by means of such terms as "inexpressible" (avaktavya); this is the ellipsis. It is not the second [alternative].

Since it is not established that multiple words can simultaneously issue from the mouth of a single speaker, their negation is untenable; furthermore, even in other cases, there are distinct openings [of the mouth].

Nor should it be argued that when there is a desire to express contradictory properties of an object simultaneously, the term "inexpressible" (avaktavya) merely intends to indicate the speaker’s own silence.
"Such a desire simply does not arise.
Furthermore, he states that the Arhat is not an authoritative person (*anāpta*) because he utters various contradictory ravings, beginning with the words "And when they are being spoken," etc.;
the grammatical connection is "and thus he raves."
The word "Arhat" is to be supplied as the subject.
The meaning is that he would be included only within the category of those who have not attained [the goal], and not within the category of those who have attained it.
Furthermore, he states "svarga... to show that the doctrine of non-ascertainment (anaikāntavāda) is also inconsistent for this reason.

Furthermore, for those who have determined the nature of the three types of living beings according to the Ārhata system—wherein the Sage Arhat is established as beginningless, while others are liberated through the practice of causes and bound by the non-practice thereof—even this threefold restriction would not exist; thus he says: "beginningless," etc.
He concludes the meaning of the sūtra that has been elaborated upon with the word "evam" (thus).
With the phrase "etena" (by this), the meaning is:
by the simultaneous rejection of both existence and non-existence in a single locus.
"The aggregates of atoms are earth and so forth"—this is the doctrine of the Digambara Jains. Why was it disregarded by the author of the Sūtras?
To this he says: "As for that which... (verse 33).
And thus, there would be a lack of completeness for the self. (BS 2.2.34)

Just as the impossibility of contradictory properties in a single substratum (*dharmin*) would constitute a fault in the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*), so too another fault—the non-omnipresence (*akārtsnya*)—would attach to the self (*ātman*), that is, the living being (*jīva*).
How so?
For the Jains maintain that the living being is of the same size as the body.

Furthermore, if the self were limited in size to that of the body, it would follow that the self is incomplete, non-omnipresent, and finite; consequently, like a jar or other such objects, the self would be subject to impermanence. Moreover, because the dimensions of embodied beings are not fixed, the life-principle (*jīva*) of a human, having been the size of a human body, would not be able to pervade the entire body of an elephant when it subsequently attains birth as an elephant due to the ripening of some karma.
Furthermore, if it were to attain birth as an ant, it could not be contained within the body of an ant.
This same difficulty applies equally even within a single birth, across the stages of childhood, youth, and old age.
It might be argued as follows:
The soul (*jīva*) has infinite parts; those very parts would contract in a small body and expand in a large one.
Now, it must be stated whether the coexistence in the same location of those infinite parts of the soul is obstructed or not.
If there were obstruction, then the infinite parts could not be gathered within a limited space.

Even if [the soul] were non-obstructive, since it would occupy the space of only a single part, it would be impossible for all its parts to possess extension; thus, the soul would necessarily be reduced to the size of an atom.
Furthermore, it is impossible even to conceive of an infinity of parts belonging to a soul that is limited to the mere dimensions of the body. (34) [Note:
*Karmavipāka* refers to the manifestation of the results of actions.]
He refutes the view that the soul has the same dimensions as the body with the words "If this were so":
"akārtsnyam" means having a middle-sized dimension;
the meaning is that by virtue of that, [the soul] would be non-eternal.
He states another point: "And of bodies.
Maturation (*vipāka*) is the manifestation of karmas.
The soul's pervading the entire body of an elephant is its non-limitedness (*akārtsnya*).
The meaning is that one part of the body would be devoid of life;
the entire soul would not enter the body of an ant,
and the soul would even exist outside the body.

Furthermore, [the opponent argues: "If the self were merely the size of the body of a child, then it would exist only in some part of the body when that same person becomes an adult; thus, the entire body would not be possessed of life. To this, he says: "It is equal" (*samāna*).

He raises the objection that the self's size is restricted to the measure of the body—just as the parts of a lamp contract within a jar and expand within a house, so too are the parts of the living being (the *jīva*)—by saying: "It might be so" (*syāt*).

Having proposed the alternatives as to whether the parts of the *jīva* occupy different locations like the parts of a lamp, or occupy a single location, he refutes the first alternative by stating: "Of those," etc., [arguing] that if the former were true, the *jīva* would exist even outside of a small body.
However, the lamp does not exist outside the jar because its constituent parts have been destroyed.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "because it is non-obstructive" (*apratighāta*).
Furthermore, he states "moreover" (*api ca*) that the permanence of the parts is unestablished, because they are minute, like the particles of the lamp itself. //34//
Now,

it might be argued that through the process of transmigration, when assuming a large body, certain parts of the soul enter [the new body], and when assuming a small body, certain parts depart from it. To this, it is replied:
Nor can there be non-contradiction even by way of succession, because of [the faults of] transformation and so forth.

(BBs 2.2.35) Nor can this state of the soul having the same dimensions as this body be established without contradiction even through succession, by means of the soul's approaching and departing from its constituent parts. Why? Because of [the faults of] transformation and so forth.
Because it would entail the defects of modification and so forth.
For if the individual soul (jīva) were constantly being filled and depleted by the arrival and departure of constituent parts, its state of being subject to modification would be unavoidable;
and if it were subject to modification, it would follow—as with leather and similar things—that it is non-eternal.
