Furthermore, the accepted doctrine of bondage and liberation would be contradicted; for it is held that the soul, enveloped by the eightfold karma and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra like a gourd, rises upward upon the severance of its bonds.
Moreover, because the parts that come and go possess the nature of arrival and departure, the body must be non-self, just like the physical body and so forth.
Consequently, it would follow that some persisting constituent part is the self;
yet that cannot be identified as "this is it.
Furthermore:
It must be explained from where these constituent parts of the living being (jīva) emerge when they arrive, and where they dissolve when they depart;
for they could not emerge from the material elements (bhūta) nor dissolve into the material elements,
because the living being is non-material (abhautika).

Nor can any other substratum for the parts of living beings— whether common or uncommon— be established, due to a lack of valid evidence. Furthermore, if this were the case, the self would have an indeterminate nature.

Because the parts that come and go possess no fixed dimension, for this reason— and due to the resulting faults such as these— it is impossible to maintain that the soul’s coming and going of parts occurs even alternately. Alternatively, by means of the previous sūtra, it was shown that if the soul were the size of the body, then upon assuming other bodies that are increased or decreased in size, it would follow that the soul is incomplete, which leads to its impermanence.

Furthermore, if it is argued that although there is no fixed limit to the measure [of the self] when it is questioned in turn, the self would nonetheless be eternal by way of the principle of the eternity of a stream or continuum— just as the Raktapaṭas maintain that even though consciousness is not permanent, its continuum is permanent, and the same applies to us— the answer is stated by this Sūtra: first of all, if the continuum is not a real entity, it follows that one falls into the doctrine of non-self (nairātmyavāda).
Even if the self were a real entity, this position is untenable because it would entail defects such as undergoing transformation (*vikāra*). [Note:
Although the dimension of the self varies with each different body and thus lacks permanence, there is nonetheless a continuous stream even through its destruction;
"those for whom the cloth has fallen off" (*visica*) means those who are naked.]
Thus, the view that the parts of the soul (*jīva*) are eternal has been refuted regarding its being limited to the size of the body.
Now, the author raises an objection with the words "Now" (*atha*): some parts of the soul are immutable (*kūṭastha*), while others are subject to coming and going.
The meaning is that when the soul occupies a large or small body, its size conforms to the body through the addition or removal of these parts.
He refutes this with a scriptural citation: "And not...
"Coming and going" (*āgamāpāyau*) refers to a process of change.
Does the nature of a self belong to those parts that come and go, or not?
Regarding the first [position], he says: "due to defects such as modification" (*vikārādidoṣa*).
To the question, "What is this acceptance of bondage and liberation? he replies: "the eightfold karma" (*karmāṣṭaka*).
This has already been explained.
Stating another defect in the first alternative, he refutes it by taking up another alternative with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The meaning is that because the remaining immutable parts are difficult to know, there is an absence of self-knowledge, and thus no liberation.

He says "Furthermore" to show that, just as the form of the parts of a lamp is light, the occurrence of coming and going is not logical for the parts of the self due to the absence of any cause for such a form.
The meaning is: whether [the self] is common to all living beings or unique to each individual.

Furthermore, if the self were composed of parts that undergo coming and going, then because one would not know how many parts arrive and how many depart, there would be no certainty regarding the self, and consequently, no liberation; thus he says, "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). Moreover, if the soul (*jīva*) were a whole (*avayavin*) produced from parts, it would be impermanent.

If the self were a collection of parts, it would be non-existent; if the nature of selfhood resided in all the parts, then even upon the loss of any single part, the body would immediately become insentient; and if it were fully present in each individual part—as in the case of "cowness"—there would be a plurality of selves in a single body. Therefore, he concludes that the self does not possess the dimensions of the body nor is it composed of parts, stating: "Therefore... (ataḥ).
He states another meaning of the Sūtra with the words "Alternatively" (*athavā*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the impermanence of the self has been stated by way of describing the non-wholeness [of the self] upon its acquisition of gross and subtle bodies, a doubt may arise—similar to that of the Sugata—that the self is permanent in the form of a continuum (*saṃtāna*); it is in response to this that the answer is given by means of this [verse].
The word "stream" (*srota*) is an explanation of the term "alternately" (*paryāyeṇa*).

Even though the measure and the self do not persist through the destruction of the body, there is nonetheless a stream, a continuous flow; because the continuum of individual selves (ātmavyakti-saṃtāna) consisting of that stream is eternal, there would be the eternity of the self. To this point, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
The meaning is that those from whom clothing has departed are "naked" (*visica*), that is, those who are sky-clad (*digambara*).
Nor is it the case that there is no contradiction regarding the permanence of the self (*ātman*) even through its states (*paryāya*) or its continuum (*saṃtāna*).
Why?
From the modifications and so forth:

if the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is not a real entity (*avastu*), it is the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*); if the continuum is a real entity but distinct from the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*), it is the doctrine of an immutable self (*kūṭasthātmavāda*).

The meaning of the sūtra is that the position that the self is a continuum (saṃtāna) is untenable, because if there were no difference [between the states], then defects already mentioned—such as the occurrence of transformations like birth and so forth, destruction, and the absence of liberation—would necessarily follow. //35//
And because of the final state and the eternity of both, there is no distinction. (BS 2.2.36)
Furthermore, the Jains maintain that the size of the soul existing in the final state of liberation is eternal;
by that same logic, it would follow that the sizes of the soul in the two prior states—namely, ignorance and the intermediate state—are also eternal, resulting in the consequence of non-distinction.
There would be only the size corresponding to a single body, and no attainment of other bodies characterized by increase or decrease.
Alternatively, because the final size of the soul (*jīva*) is fixed, the soul would have to possess that same fixed size even in its two previous states;
consequently, one would have to admit that the soul is always either atomic or large without distinction, rather than having the size of the body.
Therefore, like the Buddhist view, the Jaina doctrine (*ārhatamata*) is also inconsistent and should be disregarded. // 36 //
The Section on the Lord (Paty-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 37–41.
This refutes the restrictive rule that the individual soul (*jīva*) has the exact dimensions of whichever body it occupies, whether gross or subtle—namely, the statement "it ends" (*antyeti*).

Because the final body-dimension is observed to be stable and eternal, it follows that the other two—the initial and intermediate dimensions—would also have to be eternal; thus, there would be no distinction between the three.
The construction of the sūtra is as follows: there would be equality among eternal dimensions, because contradictory dimensions cannot coexist in a single locus.
[Objection: The initial and middle dimensions are eternal, because they are the dimensions of the self (ātman).
It is like the ultimate dimension (*antyaparimāṇa*).

Nor is there a lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatā*), because the point is that if dimension were destroyed, the self would also be destroyed, and thus the permanence of the ultimate dimension would be impossible.
He states the result of establishing the equality of the three dimensions with the words "eka" (one).

The meaning is that the previous bodies would have to be identical in dimension to the final body; for if the self possessed the dimensions of those dissimilar bodies, it would contradict the inference of the equality of the three dimensions.

Previously, having accepted three sizes across the three periods of time, the eternity [of the soul] was inferred by means of the final example and parity was established. Now, since that final size—namely the liberated size—must exist as either atomic or gross, that very same final size would also have to exist at the initial and intermediate times due to its eternity; for that which was previously non-existent cannot possess eternity. Thus, there would be no distinction in the size of the individual soul (jīva) throughout the three periods of time. To this he says: "Or rather... (athavā).
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the doctrine of the Jains—who rely solely on error—and the [Vedic] teaching of the harmony [of all things]. //36//
Because of the inconsistency of [the doctrine of] the Lord (pati). (BS 2.2.37)
Now, the doctrine that the Lord alone is the sole efficient cause is refuted.
How is this understood?

From the sūtras: "And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples" (BrSū 1.4.23), and "And because of the teaching of [His] desire-to-create" (BrSū 1.4.24).
In this context, since the Teacher himself has established that Īśvara possesses a dual nature— as both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*)—

if the mere doctrine of Īśvara as a cause were here refuted without distinction, it would follow that the author of the Sūtras has made a contradictory statement due to internal inconsistency. Therefore, the position that Īśvara is not the material cause but merely the presiding instrumental cause is here refuted with effort, because it stands in opposition to the non-duality of Brahman ordained by the Vedānta.
Furthermore, this conception of a Lord outside the Veda is of many kinds.

First, some who rely on Sāṃkhya and Yoga postulate that the Lord is the presiding overseer of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the individual soul (*puruṣa*), acting solely as the efficient cause; thus, primordial matter, the soul, and the Lord are distinct from one another.

The Māheśvaras, however, maintain that the five categories—effect, cause, yoga, ritual injunction, and the end of suffering—were taught by Paśupati, the Lord, for the sake of liberating bound souls from their fetters; they describe Paśupati, the Lord, as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
Likewise, some others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, also describe the Lord as the efficient cause in some way or another, according to their own systems.
To this, the following is stated: "On account of the lack of appropriateness of the Lord" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*).
The Lord’s status as the cause of the world by way of being the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) over primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the individual soul (*puruṣa*) is not tenable.
Why?
Because it would be inconsistent.
What, then, is this inconsistency?

For if Īśvara were to ordain the distinctions among living beings by way of inferior, middling, and superior states, he would be subject to defects such as passion and hatred; consequently, like ourselves and others, he would be reduced to the status of a non-Īśvara.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the Lord's activity] depends upon the karma of living beings, we say no;

for if karma and the Lord were respectively the impelled and the impeller, the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would follow. If it is argued that this is not so because of beginninglessness (*anāditva*), we say no.
Because the fault of mutual dependence remains unchanged even in past times— just as it is in the present time— it would result in the fallacy of a "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*).
Furthermore, it is the established doctrine of the experts in Nyāya that "the defects (*doṣas*) are characterized by incitement to action" (*Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.18).
Indeed, no one is ever seen to act for his own sake or for the sake of others unless impelled by some defect;
and even the claim that all people act for the sake of others only because they are impelled by their own self-interest is inconsistent,
as it would entail the loss of God's divinity due to His being possessed of self-interest.

Furthermore, there is inconsistency because [the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga] admit that Īśvara is a particular kind of *puruṣa*, whereas they also admit that the *puruṣa* is characterized by indifference (*audāsīnya*).
(Sūtra 37) [The commentators explain: "Those who rely on Sāṃkhya and Yoga" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, and others.
"The four types of Māheśvaras" refers to the Śaivas, [Pāśupatas, Kārukas, and Kāpālikas].
The Pāśupatas, the Kāruṇikasiddhāntins, and the Kāpālikas.

"Beings" refers to living creatures; "their bond" means their bondage; the meaning is "for the destruction of that. Regarding the Sūtra *Patyurasāmañjasyāt* (Sūtra 2.2.37): immediately after refuting the doctrine of the tonsured-headed (luñcitakeśa), the Śaiva doctrine of those who wear matted hair (*jaṭādhārin*) comes to mind and is now rejected. Thus, he states the contextual connection with the words "Now... (*idānīm*).

One might raise the doubt: "Why could this not simply be a general refutation of God? [The author] replies, "Not so," because it would contradict his own statement, using the words beginning with "prakṛtiśca" (and primordial matter).

The grammatical connection is as follows: since [the Lord] has already been established [as having both material and instrumental causes], what is understood here is specifically the negation of a Lord who is a mere instrumental cause.
"One whose utterance (*abhivyāhāra*)— that is, his statement— is *vyāhata*, meaning contradictory, is so described.

When there arises a doubt as to whether or not there is a contradiction between the Vedāntic synthesis (*samanvaya*), which asserts that the world has non-dual Brahman as its material cause (*prakṛti*), and the doctrine of the Śaivas and others, who maintain that the Lord (*Īśvara*) alone is the agent and not the material cause— if there were such a contradiction, then because the latter doctrine is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the non-dual Brahman spoken of in the Vedānta would fail to be established.

Intending the result, [the author] states an intermediate difference of opinion while presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "God alone is the agent," because—just as existence and non-existence cannot coexist in one place—the status of being an agent and the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) likewise cannot coexist in one place. He says: "And she... Here, "she" refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), who is the referent of the term *sāṃkhya*. This refers to the followers of Sāṃkhya.
There are four types of Māheśvaras: the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, the Kāruṇikasiddhāntins, and the Kāpālikas.
All of these are called Māheśvaras because they follow the scriptures (āgamas) proclaimed by Maheśvara.
The effect consists of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth.
The cause consists of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the Lord (īśvara);
yoga is meditative absorption (samādhi); and ritual practice (vidhi) refers to bathing at the three periods of the day and so forth.
The five categories are: suffering, its end, and liberation.
"Beasts" refers to living beings; their "fetter" is bondage, and the meaning is for the sake of destroying that.

Having stated the view that Paśupati is merely the efficient cause based on the authority of the Pāśupata scriptures, he states the view of the Lord as inferred through reasoning with the word "tathā" (likewise).
The Vaiśeṣikas establish the existence of God as the creator by means of the following inference: "The subject under dispute possesses a creator, because it is an effect, like a jar."

The action and its fruit possess a giver who is endowed with supernormal powers (abhijñā) and his retinue, because the fruit arises at a later time, just like the fruit of service; thus say the Gautamas and the Digambaras.

The excellence of knowledge and sovereignty must eventually come to rest somewhere, because it is subject to degrees of superiority, like any measurable magnitude; thinking thus, the Sāṃkhyas, Saugatas, and Pātañjalas have stated: "some [of these] in some way."
He establishes the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
To the question, "Since a faultless God is established through scripture (*āgama*) and other means, how can He be possessed of faults? he asks, "What [is the case]?
It is not, first of all, that the determination of God is reached through one's own respective scripture.
Because the scriptures lack a foundation, they are not authoritative; nor can omniscience serve as their foundation, for there is no proof of its existence.

Nor is scripture alone the means of valid cognition, because there would be a circular dependence: the ascertainment of the validity of scripture depends on the ascertainment of its source, and the ascertainment of that source depends on the ascertainment of the scripture's validity.
Furthermore, it is not logical for human words to possess intrinsic validity.
Furthermore, because there is mutual contradiction [among systems] and because reality remains undetermined,
it is not possible to reach a definitive conclusion through inference that "the Lord is omniscient and the sole creator.
This is because inference follows what has been observed and therefore cannot establish an object contrary to what is observed.

And thus, in the world, whatever kind of agents are observed, such alone would be established as the creators of the world— possessing passion, hatred, and so forth. If, despite not observing unity and other qualities in the creator of diverse palaces and the like in the world, one were to postulate unity, eternal knowledge, and faultlessness for the creator of the universe on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*),
then let it also be postulated that [the Creator] is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the substance.
Because the creator himself is the material cause, this is simpler; otherwise, there would be the conceptual complexity of postulating independent material causes such as *pradhāna* or atoms.
Furthermore, if it were argued that the creator is not established as the material cause because he is not perceived, then even his oneness and other attributes would not be established.

For us, however, by means of the Veda—which, being non-human in origin, possesses an intrinsically established status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—there arises, without dependence on examples, the determination of an omniscient, faultless Lord who is the opposite of a worldly agent, consisting of both a non-dual agent and material cause. Once that has been determined, there is no room for the attribution of defects such as passion, because that would be sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*). This constitutes the distinction from those who maintain an inferential Lord. With this in mind, he states the inconsistency of a non-Vedic Lord with the words "inferior" (*hīna*), etc.

If the creator’s being the material cause is not postulated because it is unobserved, then, since faultlessness is likewise unobserved, and given the observed pervasion that "one who acts unequally is faulty," the creator of the world would necessarily be faulty. Nor is there here a sublation by the inference that apprehends the subject (the creator),
for the mark of "being an effect" establishes only a creator in general and remains indifferent to qualities such as faultlessness.

Nor is the genus [of the creator] equal to excellence, because it would entail the property of pervasion, and because in the absence of defects, it is impossible for there to be an unequal agency that is pervaded by those [defects].
The fallacious rejoinder known as *utkarṣasama* (balancing by addition) consists in attributing to the subject (*pakṣa*) properties that do not pervade the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For instance: "If sound were impermanent due to the reason of being produced, like a jar, then it would also possess parts for that very same reason.
The point is that having parts does not pervade impermanence, because there are counter-examples such as odor (*gandha*), which is impermanent yet partless.

One might object: "Is it not the case that God creates beings with unequal fruits impelled by the karma of living beings, and not by His own will? To this he says: "A living being... Since it is impossible for insentient karma to be an impeller, he says: "No.
Nor can it be said that karma, impelled by God, is the impeller of God; to this he says: "Karma..."

He raises the objection: "No, because of beginninglessness. [The opponent argues: "Impelled by past karma, God impels present karma toward its fruit; thus, because the relationship between the impelled and the impeller is beginningless, there is no logical inconsistency.
[The author replies: Even past karma, being insentient (*jaḍa*), cannot be the impeller of God.
Nor can that [past karma], even while being impelled by God, impel God in turn.
This is because it has already been stated that [the two] are mutually dependent (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore, if you claim that the very same Lord, impelled by past karma, impels that Lord to bestow the fruit upon the present karma, we say no.
For this would entail an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that lacks any supporting evidence (*māna*) and results in the destruction of the root [of the argument].
Therefore, the meaning is that the inconsistency— namely, that God alone, independent of karma, is the creator of inequality— is unavoidable.
As for the claim that there is no such fault because karma is merely an instrumental cause for God in the granting of results and not its instigator,
that is not correct.
For [the opponent's view] entails that the Lord (Īśvara) who causes one to perform unequal actions would inevitably be possessed of fault;

and if he is made to cause actions in dependence upon prior karma, the aforementioned lack of authoritative basis and infinite regress (anavasthā) would follow. For us, however, [the scripture states]: "For He alone causes one to do good and evil."
Furthermore, there is a disparity because the assumption of dependence on prior karma is rooted in scripture, as indicated by the term "blameless" (*niravadya*).
Moreover, even according to the opponent's own view, it follows that the Lord would possess passion and other defects; thus he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).
It is the established position of the logicians (*tārkika*) that defects [such as passion] follow from the mark of being an instigator.
Likewise, God possesses passion and other such qualities for his own sake, because he is an initiator,
like a [common] consensus.
Nor is there an inconsistency regarding the compassionate person, because his purpose is the cessation of his own suffering prompted by the suffering of others; this is the meaning.
Regarding the contradiction that "the indifferent one is the initiator," he says "puruṣa... in response to the Yogas. //37//
And because a relationship [between the two] is untenable. (2.2.38)
Furthermore, this is indeed consistent with reason.
For a Lord distinct from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* cannot be the ruler of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* without some relation [between them].
First of all, a relation characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not possible.
Because the Pradhāna, the Puruṣa, and Īśvara are all-pervading and partless,
there can be no relation characterized by inherence (samavāya), since the relationship between substratum and superstratum cannot be established.
Nor can any other relationship cognizable through its effect be postulated, because the very nature of the causal relation remains unestablished even now.
If it is asked, "How [is this so] for the proponent of Brahman?", we say: no.
This is because for that [Advaitin], a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) is logically established.

Furthermore, since the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādī*) determines the nature of the cause and so forth on the basis of scripture (*āgama*), there is no necessity that he must accept everything exactly as it is perceived in the world.

However, for the opponent, who determines the nature of the cause and so forth by the force of empirical examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), there exists this distinction: he must accept everything exactly as it is perceived.
If it is argued that the strength of scripture (*āgama*) is equal for others as well because there exists a scripture composed by an omniscient being, we say no;

for this would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the establishment of omniscience depends upon the authority of scripture, and the establishment of scripture depends upon the authority of the omniscient one. Therefore, the conception of a Lord (*īśvara*) by the proponents of Sāṃkhya and Yoga is untenable.
In this same manner, the inconsistency should be applied, as far as possible, to other conceptions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara that are based on the Vedas. // 38 //
The author of the Sūtras states another defect in the doctrine of Pradhāna: "Because of the relation," etc.
Since it is impossible for Pradhāna and the like to be impelled if they are unrelated to Īśvara, a relation must be asserted;
however, the meaning is that neither conjunction (saṃyoga) nor inherence (samavāya) exists [between them].
To the objection that "one should postulate a relationship called 'being fit for impulsion' on the strength of the effect," he says: "Nor is it anything else.
If it were established that the world is the effect of primordial matter (pradhāna) impelled by God, then one might postulate such a relationship;
however, that [establishment] is not yet proven—this is the meaning.
However, the relationship between Māyā and Brahman is one of inexpressible identity (*anirvācya-tādātmya*), according to the Śruti text: "The power belonging to the divine Self" (*devātma-śaktim*).

Furthermore, because the Veda possesses a subject matter not previously known (*apūrva-arthatva*), the worldly relationship observed between clay and a potter need not be followed in the case of the Vedic [account].
He states the distinction that [the omniscient being] must be pursued through inference by saying "furthermore" (api ca).
There is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) regarding the cognition of both the omniscient being and the authority of scripture,
because the establishment of the omniscient being through inference has already been refuted.
The point is that knowledge cannot arise for one who lacks a mind (*amanaska*),
because the postulation of eternal knowledge is untenable due to its contradiction with the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "knowledge is produced by the mind.

Furthermore, just as in the case of *pradhāna*, atoms (*paramāṇu*)— being partless— cannot possess conjunction with a partless Lord (*īśvara*), and thus it is impossible for them to be impelled [by Him].
And if God were the impeller, He would be subject to defects; thus he says: "The same applies to the others as well" (38).
And because the existence of a presiding agent is untenable. (BS 2.2.39)
For this reason as well, the Lord imagined by the logicians is untenable.
For, being so imagined, he would have to set the *pradhāna* and other principles in motion by presiding over them, just as a potter works with clay and other materials;
yet this is not logically possible.

For it is not possible for the Pradhāna—which is imperceptible and devoid of form and other qualities—to be governed by the Lord, because it differs in nature from clay and other such materials. // 39 //

The author of the Sūtras states that there is a lack of consistency [in the Sāṅkhya view] because it is impossible for God to impel the *pradhāna* and so forth, in the words: "Because of the lack of a substratum," etc.
For the *pradhāna* and so forth cannot be controlled by a conscious being, because they are imperceptible.
The meaning is: like Īśvara, and by contrast, like deer and other such beings. //39//
If it is argued that [the self] is like an instrument, we say no, because of experience and so forth. (BBs 2.2.40)
It might be argued:
"Just as a person presides over the collection of instruments such as the eye—which are imperceptible and devoid of form and so forth—in the same way, the Lord will also preside over the Pradhāna.
Even so, this is not tenable.
For it is from the observation of enjoyment and so forth that the presided-over nature of the collection of instruments is understood;
yet here, enjoyment and such are not observed.
Furthermore, if the equality of the collection of instruments were admitted, then enjoyment and so forth would necessarily follow for the Lord as well, just as they do for transmigrating beings.

Alternatively, the two Sūtras may be explained as follows: "And because of the impossibility of a substratum" (2.2.39). For this reason also, the Lord imagined by the logicians is untenable. In the world, a king who rules over a kingdom is seen to have a substratum—that is, he possesses a body—and never one without a substratum.
Therefore, for one who wishes to postulate an unseen Lord on the basis of that analogy, some kind of body or locus for His organs would have to be described for the Lord as well.
And that cannot be described,
because since the body exists only after the time of creation, it is impossible for it to exist prior to creation; furthermore,
if the Lord were without a substratum, his status as an instigator would be untenable.
Because it is observed thus in the world:
"If it is argued that [the Lord] is like an instrument, no, because of [the need for] experience and so forth.
Now, if one were to imagine, following worldly observation, that the Lord also possesses some body as a locus for his instruments, out of desire [for such a conception].
Even this is not tenable;

for if he possessed a body, then, as with those in saṃsāra, there would follow the consequence of experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth, which would result in the Lord himself being non-Lordly. (40) [FN: *Bhoga* is the experience of pleasure and pain.]
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the apprehension of the experience of objects is included.
Because instruments exist therein, the body is called an instrument.
Anticipating the objection that this definition might deviate in the case of the eyes and other sense organs, he refutes it by stating "like an instrument."
The phrase "rūpa" clarifies that there is no manifestation of form, thereby making its imperceptibility evident.
He states "tathāpi" (even so) to show that there is no deviation [from the rule], because of the qualification "provided it is not a cause for one's own experience.
Here, "experience" (bhoga) refers to the sensation of pleasure and pain.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the apprehension of the experience of objects is included.

Nor should it be argued that there remains the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)— namely, that "whatever is to be presided over by something [the Self] must be perceptible provided it is a cause of its enjoyment"—
because the reason is qualified by the condition of being "non-perceptible while not being a cause of enjoyment."
Furthermore, because there is no qualified probans (*hetu*) due to the absence of a qualifier among the instruments (*karaṇa*),

the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not redundant; for [otherwise] there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of firewood and so forth, which are governed by a cooker who acts for the sake of another.

Nor is there a failure to establish the qualificand [the Self] on the grounds that the primal matter (pradhāna) and so forth are perceived by the Lord, because the intention is that they possess non-perceptibility in the form of being beyond the senses (atīndriya). In the case of the individual soul (jīva), experiences such as enjoyment are seen to be produced by instruments.
The literal meaning is that these [effects] caused by Pradhāna are not observed in the case of Īśvara.

By stating the defect in the opposing view, he refutes the lack of logical necessity (aprayojakatva) of the reason with the words "karaṇa" etc.: if one accepts that Pradhāna and the rest are things to be impelled, then there would have to be a cause for the experience of the impeller.
The meaning is that there is a necessary rule that an imperceptible impeller must be the cause of experience.
He states another interpretation of the two sūtras with the words "or otherwise.

Since it is observed in the world that whatever conscious being is an impeller possesses a body, and since a body is impossible for Īśvara, he states the meaning of the sūtra [beginning with] "for this reason also" as follows: [Īśvara cannot be the impeller].
It has been stated that for one who imagines, "The Self is possessed of a Lord because it is an effect, like a kingdom," the Lord would necessarily be embodied, just like a king.
In this regard, he rejects the acceptance of such a consequence with the words "nor can that be described.
Nor should it be said that a body exists eternally even prior to creation; the meaning is that a body is necessarily composed of the elements (bhautika).
To the objection that the Lord must be bodiless, he says: "And because there would be no substratum.

He dispels the doubt that the body of the Lord—unlike that of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is composed of the elements—might exist even prior [to creation] as something fashioned by His own will, by stating: "Like the organs" (*karaṇavat*).
A body is so called because the organs are present therein.

It should be understood that the postulation of a body consisting of desire alone is untenable, both because there is a lack of evidence and because it contradicts the observed law of materiality. //40//
There would either be finitude or non-omniscience. (BBs 2.2.41)
For this reason as well, the Lord (Īśvara) imagined by the logicians is untenable.
For he is accepted by them as omniscient and infinite;
yet they also accept that the primal matter (pradhāna) is infinite, and that the individual selves (puruṣas) are infinite and mutually distinct.

In that regard, would the omniscient Lord determine the measure of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), of the individual selves (*puruṣas*), and of his own self, or would he not? In either case, a logical fault remains attached.
How so?

First, regarding the former alternative: because they are limited by a definite measure (*iyattā*), it necessarily follows that the Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara must be finite, as this is observed in the world.

For whatever object in the world is limited by a definite measure, such as a cloth and so forth, is seen to be finite; likewise, the triad consisting of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara must also be finite because it is limited by a definite measure.
To begin with, their numerical measure is delimited by the form of the triad: Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara.
The Lord would also have to determine the individual size of each person contained therein,
as well as the great number of persons residing there.

Consequently, among those whose extent has been thus delimited, those transmigrating souls who are liberated from saṃsāra would find that their saṃsāra is finite, and their state of being a transmigrator would also be finite.
In this way, as the others are also liberated one after another, there would be an end to both saṃsāra and those who transmigrate.

Furthermore, primordial matter (pradhāna), along with its modifications, is intended to be that which is governed by the Lord for the sake of the Puruṣas; if that were empty, what would the Lord govern?
Or in regard to what object would his omniscience and lordship exist?
Furthermore, if the Pradhāna, the Puruṣas, and the Lord were thus finite, it would follow that they have a beginning;
and if they had both a beginning and an end, it would follow that they are subject to the doctrine of nihilism (śūnyavāda).
Now, if this fault is to be avoided, the latter alternative must be accepted: namely, that the extent of the Pradhāna, the Puruṣas, and the Self is not delimited by the Lord.
Furthermore, another fault would follow: the abandonment of the admission that the Lord is omniscient.

Therefore, the doctrine of God as the cause, as maintained by the logicians (*tārkika*), is also inconsistent. (41) [Note: *Saṃkhyā* means number; *parimāṇa* means measure; *iyattā* means limitation.]

Having thus established that the determination of God's status as a creator cannot be reached through dry logic, the author of the Sūtras states— “It would entail finitude”— that even the determination of His eternity and omniscience is not possible.
He says, “In the former case,” meaning that the triad consisting of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara would be non-eternal, because they are limited by a measurable extent, like a jar.
Number (*saṃkhyā*) or magnitude (*parimāṇa*) is limitation (*iyattā*).
Thus, there are two reasons: "because its number is determined" and "because its magnitude is determined.

Although the reason could have been simply "having a number," the word "determined" (*niścita*) is used to demonstrate that the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the certainty regarding an omniscient being.
Regarding that, he states that the first reason is not unestablished: "Number and dimension.
This means the essential nature of number.
He establishes the second reason with the words: "The essential nature..."
The meaning is that primordial matter (pradhāna) and the other categories have a determinate dimension, because they are substantially distinct, like a jar.
But surely, even if it is known that there are three—Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara—how can the number of individual souls (jīvas) be determined, given their infinity?
To this, he says: "Puruṣa...
The number of souls is also determined by Īśvara.
The meaning is that omniscience is impossible in the absence of certainty.
He states the consequence of the establishment of the reason with the words "therefore" (*tataśca*).
The meaning is that, like a heap of beans, the multitude of some living beings and their bondage would perish; thus, due to the liberation of all, the world would now be empty.
The meaning is that there would be no remainder of the eternal [self].
If it is argued, "But let the Lord (Īśvara) remain as a residue," we say no; for He too, being distinct [from the selves], would be subject to an end.
Furthermore, he states "the primal matter" (*pradhānam*) to show that there would be an absence of God due to the absence of anything to be ruled;
he states "the primal matter" (*pradhāna*) to point out another fault;
and he raises a second objection with "now" (*atha*), suggesting that it is not emptiness because there is no determination of its finite extent.
The meaning is that there is no such thing as "this much," nor is it determined;
[the sacrificial] gifts and so forth possess number and magnitude,
because they are substances.
He provides the rebuttal with the words "tataḥ" (therefore), [arguing that] the limit [of the world] exists because of the inference "like black gram and so forth";
for if that limit were unknown, there would be a lack of omniscience, and if the limit were known, its finitude would remain unrefuted.

Therefore, since the doctrine of an absolute creator God is rootless, it is established that there is no contradiction with the concordance of the Lord as both the efficient and the material cause. //41//
END BsCom_2,2.7.41 START BsCom_2,2.8.42 8. The Section on the Impossibility of Origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 42–45.
Because arising is impossible:
the position of those for whom God is intended as a mere instrumental cause, with primordial matter (*prakṛti*) acting as the presiding controller, has been refuted.
Now, the position of those for whom God is intended as a cause consisting of both—both primordial matter and the presiding controller—is being refuted.
But surely, by relying on the Śruti itself, it was already determined that the Lord is of this very nature— both the material cause and the presiding agent—
and it is an established principle that Smṛti which follows the Śruti is authoritative. For what reason, then, do you wish to reject this position?

It is said: although this kind of portion [of the doctrine] does not fall within the scope of contradiction due to its similarity [to our own views], there is another portion concerning existence that is a point of disagreement; therefore, an effort is made to refute that.
In this regard, the Bhāgavatas believe:
"The Blessed One alone, Vāsudeva, whose nature is stainless knowledge, is the ultimate reality."
He, having divided himself fourfold, is established in the form of the Vāsudeva array, the Saṃkarṣaṇa array, the Pradyumna array, and the Aniruddha array.
That which is called Vāsudeva is said to be the Supreme Self (paramātman); that which is called Saṃkarṣaṇa is the individual soul (jīva).
That which is named Pradyumna is the mind;
that which is named Aniruddha is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). Among them, Vāsudeva is the supreme, the ultimate source, while the others, Saṃkarṣaṇa and the rest, are his effects.

Having worshipped that Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, who is thus constituted, for a hundred years through the practices of approaching, procuring materials, sacrifice, self-study, and yoga, one whose afflictions are exhausted attains the Blessed One himself.

In this regard, as for what has been stated— that this Nārāyaṇa, who is well-known as the Supreme Self beyond the unmanifest, the Self of all, remains after having manifested himself in manifold forms— that is not refuted.
Because the manifold manifestation of the Supreme Self is understood from such scriptural passages as, "He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2);
and because the propitiation of that Blessed Lord— characterized by approaching Him and so forth— is intended to be performed incessantly with a mind focused on nothing else.
That too is not prohibited,
because the devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna) is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.
As for what is further stated— that from Vāsudeva arises Saṃkarṣaṇa, from Saṃkarṣaṇa arises Pradyumna, and from Pradyumna arises Aniruddha— [that is not contradicted].
To this we reply: the origination of the individual soul (jīva), designated as Saṃkarṣaṇa, from the Supreme Self, designated as Vāsudeva, is not possible;
for it would entail defects such as impermanence.
Indeed, if the individual soul were subject to origination, defects such as impermanence would necessarily follow.
Consequently, for him there would be no attainment of the Blessed One as liberation, because it would follow that upon the attainment of the cause, the effect must dissolve.

Furthermore, the Teacher will refute the origination of the individual soul in the sūtra: "The self is not [produced], because it is not heard [to be so] and because of its eternity according to those [scriptural passages]" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.17).
Therefore, this conceptualization is inconsistent. [Note:
*Vyūha* means form.
*Abhigamana* is the act of going to the deity’s abode preceded by the focused concentration of speech, body, and mind.]
The acquisition and gathering of materials for worship is *pūjā-dravyārjana*; *ijyā* is worship;
and *svādhyāya* is the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra and others.
"Yoga" means meditation (*dhyāna*).

Immediately after refuting the doctrine of the five categories (*pañcapadārtha*) held by the followers of Maheśvara, he refutes the doctrine of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) which has come to mind—on the grounds that "origination is impossible.
He states the purport of the section with the words, "Of those who... (*yeṣām*).
He raises an objection regarding the commencement of the inquiry with the words "Now, [is it not the case]...":

having accepted those portions that are not contradicted by the Vedas, he states "It is said" in order to refute the portion concerning the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) which is contradicted by the Vedas;
here, the subject matter is the Bhāgavata and Pañcarātra scriptures.

Regarding the doubt as to whether that [scripture] is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the portion concerning the origin of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) asserts that it is a means of valid knowledge because no sublation (*bādhā*) is perceived; this is indicated by the word "therein" (*tatra*).

The difference in results between the two positions is as follows: in the prima facie position, because there would be a contradiction with those [other] scriptures, the systematic unity (*samanvaya*) of Brahman as non-different from the individual soul cannot be established; whereas in the final position (*siddhānta*), because that scripture is not a means of valid knowledge regarding that specific portion, there is no contradiction, and thus that [unity] is established.
He refutes the state of having parts by saying "stainless" (nirañjana).
If so, how can there be a division of forms in Vāsudeva, who is non-dual?
To that he says: "He... (saḥ).
"Vyūha" means form.
Having explained the subject matter of the scripture with its specific distinctions, he states the purpose of the person along with its reason: "him who is thus constituted.
This refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman), who possesses the aforementioned manifestation, who is the source of all, stainless, and whose nature is consciousness.
*Abhigamana* is going to the temple preceded by concentration of speech, body, and mind.
*Upādāna* is the acquisition of the materials for worship.
*Ijyā* is worship.
"Self-study" (svādhyāya) is the recitation of the eight-syllabled mantra and so forth;
"yoga" is meditation.
In that regard, one adopts the non-contradictory portions—this is what is meant by "therein."
The Śruti passage, "Having become concentrated and possessed of faith," and "In whatever way they worship Him," etc.,
as well as the Smṛti passage, "Performing my work, with me as the supreme goal," etc.
He refutes the contradictory portion by stating "yat punar" (as for that which...).
The meaning of the word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to defects such as the loss of what has been performed (*kṛtahāni*).

The sense is that, because the *Pañcarātra* scripture lacks authority regarding its own origin—given the certainty established by the logically sound scriptural texts such as "The Self is unborn" (*aja ātmā*)—the firm establishment of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of Brahman as non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*) remains secure. //42//
And the instrument does not belong to the agent. (2.2.43)
For this reason as well, this conception is inconsistent;
for in the world, an instrument such as an axe is never seen to arise from an agent such as Devadatta.
Yet the Bhāgavatas describe that the instrument, the mind named Pradyumna, arises from the agent, the individual soul named Saṃkarṣaṇa.
And from that [intellect] which is born of the agent, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) designated as "aniruddha" arises;
yet we are not able to determine this without an illustrative example, nor do we find any such scriptural authority (śruti). // 43 //
Having refuted the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*), he now refutes the origination of the mind from the soul with the words, "Nor from the agent" (*na ca kartuḥ*).
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the origination of an instrument is never observed from an agent, this conceptualization is untenable.
The particle *hi* is used for the purpose of stating a well-known fact: that an agent is one who employs already established instruments.
He states that such a description is groundless with the words "not so" (na vai).
If it is argued: "But in the world, it is observed that some preeminent craftsman, having fashioned an axe, cuts down a tree with it," [the reply is:
True.
The agency of an axe is appropriate because the artisan possesses other instruments such as his hands; however, since the individual soul (jīva) lacks other instruments, the mind cannot be the agent.
Alternatively, if it were an agent without any instrument at all, the mind would be rendered useless—this is the intended meaning. //43//
Or, if [the pradhāna] exists as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that [consciousness]. 2.2.44.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "These [beings], Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, are not intended to be individual souls (*jīva*) and so forth; rather, all of them are accepted as being indeed the Lord (*īśvara*), endowed with the sovereign qualities of knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor.
All these are Vāsudevas alone—faultless, without a substratum, and beyond reproach."

Therefore, it might be argued that this aforementioned fault of the impossibility of origination does not apply. To this it is replied: even so, there is no refutation of that; indeed, the impossibility of origination remains unrefuted as a fault by way of another method—this is the intended meaning.
How so?

If the intention is that these four lords, Vāsudeva and the others, are indeed mutually distinct, possessing equal attributes, and do not possess a single unified nature, then the postulation of multiple lords is purposeless, since the work of a lord is accomplished by a single lord alone.
Furthermore, there would be a loss of your own tenet,
because you have accepted that each individual Vāsudeva is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*).
Now, if your intention is that these four manifestations (*vyūha*) of the one Lord alone possess identical attributes, [then...]
Nevertheless, the impossibility of origination remains exactly as it was;

for the origination of Saṃkarṣaṇa from Vāsudeva is not possible, nor that of Pradyumna from Saṃkarṣaṇa, nor that of Aniruddha from Pradyumna, because there is no distinction [of excellence] among them.
For there must indeed be a distinction between cause and effect, as in the case of clay and a jar;
for in the absence of such a distinction, it is not possible to conceive of something as being the effect and the other as the cause.

Furthermore, the proponents of the Pañcarātra system do not admit any difference—whether in one or in all [of the forms] such as Vāsudeva and the others—based on a gradation of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth.
For indeed, all these manifestations (vyūhas) are held to be Vāsudeva himself, without distinction.

Nor do these manifestations of the Blessed One remain limited to the number four alone, since it is understood that the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is a manifestation of the Blessed One. 44.
FN: "Free from defects" means empty of passion and the like; "without a basis" means not produced by nature; "blameless" means devoid of destruction and so forth—this is the meaning.

He raises an objection regarding what the Sūtra seeks to exclude—the possibility that even though the birth of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others is impossible, there might still be a fourfold manifestation (vyūha)—with the words "But it might be argued" (*athāpi syāt*).
"Power" (*śakti*) refers to internal capacity consisting of knowledge and sovereignty;
"strength" (*bala*) refers to physical capacity.
The meaning is that because Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others are endowed with vigor (*vīrya*), heroism (*śaurya*), splendor (*tejas*), and confidence (*prāgalbhya*), they are indeed lords (*īśvara*).
Regarding their lordship over all, he cites the statement from the *Pañcarātra*: "They are indeed Vāsudevas."
"Without description" means empty of passion and the like;
"without basis" means unproduced by nature;
"blameless" means devoid of destruction and so forth—this is the meaning.
He states that because of his lordship (*īśvaratva*), the impossibility of birth is indeed a merit: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He establishes the final conclusion with the Sūtra: "In this case" (*atra*).
And even so: *evam api*.
The meaning is: "even though there is the state of being consciousness, power, and so forth, by virtue of [their] lordship over the four.
He asks about another alternative: "How?
Does it mean that the four are independent and distinct, or are they non-distinct as modifications of a single entity?
Having restated the first [position], he refutes it with the words beginning "yadi" (if).
Regarding the second [position], the transformations are either equal to the material cause or inferior to it;
having raised the first of these, he negates it with the words beginning "atha" (now/if).
Regarding the position that [the manifestations] are fewer, he states the contradiction with established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*): "And not five.
If the Lord's manifestations (*vyūhas*) were fewer than that, then there would be a contradiction with the number four; thus he says: "And not these... (verse 44).
And because of contradiction. (BsCom_2,2.8.45)

Furthermore, many kinds of contradictions are observed in this scripture, characterized by the conceptualization of qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), as seen in such views as:
"Knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor are the qualities;
these Blessed Lords Vāsudevas are themselves the Self."
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the Vedas;
for we observe censures of the Vedas, such as the statement that Śāṇḍilya, having not found the highest good in the four Vedas, mastered this [other] scripture.
Therefore, it is established that this hypothesis is inconsistent. // 45 //
For this reason as well, the author of the Sūtras states that the doctrine of the production of the individual soul (jīva) is to be disregarded: "And because of contradiction" (vipratiṣedhācca).
It is contradictory for the same entity to possess both the state of being a quality (guṇatva) and the state of being a possessor of qualities (guṇitva).

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of contradictory statements such as first asserting that Pradyumna and Aniruddha are distinct from the Self, and then stating that these two are the Self itself.
Having stated the meaning of the Sūtra—that there is a lack of consistency due to internal contradictions—[the author] states another point: "The Veda... [and so on].
The meaning of the words "censure" and so forth is that even one who has studied a single syllable of this Tantra (the Upaniṣads) is superior to those who know the four Vedas.
Therefore, it is established that the non-contradictory harmony (*samanvaya*) of the impersonal Vedānta is not opposed by mutually contradictory human fabrications. //45//
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Faultiness of the Doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and Others."

Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya), composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "Demonstration of the Fallacious Nature of the Doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and Others.
The third quarter of the second chapter:
In this quarter, the resolution of apparent contradictions regarding the scriptural texts concerning the five great elements, the individual soul (jīva), and so forth.
The Section on Space (Viyan-adhikaraṇa), Sūtra 1.7.
Third Pāda of the Second Adhyāya.
[Salutation to] the creator of space and the other elements, the bee at the lotus-face of Sītā.
I worship the Lord of All, who is non-different from the Self, the universal creator whose nature is eternal consciousness. //1//
START BsCom_2,3.1.1:
"Ether [is] not [produced], because it is not mentioned in scripture.
(BBs_2,3.1) In various places throughout the Vedāntas, scriptural passages concerning origin are found that follow different approaches.
Some maintain that space has an origin, while others do not;
likewise, some maintain that wind has an origin, while others do not;
and the same applies to the soul and the vital breaths.
In this very way, contradictions based on sequence and other factors are also observed in other scriptural passages (*śruti*).

Since it has been established that the positions of others are to be disregarded due to such contradictions, one might suspect that one's own position is likewise to be disregarded because of internal contradictions.
Therefore, the subsequent section is commenced to clarify the meaning of the creation texts found throughout all the Vedāntas.
And when that [scripture] is rendered pure, the result is precisely the cessation of the aforementioned doubts.
In this regard, first of all, it is considered with reference to space: does this space have an origin, or does it not?
On this point, it is established first: "Space does not originate, because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]."
Space, indeed, is not produced.
Why?
Because it is not heard [in scripture].
For there is no mention of it in the section concerning its origin;

for in the Chāndogya, having introduced Brahman denoted by the word "Being" in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chā. 6.2.1), it continues, "It thought" (tadaikṣata).
And in the passage, "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), the origin of the triad of fire, water, and food is heard by taking fire as the starting point among the five great elements;
and scripture is our authority for the production of knowledge regarding objects beyond the reach of the senses.
Furthermore, there is no scriptural passage here that establishes the origin of space;
therefore, there is no origination of space. // 1 //

Fearing that, by the consequence of the soul's non-origination, the origination of space (ākāśa) would also be impossible, [the author] first states the view of a certain school (ekadeśin) while offering a rebuttal: "Not so, because of the lack of scriptural statement" (*na viyadaśruteḥ*).
Summarizing the meaning of the two preceding sections—on space and on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—he states the connection with the previous section: "In the Vedāntas...
He explains the difference in the introductory statements with the words beginning "Some say," and so forth.
The purpose of the section on the ether (*viyat-pāda*) is the removal of the suspicion of mutual contradiction among the scriptural texts concerning the enjoyer of the elements.
The purpose of the section on the vital breaths (*prāṇa-pāda*) is the removal of that [same suspicion] regarding the scriptural texts concerning the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*).

Since both sections are commenced because the suspicion arises that "just as the views of other schools are to be disregarded due to mutual contradictions and contradictions between earlier and later passages, so too the position of the Śruti itself should be disregarded," there is a connection by way of illustration with the preceding section.
This is the collective meaning:
the Taittirīyakas maintain that space and wind have an origin,
whereas the Chandogas do not maintain this.

The Vājasaneyins record the origin of the individual soul and the vital breaths in the passage, "All these emerge from the Self," while the followers of the Atharva-veda state, "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath," and others do not.
Thus, in some places, creation begins with ether.
In some places, [the creation] is preceded by fire, which contradicts the [established] order;
from the word "etcetera" (ādipada), there is the lack of order in [the statement], "He created these worlds";
and in some places, there are seven vital breaths (prāṇas).
In some places, contradictions based on number—such as "eight" and so forth—should also be understood.
The "elaboration" (prapañca) refers to two quarters (pāda).
Thus, because these two quarters serve to resolve mutual contradictions among the Śrutis, the connections between the Śruti, the Śāstra, and the Adhyāya are established.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether there is a mutual contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the origin and non-origin of space, based on the principles of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*).

Anticipating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that if there were origin, then these two scriptural texts would lack authority due to contradiction through syntactical split, [the author] first introduces a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*) who maintains the position of non-origination, saying: "In that regard, first... (*tatra tāvad iti*).
The explicit scriptural statement regarding origination does not exist; such is the hidden intention. //1//
But it does exist. BBs 2.3.2.
The word "tu" (but) is used to adopt an alternative position:
let there be no origination of space in the Chāndogya;
however, it exists in another Śruti.
For the Taittirīyakas record: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," and then, having introduced this, state, "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Consequently, there appears to be a contradiction between these two scriptural passages: in one case creation begins with fire, and in another it begins with ether.
But surely it is appropriate to interpret these two scriptural passages as forming a single coherent whole?
True;
that [reasoning] is logical, yet it cannot be understood.
Why?

Because it is impossible for a single creator, mentioned only once in the phrase "It created that heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), to have a connection with two things to be created, [the text continues]:
"It created that heat."
"It created space.
Now, it is observed that even when the agent is mentioned only once, he can be connected with two actions, as in the expression: "Having cooked the soup, he cooks the rice."
I shall connect the passage thus: "Having created that ether in this way, it created fire.
But it is not so connected; for in the Chāndogya, fire is understood to be the first-born, while in the Taittirīyaka, ether is.
Nor is it possible for both [ether and air] to be produced first;
by this, the contradiction with the words of the other scriptural passage is also explained:
"From that very Self, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

In this case as well, because it is impossible for the single ablative "from that" (*tasmāt*) and the single verb "was produced" (*saṃbhūtaḥ*)— heard only once— to be simultaneously connected with both ether and fire,
and because of the separate scriptural statement, "From air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*), [ether is not produced from Brahman]. // 2 //
Now the author of the Sūtras presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "But it exists" (*asti tu*).

He raises an objection—asking how there could be a lack of authority for two scriptural passages when their authority is possible through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*)—with the words, "But [if you say] syntactic unity...
He replies that a lack of authority is indeed appropriate because syntactic unity is impossible, beginning with the words, "True," and so forth.

The proponent of the primary established doctrine (*mukhya-siddhāntin*) raises an objection: "Even though a single [word] cannot be connected to two effects simultaneously, it can be connected to them sequentially; therefore, there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
The proponent of non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya-vādī*) refutes this, saying: "It is not so.
The meaning is that such a sequence is not tenable, because it would result in the subversion of the primacy of both [words] as they are heard in the text.
To the objection that both [fire and air] might be produced first from a single split seed like two halves, he says "nor" (na ca).
The ellipsis is: "because it would violate the scriptural statement of the sequence, 'From air, fire'.
Having stated that the Chāndogya Śruti has a meaning contrary to the Taittirīya Śruti, he states that the Taittirīya Śruti has a meaning contrary to that [Chāndogya] by saying "by this" (etena).
He states this meaning of the word with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
The meaning is that even in the Chāndogya, the primacy of fire (tejas) heard there would be difficult to reconcile here.
Furthermore, in the Chāndogya, the referent of the word "Being" (sat), which is the Self (ātman), is heard to be the material cause (upādāna) of fire.
But here, the phrase "vāyuḥ" (wind) does not form a single syntactical unit; thus he says: "vāyoḥ" (of wind). //2//

Because a figurative sense is impossible.
There is no origination of space precisely because it is not so stated in scripture.
As for that other scriptural passage cited which asserts the origination of space, it must be understood as figurative.
Why?
Because it is impossible.
For as long as those who follow the views of the venerable Kaṇabhuj remain alive, the arising of space cannot possibly be maintained.
For they deny the production of space because of the impossibility of a causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).
Indeed, it is said that everything being produced arises from inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*).
And for a substance, the inherent cause consists of multiple substances belonging to the same genus.
Furthermore, there exists no substance of a single class that is manifold and capable of being an originator [of ether],

such that— given that as an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) and its conjunction as a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)— ether might arise within it. Due to the absence of such [causes], an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) that functions to assist it is utterly remote from ether.

Furthermore, in the case of things that possess an origin, such as fire and the like, a distinction between their prior and subsequent states is conceivable: it is possible to determine that before its origin, the effect—such as illumination—did not exist, whereas after [its origin], it does exist. However, in the case of space, no such distinction between prior and subsequent times can be conceived.
For how could one possibly ascertain that before its origin there existed something without room, without cavities, and without apertures?

Furthermore, because of its dissimilarity to earth and other elements, and because of its characteristics such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*), the non-produced nature of space (*ākāśa*) is established. Therefore, just as in common worldly usage there occurs figurative expressions (*gauṇa-prayoga*) of this kind, such as "making space" or "space has been produced," and just as there occurs figurative designations of differentiation for that which is one and the same space— such as "the space within a jar," "the space within a water-pot," or "the space within a house"— so too [is the case here].
Even in the Veda, there is the statement, "One should sacrifice the forest animals in the open air";
likewise, the scriptural injunction regarding their origin must also be understood as figurative. // 3 //

When the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position has been reached—that the scriptures lack authority due to such contradictions—the proponent of the non-origination of space (*viyadanutpatti*) states his own view regarding their authority, beginning with the words "In this [scripture]...

It should be understood that, up until the end of the chapter, in each section (*adhikaraṇa*), the result of the prima facie position is first that the scriptures lack authority because of contradiction; then follows the partial conclusion (*ekadeśisiddhānta*);

and finally, in the principal conclusion (*mukhyasiddhānta*), the result is the establishment of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the scriptures with Brahman through their unity of purpose (*ekavākyatā*) without contradiction, as well as the sequence [of these stages].

In that regard, since there is a conflict between two scriptural passages (śruti) both of which are included within the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), and because it is impossible for both to lack authority, the author explains the view of the "partialist" (*ekadeśin*)— that there is no contradiction because the Chāndogya passage, supported by reasoning (*tarka*) regarding the impossibility of the production of ether, has its primary sense while the other is figurative— with the words beginning "it does not exist," etc.
