Having set aside the first [position], he refutes the second with the words, "so also in the other case.

The meaning is that by means of the quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) acting as a cause, a quality is superimposed upon the Self; and by virtue of that very superimposed quality of the Self, the individual soul (*jīva*) is perceived as having the size of the tip of an awl and as being limited, whereas in its own nature it is indeed infinite—as stated:
"It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other gods, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action."

Having stated, "Then, with his being purified by the clarity of knowledge, he beholds Him, the partless One, while meditating," and having said, "This Self is atomic," [the author] explains that even if [the referent] is the individual soul (jīva), the meaning of the word "atomic" refers to the superimposed atomicity; thus he says, "Of the jīva also.
As for what was stated—that because of the separate teaching, the pervasion of the body by the Self occurs solely through the quality of consciousness—[this is addressed as follows].
Regarding this, he says: "In that way, by means of wisdom (prajñā).
The meaning is that "intellect" (buddhi) is wisdom.
If consciousness (caitanya) were wisdom, then there would be a metaphorical attribution of difference; thus he says: "or it is merely a designation."
"Is it not the case that since consciousness (caitanya) is a quality (guṇa), the distinction [between the Self and consciousness] should be primary?
No," he says: "for not here.
The meaning is: because of the scriptural teaching of its being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva).
He states that other previously mentioned [states] are also conditioned by adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, using the words beginning with "hṛdaya.
He explains the scriptural illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
The term "non-existence" (asattva) is used from a superficial perspective.
The state of being non-transmigratory is what must be established;
the remainder is easily understood. //29//
To this, he recites the following reply:
And because it is cultivated as long as the self exists, there is no fault in seeing it.
This aforementioned fault should not be suspected.
Why?
This is because the conjunction with the intellect persists as long as the self exists;
as long as this self remains a transmigrating being,
and as long as its state of transmigration is not terminated by right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

The connection of this [Self] with the intellect does not cease as long as this relation with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect persists; and as long as that relation with the limiting adjunct of the intellect exists, so long does the individual soul (jīva) possess its status as a soul and its state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva).
In ultimate reality, however, there is no such thing as a "soul" apart from the nature imagined through the connection with the limiting adjunct of the intellect.
Indeed, in the exposition of the meaning of the Vedānta, no second conscious principle other than the Lord—who is of the nature of eternal liberation and omniscient—is found.
"There is no other seer, hearer, thinker, or knower than He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23);
"There is nothing else that sees, hears, thinks, or knows besides Him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
This is known from such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6) and "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
How, then, is it understood that the conjunction with intelligence persists as long as the self exists?
[The author] says: "Because that is seen.

For the scripture shows this: "This person, consisting of consciousness, who is among the vital breaths, the light within the heart—that, being common to both, moves through both worlds; it meditates, as it were, and it stirs, as it were."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.4), and so forth.
In that context, "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) means "consisting of intellect" (*buddhimaya*).

This is because in another passage—where it says, "consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing"—the term "consisting of consciousness" is recited together with the mind and the other faculties.
And its being "consisting of intelligence" (buddhimayatva) is intended precisely as having the qualities of that [intellect] as its essence;
just as in common usage one says "Devadatta consists of women," meaning he is dominated by passion for women and so forth, so it is here.
Furthermore, the statement, "Being the same [as the intellect], he wanders through both worlds," shows that there is no separation from the intellect even when going to another world.
It is understood that [the Self] appears as if possessing thought due to its proximity to that very [intellect].
And the scripture shows this: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
This is what is meant: it does not meditate by itself.
Nor does it move;
for when the intellect is meditating, the Self seems to meditate, and when the intellect is moving, it seems to move.
Furthermore, this connection of the Self with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect is preceded by false knowledge.

Furthermore, since false knowledge does not cease except through right knowledge, the connection with the limiting adjunct of the intellect (*buddhy-upādhi*) does not subside as long as there is a lack of realization of one's identity with Brahman.
And the scripture shows this: "I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness;
only by knowing Him does one pass over death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8). // 30 //
FN: Consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) means abounding in intellect (*buddhi*).
"Having the color of the sun" means self-luminous.
"Beyond darkness" means untouched by ignorance (*ajñāna*).

[The phrase] "by the existent Supreme Self" [is used]. Now, one might object: "Let transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva) belong to [the self] by its own nature; why [postulate] the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect (buddhi)? To this, he says: "And as long as this...

Being "common" (samāna), that is, having attained identity with the intellect, it is "consciousness" (vijñāna)—meaning Brahman—and its modification (vikāra) is the subtle body (aṇu); such is the meaning.
To the question "Why should this not be so?", he says: "In another passage.
The meaning is that it consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), that is, it abounds in intellect (*buddhi*).
The phrase "by what [is it similar]? is to be supplied as the expected inquiry.
Having stated, on the strength of scripture, that the nature of the intellect (buddhi) persists as long as transmigratory existence because—
as long as the root exists— the separation of the effect is impossible, he states this also through reasoning with the words "Moreover, it is false" (mithyā).
Regarding the point that the destruction of the bondage of the intellect and so forth occurs only through right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), he cites scripture with the words "It shows" (darśayati).
The grammatical construction is "he transcends death.
"Having the splendor of the sun" means self-luminous;
"beyond darkness" means untouched by ignorance—this is the meaning. //30//
Now, it may be objected that in the states of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, it is impossible to admit a connection of the self with the intellect.
This is because of the scriptural statement, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1),
and because it is accepted that there is a dissolution of all modifications.
How, then, can there be a persistence of the connection with intelligence throughout the entire existence of the self? To this it is replied:
"But because, while existing, it becomes manifest like virility and so forth" (BBs 2.3.31).

Just as in the world, virility and other such qualities exist in the form of seeds during childhood and other stages, yet being unperceived they are regarded as non-existent, only to become manifest during youth and so on; [so too is the case here].
Things that do not exist do not arise, because it would follow that even eunuchs and the like could produce them;
likewise, this connection with the intellect, existing already in the form of a potentiality during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, manifests again upon awakening and creation.
For it is only in this way that this is logically consistent.
For the arising of anything cannot occur without a cause, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the scripture demonstrates that rising from deep sleep is brought about by the existence of the seed consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*): "Having reached Being, they do not know; having reached Being, they say" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2), and "They become here a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3).

By such passages as these, it is established that the connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, persists as long as the self-existence (ātmabhāva). // 31 //
He raises the objection regarding the non-establishment of [the self] being co-existent with the body, beginning with "But surely" (nanu).

The meaning is that if the intellect (*buddhisattva*) exists during deep sleep, there would be no merging with Brahman; if it exists at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), that dissolution would be contradicted.
He states that the intellect (buddhi) persists as long as there is the state of being a self in its gross and subtle forms, beginning with the words "puṃstva" and so forth.
"Puṃstva" means semen;
by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the beard and other such features are included.
The meaning is "of this connection with the intellect.
Regarding the point that the intellect and so forth, which exist in the state of deep sleep (svāpa) in the form of seeds, become manifest upon awakening, he cites scripture, saying "it shows.
The phrase "they do not know" expresses the existence of the seed whose nature is ignorance (avidyā).
The statement regarding manifestation is that those [beings], such as tigers and the like, manifest once again. //31//
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other.

And that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the Self, is designated in various places by many names such as *manas*, *buddhi*, *vijñāna*, and *citta*. Furthermore,
according to the distinction of its functions (*vṛtti*), that which possesses functions such as doubt is called *manas*, while that which possesses functions such as ascertainment is called *buddhi*.
Moreover, it must necessarily be admitted that such an internal organ exists;
for otherwise, if it were not admitted, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception.
Since the self, the sense organs, and the objects—the means of perception—are present, constant perception would necessarily result.
Furthermore, if the effect were absent despite the presence of the collection of causes, then non-perception would necessarily follow eternally;
yet this is not observed.
Alternatively, one must admit an obstruction of the power of either the self or the sense organ.
Nor is an obstruction of the self's power possible,
because it is changeless;
nor is it possible for the sense organ.
For its power, being unimpeded in the preceding and succeeding moments, could not suddenly be obstructed.
Therefore, that by whose attention and non-attention perception and non-perception occur is the mind (*manas*).
And thus says the Śruti: "I was elsewhere with my self [the mind], I did not see; I was elsewhere with my mind, I did not hear" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
Thus it is said: "For by the mind alone one sees, by the mind one hears" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).

Furthermore, it shows that desire and the rest are its modifications: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, fear—all this is indeed the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
Therefore, this is logical.
"Because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by them. (Sūtra 32)
The author of the Sūtras states the proof for the existence of the intellect (buddhi) with the word "eternal" (nitya):
"For one sees indeed by means of the mind;
and the intellect does not act."

The meaning is that, as it is stated in various scriptural passages— such as "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," "It is to be known by the mind," and "The mind and that which is to be thought"— the substance of the intellect (buddhi-dravya) is well-known as being denoted by terms such as "manas" and so forth.
How can there be a manifold expression for that which is one?
To this he says: "In some cases...
It should also be understood that *ahaṅkāra* is characterized by pride (*garva*), while *vijñāna* is primarily consciousness (*cit*) or primarily memory (*smṛti*), and is thus called *citta*.

Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is established by the perception of witnesses and is also restated in scripture, nevertheless, for one who disputes its existence on the basis of perception and scripture, [the author] establishes it through the impossibility of simultaneous engagement (*vyāsaṅgānupapatti*), connecting the Sūtra beginning with "And that" (*tac ca*) and stating "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).
For if there were a connection between the five sense organs and their five respective objects, there would necessarily be five simultaneous perceptions at once.
This is because the causal complex (sāmagrī) is present even when the mind is absent.
The meaning is that if there were no perception despite the presence of the causal complex, then there would follow the consequence of never perceiving [the object] at all.
Therefore, the implication is that the mind must be accepted as the factor that determines its occasional perception.

One might object: "Even when there is contact with fire, just as burning is only occasional, let perception also be occasional; what need is there for the mind? Anticipating this doubt, the author explains the phrase "or else there would be a restriction to one of the two" with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*). The meaning of the word "or" (*vā*) is this: either constant perception must be admitted despite the presence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or else a restriction must be admitted regarding the power of one of the causes being obstructed by something—just as, for example, the power of fire is obstructed by a magnet-stone (*maṇi*).
To the objection that "let there be an obstruction," he says:
"And not... It should not be said that the obstruction belongs to the sense organ itself, because there is no obstructing agent.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that when the visible causal complex is present, the unseen (adṛṣṭa) acts as an obstructer, for this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor can inattention (vyāsaṅga) be the obstructer, because that is impossible in the absence of a mind that acts as an obstructer.

For instance, when the simultaneous perception of taste and other objects occurs, a distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) consisting of the desire to perceive taste must be admitted as an obstacle to the perception of form and so forth.

And since that [distraction], being a quality (*guṇa*), must—like color—have a substratum that is a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), it cannot belong to the Self, which is unattached, devoid of qualities, and immutable; therefore, the mind alone must be accepted as the possessor of qualities. Thus, the existence of the mind is established through the impossibility of such distraction otherwise.
Intending this, he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
"Attention" (*avadhāna*) means the desire to know (*bubhutsā*).
Nor should it be argued that the desire to know is not the determining factor for perception, since one perceives foul odors and the like even without such a desire.
This is because, even when many objects are present, it is accepted that [the mind] acts as a restrictor for that [desire] in only one particular instance.
Furthermore, according to their view, since desire and the like are attributes of the self (*ātman*), it should be understood that the mind is difficult for them to obtain;
for distraction is possible through the self itself, which possesses the attributes of desire and so forth.
Now, he cites scripture (*śruti*) to show that distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) is mental in nature, using the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

Not only is the existence of the mind established through distraction, but it is also established as the locus of desire and so forth; this is what he states with the words "And desire and so forth" (*kāmādayaś ca*).
He states the result of declaring that cognition is a valid means of knowledge: "Therefore," etc. (32).
