The soul is an agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless.
Under the heading of its having the qualities of that [intellect] as its essence, yet another attribute of the living being is further elaborated:
this living being must be an agent.
Why?
Because it is the purpose of the scripture.
And in this way, the scriptural injunctions of such a nature as "one should sacrifice," "one should offer oblations," and "one should give" become meaningful.
Otherwise, it would be purposeless;
for that [scripture] teaches a specific duty for one who exists as an agent,
and that would not be possible if agency did not exist.

In this way, this treatise also becomes meaningful, for it says: "For he is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the doer—the Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.9). // 33 //

Thus, by stating the superimposition of atomicity upon the Self, its natural greatness has been established. Now, he establishes agency as residing outside of that [atomicity]: "The agent exists, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. Whether that eternal, conscious, and great Self is an agent or not is a matter of dispute between the scriptural texts concerning its lack of attachment (*asaṅga*) and those concerning injunctions and the like.

Since the validity of the scriptures, such as injunctions, is established by the fact that the intellect alone is the agent in cases of doubt, the Sāṃkhya position—that the Self is a non-agent—is reached.

Anticipating the objection that this would be a mere repetition—given that the superimposition of agency upon the Self is already established by the statement that the Self has the qualities of the intellect as its essence—the author states "tadguṇa... (by the statement of having those qualities as its essence).
He asserts that there is no tautology because he elaborates upon the superimposition of agency in the Self for the purpose of refuting the Sāṃkhya view.
The *adhikāra* (contextual connection) is the *prasaṅga* (logical sequence).

Since it has been stated that there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning "non-attachment" (*asaṅgatva*) and "agency" (*kartṛtva*)— namely, that while in reality there is non-attachment, agency arises from ignorance— the three sections (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of the inquiry into agency are connected to this chapter (*pāda*).
The mutual contradiction or non-contradiction of the scriptures is the result of the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions.

Alternatively, the distinction here is that in the prima facie position the result is the futility of the scripture due to the absence of bondage, whereas in the established conclusion (siddhānta), the result is the meaningfulness of the scripture because of the existence of the connection with agency and so forth.

[Objection: "Surely, let the purposefulness of the scripture be established by the intellect being the agent; what is the use of the individual soul (jīva) being the agent? To this, he says: "For that [activity] belongs to one who is an agent. Agency must be attributed only to a conscious being capable of the cognition, "This is to be done by me," and not to the insentient intellect. Furthermore, agency must belong to the experiencing self alone, according to the maxim, "The fruit of the scripture accrues to the performer"—this is the intended meaning. //33//
Because of the teaching regarding his wandering about. (BBs 2.3.34)

Furthermore, the soul possesses agency, because in the section concerning the individual soul, the scripture teaches its wandering in the intermediate state (*sandhya-sthāna*): "He, being immortal, goes wherever he desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12), and "He moves about at will within his own body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18). // 34 //
FN: The intermediate state (*saṃdhyam sthānam*) is the state of dreaming. It is called "intermediate" because one goes (*īyate*) [to it]; the intermediate state is the dream.
That Self is immortal; because of the teaching regarding its "wandering" (vihāra)—that it moves or goes according to its desire—the Self is the agent. //34//
Because of appropriation. (BBs 2.3.35)

Moreover, its agency is established by the fact that, in the very context concerning the individual soul (*jīva*), it mentions the taking up of the instruments: "Therefore, having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by means of [his own] consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17), and "having grasped the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18). // 35 //

Note: The construction is as follows: "In sleep, the individual soul (jīva) goes to the heart, having taken up the consciousness—that is, the power of apprehension—of the vital breaths (prāṇas), which are the sense organs, by means of consciousness, which is the intellect (buddhi). Among the vital breaths, [the soul] sleeps having taken up the collection of sense organs capable of consciousness by means of consciousness, which is the intellect; thus, it "turns away having grasped the vital breaths. The meaning is that the self possesses the agency of appropriation (*upādāna-kartṛtva*), because appropriation would be impossible in the absence of agency. //35//
And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action, [the agent exists], provided there is no reversal of the grammatical indication. (BS 2.3.36)

Furthermore, the soul possesses agency, because the scripture designates its agency in both worldly and Vedic actions, stating: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs the ritual acts" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1).
But surely, the word *vijñāna* is understood to refer to the intellect (*buddhi*).
How is the agency of the individual soul (jīva) indicated by this?
It is not so stated;
for this designation refers to the soul alone, not to the intellect (buddhi).
If it were not the soul (*jīva*), there would be a reversal in the designation;
[the text] would have designated it as "by means of consciousness" (*vijñānena*).

For elsewhere, when the intention is to express the intellect (*buddhi*), the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is seen to be designated with an instrumental case ending, as in: "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths (*prāṇānām*) by means of consciousness" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.17).

But here, because of the designation in grammatical apposition with the agent in the statement, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1), the agency of the Self as distinct from the intellect is indicated; thus, there is no fault. // 36 //

To this, it is said: If the individual soul (*jīva*) were an agent distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*), being independent, it would necessarily accomplish for itself only what is pleasant and beneficial, and never the opposite.
Yet, it is observed accomplishing even the opposite;
and such an irregular activity is not possible for an independent self.
If the word *vijñāna* were not a designation for the *jīva*, then there would be a contradiction with its being designated in the nominative case;
rather, it would have been designated with the instrumental case to indicate an instrument.

Therefore, since in this scriptural passage the word *vijñāna* is used in grammatical apposition with the verb "spreads" (*tanute*), which denotes the agent, the meaning of the Sūtra and its Bhāṣya is that the self's status as the agent in the action is indicated.
To this, he recites the following reply:
There is no lack of restriction, just as in the case of perception.

Just as this self, although independent with respect to perception, perceives both the desirable and the undesirable without restriction, so too will it bring about the desirable and the undesirable without restriction.
If it is argued that there is a lack of independence even regarding perception because one observes the appropriation of the causes of perception, we say: no.
Since the causes of perception have as their sole purpose the conceptualization of objects,
the self possesses independence with respect to perception due to its association with consciousness (*caitanya*).
Furthermore, even in regard to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the self does not possess absolute independence, because it depends upon specific conditions of place, time, and causal factors.
Moreover, the agency of an agent who depends on auxiliaries does not cease;
for indeed, even a cook who depends on fuel, water, and so forth, still possesses the status of a cook.
And due to the diversity of auxiliary factors, the soul's engagement in the performance of desired or undesired effects without fixed necessity is not contradictory. // 37 //
He introduces another sutra with the words "here he says":

"If the *jīva* were independent, it would do only what is desired; if it were not independent, it would not be an agent," according to the principle that "the independent one is the agent"—this is the meaning.
Even though there is independence [of the self], activity is not restricted due to the diversity of causal factors (*kāraka*); he refutes this with the sūtra, beginning with "just as" (*yathā*).
He raises an objection based on a lack of consensus regarding the example, saying, "even in the case of perception" (*upalabdhāv api*).

He replies, "no," stating that because the eyes and other senses exist for the purpose of connecting with objects through consciousness, and because the self possesses the nature of consciousness and thus has independence regarding the perception of its own connection, the example is established.
One might object: "If the self depends upon the instruments for the sake of connection with objects, how can it be independent? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Independence does not mean being independent of anything other than itself;
for if that were so, even the Lord (*īśvara*) would lack independence, as he too depends upon the karma of living beings.

However, independence (*svātantrya*) consists in being the instigator of other causal factors while not being impelled by them; thus, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is independent, it performs even that which is an undesirable means due to the delusion that it is a desirable means. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction between the fact that its activity is non-deterministic and its independence. //37//
Because of the reversal of capacity. (BBs 2.3.38)
For this reason as well, the individual soul (jīva) must be the agent distinct from consciousness (vijñāna).
If, on the other hand, the intellect (buddhi)—which is denoted by the term "consciousness"—were itself the agent, then there would be a reversal of capacities:
the intellect's capacity as an instrument would be lost, and it would incur the capacity of being an agent.

Furthermore, since the intellect possesses the capacity for agency, it must be admitted that it alone is the object of the notion of "I," because activity is everywhere seen to be preceded by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), as in such expressions as:
"I go," "I come," "I eat," and "I drink."
And for that [agency] which is endowed with the power of an agent, another instrument must be postulated as the producer of all effects;
for even a capable agent is seen to engage in actions only by employing an instrument.
Consequently, there would be a dispute over mere terminology, but no difference whatsoever in the underlying reality.
Because agency is admitted for that which is distinct from the instruments. // 38 //
To provide another reason for the soul's status as an agent, the Sūtra states: "Because of [its] power" (śakti).
The meaning is that the power of agency must belong to the intellect (buddhi), as it is the opposite of its power as an instrument.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And since the intellect possesses... and so forth.

The sense is that he who is the perceiver is the agent; that very soul (jīva) is the one who perceives, and the instrument required for that [perception] is the mind (manas). Thus, the agency of the soul is established. //38//
And because of the absence of meditative concentration (samādhi). BBs 2.3.39.

Furthermore, this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which has as its purpose the realization of the Self according to the Upaniṣads, is taught in the Vedāntas: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon; it is to be sought after, it is to be desired to be known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5);
and "Meditate on the Self as 'the Self'" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.6).
Having such characteristics as these, that [activity] too would not be possible if the self lacked agency;
therefore, from this also, its agency is established. // 39 //
He states that the agency of the self must also be admitted because the injunction for the means of knowledge would otherwise be inexplicable—this is expressed by the word "samādhi.
The meaning is that it is only for one who is the enjoyer of the fruit of liberation that agency in the meditative concentration (samādhi), which is the means to that fruit, is logical;

otherwise, if the self were not an agent, the intellect—which is not the enjoyer—could not possibly be an agent, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the absence of meditative concentration. //39//
END BsCom_2,3.14.39 START BsCom_2,3.15.40 15.
The Section Concerning the Carpenter (Takṣādhikaraṇam) // Sūtra 40.
And just as the carpenter [acts] in both ways (BBs 2.3.40),
so first has the agency of the embodied soul been demonstrated by reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scripture; now,
however, it is considered whether that agency is inherent or caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
In this regard, by these very reasons—such as the purposefulness of the scriptures and so forth—it might be argued that agency is inherent [to the Self] because there is no cause for its negation.
This being the position reached, we reply:
inherent agency is not possible for the Self.
Because it would follow that liberation is impossible;
for if the self has agency as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), liberation from agency is not possible, just as heat cannot be removed from fire.
Furthermore, for one who is not liberated from agency, there is no accomplishment of the human goal (puruṣārtha), because agency is of the nature of suffering.
[Objection: Even while the power of agency remains, the human goal will be accomplished by avoiding the effects of agency.
And the avoidance of that [defect] results from the avoidance of its cause;
for example, although fire possesses the power to burn, the effect of burning does not occur when it is separated from wood. [To this we reply:
No, because it is impossible to completely avoid even those causes that are connected to the self through a relationship characterized by their inherent powers.
[Objection: Surely liberation will be accomplished through the prescription of the means to liberation. [Reply: No; for that which depends on a means is impermanent.
Furthermore, it is intended that the establishment of liberation results from the teaching of the Self as eternally pure, enlightened, and free.
Furthermore, such a presentation of the Self would not be possible if agency were inherent to it.
Therefore, the agency of the Self is due solely to the superimposition of the attributes of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and is not inherent.
Thus says the Śruti: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
And the statement, "The wise say that the self, when joined with the body, the senses, and the mind, is the enjoyer" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.4),
shows that the acquisition of specific attributes such as being an enjoyer belongs only to the self when it is conjoined with limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
For among those who possess discrimination, there exists no separate living being (jīva) other than the Supreme Self who is a doer or an enjoyer.
Because of scriptural passages such as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sand 4.3.23),
it would follow that the transmigrating being alone is the agent and the enjoyer.
If the conscious individual soul (*jīva*) were something other than the Supreme, it would not exist as an agent distinct from the aggregate of the intellect and so forth. This is not so;
for agency and enjoyership are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus says the scripture: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

Having thus demonstrated agency and enjoyership in the state of ignorance, [the text] precludes those very same agency and enjoyership in the state of knowledge: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
Likewise, [it shows] that the exhaustion of the Self in the states of dreaming and waking is caused by contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like that of a hawk flying about in the sky.

Having taught the absence [of distinctions] in deep sleep, the text teaches that for one who is embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātman*), [the state is such]: "Now, this is his form in which desires have been attained, which consists of the Self, which is desireless, and which is beyond sorrow" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21), beginning thus, up to:
"This is his highest goal, this is his highest attainment, this is his highest world, this is his highest bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).
Because of this conclusion, the Teacher says: "And just as a carpenter [acts] in both ways. And this particle *ca* is read here in the sense of *tu* (but/rather).

One should not think that the agency of the Self is inherent, like the heat of fire. Rather, just as in the world a carpenter, with an axe and other tools in his hands, becomes an agent and suffers, yet upon reaching his own home, having set aside those tools, becomes at ease, withdrawn from activity, devoid of effort, and happy— so too does the Self, when associated with the duality presented by ignorance, [become an agent].

The self, being the agent and subject to suffering in the states of dream and waking, enters its own supreme Brahman-self in order to dispel that weariness; having become free from the aggregate of effects and instruments, it becomes a non-agent and happy in the state of profound serenity (*saṃprasāda*). Likewise, even in the state of liberation, having shaken off the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge, the self alone remains, and being thus ceased [from all activity], it becomes happy.
The analogy of the carpenter is to be understood in this respect:
for a carpenter becomes an agent only by depending on specific instruments such as an adze for specialized operations like carving;
however, with his own body, he is indeed a non-agent.
Thus, this Self becomes an agent only by depending upon the instruments such as the mind and so forth in all its activities; by its own nature, however, it is indeed a non-agent.

For the Self does not possess parts like those of a carpenter, by means of which it might take up or set aside the instruments such as the mind and so forth, just as a carpenter takes up or sets aside tools such as an axe.
As for the claim that the self's agency is inherent because of reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures and so forth—that is not so.

First of all, the injunctive scripture (vidhi-śāstra), taking up agency as it is already established, teaches specific duties to be performed; it does not establish the self's agency [as an inherent property].
Furthermore, we have already stated that its agency is not inherent, because of the teaching that Brahman is the Self.
Therefore, the scripture of injunctions will proceed by taking up an agency created by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Even scriptural passages of this kind, such as "The agent is the person consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānātmā puruṣaḥ*), being of the nature of restatement (*anuvāda*), will merely restate the agency created by ignorance exactly as it is found [in worldly experience].
By this, the objections regarding the appropriation of the state of roaming (*vihāra*) have been refuted, since those two [objections] are likewise of the nature of restatements.

Now, an objection may be raised: when it is taught that "in the intermediate state, while the organs are asleep, he moves about at will within his own body," this description of roaming implies that the Self alone possesses agency.

Likewise, regarding the passage concerning "appropriation" (*upādāna*), where it is heard that among the instruments there are both accusative and instrumental case-endings in the statement, "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of [his own] consciousness," one might infer that the Self alone is the agent.
To this, it is replied: First of all, in the intermediate state (*saṃdhya-sthāna*), there is no absolute cessation of the instruments for the Self.
For it is said, "Becoming a dreamer endowed with intellect (*sadhīḥ*), he transcends this world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
For even in that state, there is mention of a connection with the intellect;
and thus they record in their tradition: "If the mind does not cease even when the senses have ceased, and it continues to experience objects, one should know that to be the perception of a dream."
"The functions of the mind are desire and the rest," so says the Śruti.
And these are perceived in the dream state;
therefore, it is indeed together with the mind that one wanders in the dream state.
Furthermore, even the dwelling there consists merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and does not exist in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*).

Thus, scripture describes the activity of dreaming as being bound to forms, just like a perception: "As if rejoicing with women, as if eating, or even as if seeing terrors" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.13).
Ordinary people also describe their dreams in the same way: "I climbed, as it were, a mountain peak; I saw, as it were, a row of forests."

Likewise, even with respect to appropriation (*upādāna*), although there is an indication of the instruments by means of the case-terminations for object and instrument, nevertheless the agency (*kartṛtva*) must be understood as belonging only to the self (*ātman*) conjoined with that [appropriation],

since it has been shown that agency is impossible for the [self] alone. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, there are various modes of intention (*vivakṣā*), such as "the warriors fight" (*yodhā yudhyante*) and "the king fights by means of the warriors" (*yodhai rājā yudhyate*).

Moreover, in this context of "appropriation" (upādāna), what is intended is merely the cessation of the activity of the instruments (karaṇa), not the independence of anything whatsoever; for even in sleep, the cessation of the activity of the instruments is observed even when it is not preceded by conscious intent.
As for this designation shown—namely, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice"—that establishes the agency of the intellect (buddhi) alone.
Because the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) is well-known in that context, and because it is recited immediately after "mind" (manas), as in:
"Faith is its head" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).
And because it is stated that the self consisting of consciousness has faith and so forth as its limbs,
and because it is well known that faith and the rest are attributes of the intellect,
[it is said]: "All the gods worship Brahman, the eldest, as consciousness" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1).
And this is because of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*);
because "being the eldest" is well-known in common understanding as being born first;

and because in another Vedic text—namely, "This sacrifice is indeed the successive progression of speech and mind"—it is determined that the sacrifice is accomplished by means of speech and the intellect.
Nor does a reversal of the capacity of the intellect occur when the instruments are admitted to be agents;
for it is necessarily the case that all causal factors possess agency with respect to their own respective operations.
Rather, the status of these instruments as instruments is contingent upon perception.
And that [knowledge] belongs to the self;
yet even in that [knowledge], there is no agency for it,
because its nature is eternally one of attainment.
Even agency preceded by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) cannot belong to the perceiver,
because the ego-sense itself is an object of perception.
And this being the case, there is no contingency of postulating yet another instrument.
Because it is accepted that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the instrument;
as for the absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is already resolved by the fact that this is the very meaning of the treatise,
since the injunction for concentration is based upon agency exactly as it is attained [in ordinary experience].
Therefore, it is established that even the agency of the self is caused solely by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). [Verse 40] — [Note: "Sorrow" refers to that which is untouched by suffering;
"gati" refers to that which is to be attained.]
The world is that which is to be enjoyed; happiness is pleasure. Being unimpelled by others is self-abidance (*svasthatva*); being free from mental effort is tranquility (*nirvṛtatva*).
The emptiness of bodily movement is the state of being devoid of activity;
*saṃprasāda* is deep sleep;
*jakṣat* means "as if eating."
And just as with the carpenter, who acts in both ways;
having relied upon the previously stated agency of the self, he states the doubt and the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "In this way, first... and so forth.

Since the agency of the self has been established by refuting the Sāṃkhya view, and there being no subverting evidence (bādhaka), the position of the Mīmāṃsakas and others—that this [agency] is real—is reached.

Nor can there be a sublation by the scripture concerning non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*), because that scripture serves as a mere eulogy (*stāvaka*) due to the strength of the scriptural statements on agency accompanied by the experience "I am the agent. Having reached this preliminary position, the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) even outside the scope of the sūtra itself with the words "not natural" (*na svābhāvikam*).
Regarding what was stated—that there is no sublator—he says "non-liberation" (*anirmokṣa*) to show that such a claim is unproven.

An objection is raised: "Surely agency is indeed the power of action, which exists even in liberation; nevertheless, because the effect of that power—the capacity in the form of action—is absent, the status of liberation as the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha) is established. To this, he replies with the words "nanu sthitāyām" and "tatparihāraśca": "If the power remains present, how can there be an avoidance of its effect?
To that, he says: "And the avoidance of that [is as follows]."

If power (śakti) exists in liberation, then the effect (kārya) must also exist, because where there is no capacity for being produced (śakya), power is impossible. For even during the dissolution (pralaya), there exists a subtle, producible effect that is capable of arising again.

And thus, he offers a rebuttal—stating that "there is no loss of liberation"—on the grounds that the causal efficiency (śakti) implies the effect together with its causes such as merit (dharma) and so forth;

for since the effect, along with its causes, is capable [of being produced], it is connected to causal efficiency, and therefore it should be understood that the causes themselves are also connected to causal efficiency through a mediated succession.
The meaning is: "by means of the connection, [the causes become] connected [to the efficiency]."

Alternatively, [the compound may be analyzed as] *śakti-lakṣaṇa-ākṣepakam* (that which has power as its characteristic and implies) belonging to a certain effect; thus, by that effect, there is a connection—this being a case of two different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*) expressed with two instrumental endings. One might object: "But surely, just as a human attains divinity through ritual action, the status of being a non-agent for the agent is established by the force of the scriptures. To this he raises the doubt with the word "nanu" (but surely). [The reply is:
Since liberation, known as non-agency, results from knowledge, one must understand that agency is merely illusory (*āvidyaka*); therefore, knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone.
If liberation were [attained] through action, the author says "no" to that. Previously, it was stated that there would be no liberation by accepting that agency is inherent to the Self;
now, he says "moreover" (apica) that it is not inherent, because that would contradict numerous scriptural passages concerning its being unattached and changeless.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume that those [passages] which have been repeatedly heard as having multiple meanings are merely commendatory;

nor is the experience "I am the agent" contradicted, because that experience—which apprehends an agency that is indifferent to both truth and falsehood—is intelligible even as a superimposition (adhyāsa). This is the meaning.
Regarding the superimposition of agency, he cites scripture: "And thus...
He further states that agency is sublated by the experience of the wise: "For not...

If there were no conscious being distinct from the aggregate of the intellect and so forth, and other than the Supreme, then it would follow that the Supreme itself is the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī).
And that is undesirable, because it would contradict the eternal liberation of the Supreme; thus he raises the objection: "The Supreme itself [is bound].
We do not assert that there is bondage for the Supreme, which is the pure element of consciousness.

However, we maintain that bondage and liberation belong to that very [Self] which, being reflected in ignorance, intellect, and so forth, has attained the state of a *jīva* through its differentiation by ignorance.

He provides a rebuttal—stating "not [due to] ignorance"—on the grounds that even an imagined difference is seen in the world to establish the distinction between the attributes of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
Regarding the point that bondage is conditioned by ignorance and does not belong to the pure Self, he cites scripture, saying "and thus."
Because agency conforms to the presence and absence of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect, and because of scriptural testimony, it is not inherent; thus he says, "Likewise in dream...

Since the Self alone is desired because of its nature as bliss, its essential form is "desirous of the Self" (ātmakāma); since there is no object of desire other than itself, it is "desireless" (akāma);
and because it is desirous of the Self and free from desire, it is "one whose desires are fulfilled" (āptakāma), and because it is free from sorrow, he says, "free from grief" (aśoka).
The meaning is that it is beyond sorrow and untouched by suffering.
He states that this very nature of the self in deep sleep is the supreme human goal: "This... [eṣa].
The meaning is that destiny, the goal to be attained, prosperity, sovereignty, the world, the object of experience, and happiness do not exist elsewhere than from this [Brahman].
It has been stated that the Self is non-agent by its own nature, yet it is an agent through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi); thus, both states have been described.
He applies the Sūtra to that point, beginning with "He says this... and so forth.
"Saṃprasāda" refers to deep sleep (suṣupti).

Just as the redness of a crystal is caused by an external adjunct such as a flower, so too the agency of the Self is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be caused by adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*).
Nor is it reasonable to claim that these two [concomitances] concern the intellect’s status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) rather than its status as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the Self’s agency;

for since being a material cause—which persists in the effect—is more intrinsic than being an instrument, it is established by those two concomitances that the intellect, when conjoined with consciousness, is indeed the material cause.

The point is that there is agreement with the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) regarding the agency of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)—known as the intellect (buddhi)—which is superimposed non-differently upon Consciousness (cit), because it is the material cause of agency.

Now, one might object that there is a disparity between the illustration and the illustrated: a carpenter is an agent by himself because he possesses the power to wield tools such as axes with his own hands, whereas the Self, being partless, lacks such power.

Anticipating this objection, the author states, "And the illustration of the carpenter," expressing the similarity intended on the basis of the aspect of agency conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
To the objection, "Why might the agency being restated by the scripture not be inherent? he says: "And it is not inherent.
He raises the doubt: "But [agency] in the intermediate state," meaning that the agency heard [in the scripture] during the time when limiting adjuncts are absent must indeed be inherent.

Furthermore, if agency belongs to that which is qualified by the instruments, then since those instruments would be included within the agent, the case-ending for the agent (the third case) would have to apply to them as well.
And since this is not the case, he says "likewise" (tathā) to show that agency belongs to the isolated self alone.
First, he says "not indeed in the intermediate state" (na tāvat saṃdhye), because the absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in the dream-state is unestablished.
He then says "the wandering [in dreams] also" (vihāro 'pi) to show that because the wandering is false, the agency therein is also false.
"Jakṣat" means "as if eating.

It has been stated that if the agent were characterized by the act of making a sound (*kaṇatva*), then the agentive case-ending (*kartṛvibhakti*) would apply to the instruments (*karaṇa*), rather than the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇavibhakti*); to this he replies: "And it occurs thus in common usage (*loke*)."
The use of the instrumental case even for agents is not contradictory, because it is observed [in usage].
Furthermore, there is indeed the application of agency, as in such passages as "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," and so forth; this is the intended meaning.
Having accepted that appropriation (*upādāna*) possesses an agent, the agency of the isolated self (*ātman*) alone was refuted.
Now, [the author] says "Moreover" (*apica*) to show that because the self is inactive (*akriyatva*), it has no need for an agent.
Previously, accepting that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the living being (*jīva*), the scriptural statement "he expands" (*tanute*) was cited regarding the agency of the living being.

Now, since it might be concluded from that scriptural passage that agency belongs to the Self as unconditioned by anything else, [the author] says "But he who... with the intention of establishing that agency belongs to the Self only when conditioned by that [intellect]. Since the word *vijñāna* is well-known in such scriptural passages as "this which consists of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) to refer to the intellect (*buddhi*), and because it is mentioned here immediately after the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kosa*) and because of the indicative marks such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, it is indeed the intellect [that is meant].
The meaning is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
He states another indicative mark regarding that very point: "Consciousness is the gods.

Since the Śruti passage beginning with "The great being, the first-born" declares that the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is Brahmā as Hiraṇyagarbha, is the eldest, here "consciousness" refers to the eldest Brahman who is worshipped by the gods, i.e., the sense organs.
The meaning is that it is simply the intellect (*buddhi*).
A *yakṣa* is one who is worthy of worship.

Furthermore, since another Vedic scripture states that sacrifice is an effect of the intellect, he says "This very [intellect]" to indicate that here too, the knowledge of the performer of the sacrifice is the intellect.

Having meditated with the mind, the sacrifice arises through the utterance of mantras by speech; therefore, the meaning is that the sacrifice is the sequential relationship between the mind and speech. As for what was said—that if the intellect were the agent, there would be the consequence of a reversal of causal power—that is not so, for rice grains do not soften [without it].

"The pieces of wood burn" and "the pot supports [the rice]"—since all factors of action (*kāraka*) assume the status of agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to their respective functions, he says "nor... [in the verse].
If that is so, then if the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors were agents, there would be no talk of them being instruments (*karaṇa*); to this he replies: "perception... [and so forth].

The meaning is that just as wood, although it is the agent (*kartṛ*) in its own operation, is an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of cooking, so too the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, although they are agents in actions such as determination (*adhyavasāya*) and volition (*saṃkalpa*), are instruments with respect to perception (*upalabdhi*). Now, [the opponent asks: "In that case, whose operation is perception? To this he says: "And that...
[referring to the verse]. In that case, the Self (*ātman*) would be the sole agent in that [perception].
Based on the established principle that "he who possesses a particular activity is the agent of that [activity]," the author says: "And not...

If it is asked, "Since perception (*upalabdhi*) is eternal, how can the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties be said to be instruments (*karaṇa*)," the answer is as follows: The indivisible witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), becoming differentiated by the modifications of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), arises as delimited by objects.

Thus, while the intellect and other faculties function as instruments with respect to perception—which is termed consciousness delimited by objects—the self, when conditioned by the intellect and so forth, functions as the agent; it is not the isolated [witness-consciousness] alone.
Nor can agency belong to the intellect alone, because consciousness cannot be the operation of something insentient; this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that if the intellect were the agent, it would follow that the individual soul (jīva)—which is the object of the notion of "I"—must have some other instrument, and thus there would be a dispute over mere names: he dispels the delusion that agency belongs to the isolated Self by stating "the ego... (ahaṅkāra...).

Regarding the agency attributed to the *ahaṅkāra*—which consists of consciousness superimposed through non-difference from the intellect (*buddhi*) for the purpose of refuting the Sāṃkhya—it belongs only to the Self as qualified by the intellect, which is accessible to the notion of "I," and not to the pure Witness (*sākṣin*), because it is impossible for the Witness, whose nature is that of the seer, to possess the attributes of the seen.

Thus, since agency belongs to the qualified Self, the instrumentality is appropriately attributed to the insentient intellect itself as its qualifying attribute; consequently, there is no contingency of having to postulate another instrument.

The meaning is that for one who maintains that the agency belongs solely to the intellect (*buddhi*) without superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the consequence of having to postulate another instrument (*karaṇāntara*) is unavoidable.

Thus, although reasons such as "the meaningfulness of the scriptures" (*śāstrārthavattva*) establish only the mere agency of the Self, they lack the capacity to prove intrinsic agency; therefore, agency is merely superimposed and serves as the basis for the scriptural texts concerning the agency of those enjoined by injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth.

Consequently, it is established that there is no contradiction between the [scriptures on] the Self's lack of attachment (*asaṅgatva*) and the scriptural texts concerning its agency in injunctions and so forth. //40//
END BsCom_2,3.15.40 START BsCom_2,3.16.41 16. The Section Concerning Dependence on Another (Parāyattādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 41–42.
"But [the agency] is from the Highest, because of the scriptural statement regarding Him.
(BS 2.3.41) Regarding this agency of the individual soul (jīva), which was described as being based on the appropriation [of the body] during the state of ignorance:
is that agency independent of the Lord, or does it depend upon the Lord? Such is the inquiry.
In this regard, it has already been established that the individual soul (jīva) does not depend upon Īśvara for its agency.
Why?
Because there is no purpose for such dependence.
For this individual soul (jīva), being itself impelled by defects such as attachment and aversion and endowed with the collection of other causal factors, is capable of experiencing agency;
what, then, will the Lord do for it?
Furthermore, there is no common worldly consensus that in actions such as agriculture and the like, another—the Lord—must be depended upon, as one would depend on oxen and so forth.

Furthermore, if the Lord were to create living beings through an agency consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), the consequence would be His cruelty; and if He were to ordain their agency for unequal results, the consequence would be partiality.
But has it not been stated [in the Sūtra]: "Partiality and cruelty do not apply, because [the Lord] takes things into consideration" (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.17)?
It has been rightly said that the dependence of the Lord is possible only if there exist sentient beings;

and the existence of sentient beings is possible only if there exist their merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); and the existence of those two is possible only if the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses agency (*kartṛtva*).
If that very agency were dependent upon the Lord, then with reference to what object would the Lord’s dependence be said to exist?
Furthermore, in this way, the consequence would follow that the living being (jīva) undergoes the results of actions not performed by it.
Therefore, its agency must belong to itself. Refuting this position with the word "but" (tu), he asserts: "From another" (parāt).

In the state of ignorance, for the individual soul (jīva)— who perceives no distinction between the aggregate of causes and effects, who is blinded by the cataract of nescience, and who exists as distinct from the Supreme Self— the accomplishment of transmigratory existence, characterized by agency and enjoyership, occurs through the permission of that Lord, the supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, and the conscious one.
And it is by means of that very consciousness, which has his grace as its cause, that the attainment of liberation ought to occur.
Why?
Because of the scriptural testimony to that effect.
Although the individual soul (jīva) is impelled by defects and possesses the necessary causal complex, and although in worldly activities such as agriculture the causality of God is not well-known,
nevertheless, it is determined from scripture that in all undertakings God is the causal agent.
For there is a scriptural passage: "He indeed makes him perform good deeds whom He leads upward from these worlds;
He indeed makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8).
And there are other passages of this kind, such as: "He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within. [41]
"But [the superimposition] is from another, because of scriptural testimony.
Just as in the case of the superimposition of redness upon a crystal, a red substance is the instrument— since there is the experience, "This crystal is red"—

so too it has been stated that the intellect (buddhi), which undergoes transformation through desire and so forth, is the instrument for the superimposition of agency and other attributes upon the Self.

Having raised a doubt based on the fact that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the status of an agent by depending upon that [agency] superimposed [upon it], and because of the scriptural texts concerning the Lord’s status as the "causer" (kārayitṛ), he states the doubt with the words "yad idam" (as for this...).

Here, the connection to the chapter (pāda) is established through the resolution of the contradiction between such scriptural passages as "eṣa hy eva" (for He alone... and others which indicate the independence of the agent, and those scriptural passages concerning injunctions (vidhi) and so forth.
He presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) according to the doctrine of the Karma-mīmāṃsakas, starting with the words "tatra" (in that regard).
Since no absence of agency is observed when there is an absence of God, despite the presence of causal factors such as the intellect (buddhi), God is not the instigator.
Furthermore, if He were the instigator, it would entail consequences such as cruelty; thus he says, "And by that which consists of affliction.
He raises an objection, suggesting this challenge has already been answered, with the words, "But surely... (nanu).

Previously, it was stated that— taking for granted as established the soul's possession of merit and demerit— the Lord’s authorship of an unequal world is not contradictory because He is dependent upon those factors; however, now, since the soul’s agency is established as being subordinate to the Lord,
the soul’s possession of merit and demerit is established, and once that possession is established,
the Lord’s status as a director who is dependent upon those factors is established.

If it is argued that once God’s status as the instigator is established, the soul’s status as the agent is thereby established—resulting in a circular argument—it is said that dependence on karma is therefore impossible; to this he replies, "True. Let it be granted that [God] acts without depending on karma; to that he replies, "unearned" (akṛta).
If [the Lord] were to act without regard [for merit or demerit], he would join righteous men with suffering and unrighteous men with happiness;
or, if he were compassionate, all beings would be uniform in happiness. Consequently, neither the diversity of the world nor the scriptures prescribing injunctions and so forth would exist.

Therefore, for the sake of making the meaning of the scriptures on injunctions and so forth purposeful, the agency of the individual soul (jīva) must be stated as being dependent upon passion and hatred, and as arising from itself alone.
And thus, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning God's status as the agent.
Since it might be argued that such a scripture is merely laudatory of the Lord, the author establishes the final conclusion with the words "etām" (this).

Just as, when the collection of causes such as sandalwood paste is present, although there is no perception of pleasure apart from merit (*dharma*), yet by the authority of scriptures such as "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action," [the causal efficacy] of merit is established.
The sense is that, in this way, the Lord's status as an enforcer by means of the authority of the scriptures is also established. //41//

[Objection: But if it is thus that the Lord is the cause of action, would there not result partiality and cruelty on His part, and for the individual soul (jīva), the acquisition of what was not earned?
It is said:

"But [the Lord] has regard for the effort made, on account of the non-futility of what is enjoined and what is prohibited, and so forth. The word "but" (tu) is intended to exclude the previously mentioned objection.
The effort made by the individual soul (jīva), characterized as merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), is precisely what the Lord (Īśvara) takes into account when causing him to act.
Consequently, the faults previously urged do not apply.

Depending solely upon the diversity of the merit and demerit performed by the soul, the Lord distributes the various fruits unequally, acting merely as the instrumental cause (nimitta), just like a rain-cloud.

Just as in the world, for various kinds of shrubs, bushes, and so forth, as well as for rice, barley, and the like— which arise from their own respective specific seeds— the rain-cloud serves as the common cause;
for if there were no rain-cloud, the irregularity in their sap, flowers, leaves, and so on would not arise,
nor would it arise if their own respective seeds were absent.
Thus, it follows that God, depending upon the effort exerted by the individual soul, would ordain its good and evil.
But surely, if the soul's agency is dependent on another, its dependence on exerted effort is not tenable.
This is not a fault.
For even though agency is dependent on another, the individual soul (jīva) indeed acts;
for the Lord causes him to act while he is acting.

Moreover, He causes him to act now in dependence upon his prior effort, and caused him to act previously in dependence upon an even earlier effort; thus, because saṃsāra is beginningless, there is no fault.
But how is it understood that Īśvara depends upon what has been done and what is ancient?
He says: "Because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless," and so forth.
For instance: "One who desires heaven should sacrifice," and "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed."
In this way, there is no purposelessness for that which is enjoined and that which is prohibited;
otherwise, it would be meaningless,
and the Lord alone would be subject to injunctions and prohibitions.
Because the individual soul is absolutely dependent [on God],
[if God were to act arbitrarily], He might unite even one who performs what is enjoined with misfortune, and likewise unite even one who performs what is prohibited with prosperity;
and consequently, the authority of the Veda would come to an end.

And if the Lord were absolutely independent, human effort (puruṣakāra) would likewise be useless for worldly beings; furthermore, the aforementioned defects regarding place, time, and causal conditions would follow as a consequence. By the use of the word "etcetera" (ādigrāhaṇena), he indicates such a collection of defects. // 42 //

Anticipating the objection that "since the diversity of results is established by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) alone, there is no need for a Lord (*īśvara*)," he replies: "If the diversity of sprouts were established by seeds alone, then the rain-cloud (*parjanya*) would be rendered useless.

If it is argued that the rain-cloud is not useless because specific causes depend upon general causes, then the Lord is also not useless, as He too serves as a general cause. Thus he says, "Like the rain-cloud.
He explains the illustration with the words, "Just as... (yathā).
The distinction is that *gucchās* are clusters or bunches of flowers consisting of very long creeper-joints, whereas *gulmas* are short creepers.

Is it being argued that if God is the causal agent (*kārayitṛ*), the individual soul (*jīva*) would lack agency (*kartṛtva*), or is it an objection regarding the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*)?

He says "not so" to [the objection], meaning "this is not a fault," because we observe that a student who is dependent on a teacher possesses primary agency in the act of studying. He refutes the circular argument (cakraka) with the words "furthermore" (apica).

The remainder [of the argument] is that the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the causative agency (*kārayitṛtva*) of God (*īśvara*) are both irreproachable. He provides the proof for the necessity of God being dependent on other factors through the words beginning with "How so?": if God were thus dependent, the scriptures such as the injunctions (*vidhi*) would not be rendered purposeless.
He elaborates on the pointlessness [of the two] if they were otherwise independent, stating: "The Lord.
This means that He alone would be appointed—that is, consecrated—in their place; He alone would perform their work.

And thus, because the individual soul (jīva) is entirely dependent on the independent Lord, the scripture concerning injunctions and so forth would be ineffective and useless; this is the connection [of the argument]. "Human effort" means exertion.
He states the meaning of the word "and so forth" with the word "tathā" (thus).
The aforementioned defect, such as the arrival of what was not performed (*akṛtābhyāgama*), [does not apply].

Therefore, since the Lord acts as the impeller while being dependent upon karma, it is established that there is no contradiction between the scriptural passages such as "For he alone" (*eṣa hy eva*) and those concerning injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth. //42//

END BsCom_2,3.16.42 START BsCom_2,3.17.43 17. The Section on the Portion (Aṃśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 43–53 17. The Section on the Portion (Aṃśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 43–53 [The following is a translation of the relevant portion of the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*: **Sūtra 43:** But [the individual soul] is a part [of Brahman], because of the scriptural statement and because of the possibility. **Commentary:** It has been stated that the individual soul is not a reflection (*pratibimba*) of Brahman, nor is it a transformation (*vikāra*). What, then, is its relationship to Brahman? To this, the author of the aphorisms replies: "But [the individual soul] is a part. The word "but" serves to exclude other views. The individual soul is a part of Brahman, just as a spark is a part of fire. Why? "Because of the scriptural statement," as in: "Having created it, He entered into it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), and "From that, indeed, [comes] the breath; from the breath, faith; from faith, the sacred utterance (*om*); from the sacred utterance, the Ṛg-veda, Yajur-veda, Sāma-veda, and Atharva-veda; from these, the sacrifices; from the sacrifices, the worlds; from the worlds, the beings; from the beings, food; from food, life-breath; from the life-breath, fire; from fire, the hymns; from the hymns, the worlds; from the worlds, the moon; from the moon, the stars; from the stars, the immortals; from the immortals, the vital force; from the vital force, the self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). And "because of the possibility": the state of being a part is possible for the individual soul, since it is non-different from Brahman in essence, yet distinct in its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, the scriptural texts regarding difference and non-difference are reconciled by this doctrine of parts. Moreover, the Lord’s possession of infinite power is thus established, and the individual soul’s experience of pleasure and pain is accounted for by its limited nature. Therefore, the individual soul is a part of Brahman. **Sūtra 44:** Or rather, [it is] like light and so forth. **Commentary:** Or rather, the relationship may be understood as being like that of light, heat, and color to the sun, or like the ether within a jar to the universal ether. Just as the sun is one, yet appears diverse through its rays, or as the ether is one, yet appears divided by jars and other vessels, so too is the Lord one, yet appears as many through His powers and limiting adjuncts. This explains how the Lord remains one while the individual souls appear manifold. **Sūtra 45:** Because of the designation of difference. **Commentary:** The individual soul is a part of Brahman because of the designation of difference between them in scripture, such as: "Two birds, inseparable friends" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), and "The two unborn ones, the knower and the known" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.9). **Sūtra 46:** And because of the teaching of entering. **Commentary:** Furthermore, the fact that the Lord is taught to have entered into the individual soul supports the view that the soul is a part of Him: "Having created it, He entered into it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1). **Sūtra 47:** And because of the teaching of being of the same nature. **Commentary:** Also, because the individual soul is taught to be of the same nature as Brahman—being essentially consciousness—it cannot be a separate entity, but must be a part of Him. **Sūtra 48:** And because of the teaching of the smallness [of the soul]. **Commentary:** The teaching that the individual soul is minute in size—as in "He is the inner self, smaller than a grain of rice, smaller than a grain of barley" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.1)—is consistent with its being a part of the infinite Brahman. **Sūtra 49:** Not so, because of the denial [of such smallness]. **Commentary:** Some argue that the soul is not truly minute, because scripture denies its minuteness: "He is the great, all-pervading self" (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). However, this objection does not hold. **Sūtra 50:** On account of the reference to the body. **Commentary:** The denial of minuteness refers to the soul when it is considered in relation to its body, which is vast. The soul itself, however, remains minute as a part of the infinite Brahman. **Sūtra 51:** And because of the observation of the manifestation of power. **Commentary:** Furthermore, we observe the manifestation of various powers in the individual soul, such as the capacity for knowledge and action, which indicates its nature as a part of the omnipotent Brahman. **Sūtra 52:** And because of the teaching of the distinction [between the two states]. **Commentary:** Scripture teaches the distinction between the soul's state of bondage and its state of liberation, which would be impossible if the soul were not a part of Brahman subject to change in condition. **Sūtra 53:** And because of the teaching of the going out [of the soul]. **Commentary:** Finally, the teaching that the soul goes out from the body at death—as in "When he departs, he departs together with the vital force" (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2)—confirms that it is a part of Brahman, moving from one locus to another. Thus ends the section on the portion. The individual soul is a part of Brahman, established by scriptural authority and logical possibility. This doctrine resolves all contradictions and accounts for both the unity of the Self and the diversity of individual experiences. END BsCom_2,3.17.43 START BsCom_2,3.18.44 18. The Section on the Non-Separation of the Released Soul (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 54–55 18. The Section on the Non-Separation of the Released Soul (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 54–55 **Sūtra 54:** But there is non-separation, because of the declaration of that [state]. **Commentary:** When the individual soul is released and attains the state of Brahman, is it separated from Him or not? The answer is: "But there is non-separation. Why? "Because of the declaration of that [state]," as in: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9), and "Being Brahman, he goes to Brahman" (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6). **Sūtra 55:** For [the released soul] is like the light and so forth. **Commentary:** The released soul is non-separate from Brahman, just as light, heat, and color are non-separate from the sun, or as the ether within a jar is non-separate from the universal ether. Upon liberation, the soul's limiting adjuncts vanish, and it exists in its true nature as a part of the infinite Brahman, free from all distinctions of name and form. Thus, the released soul is non-separate from the Supreme Self. END BsCom_2,3.18.45 START BsCom_2,3.19.46 19. The Section on the Attainment of the World of Brahman (Prāptādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 56–58 19. The Section on the Attainment of the World of Brahman (Prāptādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 56–58 **Sūtra 56:** But [the soul] attains [the world of Brahman], because of the scriptural statement. **Commentary:** Does the released soul merely become non-separate from Brahman, or does it also attain the world of Brahman? The answer is: "But [the soul] attains
"He is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of manifoldness, and also because otherwise some record Him as being a fisherman, a woodcutter, and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.43).
The relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) has been stated;
and that [relationship] is observed in the world only between things that are connected, such as a master and a servant, or as fire and its sparks.

Furthermore, since it is admitted that there exists a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), a doubt arises as to whether this connection is like that of a master and a servant, or like that of fire and its sparks; thus, one might conclude that there is no fixed rule. Alternatively, since the relationship of ruler and ruled is well-known only in the case of masters and servants, one might conclude that the connection must be of that very kind.
Therefore, he says "a part":
the individual soul (jīva) must be a part of the Lord (īśvara),
just as a spark is of fire.
A "part" (aṃśa) is like a portion; for that which is partless, a primary part is not possible.
Why, moreover, on account of its partlessness, is it not [itself] that [very thing]?
Because of the designation of diversity (nānāvyapadeśāt).
"He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1);
"Only by knowing this one becomes a sage"; and "He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within"—such designations of difference are not tenable if there were no actual difference.
Now, one might argue that this various designation of difference is even more appropriate in the case of a master and a servant; to this, he says: "And otherwise also."
Nor is the state of being a part established by the mention of diversity alone.
Rather, there is also another way of describing [the Lord] which establishes His non-differentiation.

For instance, some followers of a Vedic school (śākhins) declare that Brahman possesses the nature of the Dāśas, Kitavas, and so forth, in the *Brahmasūkta* of the Atharvaṇikas: "Brahman is the Dāśas, Brahman is the Dāsas, Brahman indeed are these Kitavas," and so on.
These fishermen who are well known as *dāśas*,
those slaves (*dāsas*) who exhaust themselves for their masters,

and others who are gamblers (*kitavas*)— all these are Brahman indeed. By citing these lowly beings as examples, he declares that all individual souls (*jīvas*), having entered into the aggregate of name-and-form consisting of the body and its organs, are Brahman.

Likewise, in another passage concerning the nature of Brahman, this same meaning is elaborated: "You are female, you are male, you are a youth, or even a maiden; you are an old man tottering with a staff; you are born, facing every direction" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.3).
And: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth."
The establishment of this point is also due to scriptural passages such as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
Furthermore, consciousness is common to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), just as heat is common to fire and its sparks.
Therefore, from the cognitions of difference and non-difference, there follows the cognition of being a part. // 43 //

"One part [is eternal]; the soul is eternal, self-luminous, non-atomic, and a non-agent"—by establishing here the identity of Brahman with the purified meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (the "Thou"), there is a resolution of the contradiction between the scriptural texts on difference and non-difference; thus, there is a connection to the chapter (*pāda*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no establishment of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
The difference [between this view and others] is that in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), that [relationship] is proven.

Having taken as the subject matter the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which is implied by the previously mentioned relation of the beneficiary and the benefactor, he states a doubt based on the observation of two kinds of examples—beginning with the words "tataśca" (and therefore).

He says "or rather" (*athavā*) because he finds the [previous] position unsatisfactory, since it would lead to the undesirable conclusion of an indefinite relationship, such as any mere relationship like that of master and servant, which is already well-known.
By this, the dimension of difference well-known from such scriptural passages as "He who dwells in the self" has been shown.
In the same way, the dimension of non-difference established by such scriptural passages as "That thou art" is to be understood.

Thus, since the scriptures concerning difference and non-difference possess equal force, there arises a contradiction; and because no specific relation can be determined, the previously mentioned relationship of beneficiary and benefactor—which depends upon a specific relation—remains unestablished. It is on the basis of this objection that the connection [of the present section] is established.

He establishes the final conclusion—that the relationship of part and whole is based on a distinction superimposed in accordance with the non-dualistic scriptures, which possess unattained fruits and are therefore stronger than the dualistic scriptures that merely restate distinctions already established in worldly experience—by the words beginning with "ataḥ" (therefore).
To the objection, "Even if fire has parts, how can the partless Lord have parts?", he says: "like a part."

The word "jīva" is to be supplied [to the previous statement]. One might object: "If there is only difference, then the relation of owner and owned is appropriate, not the relation of part and whole. To this he replies: "Therefore," because non-difference also exists, there is the relation of part and whole.
The meaning of the Śruti is that one becomes immortal by knowing Him who, having fashioned name and form, enters them and exists acting within them—He whom you deceive when He goes or stays.
Regarding the non-difference established by Śruti, he states the reasoning: "And consciousness...
The meaning is: the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Brahman, because it possesses consciousness, just like Brahman. //43//
And from what source is the understanding of being a part derived?
And from the wording of the mantra:

"The wording of the mantra also makes this meaning understood: 'Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is greater than that; all beings constitute one quarter of him, while his three quarters are the immortal in heaven'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
Here, by the word *bhūta*, he indicates all moving and stationary beings, primarily consisting of living souls (*jīva*), as seen in the usage:
"Not harming any beings, except at [sacrificial] stations" (*ahiṃsansarvabhūtānyanyatra tīrthebhyaḥ*). "Part" (*aṃśaḥ*), "quarter" (*pādaḥ*), and "portion" (*bhāgaḥ*) are synonymous.
Therefore, from this as well, there is the comprehension of being a part. // 44 //
The expansion, greatness, and manifestation of this thousand-headed Puruṣa is coextensive with that [universe]; yet the Puruṣa is greater, more vast, than that expansion.
Regarding the term "beings" (*bhūtāni*)—meaning embodied living beings—he provides the restrictive rule here by saying "not harming.
"Sacred fords" (*tīrthāni*) refers to the ritual acts prescribed in the scriptures.
The meaning is that by refraining from harming any living beings other than those [specific ones], one attains the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).
Here, because the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of "living beings," the intention is that it is likewise so in the mantra mentioned in the Sūtra.
Even though living beings constitute a quarter [of the sacrifice], how is it that they possess the nature of being a constituent part (*aṃśatva*)?
Regarding this, he says: "A part is a quarter. (44)
And from what source is the understanding of its being a part derived?
Moreover, it is recorded in tradition;
even in the *Īśvaragītās*, the soul's status as a part of the Lord is recorded: "In the world of living beings, my very own eternal part has become the individual soul" (BhG 15.7).
Therefore, from this too, the understanding of its being a part [of the Lord] follows.

As for what was said—that in the world the relationship of ruler and ruled is well-known only in cases such as master and servant—even though this is well-known in the world, nevertheless, from the scripture (śāstra), the relationship of part and whole and the relationship of ruler and ruled are determined here. Since the Lord (Īśvara), endowed with unsurpassed limiting adjuncts (upādhi), governs the individual souls (jīvas) who are endowed with inferior limiting adjuncts, nothing at all is contradicted. // 45 //

To this, it is said: Surely, if it is admitted that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of the Lord (*īśvara*), then by virtue of the individual soul’s experience of the suffering of saṃsāra, the Lord as the whole (*aṃśin*) would also become subject to suffering.
Just as in the world, Devadatta, the possessor of limbs, becomes subject to suffering through pain occurring in any one of his limbs, such as the hand or foot, so it would be here.
And consequently, those who have attained that [state of liberation] would incur even greater suffering.
Therefore, it would follow that right vision (samyagdarśana) is useless, on the grounds that it would be better for transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) itself to remain in its prior state.

To show that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of the Blessed Lord as stated in the *Puruṣasūkta* mantra, the author of the Sūtras cites the *Bhagavadgītā*, beginning with the words "And also" (*api ca*). Having raised the objection—given the well-known state of absolute difference between the ruler and the ruled, how can the individual soul, who is the object of rule, be a portion of the Lord?—[the author replies] that being the object of rule is possible even through an imagined (kalpita) distinction.

He states that [the Lord] possesses the nature of being a part (*aṃśatva*) by virtue of the scriptural authority establishing an absolute non-difference, beginning with the words "As for that which...

If it is argued that if the Lord's status as a controller is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), why should the individual soul (*jīva*) not be that controller instead, he replies: "Because of the unsurpassed...
The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body are "utterly inferior" (*nitarāṃ hīna*).
The distinction between the Lord and the object of his lordship arises from the gradations of the limiting adjuncts of ignorance (ājñānika-upādhi), not from reality itself.
As it was said by Sureśvarācārya: "The relationship between the Lord and the object of his lordship is born of the ignorance of the inner self (pratyag-ajñāna)."
Through right knowledge, one who has destroyed darkness becomes the lord even of lords.
Thus //45//
