The Supreme is not like this, as in the case of light and so forth.
We maintain that the Supreme Lord does not experience the suffering of saṃsāra in the same way that the individual soul (jīva) does.

For the individual soul, under the influence of the onset of ignorance (avidyā), comes to identify with the body and so forth as if they were its self; it then, through ignorance, falsely imagines itself to be suffering, thinking "I am miserable," thus attributing to itself the experience of suffering produced by those [identifications].
The Supreme Lord does not possess such identification with a body or the like, nor does He have the conceit of suffering.

Even for the individual soul (*jīva*), the conceit of suffering is caused solely by the delusion of non-discrimination from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—such as the body and senses—which are produced from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) created by ignorance; it does not exist in an ultimate sense.
And just as one experiences suffering caused by burning, cutting, and so forth occurring in one's own body through the delusion of identifying with it, so too [is the case for the soul].

Even suffering that has sons, friends, and so forth as its object is experienced solely through the delusion of false identification, thinking "I am the son" and "I am the friend," thus becoming attached to sons, friends, and the like under the influence of affection.
From this, it is understood with certainty that the experience of suffering is caused exclusively by the error of false identification.
This is understood from the observation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For instance, when many people are seated together— some possessing sons, friends, and so forth, who identify with those relationships, while others do not— and it is proclaimed that "a son has died," "a friend has died," and so on, it is only those who possess the conceit (*abhimāna*) of having sons, friends, and the like, who [experience grief].
Suffering arises from that cause [of false attribution] for those who possess such conceit, but not for wandering mendicants and others who are free from it.
Therefore, even in the case of an ordinary worldly person, the efficacy of right vision is observed;
how much more so, then, in the case of one who perceives no object other than the Self—which is devoid of objective qualities and whose nature is solely eternal consciousness?
Therefore, there is no consequence of the futility of right vision (*samyagdarśana*).
The phrase "like light and so forth" (*prakāśādivat*) is an introduction of an illustrative example.

Just as sunlight or moonlight, while remaining pervading the sky, assumes the states of being straight, curved, and so on in relation to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as a finger; [so too does the Self appear].
Even while assuming various states as it were among those undergoing transformation, it does not, in the ultimate sense, assume those states.
Just as space, though appearing to move when jars and other objects move, does not move in the ultimate sense;
and just as the sun, which possesses the reflection, does not tremble even when the reflection of the sun in a water-basin trembles due to the shaking of that basin.

Thus, although the portion called the *jīva*—which is presented by ignorance (*avidyā*) and conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—is subject to suffering, the Lord who possesses that [portion] does not suffer.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the *jīva*'s attainment of suffering is caused solely by ignorance.
Accordingly, the Vedānta texts, such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), establish the very nature of Brahman for the *jīva* by setting aside its state as a *jīva* which is caused by ignorance.

Therefore, there is no consequence of the Supreme Self being subject to suffering on account of the suffering of the individual soul. [This concludes the commentary on the previous sūtra. He introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words: "Regarding this, he says."
The meaning is: Īśvara is suffering due to the sufferings of his own parts (aṃśa), because he possesses parts, just like Devadatta.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

The meaning is that, in comparison with the attainment of the totality of all aspects of suffering [resulting] from knowledge, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is better, because there one experiences only one's own suffering.
He analyzes the proposition "it is not for this purpose" with the words: "Just as the individual soul" (*yathā jīvaḥ*).

In the example of Devadatta, the presence of the causal complex consisting of delusion, desire, karma, and form is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); due to the absence of that, the Lord does not incur suffering.

And this has been stated: even though there is non-difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), there is a distinction in their properties—this is the intended meaning.
He elaborates upon the fact that suffering is produced by delusion with the words "of the living being as well," and so forth.

Having stated the positive concomitance—that when there is delusion, there is suffering—he says "by way of negative concomitance" (vyatireka) to show that because the absence of suffering is observed when delusion is absent, it is certain that suffering is produced by delusion;
the meaning is "in others who are devoid of such conceit."

He states "and therefore" (*ataśca*) to show that if even for a *jīva* the absence of suffering is observed upon the attainment of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), what need is there to speak of the eternal, omniscient Lord?

Having thus stated that the reason [for the Lord being a part-whole] is vitiated by a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), he demonstrates the lack of pervasion (*vyabhicāra*) in three instances regarding the rule that "whatever is a whole (*aṃśin*) must, in reality, possess the qualities of its own parts": namely, "like light and so forth" (*prakāśādivat*).
Furthermore, he points out the deficiency in the example of Devadatta regarding the probandum—that the whole is in reality suffering due to its parts—by stating "of the *jīva*" (*jīvasya*).
However, it has been stated that the probandum of "suffering," which is merely imagined, does not exist in the Lord because of the absence of delusion and so forth.
Furthermore, the inference of suffering—whether for the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord—is not tenable because it is contradicted by scripture; thus he says, "And so" (tathā ca).
The meaning is that if [the Lord] were a sufferer, there would be no teaching regarding His state [as being free from suffering]. //46//
And they remember it as well. (BBs 2.3.47)
And Vyāsa and others record that the supreme self (paramātman) does not suffer due to the suffering of the individual soul (jīva):
"In this regard, that which is indeed the supreme self is remembered as eternal and devoid of qualities;
it is not smeared by fruits [of action], just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water."
"But that other one, whose essence is action, is joined with liberation and bondage;
he is further joined with the group of seventeen"—
the word "and" (ca) implies that they recite [this] as well, such is the completion of the sentence.
"One of the two eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6);
and "So the one Inner Self of all beings, being external [to them], is not tainted by the suffering of the world" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.11). // 47 //
Here it is asked: "If, then, there were only one inner self for all beings, how could there be worldly and Vedic permissions and prohibitions?
But has it not been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is a part of the Lord?
And because of the distinction between them, permissions and prohibitions based upon them are logically established as non-confused; so what is the objection here?"
It is replied: this is not so;

for even the partlessness of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by those scriptural passages that teach non-duality, such as: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), and "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19);
"That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7); "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
Such are the types of [objections].
Now, was it not stated that the status of being a part (aṃśatva) is established through the cognition of both difference and non-difference?
This would indeed be so if both difference and non-difference were intended to be demonstrated.
However, it is non-difference alone that is intended to be established here, since the human goal is accomplished through the realization of Brahman as the Self.
Difference, which is obtained by its very nature, is merely restated;
moreover, it has already been stated that the individual soul cannot be a literal part of the partless Brahman.

Therefore, since the one Supreme alone is the inner self of all beings, existing in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), the logical consistency of injunctions and prohibitions must be explained [in this way]. (47) [Note: In that context, between the individual soul and the Supreme, the "karmic self" is the individual soul which is the locus of karma.]
The group consisting of seventeen—the ten organs of sense, the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—is the subtle body (*liṅga*).

"Death after death" means that he who perceives here in Brahman this universe, which consists of the sentient and the insentient and is characterized by imagined diversity as if it were manifold, attains after death a further death: the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) in the form of a succession of births and deaths. This is the meaning.
He states that even inference is sublated by scripture with the words "And they remember.
He explains the Sūtra with the words "They cause [them] to remember.
In that context, between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*), the *karmātmā* is the individual soul who is the locus of karma.
The aggregate consisting of seventeen members— the ten sense organs, the five vital breaths, the mind, and the intellect— is the subtle body (*liṅga*).
Regarding the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra, he states "by the word 'and'" (*caśabdāt*), explaining that its purpose is to include what is mentioned in the Śruti.

The meaning is: "Just as the sun is not tainted by the defects of visibility, so too [the Lord is not tainted]. Since He is external and unattached, He is therefore not tainted. Having thus refuted the defect in the Lord caused by His being a possessor of parts (*aṃśin*), the author now raises an objection—beginning with the words "Here he says" (*atrāha*)—by taking up the absolute identity of essential nature (*atyantasvarūpaikya*), in order to clarify that the status of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a part, which was previously mentioned, is merely conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body. The syntactical connection is: "How then? (*kathaṃ tarhi*).
"Due to that difference" means due to a difference in parts (*aṃśabheda*).

The intention of the objection is this: by the proponent (siddhāntin) stating that a primary part is not possible for the partless Brahman, it is effectively asserted that there is no difference; and since there is no difference, there is an absence of the relationship between part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*), which renders the conventional usage of distinctions such as "permission" (*anujñā*) and so forth untenable.
We do not assert that difference is non-existent like a man’s horn; rather, we declare it to be false (mithyātva).

Thus, the Sūtra provides the resolution with the words beginning "tām" [and so forth], stating that the empirical usage of difference is possible due to the imagined difference among the partial selves (aṃśajīva) arising from the distinctions of limiting adjuncts such as the body, until the realization of Brahman occurs. //47//
We shall explain that [objection]: *tāṃ brūmaḥ*—
Permission and prohibition [apply] due to the connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth.
"One should approach one's wife during her season" is a permission;
"One should not approach the wife of a teacher" is a prohibition.
Likewise, "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" is an injunction (*anujñā*);
"One should not harm any living beings" is its exception (*parihāra*). Similarly, in common worldly usage as well, "A friend should be served" is an injunction.
"One must avoid the enemy"—this is avoidance.
In this manner, both permission and avoidance would be possible for the self, even though it is one, due to its connection with bodies.
Connection with bodies is "dehasambandha" (body-connection).
What, then, is the connection with the body?
It is the arising of a contrary notion within the self, such as "I am this very aggregate consisting of the body and so forth.
And this is observed in all living beings, taking the form: "I go," "I come," "I am blind," "I am not blind," "I am deluded," "I am not deluded," and so on.
For there is nothing other than right vision (*samyagdarśana*) that can prevent this [delusion].
Prior to right vision, however, this delusion persists among all living beings.

Thus, even while accepting the non-duality of the Self (*aikātmya*), the concepts of permission and prohibition are logically tenable due to the distinctions created by the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, which have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause.

In that case, it follows that for one who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśin*), injunctions and prohibitions would be purposeless. No; because such a person has already accomplished their goal, it is impossible for them to be subject to a mandate.
For it is only with respect to what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted that a person is to be enjoined—that is, they must be directed by an authority.
But seeing no object—whether to be abandoned or to be adopted—as distinct from the self, how could one be enjoined?
Nor could the self be enjoined by the self alone.
If it is argued that only one who perceives a distinction from the body can be subject to an injunction, we say no.
This is due to the conceit of being a composite [of the body and so forth].

It is true that for one who perceives [the self's] distinction [from the body], there is no status of being subject to injunction; nevertheless, it is precisely for the self who does not perceive its non-composition with the body and so forth—just like space—that there is the conceit of being subject to injunction.
Indeed, an injunction is never observed for anyone who perceives their own non-composition with the body and so forth.
How much more so for one who perceives the identity of the Self?
Nor does the absence of injunctions lead to the consequence of acting as one pleases for the one who possesses right vision;
for in all cases, it is precisely self-conceit (*abhimāna*) that is the motivator, and such conceit is absent in the one who possesses right vision.
Therefore, permission and avoidance arise solely from the connection with a body,
as in the case of light and so forth; just as, although fire is one, the crematory fire (kravyād) is avoided while the other is not.
Just as the light of even a single sun is avoided when it is connected with an impure place, while that which rests upon pure ground is not;
and just as terrestrial regions such as those containing diamonds and lapis lazuli are accepted,
whereas even though they are also terrestrial, things like corpses from hell are avoided.
Just as cow's urine is accepted as pure, yet that very same substance is rejected when it comes from another species, so it is with this case. (48) [FN:
*Pratatā* means continuous;
*viśeṣa* means distinction.]

The term *kravyāt* refers to the cremation fire (*smāśānāgni*), so called because it "eats raw flesh" (*kravyam atti*). Now, one might object that if error were to cease for some reason, there would be a cessation of worldly discourse (*vyavahāra-viccheda*); to this, he says: "For not of this... and so forth.
*Pratatā* means continuous (*saṃtatā*).
"Distinction" (*viśe�sa*) means difference.
He says, "Not for him," because since the knower of Brahman is not subject to injunctions, the futility of the scripture is accepted as a desired consequence.

The meaning is that because of the absence of duality—which is the object of an injunction—and because an injunction is untenable with respect to the Self which is not something to be accomplished, the knower of Brahman is not one to be enjoined.
Now, it must be said that only one who possesses the discrimination of a self distinct from the body is qualified for action whose fruit is to be experienced in the hereafter;
and thus, the knower of Brahman is not subject to injunctions, because he possesses such discrimination.
He raises an objection, saying "like one authorized for ritual action," with the words "despite the distinction from the body.

He refutes this with the words beginning with "no," arguing that because indirect discrimination does not contradict immediate delusion, the agent of action still possesses the delusion of non-difference from the body; thus, such delusion serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
The meaning is that it is for one who is deluded and does not perceive that "I" am distinct from the body, just as the sky is distinct from the body.
One who knows Brahman is not subject to injunctions,
because he is free from delusion.

He says "not so" by comparing [the knower] to one in deep sleep (*suṣuptavat*). The meaning is as follows: for one who perceives the non-composite nature of the body and so forth, who is devoid of the perception of compositeness, and who is free from the delusion of difference—that is, for one in deep sleep—even an ignorant person is not seen to be subject to injunction at a time when delusion is absent; how much more so, then, can this be said of the knower of the Self?
Anticipating an objection regarding the impossibility of non-injunction, he refutes it with the words "And not...

The meaning is that there is no over-extension [of the rule], because once detachment from objects—which has been practiced for the sake of knowledge—persists even after knowledge is attained, the passion that impels one toward objects ceases.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Even his taste for objects ceases upon seeing the Supreme."
Having thus stated that the Knower is not subject to injunction by way of the discussion on permission and so forth, he concludes the subject matter with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
He provides an illustration for both permission and avoidance based on the difference of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) even for a single entity with the word "Light" (jyotiḥ).
One who eats raw flesh (kravya) is a meat-eater; the meaning is that the fire of the cremation ground is impure. //48//
And because there is no continuity, there is no confusion [of karmic results]. (BBs 2.3.49)
It may be granted that permission and avoidance could belong even to a single self due to its connection with different bodies.
But if it is argued that the connection with the fruits of one's own karma would then become confused under the assumption of a single self—because the owner is one—the answer is:
this is not so.
Because there is no continuity;
for there is no continuous connection of the self—as agent and enjoyer—with all bodies.
For it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Furthermore, because there is no continuum of a soul due to the absence of a continuum of a self, there will be neither a confusion of karma nor a confusion of its results. // 49 //
He explains the Sūtra as a response to this doubt, beginning with the words "syātām" (they might be).

Even if the taking up and abandoning [of states] were to occur due to the connection with a gross body, there would nonetheless be a confusion (*vyatikara*) or intermixture (*sāṃkarya*) of the fruits of karma, because the fruit of an action performed by one person might be experienced by another. This is because it is impossible for a self qualified by a body to experience heaven and so forth; rather, it must be the unqualified Self.
Because there is only one experiencer,
the objection is that a distinction in the nature of the self must be asserted in order to establish the systematic arrangement [of states] such as "one who goes to heaven" and "one who goes to hell.
That confusion would indeed arise if the state of being an experiencer belonged to the unconditioned self alone.
But this is not the case;

for in the [sūtra] "because that [intellect] is its essence" (tadguṇasāratvāt), agency and so forth are established as belonging only to the Self when it is conditioned by the intellect, and this applies to liberation as well.

And thus, since the intellect has no connection with another body, the individual soul (jīva) conditioned by it likewise lacks a connection with that other body; therefore, because there is a distinction among enjoyers due to the distinction of their intellects, there is no confusion of karma and so forth— this is the meaning of the resolution.
And it is merely a reflection.
This individual soul (jīva) is to be understood as a mere reflection of the Supreme Self, like the sun reflected in water and so forth;
it is not the Self itself directly.
Nor is it a separate entity.

Therefore, just as when one reflection of the sun in water trembles, another reflection of the sun in water does not tremble, so too when one living being is connected with the fruit of karma, another living being does not have that connection.
Thus, there is indeed no confusion between action and its fruit;
and since the appearance is produced by ignorance, it is logically established that the transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) which has that appearance as its basis is also produced by ignorance.
Consequently, by means of the removal of that [ignorance], the teaching of the ultimate reality—the identity of Brahman and the Self—is logically possible.
However, for those who maintain that there are many selves and that all of them are omnipresent, this very confusion necessarily follows.
How so?

The Sāṃkhyas hold that there are many, all-pervading selves whose nature consists solely of consciousness, who are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and beyond distinction; for their sake, *pradhāna* (primordial matter) exists as a common substrate, and through it, the accomplishment of their experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) occurs.

In their plurality and pervasiveness, [the elements] are identical in nature to jars, walls, and so forth; being merely substantial entities, they are inherently insentient. Likewise, the selves (*ātman*) and the minute internal organs (*manas*), which serve as their instruments, are insentient. Therein, through the conjunction of the substances of the selves and the substances of the internal organs, the specific qualities of the self, such as desire and the rest, arise.
These [qualities] inhere individually in each self without distinction; that is *saṃsāra*.
The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that liberation is the absolute non-arising of these nine qualities of the self.

In this regard, first for the Sāṃkhyas, since all selves consist of the nature of consciousness and there is no distinction in their proximity [to the intellect], it would follow that when one self is connected with pleasure and pain, all selves would be connected with pleasure and pain.
This might be so.
The established order will exist because the activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of the isolation (kaivalya) of the Puruṣas;
otherwise, the activity of the Pradhāna would be for the purpose of manifesting its own power,
and thus the consequence of non-liberation would follow.
This is not sound.
For an arrangement based on the attainment of one's desired goal cannot be understood [as valid];
rather, an arrangement might be stated by means of some logical justification (*upapatti*).
Furthermore, if rebirth were non-existent, even if the desired isolation of the self (*puruṣakaivalya*) were not to occur,
a confusion of states would nonetheless result due to the absence of any cause for distinction.

Even according to the followers of Kaṇāda, when the mind is conjoined with one self, it would necessarily be conjoined with other selves as well, since there is no difference in their proximity and so forth.

Furthermore, since there would be no distinction in the cause, there would be no distinction in the result; thus, if one self were joined with pleasure and pain, it would follow as a logical consequence that all selves would likewise equally experience pleasure and pain. // 50 //
In the first sūtra beginning with "aṃśa," the soul's status as a part was explained through the notion of being delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like the space within a jar;

now, indicating his lack of preference for the theory of delimitation by means of the word "eva" (only/itself), the venerable author of the sūtras presents the theory of reflection, which is established by such scriptural texts as "He became the counterpart of every form," stating: "And it is only a reflection."
The Supreme Self itself, when unconditioned, does not become the individual soul (jīva),
because of the experience of limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
nor is it different from that [Supreme Self].

Because this would contradict scriptural and traditional texts on non-difference, such as "He has entered here," the meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is simply the reflection [of the Self] in the intellect and its effects, which are products of ignorance (avidyā). In this view, the distinction between one who goes to heaven and one who goes to hell is established based on the differences among the reflections in the intellect; furthermore, since the state of being an individual soul is caused by ignorance, liberation through knowledge (vidyā) is logically consistent. He states this with the words beginning "And therefore" (ataśca).
As for this prattle of Bhāskara— that the reflection is not imagined through its association with an adjunct (*upādhi*), but rather by its very nature,

and therefore a reflected image that is imagined cannot persist in liberation and thus lacks the status of a *jīva*— this must be disregarded as being caused by ignorance of the secret of our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

For if the face in a mirror were imagined like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, then there would be a sublation of its very nature, such that one would have the sublation "This is not a face," just as one has the sublation "This is not silver."

Therefore, since there is no sublation of the face itself—because while the mere relation [of the face] with the mirror is sublated by the cognition "there is no face in the mirror," the non-difference from one's own face remains unsublated through the experience "this is indeed my face"—the face is merely imagined as being in a state of conjunction.
Furthermore, because the statements regarding entry speak of the very unmodified Brahman entering in the form of a reflection, there is no imagination of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The teachers have already exerted great effort on this point in the *Darpaṇa-ṭīkā*, so we shall desist here.

Thus, it has been stated that even though there is identity of essential nature (*svarūpa*) according to our own view, there is no confusion (*asāṃkarya*) due to the difference between the conditioned selves (*upahita-jīva*).
Now, he begins to explain the confusion belonging to others, which is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra, with the words beginning with "yeṣām" (of those for whom...).
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression—these nine are the specific qualities of the self;
by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "proximity and so forth," neutrality is expressed.
The Sāṃkhya raises his own objection: "It might be thus."

Although there is no distinction among all persons regarding the proximity of *prakṛti*, it is *prakṛti* alone that proceeds in a restrictive manner for each individual person for the sake of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).
Thus, the activity of *pradhāna* is determined by the purpose of the person to be served; this constitutes the established order of experience and so forth.

Otherwise, if one does not accept this restricted activity, the activity of *pradhāna* would be for the sake of manifesting its own majesty, which would result in a failure of its intended purpose. This is the meaning.

Because the insentient *pradhāna* lacks the discernment required for a purpose, and because the future goal of the *puruṣa*—being itself insentient—is incapable of acting as a regulator, there can be no established order; this is due to its being devoid of both authority and logical justification. Thus he says, "This is not so.
The sense is that against one who brings about the frustration of a purpose by acting as a regulator, it is precisely that [frustration] which is intended as the consequence.
He states that even in the view of the logicians (tārkika), there is a confusion regarding experience and so forth, saying: "Of the followers of Kaṇāda.
The cause is the conjunction with the mind;
the result is pleasure and so forth.

He raises the objection that the conjunction of the mind with a particular self, produced by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of that self, is the cause of pleasure and so forth for that very self—this is the established position he questions with the words "syādetat" ("it might be so"). He refutes it with the Sūtra, saying "no" (na). //50//
It might be argued as follows: [text begins] BsCom_2,3.17.51. [text ends] BsCom_2,3.17.50. Start BsCom_2,3.17.51. It might be so.
"It might be that the restriction is caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa)," [the author] says:
"No, because there would be no restriction regarding the unseen. (BBs 2.3.51)

When many selves—like space, omnipresent and present in every body without distinction between external and internal—produce the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), characterized as dharma, through mind, speech, and body, the following applies:

For the Sāṃkhyas, that [unseen merit] does not inhere in the self but resides in the Pradhāna; because it belongs to the Pradhāna in common, it cannot logically serve as the regulator for the individual experience of pleasure and pain for each self.

For the followers of Kaṇāda as well, since the unseen merit is produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind—which, as before, is common to all—there is no reason for the restriction that "this unseen merit belongs to this specific self alone"; thus, the same fault remains. (51)
It might be argued:

intentions (*abhisaṃdhi*) and the like— such as "I shall attain this fruit," "I shall avoid this," "I shall strive in this way," or "I shall act in this manner"— which operate within each individual, will determine the relationship of owner and owned between the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and the selves (*ātman*).
He says "no"—the meaning is that, as in the previous case, because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is common to all selves (*sarvātmasādhāraṇatva*), there is no fixed distribution (*vyavasthā*).

Anticipating the objection that "there is a restriction of the unseen force arising from that [unseen force] due to the restriction of passion (*rāga*) and so forth," he takes up the next sūtra with the words beginning "this might be so" (*syādetat*). //51//
And the same applies to intentions and so forth as well. (BBs 2.3.52)

Even in the case of intentions (*abhisaṃdhi*) and so forth, since they are produced in the proximity of all selves through the common conjunction of the self and the mind, it is impossible for them to serve as the cause for restriction; thus, the aforementioned defect necessarily follows. // 52 //
The lack of restriction [of the soul's location] entails the aforementioned fault.
The meaning of the objection is that there would be a fixed order because a portion of one soul would be contained within another body. //52//
If it is argued that [the whole exists] because of its spatial location, we say no, because [that location] is included within [the parts]. (BS 2.3.53)

Now, it might be argued that even though the self is all-pervading, its conjunction with the mind—which is itself restricted to the body—will occur only in that portion of the self delimited by the body; therefore, there will be a restriction based on spatial location regarding intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) and so forth, as well as regarding the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and pleasure and pain.
That too is not tenable.
Why?
Because of inclusion;
for, due to the non-distinction of their sovereign power (*vibhutva*), all selves are included within all bodies.

In this regard, the Vaiśeṣikas cannot postulate that even for the self, which is omnipresent, there is a specific spatial location delimited by the body. Even if such a location were postulated, it would be merely conceptual; as a part of an omnipresent self, it could not, by virtue of its conceptual nature alone, determine a real effect. Furthermore, since the body arises in the proximity of all selves, it is impossible to determine that it belongs to this particular self alone and not to others.

Moreover, even if one accepts that [the self] occupies a specific location, it would be possible for two selves experiencing identical pleasure and pain to achieve their enjoyment through a single body at some time,
because it is possible for the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of two selves to occupy the same location.
For instance, when Devadatta’s body has departed from the place where he experienced pleasure and pain, [that place remains occupied by his *adṛṣṭa*].

Furthermore, when that [self] reaches the body of Yajñadatta, an experience of pleasure and pain identical to that of the other [Devadatta] is observed; this would not occur if there were no undesirable [consequence] of Devadatta and Yajñadatta occupying the same location.
Moreover, for one who maintains the doctrine of spatial localization (*pradeśavādin*), it would follow that the enjoyment of heaven and so forth would be impossible.

Furthermore, because the production of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) occurs in specific regions of the body of a Brahmin and others, and because the enjoyment of heaven and so forth takes place in other locations,
it is impossible for many selves to be omnipresent;
this is because there is no illustrative example [to the contrary].
Tell me, first of all: what are those many things that occupy the same location?
If you say they are "form" (rūpa) and so forth, no; for even these are non-different in their substantial aspect (dharmyaṃśa), and yet they differ in their defining characteristics (lakṣaṇabheda).
But there is no difference in the characteristics of multiple selves.

If it is argued that the establishment of their difference occurs by virtue of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), we say no; for the postulation of ultimate particularities and the postulation of the difference between them are mutually dependent (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of space and so forth is not established for the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), because they admit that these are effects;
therefore, it is established that only in the position of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) is there an absence of all defects. // 53 //
Is the self that is conjoined with the mind merely a spatial part of the self, or is it an imagined one?
In the first case, since all selves would be contained within all bodies, there would be a lack of distinction between them.
He refutes the second [position] with the words, "In that case, not by the Vaiśeṣikas.
Since all selves are in proximity, it is impossible to postulate a specific location for any one of them; the meaning is that there is no determining factor.
Even while accepting the conception of spatial parts (*pradeśa*), he says "kalpyā" (it must be postulated).
Anticipating the objection that there is a fixed rule—that the experience belongs only to that self whose body is directed toward a particular effect such as intention—he says "the body also.
He states another fault regarding the position of spatial parts with the words "pradeśa... (regarding the spatial parts).
In whichever part of the self the production of *adṛṣṭa* occurs, is that part mobile or stationary?
Not the first, because it is impossible for a part to have motion or division within an immobile whole, and because this would result in the fallacy of the doctrine of atomic selves (*aṇvātmavāda*).

In the second case, since the experience of another person is also observed in that very same location, *adṛṣṭa* must exist there as well; thus, the undesirable consequence follows that both selves would experience [the results] through a single body.

If the distinction between the two [experiences] is due to a distinction in the spatial parts (*pradeśa*) of the self, even then, because those two parts are contained within a single body, the confusion of experiences (*bhoga-sāṃkarya*) remains as it was; furthermore, this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of asserting that the self possesses parts (*sāvayava*). Moreover, since the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the conjunction of the body and so forth occurs only in that specific part of the self where it arises, it would remain fixed in that very immobile part; consequently, there would be no experience in the self as delimited by a heavenly body (*svarga-śarīra*) and so on, because the *adṛṣṭa* would not be present there. Therefore, the distinction of spatial parts is not a determining factor for the restriction of experience.

As for the claim that the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) produced here [in this life] is the cause of experience for its own substrate wherever it may be, thereby establishing experiences such as those in heaven—
that is not so;
the point is that there is no evidence for an unseen merit located at a distance from the body of experience.

As for what some say— that even though the mind is one, because of the difference between individual selves, there is a difference in the specific instances of conjunction, such that through a particular instance of conjunction, merit (adṛṣṭa) and so forth belong to a specific self alone, and thus there is no confusion— this is not correct.

Since there is no difference in the nature (vaijātya) of the specific instances of conjunction, it would follow that all of them would cause merit and so forth to reside within all the selves located inside a single body.
And thus, the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) by all selves within a single body would be unavoidable.

Furthermore, having previously stated the confusion resulting from the admission of the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of many [selves], he now says, "and the impossibility of omnipresence," because the omnipresence of agents is unestablished; for there is the experience of their limitedness, as in "I am right here," and there is a lack of evidence [for their ubiquity].
Furthermore, if many [entities] were all-pervasive, they would have to occupy the same location, and that is untenable because it is never observed; thus he says, "he speaks.
If it is argued: "But is it not observed that color, taste, and so forth reside in a single pot?"
This example is not accepted by us.

Since color consists of fire alone, taste of water alone, and smell of earth alone, there is no non-difference between each respective quality and its own substratum; thus, because there is no jar existing apart from the substrata such as fire and so forth, the plurality of selves is also unestablished.
Because the defining characteristic of being a self (ātmatva) is non-different;
thus, Devadatta’s self is not different from Yajñadatta’s self, because it possesses the nature of a self,
just like Yajñadatta’s self.
Here the Vaiśeṣika raises an objection: "Regarding 'ultimate particulars' (*antyaviśeṣa*).

Particulars (*viśeṣas*) reside only in eternal substances; they are themselves the differentiators of their own substrata and do not require a further differentiator for themselves, and thus they are called "ultimate.
Consequently, the meaning is that a distinction between selves arises from the difference characterized by the nature of these particulars.
First of all, the postulation of specific qualities is not for the sake of knowing the distinction of the Self from non-Selfs,
because the distinction from non-Selfs is established by the very fact of being the Self.
Nor is that postulation for the sake of knowing the mutual distinction among Selves.

The meaning of the rebuttal is as follows: since the distinction between selves has not yet been established even now, it is not logical to postulate a distinction between selves based solely on the postulation of a distinction between their specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).

For there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of a distinction between selves would depend upon the establishment of a distinction between their specific qualities within those selves, while the establishment of that [quality-distinction] would depend upon the cognition of the distinction between the selves.
As for the claim that space, direction, and time serve as examples for the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of many [entities], that too is untenable; thus he says: "Of space and the rest.
Since omnipresence resides in a single locus, there is no plurality of omnipresent entities due to parsimony (*lāghava*).

Just as within a single space, the arrangement of sounds such as high-pitched or low-pitched is established through the distinctions of drums, lutes, and so forth, so too it is within a single Self (*ātman*).

He concludes that the postulation of difference is futile with the words "Therefore," because the establishment of distinctions such as pleasure and so forth is possible through the differences in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the intellect, whereas it has already been stated that such establishment is impossible even if there were a plurality of selves.

Thus, since there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the elements and those concerning the enjoyer, it is established that the non-dual Brahman is the consistent purport of the scriptures. //53//
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.

Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the third section (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Resolution of the Contradiction Regarding the Scriptural Passages on the Five Great Elements and the Living Self.
Now begins the fourth section of the second chapter.
In this section, there is a resolution of the contradictions regarding the scriptural passages concerning the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra).
The Fourth Pāda of the Second Chapter. Section 1:
The Origin of the Vital Breaths (Prāṇa). Sūtras 1–4.
Likewise, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
The contradiction in the scriptures regarding the objects beginning with space was resolved in the third quarter;
now, in the fourth, the contradiction regarding the vital breaths is resolved.

In those passages concerning origination, such as "It created that heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3) and "From this very Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the origination of the vital breaths is not mentioned; moreover, in some places their non-origination is explicitly taught, as in "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
Regarding this, they ask: "What was that non-existence (asat)? [The reply is: "In the beginning, those very sages (ṛṣis) were non-existence. They ask: "Who are those sages? [The reply is:
"The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the sages. Since, in this passage, the existence of the vital breaths prior to creation is heard [to be stated], [it follows that they are eternal].

In other places, however, the origination of even the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is taught: "Just as from a blazing fire tiny sparks fly forth, even so from this Self all the vital breaths [proceed]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20);
"From this is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3);
and "From that the seven vital breaths arise" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8).
Thus, in such passages as, "He created Prāṇa; from Prāṇa, faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the sense-organs, mind, and food" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4),
there arises a state of non-comprehension due to the contradiction between various scriptural statements and the lack of a discernible means for determining one over the other.
Alternatively, since their existence is heard of prior to origination, it follows that the origination of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is figurative;
therefore, he reads this reply: "In the same way, the prāṇas.
But how, in this case, is there a conformity with the word "in the same way" (tathā), given the absence of a relevant point of comparison?

The refutation of those who assert a self that is omnipresent and manifold, which was introduced at the end of the immediately preceding section, is as follows: first of all, an analogy is not possible because of the absence of similarity;
for an analogy would exist only if there were similarity, such as "as is a lion, so is Balavarman."
If it should be argued that this is for the purpose of establishing a similarity with what is observed—
namely, that just as that which arises in the proximity of all selves is unrestricted, so too the vital breaths are unrestricted with respect to every self—
that too would be a mere repetition, since this has already been stated by way of the non-restriction of the body.

Furthermore, the vital breaths (prāṇas) cannot be compared with the individual soul (jīva), because that would contradict our established doctrine; for the non-origination of the soul has been declared,
whereas the origination of the vital breaths is what we intend to explain.

Therefore, it may appear that the phrase "in that manner" (*tathā*) is incoherent; however, this is not so, because a connection is established through the analogy provided by the illustrative example.

Here, the collection of statements from those who maintain the origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) serves as the illustration: "From this Self, all vital breaths, all worlds, all gods, and all beings emerge" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20).
This refers to such passages as these.
The meaning is that just as the worlds and so forth arise from the Supreme Brahman, so too do the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Accordingly: "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs; [and] space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports all" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3).
In such passages as these, it should be understood that the origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) occurs just like that of ether (*ākāśa*) and the other elements;
or alternatively, because in cases such as "And the failure of the *apāna* is like that" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.15), a connection with a remote point of comparison is also accepted.

Just as ether and the other elements mentioned in the immediately preceding section were established as modifications of the supreme Brahman, so too must it be understood that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are also modifications of the supreme Brahman.
What, then, is the reason for the vital breaths being modifications?
It is simply because they are so stated in scripture (*śruti*).
Now, as for the objection that in certain passages the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is not heard of—that is incorrect;
for it is heard of in other passages.
Indeed, the fact that something is not heard of in one place cannot prevail to negate what is heard of elsewhere.
Therefore, since there is no difference in their being mentioned in scripture, it is well said that the vital breaths (prāṇas) also originate, just like ether and the other elements. [Note:
The subject matter concerning the vital breaths includes the origin of the vital breaths, their number, their true nature, and so forth;
*ānulomya* means consistency or logical coherence.]

Just as in the third chapter, fourth quarter, the principle of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding non-receiving (*apratigraha*), though separated by many sūtras, is referred back to in the case of vomiting Soma, so too should it be understood here.

Having examined the nature of the agent in the preceding section, [the author] establishes the production of the sense organs, which are his instruments, with the words: "In the same way, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*).

He states the connection between the two quarters—namely, the relationship of cause and effect—by saying: "The ether and so forth," indicating that the examination of the elemental vital breaths follows immediately after the examination of the elements and the enjoyer.
He states that very contradiction with the words "In that regard," and so forth.

Although the origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is established by the logic of the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*), because the proposition of the single knowledge (*ekavijñāna*) would otherwise be untenable if the breaths were unoriginated, nevertheless, this section is not redundant; for its purpose is to explain the status of the breaths during dissolution (*pralaya*), as attested by scriptural texts concerning their existence at that time.
In this context, the "vital breaths" (prāṇas) are the objects [of discussion].

Since there is a doubt as to whether they arise or not due to conflicting scriptural statements (śruti), and because these statements are of equal force, there is no definitive conclusion; thus, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) results in their lack of authority.
To that, the proponent of the figurative interpretation (gauṇavādī) offers a resolution, beginning with "Or rather" (athavā).

The meaning is that there is no contradiction because the scriptural statement regarding the existence [of the vital breaths] at the time of dissolution is more powerful due to its lack of any other possible application (niravakāśatva), whereas the scriptural statement regarding their origination is figurative, just like the scriptural statement regarding the origination of the individual soul (jīva).

The phrase "or rather" (athavā) is stated to indicate that the figurative position, like the non-authoritative position, is merely a prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) for the proponent of the primary conclusion (mukhya-siddhāntin).
The proponent of the primary conclusion says: "Therefore... (ata iti).
The word "tathā" implies the question "how?"—
meaning "in accordance with" or "straightforwardly. He clarifies the sense of "similarity" by saying "of that which has been observed."
The statement "the vital breaths (prāṇas) are like defects" is incoherent.
Even if the sūtra were to follow as "the vital breaths, like unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), are also non-restrictive," it would still be a mere repetition.

If the meaning of the sūtra is that "the vital breaths do not originate, like the individual soul (jīva)," then the objection is that this constitutes a departure from established tenets (apasiddhānta).
He responds: "No;
in the case of an example.

Having accepted that an example (dṛṣṭānta) must be stated in proximity to the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika), he speaks of this proximity by virtue of their being situated within a single sentence.
This restriction does not apply at present; for the venerable Jaimini has relied upon a remote example, as he says: "Alternatively.
There exists in the third chapter the section concerning the "Sacrifice on Receiving a Horse" (*aśvapratigraheṣṭyadhikaraṇa*).
The scriptural passage concerning this is:

"As many horses as one might accept as a gift, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he perform. In the subsequent section, there arises the doubt whether this offering to Varuṇa belongs to the giver or the receiver; having raised the objection that it belongs to the receiver because of the scriptural hearing of the word "pratigṛhṇīyāt" ("one should accept"), [the author proceeds].
Since the opening statement, "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa," mentions the giver, it will be established by this indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the rite belongs to the giver of the horse alone;

therefore, the word "should receive" (*pratigṛhṇīyāt*) means "one who should cause [another] to give a horse," which is to say, "he should give. Once the meaning of the sentence—"He who is the giver of a horse should perform the Varuṇī sacrifice"—is established, the inquiry arises: is this sacrifice occasioned by the giving of a horse performed in a worldly (*laukika*) context or in a Vedic (*vaidika*) context?

In this regard, since a fault arises from the prohibited worldly gift of a horse—as in the injunction "one does not give a horse"—this *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering) is intended to remove that fault. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) established by the sūtra, "But the *iṣṭi* should apply to the worldly [gift] because of the fault," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "For here, Varuṇa indeed seizes him who accepts a horse."
A sacrifice is prescribed for the purpose of proclaiming the fault of the donor;
the word *varuṇa* is conventionally established as denoting the disease known as dropsy (*jalodara*).
Furthermore, it is not well-known that this disease occurs in the case of giving a horse according to worldly custom.
Nor can the well-known meaning [of Varuṇa] be established by this very sentence alone;

for, as in the case of the statement "there is a fault in giving, and the ritual action is performed for the sake of removing it," there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) because of the difference in meaning.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that the word *varuṇa*—derived through the etymology "he covers" (*vṛṇoti*)—is merely a restatement of the fault incurred by transgressing a prohibition.
Because it would result in the abandonment of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*);
and if that were abandoned, then even in the case of Vedic giving, one could—by means of the aforementioned etymological derivation—refer to the pain produced by the loss of a horse as a gift.

Therefore, this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) restating what is already established. Having thus deliberated that "this sacrifice pertains to the giving of a horse connected with the sacrifice," it was stated: "And the mishap involving the drink is like that."
It is heard in the scripture: "If, while the Soma-drinking is being performed, there should be a mishap consisting of vomiting, then one should offer this Śyāmāka rice-oblation to Soma-Indra.

In that context, the logic of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position from the section on the "Sacrifice for the Acceptance of Horses" (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*), though separated by many sūtras, is referred to here by the word "tadvat" (in the same manner). Accordingly, in the case of ordinary (non-Vedic) vomiting of Soma drunk for the sake of balancing the bodily humors (*dhātusāmya*), this oblation should be offered because of the defect known as the emaciation of the senses caused by the vomiting.

The meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra is that the statement, "He who vomits the Soma loses his sensory power through [the loss of] vigor," is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already observed.
The *siddhānta* (conclusion), however, is that since the disposal of the remnant occurs during Vedic Soma-drinking, there is no fault even in vomiting;
furthermore, in common worldly experience, the drying up of the senses caused by vomiting is not a defect, as it serves as a quality by restoring the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

In the Veda, however, from the indicative mark of the mantra for the sake of proper digestion—"May my speech not go beyond the navel"—it follows that in the case of vomiting, there is a deficiency in the ritual act, and thus it constitutes a fault.
Therefore, it is established that in the case of vomiting the Vedic Soma, there is an offering of cooked rice (caru) to Soma-Indra; such is the meaning in these and other sūtras. //1//
Because figurative interpretation is impossible. (BS 2.4.2)

As for the argument previously stated—that because of the scriptural hearing of the existence [of the vital breaths] prior to their origin, the scriptural account of the origin of the vital breaths is figurative—the author replies: "Because of the impossibility of it being figurative" (*gauṇyasaṃbhavāt*).
The impossibility of its being figurative is "the impossibility of figurativeness."
For the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths cannot be figurative, as that would entail the abandonment of the initial proposition:
"O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3).

For, having thus asserted that by the knowledge of one there is the knowledge of all, this is handed down as its proof: "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3), and so forth.
And that assertion is established only when the entire world, beginning with the vital breaths, is an evolution of Brahman, because there can be no modification apart from its material cause.
But if the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths were taken in a figurative sense, this fundamental assertion would be undermined.

And thus he concludes the matter proposed: "The Person alone is this universe—action, austerity, Brahman, the supreme immortal" (Muṇḍaka 2.2.11), and "Brahman alone is this universe, this most excellent" (Muṇḍaka 2.2.11).
Likewise, in such scriptural passages as, "Verily, my dear, by the seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing of the Self, all this is known," this very proposition is to be applied.
But how is it that there is a scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) prior to their origination?
This does not refer to the Root Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), for [the scripture says]:
"For he is without vital breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
Thus, because it is determined that the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is devoid of all specific distinctions such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),

this determination of the existence of the vital breaths prior to their origination must be understood as referring to intermediate primal natures (*avāntaraprakṛti*) in relation to their own respective transformations.
This is because, among the numerous states belonging to the realm of the evolved (*vyākṛta*), the relationship between primal nature and its modifications is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.

For in the section concerning the ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*), since the sūtra "Because of the impossibility of a figurative [sense]" (*gauṇy-asambhavāt*) is a sūtra stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was explained as: "The scriptural statement of birth is figurative because of its impossibility.
And there, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was stated by means of the abandonment of that proposition.
Here, however, since it is a sūtra of the final conclusion, it is explained as: "Because of the impossibility of a figurative scriptural statement of birth."

However, by those who, following that [interpretation], explain here as well that the scriptural mention of "birth" is figurative because such a possibility exists, the abandonment of their own initial thesis would have been overlooked. // 2 //
[Objection: "But would not even the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) be figurative? To this he says: "And thus, in accordance with the meaning of the proposition.

The sense is that, in conformity with the proposition intended to be taught through the introduction and conclusion—that there is no second—this origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) must be taken in its primary sense.
He states "likewise" because the proposition is seen in other Vedic texts as well, such as the *Muṇḍaka*, and therefore it is primary.
The meaning is that this proposition (pratijñā) is to be understood as the reason for the primacy of the origin of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Now, he explains the purport of the scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breath during dissolution by means of a question, beginning with "How?

This sentence does not intend to convey that the Supreme Cause, Brahman, possesses vital breath at the time of the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya); rather, its meaning is that it refers to the existence of the vital breath in the form of the intermediate primordial nature (prakṛti) known as Hiraṇyagarbha during the intermediate dissolution (avāntarapralaya).
Now, one might object: "If the modification in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha exists, how can it be said that at that time there is no modification?
To this, he says: *svavikāra* (its own modification). The meaning is: the production of that which is the gross effect of the *kāryabrahman* (the Brahma as effect), which is itself [the subtle body].

If it is asked: "But why is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the existence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), as stated in scripture, interpreted as referring to the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*)—since it serves to prove that the vital breaths are not produced?"—we reply: "On the strength of the powerful scriptural texts concerning birth, such as 'From this [Self] is born the vital breath' (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*).
If it is further asked: "How can Brahman, which is a modification (*vikāra*), be the material cause (*prakṛti*)?"—to this he says: "The differentiated... (*vyākṛta*).

In the Śruti passage beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," and in the Smṛti passage beginning with "He is the first creator of beings," there is a well-known relationship of material cause and effect between Brahman, Virāṭ, and others— even though they are of the nature of modifications—
since they exist in the state of the root cause relative to what precedes them.

The meaning is that even a modification (vikāra) may be considered a material cause (prakṛti) in relation to what follows it. Some explain this sūtra in accordance with the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*); he refutes them with the words "ether" (*viyat*). //2//
And because it is heard [in scripture] prior to that. (BBs 2.4.3)
Furthermore, for the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) as well, the scriptural statement regarding their birth is primary, just as it is for ether (*ākāśa*) and the rest.
This is because the single word denoting birth, "is born" (*jāyate*), which is heard first in reference to the *prāṇas* in the passage,
"From this [Self] the *prāṇa* is born" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3), continues to apply to the subsequent elements such as ether.
Thus, it has been established here that "birth" in the case of ether and the other elements is primary; by analogy with that, birth in the case of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) must also be primary.

For it is not possible, within a single context and a single sentence, to determine that a single word uttered once, when connected with many things, is primary in one instance and secondary in another, as that would entail the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*).

Likewise, in the passage "He created Prāṇa; from Prāṇa, Śraddhā" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4), the verb "created," though heard in connection with the vital breaths, is also connected by implication to the subsequent entities such as Śraddhā that possess an origin.
Even where a word expressing origination is heard later in the sequence and is syntactically connected with preceding items, this same principle applies.

Just as the word "issue forth" (vyuccaranti), which is read at the end in the phrase "all beings issue forth," is connected with the preceding elements such as the vital breaths (prāṇa) as well. // 3 //

The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: "Because of its being primary" (*tatsāmānyāt*). This means that since the word "is born" (*jāyate*) is primarily applied to ether and the rest [in later passages], its application to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) mentioned earlier is also primary.
"On account of similarity with that" (*tena sāmānyam*): the similarity consists in being expressed by the same word; therefore, this is the meaning.

He extends the principle elsewhere as well—that it is not appropriate for there to be a discrepancy where one word is used in its primary sense in one place and in a secondary sense in another within a single sentence—by stating: "Even where it is heard later" (*yatrāpi paścācchrutaḥ*). //3//
Because speech is preceded by that [mind]. (BBs 2.4.4)
Although the origin of the vital breaths is not mentioned in this context— namely, "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3)—
because only the origin of the three elements, fire, water, and food, is heard there;

Nevertheless, because it is stated that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by fire, water, and food—which themselves have Brahman as their material cause—and because they share that same nature, it is established that all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) originate from Brahman.

For instance, in this very context, the fact that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by fire, water, and food is recorded in scripture: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).

In this regard, if their consisting of food and so forth is indeed primary, then their origin from Brahman certainly exists. Even if it is figurative, nevertheless, because of the scriptural hearing of the differentiation of names and forms having Brahman as its agent, and because of the introductory statement, "By which the unheard becomes heard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3),
and the conclusion, "All this has that as its self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).

Thus, from this concluding summary as well as from what is well-known in other scriptural passages, it is understood that the statement regarding the mind and the other organs being composed of food and so forth is intended solely to elaborate upon their being effects of Brahman.
Therefore, for this reason also, the fact that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are modifications of Brahman is established. // 4 //
Regarding the claim that even in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is not heard, he says in response: "Because speech is preceded by that.
In this sūtra, the word "speech" (vāk) is an elliptical indication for both the vital breath and the mind.

The construction is as follows: since it is stated that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by fire, water, and earth respectively, the claim that their non-hearing [in the text] is unestablished is refuted.
The meaning of "on account of that similarity" (tatsāmānyāt) is that the eyes and other organs share a commonality with speech and the rest, namely, the state of being instruments (karaṇatva).

In this context, according to the view where the suffix *mayaṭ* primarily denotes a modification (*vikāra*), the fact that the vital breaths are effects of Brahman remains established, because fire, water, and earth are modifications of Brahman.
Even if it is argued that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used figuratively because the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being air, cannot be a modification of water, but rather exists dependent upon it;

nevertheless, the fact that the vital breaths are modifications [of the elements] and thus exist dependent on the elements is established as the mark indicated by *mayaṭ*. This is further confirmed by other scriptural passages such as "He created the vital breath," which explicitly state that they are effects of Brahman.

Therefore, it is established that because the scriptural texts concerning the origin of the vital breaths do not contradict the scriptural texts concerning their existence [in Brahman], there is a coherent connection (*samanvaya*) with Brahman as the cause.

It should be understood that the fruit of these sections, which consist of an investigation into the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), is the realization of the distinction between the "you" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*) and the "that" (*tat-padārtha*) based on the subtle body. //4//

Section on the Seven Courses of Rebirth (Saptagatyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 5–6.
And because the sevenfold course has been specified [in scripture],
the contradiction with the Vedic texts regarding the destination of rebirth for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) has been resolved. Now, the contradiction concerning their number is being resolved.

Among those, he will explain the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) later on; for now, however, he determines how many other vital breaths there are. Furthermore, there is a doubt in this matter due to conflicting scriptural statements.
In some places, seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are mentioned: "From him the seven vital breaths arise" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.8).
In other places, eight vital breaths are mentioned by way of their quality as "seizers" (*graha*): "There are eight seizers and eight over-seizers" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.1).
In yet other places, nine are mentioned: "There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head and two directed downwards" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.7.1).

In some places there are ten: "Indeed, there are nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.4). In other places there are eleven: "These ten are the vital breaths in a person, and the self is the eleventh" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.4).
In yet other places there are twelve, as in the passage: "The skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.11).

In some places there are thirteen, as in the passage, "The eye and that which is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.8). Thus, the Śruti texts are indeed in disagreement regarding the number of prāṇas. What, then, is the prima facie conclusion?
"There are only seven vital breaths. Why? Because of their departure; for that many are understood from the passage: "From him the seven vital breaths arise" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8).
In such scriptural passages as these, they are specifically distinguished: "Indeed, there are seven vital breaths located in the head.
But [one might object]: "The vital breaths, dwelling in the cave, are deposited seven by seven" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8).
Thus, the distributive repetition (vīpsā) is heard; it indicates that there are vital breaths (prāṇas) in addition to the seven.
This is not a fault.

This distributive repetition—"seven, seven vital breaths for each person"—is intended with reference to the distinction between individuals, not with reference to a distinction in the principles (tattvas), as if there were different sets of seven vital breaths for each.
[Objection: But since numbers such as eight and others have also been cited regarding the vital breaths, how can there be only seven?
Truth has been thus illustrated;
however, due to contradiction, one of the others must be determined through calculation.
In that regard, following the principle of parsimony (*stokakalpanā*), the number seven is determined.
And it is held that the mention of a different number [of vessels] is with reference to the distinction in their functions (*vṛtti*). (5) [Note:
*viṣaya* means doubt;
*grahatva* means the state of being a binder.]
The *grahas* (seizers) are the sense organs because they seize and bind;
the *atigrahas* (over-seizers) are the objects that transcend the *grahas*.
The two downward [organs] are the anus and the generative organ.

Regarding the understanding of the departure [of the vital breaths]: thus, since there is doubt arising from the contradiction among the Śruti texts concerning the determination of their number—due to the relationship of supporter and supported among the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) whose existence has been established by birth—the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) states: "There is doubt because of the specific mention of seven [breaths] and because of the ambiguity.
This "doubt" (*viśaya*) is the uncertainty.
In this context, the sense-faculties are the objects;
namely, the five faculties of cognition, speech, and mind—these seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), together with the hand, make eight.
Their state as "seizers" (*graha*) consists in their quality of being binders.

They are called *grahas* (seizers) because they seize and bind; their state of being binders is dependent upon their objects, and thus they are called *atigrahas*. The meaning is that the objects transcend the *grahas*.
There are two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, and speech—these seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) located in the head; plus the two downward ones, namely the anus and the generative organ, making nine.

These ten, along with the intellect and the organs of action, are the vital breaths in the person's body; the established conclusion (*siddhāntakoṭi*) states that the self and the mind constitute the eleventh vital breath.
These same [senses], together with that which is called the heart—the intellect—make twelve;
together with the ego (ahaṅkāra), they make thirteen.

Alternatively, because the Veda understands them as seven, or because the quality of being a "prāṇa" is specifically attributed to the head-senses by the statement "those seven which are in the head are the prāṇas," the head-senses are designated by the term "prāṇa."
The application of the Sūtra is that there are exactly seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) by way of an exhaustive enumeration of their nature as faculties (*indriyatva*).
One raises the objection—"But surely..."—on the grounds that the number seven is contradicted by the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
They are called "those who lie in the cave" (*guhāśaya*) because they rest in the cave, namely, the heart.
"Placed in their own locations" means deposited.
This fourteen-fold nature should be understood by means of the mind.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) resolves this: "This is not a fault. //5//
