"But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the triplication, because of the teaching.

(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2): Having described the creation of fire, water, and food within the context of the evolution of "Being," it is taught: "That divinity thought: 'Well, let me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate names and forms; let me make each of them threefold.'"
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this differentiation of names and forms (nāmarūpavyākaraṇa) performed by the individual soul (jīva), or is it performed by the Supreme Lord?
On this point, the initial position is that this differentiation of names and forms is indeed performed by the individual soul.
Why? Because of the qualification "by this living self" (anena jīvenātmanā).

Just as in the world, when one says, "I shall enter the enemy army through a spy and marshal it," in such an application, the king— by means of the use of the first person in the phrase "I shall marshal"— superimposes upon himself the act of marshaling the army, which in reality is performed by the spy, because he is the causal agent; so too, [the text] superimposes upon the Deity the differentiation of names and forms, which in reality is performed by the individual soul (jīva), because the Deity is the causal agent, by means of the use of the first person in the phrase "I shall differentiate."
Moreover, in names such as "Ḍittha" and "Ḍavittha," and in forms such as jars and bowls, it is observed that the soul alone is the agent of manifestation.
Therefore, when it is argued that this manifestation of name and form has the soul as its sole agent, the author replies:
"But [the manifestation] of names and forms [is effected by the Lord]."
By the word "tu" (but), he sets aside the [opposing] position.
"The fashioning of names and forms" means the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*).
By the phrase "making tripartite," he indicates the Supreme Lord.
Because in the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), he is designated as the author without exception;
this includes the arrangement of names and the arrangement of forms— such as fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning—

as well as the many various types found in each genus and each individual, such as among *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, *palāśa* trees, and so forth, as well as among cattle, wild animals, humans, and the like.
Indeed, that [creation] must be the work of the Supreme Lord alone, the creator of fire, water, and food.
Why? Because of the scriptural instruction.

For instance, beginning with "That divinity thought," and employing the first-person form in the phrase "Let me evolve [the names and forms]," it is taught here that the agency of evolution belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone.
[Objection: But surely, because of the qualification "by means of the living self" (jīvena), the agency of the creation is determined to belong to the living self.
[Reply: This is not so;
for the word "by means of the living self" is connected with the immediately preceding word "having entered" (anupraviśya).

By the phrase "I shall not explain," [the opponent argues that] if there were a connection with that [act of explaining], then the first-person singular form "I shall explain" (vyākaravāṇi) would have to be understood as a figurative usage directed toward the deities.
Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva), which is not the Lord, lacks the capacity to bring about the manifestation of the various names and forms found in mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth.
Even in those things which possess such capacity, that capacity is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Lord;
nor is the so-called individual soul (jīva) absolutely distinct from the Supreme Lord like a servant is from a king,
because of the qualification "by the Self" (ātmanā).
Furthermore, because the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) is based solely upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
even the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) effected by that [individual soul] is in fact effected by the Supreme Lord alone.
And it is the established doctrine of all the Upaniṣads that the Supreme Lord alone is the differentiator of names and forms.
"Space, indeed, by name, is the evolver of name and form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1),
and so forth from such scriptural passages.
Therefore, the differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Lord alone as he performs the tripartition.

It is precisely this differentiation of name and form preceded by tripartition that is intended here, because the differentiation of name and form for each individual element has already been stated through the description of the production of fire, water, and food.

And the scripture demonstrates that tripartition with respect to fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning: "That which was the red color there is the color of fire, that which was white is the color of water, and that which was black is the color of food."
By such passages as [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1],
the form "fire" is first differentiated;
and once the form has been differentiated, because the object is thereby apprehended, the name "fire" is subsequently differentiated.
The same should be understood regarding the sun, the moon, and lightning as well.

By this illustration of fire and the others, it is stated that the threefold compounding (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) applies without distinction to all three substances—earthly, aqueous, and fiery. This is because the opening and the conclusion are common to all.

For thus the introduction is made without distinction: "These three deities, each one becomes tripartite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.4). And likewise the conclusion is made without distinction, beginning with: "That which appeared as if red was the form of fire," and ending with: "That which appeared as if unknown was the combination of these very deities" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.6–7). // 20 //
Note: *Prakriyā* means the process of development.
The Śruti statement, "I shall make each one of those three deities threefold by means of fire, water, and food," is intended as an illustration of the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).

The activities of the agent and the object—namely, "origination" (*utpatti*) and "causing to originate" (*utpādana*)—are well known; among these, the contradiction with the Śruti regarding the origination of the world has been refuted by the preceding two chapters.
Now, the contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding origination is being refuted.
Even in that regard, the origination of subtle elements is not subject to dispute in the scriptures as being the work of the Supreme Lord alone;

however, since there is a conflict among the scriptures concerning the origination of gross elements, he says the following for the purpose of refuting that: "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching [to that effect]."

It has been stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is differentiated by its instruments due to the differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); following upon that, the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṃgati*) is this: it is now considered whose agency constitutes the formation of gross name-and-form. "Process" (*prakriyā*) means the section (*prakaraṇa*).
He states the very act of observation with the words beginning "Hanta" (Come now).
The connection is: "Come now, let me enter into the subtle deities.
The Śruti statement, "I shall make each one of those three deities tripartite by means of fire, water, and food," is intended to indicate the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
Since the inclusion of ether and air has also been stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,
the intention of the Supreme Deity is that the practical activity of living beings will be established when the elements have thus become gross.
He states the doubt regarding the possibility or impossibility of connecting the word "jīvena" with the phrase "vyākaravāṇi" (I shall manifest) by saying "tatra" (therein).

The result [of the inquiry] is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the creator of material things, Brahman’s status as the creator of all is not established; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that status is established.

Regarding the phrase "by the soul" (*jīvena*), the prima facie proponent states, "In this regard, the following is obtained," asserting its connection with the principal verb "I shall manifest" (*vyākaravāṇi*).

Anticipating the objection—"If the Supreme Deity is not the agent, how can the first-person pronoun be used?"—he replies, "As in the world," stating that the designation of agency is figurative because [the Deity] is the instigator.
He establishes the conclusion with the words "by the word 'tu'," etc.;
"pratyākṛti" means "with respect to each individual form" (or "each species").
By this, the incapacity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with respect to the entire gross creation is illuminated.

Furthermore, since the syntactic connection of words depends upon the fitness of their meanings, the construction is: "Having entered as the individual soul, I alone shall evolve [the world]," and not "I shall evolve by means of the individual soul."

[Objection: In that case, since the act of entering has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its agent and the act of explaining (*vyākaraṇa*) has the Lord (*īśvara*) as its agent, the suffix *-kṛtvā* would not be grammatically valid due to the difference in agents. To this, he says: "And there is no such thing as a so-called *jīva*. In reality, however, because the usage of the sun itself as the agent occurs in the context of the "entry" known as the state of reflection—expressed as "the sun has entered the water"—it should be understood that even in the entry by way of the individual self (*jīvātman*), the Lord alone is the agent; thus, the scriptural use of the suffix *-kṛtvā* is justified.

Now, one might object: "If there is non-difference [between the individual soul and the Supreme], why should the individual soul itself not be the creator? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "The Supreme Lord," to show that such is not the case because the soul, being differentiated only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), lacks the power [to create], and because it would contradict the Śruti.

Since the creation of each of the great elements was previously described, he states here—in this sentence concerning evolution—that the creation of stable material objects is spoken of with specific effort; thus, by rearranging the order of the words, he expresses the meaning of the Śruti as indicated by the Sūtra: "preceded by the tripartition" (*trivṛtkaraṇapūrvakam*).
To the question, "Where is it seen that the threefold nature [of the elements] is created by the Lord? he replies: "And that... (*tac ca*).
Now he states the sequence regarding the manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*): "In that regard, fire...

Although it was stated in the passage "Because [the world] originates from this" that the creation of objects is preceded by the Vedic word, there is no contradiction here; for while the creation of objects occurs from the unmanifest word as remembered, it is the manifestation of the clear relationship between name and object that is described in this context.
[Objection: But since only fiery things such as fire are cited in the scripture, is it not the case that the triadic nature of earth and water is not intended? To this he says: "And by this..."
"At the beginning," the phrase "among them" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that whatever form, such as that of a pigeon, appears as if cognized through specific characteristics like blackness and so forth, that is the collective form of the deities. //20//

Regarding those three deities which have been made tripartite externally, another internal tripartition has been stated: "These three deities, having reached the person, each become tripartite. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7)
"It becomes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7).
Now, the Teacher, wishing to remove a certain suspected defect, demonstrates this according to the scripture itself:
"Flesh and so forth [arise] from the earth, according to the literal statement; and likewise for the other two. (Brahma Sūtra 2.4.21).
From the threefold-constituted earth, when consumed by a person, the effects such as flesh and so forth are produced according to the scriptural texts.

For thus says the Śruti: "Food, when eaten, becomes divided into three parts: its coarsest constituent becomes feces, its middle constituent becomes flesh, and its finest constituent becomes the mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.1).
The intention is that this very earth, made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛtā*), is eaten in the form of food such as rice and barley.
Of that [earth], its coarsest form goes outwards in the state of excrement;
its middling form nourishes the flesh within the body.
But the mind is the subtlest.
In this same way, the effects of the other two—water and fire—should be understood according to their respective designations.
Thus, urine, blood, and the vital breath (prāṇa) are the effects of water.
"Bone and marrow are your brilliance," he says. // 21 //

Having explained the external tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), [the author] introduces the next aphorism—beginning with "Of these" (*tāsām*)—to present another internal tripartition that differs from what was previously stated.
The meaning is that, having entered the human body, each [element] becomes threefold, existing in the form of the three effects.
The sense of the commentary is that, in order to refute the objection raised by the subsequent aphorism, it first demonstrates the internal tripartition which is the subject of that doubt.
Now, one might ask: since flesh and other such things consist of food (annamaya), how can they be said to be "earthy" (bhauma)? To this he says: "The earth itself is made tripartite.
It should be understood that the status of the vital breath (prāṇa) as air being an effect of water is merely figurative. //21//
Here it is said: If all elements and elemental derivatives are indeed made tripartite without distinction, because of the scriptural statement, "He made each of those three into a triad."
But then, on what basis is this specific designation made: "this is fire, these are waters, this is food"?
Likewise: "In the case of the self, this is the effect of food that has been eaten, such as flesh and so forth;
this is the effect of water that has been drunk, such as blood and so forth."
"This—bones and so forth—is the effect of the fire-element that has been consumed.
To this it is replied:
"But on account of its predominance, there is that designation; there is that designation" (BBs 2.4.22).
With the word "tu" (but), he dispels the objection raised.
"Vaiśeṣya" is the state of being distinguished (*viśeṣa*);
that is to say, it means "abundance."

Even though the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) has taken place, a preponderance of a particular elemental constituent is observed in certain cases: "in fire there is a preponderance of light, in water a preponderance of water, and in earth a preponderance of food.
And this tripartition is for the sake of establishing worldly usage (*vyavahāra*).
For if, through the attainment of unity—as in the case of a rope made of three strands—the three elements were not distinguished, worldly usage regarding them would not be established by the world.

Therefore, even though the threefold combination exists, the specific designation of fire, water, and food with respect to the elements and their derivatives is justified precisely because of their predominance.
The repetition of the phrase "that designation, that designation" indicates the conclusion of the chapter. // 22 //
Having thus stated the subject matter, he raises an objection regarding the fault with the words "here [someone] says.
He explains the Sūtra as a response to that, beginning with the word "but" (*tu*).

To the question, "For what purpose is 'distinction' (*vaiśeṣya*)—meaning an excess of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—established? he replies: "For the sake of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)."
Thus, it is established that there is no contradiction with Smṛti, logic, other doctrines, or Śruti regarding the Vedāntic purport concerning Brahman. //22//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the worshipful Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. // 4 //
Thus ends the second chapter, named "Non-contradiction," in the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the fourth quarter, titled "The Resolution of Contradictions Regarding the Śruti Texts on the Subtle Body."
Thus ends the second chapter, named "Non-contradiction," in the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras.
